rationale: Cost pressures push toward using less expensive materials and simpler fabrication methods for the frame.

name: Adequate dimensional stability
rationale: The frame must maintain its shape and size under temperature changes and moisture to ensure proper operation of windows and avoid binding.

name: Reduced condensation risk
rationale: Frame design and materials should minimise thermal bridging to reduce interior surface condensation and potential mould growth.

name: Enhanced durability against corrosion
rationale: Window frames exposed to weather require corrosion-resistant materials or coatings to ensure long service life.

name: Improved aesthetic finish
rationale: Architectural design often demands specific visual appearance, colour, and finish quality for window frames to match the building's character.

name: Increased structural integrity
rationale: The window sash must withstand wind loads and support the glass pane, requiring adequate structural strength.

name: Improved thermal insulation
rationale: Energy efficiency requirements drive better thermal performance of the sash frame and glazing interface.

name: Reduced air infiltration
rationale: Weather sealing and airtightness are critical to prevent drafts and energy loss around the operable sash.

name: Enhanced water tightness
rationale: The sash must resist rainwater penetration through proper drainage, seals, and joinery details.

name: Optimised ease of operation
rationale: User accessibility and smooth opening/closing functionality influence sash design and hardware selection.

name: Reduced material weight
rationale: Lighter sashes reduce handling loads on hinges and operators, but must be balanced against structural needs.

name: Improved durability against weathering
rationale: UV exposure, moisture, and temperature cycles require robust materials and protective finishes for long service life.

name: Greater dimensional stability
rationale: Minimising warping, swelling, or contraction under temperature and humidity changes ensures consistent fit and performance.

name: Eliminated thermal bridging
rationale: Thermally broken frames or insulating materials in the sash reduce heat loss through the frame.

name: increased thermal insulation
rationale: Window sills should provide adequate thermal insulation to reduce heat loss through the window assembly.

name: improved water runoff
rationale: Window sills must be designed with proper slope and overhang to direct rainwater away from the facade, preventing moisture ingress.

name: higher structural load capacity
rationale: Window sills must support self-weight, wind loads, and potentially maintenance loads to ensure structural integrity.

name: reduced thermal bridging
rationale: Window sills are common locations for thermal bridging; details should minimise heat flow through conductive materials.

name: minimised moisture penetration
rationale: Joints between the sill and window frame/wall must be sealed to prevent water ingress that could cause decay or mould.

name: limited condensate accumulation
rationale: Proper design should avoid cold surfaces on sills that could lead to condensation and subsequent material deterioration.

name: expanded durability
rationale: Materials chosen for window sills should resist UV exposure, thermal cycling, and moisture for long service life.

name: adequate acoustic insulation
rationale: Window sill assemblies can contribute to sound transmission paths; adequate mass and sealing improve acoustic performance.

name: reduced thermal bridging
rationale: Thermal bridging at window heads is a common source of heat loss; reducing it improves energy performance.

name: improved weathertightness
rationale: Window heads are vulnerable to water ingress; improved detailing and flashing enhance weathertightness.

name: adequate structural support
rationale: The window head must support the lintel or structure above; adequate support is critical for safety.

name: reduced air leakage
rationale: Sealing at the window head reduces uncontrolled air infiltration, improving energy efficiency and comfort.

name: minimised condensation risk
rationale: Proper insulation and positioning at the window head reduces the risk of condensation and mould growth.

name: optimised head height
rationale: Window head height affects daylight penetration and spatial perception; optimising it improves occupant experience.

name: greater daylight penetration
rationale: Higher window heads allow deeper daylight penetration into the room.

name: sufficient insulation continuity
rationale: Continuous insulation around the window head prevents thermal bypass and ensures energy code compliance.

name: Improved thermal performance
rationale: Window jambs should provide adequate thermal insulation to reduce heat loss/gain around the window perimeter.

name: Increased structural rigidity
rationale: The window jamb must resist wind loads and support the window frame, requiring sufficient stiffness and strength.

name: Reduced air infiltration
rationale: Air leakage around the window jamb compromises energy efficiency and comfort; sealing and tightness are critical.

name: Reduced moisture penetration
rationale: Window jambs are vulnerable to water ingress; waterproofing and drainage must be ensured to prevent rot and damage.

name: Optimised material durability
rationale: The jamb material must withstand environmental exposure over time without degrading.

name: Minimised thermal bridging
rationale: Thermal bridging through the jamb can significantly reduce overall wall thermal performance; insulation continuity is important.

name: Enhanced structural connection to wall
rationale: The jamb must be securely anchored to the surrounding wall structure to transfer loads properly.

name: Adequate accommodation of thermal movement
rationale: Thermal expansion and contraction of materials must be accommodated to prevent cracking or binding.

name: Restricted installation tolerances
rationale: Tight tolerances are needed to ensure proper fit, sealing, and operation of the window system.

name: Increased structural strength
rationale: Window mullions must be structurally strong enough to support the weight of the glazing and resist wind loads, especially in tall buildings or curtain wall systems.

name: Reduced thermal bridging
rationale: Mullions that are highly conductive can create thermal bridges, reducing energy efficiency; thus there is pressure to minimise thermal conductivity through the mullion.

name: Reduced material weight
rationale: Lighter mullions reduce structural load on the building frame and make installation easier, creating pressure to minimise weight.

name: Improved water tightness
rationale: Mullions are critical junctions in facade systems where water infiltration can occur, so there is pressure to enhance sealing and drainage performance.

name: Enhanced acoustic insulation
rationale: Mullions contribute to the overall acoustic performance of the facade; higher-performing mullion designs help reduce sound transmission.

name: Reduced manufacturing cost
rationale: Cost efficiency is a common design pressure—mullion profiles and materials should be chosen to keep fabrication and installation expenses lower.

name: Improved fire resistance
rationale: Building codes often require mullions to resist fire spread between floors or compartments, pressuring designs to use fire-rated materials or intumescent coatings.

name: Reduced visual obstruction
rationale: From an architectural perspective, slimmer mullions provide better views and more daylight, creating pressure to minimise the visual bulk of the mullion.

name: Expanded tolerance for thermal movement
rationale: Mullions expand and contract with temperature changes; designs need adequate allowance for thermal movement to avoid stress and failure.

name: Improved thermal performance pressure
rationale: Window transoms should provide adequate thermal insulation to reduce heat transfer between interior and exterior.

name: Higher structural load capacity pressure
rationale: The transom must support wind loads and potentially the weight of surrounding glazing or framing elements.

name: Reduced air infiltration pressure
rationale: Minimizing air leakage through transom joints is critical for energy efficiency and occupant comfort.

name: Maximised daylight transmission pressure
rationale: Transoms are often positioned above doors or windows to allow more natural light deeper into a space.

name: Sufficient water penetration resistance pressure
rationale: The transom must resist rainwater ingress through its seals and joints to prevent moisture damage.

name: Restricted visual obstruction pressure
rationale: Transom framing should be minimized in profile to avoid obstructing views and light transmission.

name: Lower material cost pressure
rationale: Cost-effective material selection is important to keep the overall window assembly within budget.

name: Enhanced acoustic insulation pressure
rationale: The transom assembly should help reduce sound transmission between interior and exterior or between adjacent spaces.

name: Adequate structural integration pressure
rationale: The transom must integrate properly with the surrounding window frame, mullions, and wall structure.

name: Improved operability
rationale: Window hardware such as handles, locks, and hinges must be designed for smooth and reliable operation to allow easy opening and closing of windows.

name: Reduced maintenance requirements
rationale: Window hardware components are subject to wear and corrosion; designs aim to minimise the need for frequent maintenance or replacement.

name: Enhanced security
rationale: Locks and latching mechanisms on windows must provide adequate security against intrusion, a key design pressure for window hardware.

name: Optimised material durability
rationale: Hardware materials (e.g., stainless steel, brass, engineered polymers) are selected for corrosion resistance and long-term durability under environmental exposure.

name: Reduced manufacturing cost
rationale: Cost constraints drive the selection of simpler, mass-producible hardware designs without compromising essential performance.

name: Better ergonomic design
rationale: Handles and operating mechanisms should be comfortable and intuitive for users of varying abilities, influencing hardware shape, size, and placement.

name: Improved security
rationale: The primary function of a window locking mechanism is to secure the window against unauthorized entry, demanding high security performance.

name: Enhanced ease of operation
rationale: Users require locking mechanisms that are simple and convenient to operate, especially in emergency egress situations.

name: Reduced mechanical failure risk
rationale: Mechanical robustness and reliability are critical to avoid jamming, breakage, or malfunction over the building's lifespan.

name: Lower manufacturing cost
rationale: Cost constraints from project budgets drive the need for economical design and material choices in window hardware.

name: Greater durability against weathering
rationale: The mechanism is exposed to environmental conditions (moisture, UV, temperature cycles) and must resist corrosion and degradation.

name: Reduced maintenance requirements
rationale: Building owners prefer low-maintenance components to minimize lifecycle costs and operational disruptions.

name: Increased load-bearing capacity
rationale: Window hinges must bear the weight of the window sash; higher load-bearing capacity ensures structural integrity and durability.

name: Improved corrosion resistance
rationale: Hinges exposed to outdoor conditions require resistance to rust and corrosion to maintain functionality over time.

name: Enhanced durability
rationale: Frequent opening and closing cycles necessitate durable hinge materials and construction.

name: Reduced manufacturing cost
rationale: Cost constraints in building projects drive the need for affordable hinge designs.

name: Minimised friction
rationale: Lower friction between hinge moving parts reduces wear and allows smooth window operation.

name: Restricted size and profile
rationale: Architectural aesthetics often require compact hinge profiles that are minimally visible.

name: Maximised ease of installation
rationale: Simpler installation processes reduce labor time and errors during window assembly.

name: Greater thermal performance
rationale: Hinges that minimize thermal bridging help maintain window energy efficiency.

name: Eliminated loosening over time
rationale: Hinge fasteners and mechanisms should resist loosening from vibration and repeated use.

name: Improved water resistance
rationale: Window flashing primarily serves to direct water away from the window opening, preventing moisture intrusion into the wall assembly. Higher water resistance is a core design pressure.

name: Enhanced durability against weather exposure
rationale: Flashing must withstand UV radiation, temperature cycling, and moisture over the building's lifespan. Greater durability ensures long-term performance.

name: Reduced installation complexity
rationale: Simpler installation reduces labor costs and the likelihood of field errors that compromise flashing performance.

name: Eliminated thermal bridging risk
rationale: Metal flashings can conduct heat/cold, creating thermal bridges. Minimizing this improves overall building energy performance.

name: Adequate sealant compatibility
rationale: Flashing materials must be chemically compatible with adjoining sealants to maintain a continuous, durable weather barrier.

name: Lower material cost
rationale: Cost constraints often push toward less expensive flashing materials (e.g., plastic vs. metal), though this may trade off against durability.

name: Restricted air leakage paths
rationale: Properly designed flashing contributes to the air barrier continuity around windows, reducing uncontrolled air infiltration and energy loss.

name: Improved drainage performance
rationale: Effective flashing incorporates weep paths and sloped surfaces to drain any water that penetrates the outer seal, preventing accumulation behind the cladding.

name: Better integration with adjacent cladding
rationale: Flashing details must interface seamlessly with siding, brick veneer, or other cladding systems to ensure continuous water shedding and a clean appearance.

name: Improved moisture resistance
rationale: Window trim/casing must resist moisture intrusion to prevent rot and decay, especially in exterior applications.

name: Enhanced aesthetic appeal
rationale: Trim/casing contributes to the visual character of the building and must be visually pleasing.

name: Reduced maintenance requirements
rationale: Minimising upkeep effort is desirable for durability and lifecycle cost of trim components.

name: Greater dimensional stability
rationale: Trim must resist warping, shrinking, or swelling due to temperature and humidity changes.

name: Eliminated thermal bridging
rationale: Trim/casing should avoid creating paths for unwanted heat transfer around window openings.

name: Improved weather sealing
rationale: Proper sealing between trim and wall/window prevents air and water infiltration.

name: Reduced material cost
rationale: Budget constraints often push for lower-cost materials for trim components.

name: Higher structural rigidity
rationale: Trim must be stiff enough to hold shape and resist impact or wind loads.

name: Eliminated rot susceptibility
rationale: Using rot-resistant materials (e.g., PVC, fiber cement, treated wood) prevents decay over time.

name: Increased durability against impact
rationale: Window screens need to withstand wind, debris, and daily use without tearing or deforming.

name: Improved insect protection
rationale: Primary function of window screens is to prevent insects from entering while allowing airflow.

name: Enhanced airflow permeability
rationale: Screens must allow adequate air circulation for natural ventilation.

name: Reduced visibility obstruction
rationale: Screens should minimally obstruct the view from inside to outside.

name: Lower UV degradation
rationale: Sunlight exposure causes material breakdown; UV-resistant materials extend screen lifespan.

name: Greater corrosion resistance
rationale: Metal screens (e.g., aluminum, stainless steel) must resist corrosion from moisture and environmental exposure.

name: Restricted maintenance requirement
rationale: Screens should not require frequent cleaning or repair to remain functional.

name: Sufficient daylight transmittance
rationale: Screens should allow adequate natural light to pass through for interior illumination.

name: Minimised installation complexity
rationale: Installation should be straightforward to reduce labor cost and ensure proper fit.

name: Improved thermal insulation
rationale: Window blinds and shades provide an additional layer of insulation, reducing heat transfer through windows.

name: Reduced solar heat gain
rationale: Blinds and shades block or reflect solar radiation, reducing the amount of solar heat entering the space.

name: Enhanced glare control
rationale: Adjustable blinds and shades allow occupants to control direct sunlight and reduce glare on screens and surfaces.

name: Increased daylight harvesting
rationale: Some blind/shade systems can redirect daylight deeper into the space, improving natural light distribution.

name: Reduced visual privacy
rationale: When blinds are open or made of translucent materials, they may provide less privacy compared to opaque alternatives.

name: Increased operational complexity
rationale: Motorized or automated blind systems add complexity to building controls and require maintenance.

name: Lower cooling energy demand
rationale: By reducing solar heat gain, blinds and shades lower the cooling load on HVAC systems, reducing energy consumption.

name: Minimized fading of interior furnishings
rationale: Blinds and shades block UV radiation, protecting furniture, flooring, and fabrics from sun damage and fading.

name: Greater user comfort control
rationale: Manual or automated adjustability gives occupants control over their immediate environment, improving satisfaction.

name: Improved weather protection
rationale: Window shutters are designed to protect windows from weather elements such as rain, wind, and sun.

name: Enhanced security
rationale: Shutters provide a barrier against intrusion and break-ins, improving building security.

name: Increased light control
rationale: Shutters allow occupants to adjust the amount of natural light entering through windows.

name: Improved ventilation
rationale: Operable shutters can direct airflow into the building when open.

name: Reduced heat gain
rationale: Shutters provide shading and insulation that lowers solar heat gain through windows.

name: Reduced maintenance
rationale: Shutters require periodic painting, cleaning, and repair, and there is pressure to minimize this upkeep.

name: Lower cost
rationale: Budget constraints create pressure to reduce the cost of shutter materials, installation, and maintenance.

name: Improved thermal insulation
rationale: Bay windows typically have higher heat loss than standard walls; improving insulation reduces energy costs and enhances comfort.

name: Reduced heat loss
rationale: Bay windows are a common source of thermal bridging and heat loss; minimizing this is a key design pressure.

name: Increased natural light
rationale: Bay windows project outward and often have multiple glazing panels to maximize daylight admission into the interior.

name: Expanded interior space perception
rationale: The projecting nature of a bay window creates a sense of additional floor area or a cozy alcove within a room.

name: Reduced structural overhang load
rationale: The cantilevered or projecting structure of a bay window must be designed to support its own weight and snow/live loads without excessive deflection.

name: Improved aesthetic appeal
rationale: Bay windows are often added to enhance the exterior architectural character and curb appeal of a building.

name: Higher construction cost
rationale: The complexity of framing, glazing, and waterproofing a bay window makes it more expensive than a standard flat window.

name: Reduced condensation risk
rationale: Proper thermal design and ventilation are needed to prevent moisture condensation on the large glazed surfaces of a bay window.

name: Optimized daylight factor
rationale: The geometry and orientation of a bay window can be tuned to achieve uniform daylight distribution deeper into the room.

name: enhanced thermal insulation pressure
rationale: Curtain wall window units must provide adequate thermal insulation to meet energy codes and occupant comfort requirements.

name: reduced air infiltration pressure
rationale: Building envelopes require minimized air leakage through curtain wall assemblies to maintain energy efficiency and prevent moisture damage.

name: higher structural wind load resistance pressure
rationale: Curtain walls must resist wind loads as a primary structural function of the building envelope.

name: improved water penetration resistance pressure
rationale: Curtain wall systems require effective water barriers to prevent rain penetration into the building interior.

name: reduced solar heat gain pressure
rationale: Glazed curtain wall areas should minimize solar heat gain to reduce cooling loads and improve thermal comfort.

name: optimized daylight transmission pressure
rationale: Curtain walls serve as primary daylight apertures, requiring adequate visible light transmittance for interior daylighting.

name: greater acoustic performance pressure
rationale: Building facades with curtain walls need sound transmission control for occupant comfort in noisy urban environments.

name: minimised condensation risk pressure
rationale: Thermal bridging in curtain wall frames must be managed to prevent interior surface condensation and associated mold growth.

name: lower embodied carbon pressure
rationale: Sustainable design trends increasingly demand reduced embodied carbon in building envelope materials and assemblies.

name: Improved thermal insulation
rationale: Double-hung windows are a primary source of heat loss; improved insulation reduces energy consumption.

name: Reduced air infiltration
rationale: The sliding mechanism of double-hung windows often allows air leakage; reducing air infiltration improves energy efficiency.

name: Enhanced durability
rationale: Double-hung windows are exposed to weathering and frequent operation; durability ensures long service life.

name: Lower maintenance requirements
rationale: Homeowners prefer windows that require less frequent painting, cleaning, and repair.

name: Increased natural ventilation
rationale: Double-hung windows can be opened at top and bottom to promote stack-effect ventilation.

name: Restricted operational force
rationale: The sashes should slide easily; excessive friction or binding must be avoided for proper function.

name: Greater security against intrusion
rationale: Double-hung windows can be vulnerable; enhanced locking mechanisms and reinforced frames improve security.

name: Minimised condensation risk
rationale: Condensation on double-hung windows can lead to mold and frame damage; improved thermal performance reduces risk.

name: Adequate daylight admittance
rationale: Windows must allow sufficient natural light; larger or clearer glazing improves interior daylighting.

name: Improved thermal insulation pressure
rationale: Casement windows must provide adequate thermal insulation to reduce heat loss, especially when sealed properly. This is an engineering requirement for energy efficiency.

name: Enhanced weather sealing pressure
rationale: Casement windows require robust weatherstripping and sealing to prevent air and water infiltration due to their operable nature.

name: Reduced air infiltration pressure
rationale: Minimizing unwanted air leakage through the window assembly is critical for indoor comfort and energy performance.

name: Greater structural rigidity pressure
rationale: The frame and sash of a casement window need sufficient stiffness to resist wind loads and maintain operation over time.

name: Improved ease of operation pressure
rationale: Casement windows typically use crank or hinge mechanisms; ergonomic and reliable operability is an architectural and usability requirement.

name: Reduced condensation risk pressure
rationale: Proper design of thermal breaks and glazing helps avoid condensation on interior surfaces, which can cause mold and material degradation.

name: Enhanced daylight penetration pressure
rationale: Casement windows can have large glazed areas; maximizing visible light transmittance supports natural lighting strategies.

name: Restricted hardware complexity pressure
rationale: Minimizing the number of moving parts and complexity in hinges, cranks, and locks improves reliability and reduces maintenance.

name: Greater security resistance pressure
rationale: Casement windows need robust locking mechanisms and impact-resistant glazing or frames to deter forced entry.

name: Improved thermal performance pressure
rationale: Awning windows, when closed, provide better sealing than sliding windows due to the compression of weatherstripping when the crank is tightened, reducing air infiltration and improving thermal insulation.

name: Enhanced ventilation control pressure
rationale: Awning windows can be opened during light rain without letting water in, and they catch breezes effectively, promoting natural ventilation while keeping the interior dry.

name: Increased structural integrity pressure
rationale: The hinged-top design and multi-point locking mechanisms in awning windows distribute wind loads more evenly across the frame than sliding or single-hung windows, making them more resistant to wind pressure.

name: Reduced hardware complexity pressure
rationale: Simpler crank or push-bar mechanisms could reduce long-term maintenance issues compared to more complex multi-point locking systems, though this trades off against security and sealing benefits.

name: Maximized unobstructed views pressure
rationale: Awning windows, being taller than they are wide, offer narrower sightlines compared to casement or picture windows, creating pressure to optimise placement or combine with other window types for views.

name: Increased thermal insulation
rationale: Fixed/picture windows are non-operable and typically have larger glazed areas, so increasing thermal insulation (e.g., double/triple glazing, low-E coatings) improves energy efficiency and prevents heat loss.

name: Reduced heat transfer
rationale: Minimizing conductive and convective heat transfer through the window assembly is critical for thermal comfort and energy performance.

name: Increased structural strength
rationale: Fixed windows must withstand wind loads and other structural forces, so stronger framing and glazing are required, especially for large spans.

name: Reduced air leakage
rationale: Since fixed windows are not operable, they should have minimized air infiltration through proper sealing and gasketing to maintain building envelope integrity.

name: Increased natural light transmission
rationale: Fixed/picture windows are often used for expansive views and daylighting; maximizing visible light transmittance enhances interior daylight quality.

name: Reduced solar heat gain
rationale: Large fixed glazing can lead to overheating; limiting solar heat gain coefficient (SHGC) with appropriate glazing or shading reduces cooling loads.

name: Improved water penetration resistance
rationale: Fixed windows must have better weather sealing to prevent water ingress at the perimeter joints and between frame and glazing.

name: Reduced condensation risk
rationale: Minimizing condensation on interior surfaces of fixed windows through improved thermal performance of edge seals and glazing units prevents moisture damage.

name: Greater aesthetic integration
rationale: Fixed/picture windows are prominent architectural features; optimizing frame profiles, sightlines, and proportions enhances visual appeal and design coherence.

name: Increased solar heat gain
rationale: The louvre window design allows passive solar heat gain in winter when the sun is lower, providing free heating.

name: Reduced unwanted solar heat gain
rationale: Louvre windows can be angled to block high summer sun, reducing cooling loads.

name: Improved natural ventilation
rationale: Louvre windows allow air flow even when closed, enhancing natural cross-ventilation.

name: Reduced rain ingress
rationale: The angled slats of a louvre system help deflect rain while allowing ventilation.

name: Greater daylight penetration
rationale: Louvre windows can be oriented to optimise daylight while reducing glare.

name: Lower heat loss at night
rationale: When closed, louvre windows create an insulating air layer reducing night-time heat loss.

name: Enhanced privacy control
rationale: Adjustable louvres allow occupants to control sightlines and privacy.

name: Restricted airflow in storm conditions
rationale: Louvre windows can be closed or locked to restrict airflow during storms.

name: Optimised passive cooling
rationale: The design of louvre windows facilitates natural convection and passive cooling strategies.

name: Improved thermal insulation pressure
rationale: Sliding windows often have less effective sealing than fixed or casement windows, creating a design pressure to improve their thermal insulation performance through better frame materials, double/triple glazing, or improved weatherstripping.

name: Reduced air infiltration pressure
rationale: Sliding windows are prone to air leakage at the interface between sliding panels; there is a design pressure to minimise air infiltration to meet building energy code requirements and maintain occupant comfort.

name: Enhanced operational smoothness pressure
rationale: The sliding mechanism must operate smoothly over time; design decisions around track design, roller quality, and frame alignment are driven by the need for easy and reliable operation.

name: Greater structural wind load resistance pressure
rationale: Sliding windows must resist wind loads, especially in tall buildings or exposed locations. Larger glass panels and wider spans increase the need for reinforced frames and thicker glass to meet structural safety requirements.

name: Lower manufacturing cost pressure
rationale: Cost considerations drive decisions about frame materials (e.g., aluminium vs. uPVC vs. timber), glazing options, and hardware quality to keep the sliding window product affordable and competitive.

name: Minimised water ingress pressure
rationale: Sliding windows are vulnerable to water penetration at the sill and inter-panel joints; design pressures focus on drainage systems, weatherstripping, and sloping sills to prevent water ingress.

name: Expanded daylight opening pressure
rationale: Architects often desire larger glazed areas in sliding windows to maximise natural light and views, which affects decisions about frame proportions, glass size, and the number of sliding panels.

name: Adequate acoustic performance pressure
rationale: In noisy urban environments, sliding windows may underperform acoustically compared to fixed windows; there is pressure to specify laminated glass, wider air gaps, or better sealing to achieve adequate sound insulation.

name: Improved drainage capacity
rationale: Adequate drainage capacity is needed to handle condensation loads and prevent water damage to window frames and surrounding structures.

name: Optimised drainage path slope
rationale: Proper slope ensures gravity-driven flow of condensation water to prevent pooling and potential leakage.

name: Reduced water intrusion risk
rationale: Effective condensation drainage prevents water from seeping into wall assemblies, reducing moisture damage.

name: Enhanced material corrosion resistance
rationale: Drainage system components should resist corrosion from prolonged exposure to condensed moisture.

name: Lower maintenance requirements
rationale: Design should minimise the need for frequent cleaning or unclogging of drainage paths.

name: Increased thermal insulation demand
rationale: Building energy codes and standards (e.g., ASHRAE, IECC) require lower U-values (better insulation) to reduce heat transfer through windows, thereby improving overall building energy efficiency.

name: Reduced heat loss requirement
rationale: Thermal performance targets aim to minimise heat loss through fenestration; a lower U-value directly reduces thermal transmittance, which is a key design objective for energy-efficient building envelopes.

name: Lower solar heat gain constraint
rationale: In cooling-dominated climates, low U-values often pair with low solar heat gain coefficients (SHGC) to reduce overall cooling loads, creating a downward pressure on acceptable U-values.

name: Improved occupant comfort pressure
rationale: Lower U-values reduce cold drafts near windows and minimise radiant temperature asymmetry, enhancing thermal comfort for occupants, which pressures designers toward specifying better-performing windows.

name: Reduced thermal transmittance
rationale: Lower U-value for the door leaf improves thermal insulation performance.

name: Increased structural stiffness
rationale: Greater stiffness reduces deflection under wind or impact loads.

name: Reduced weight
rationale: Lighter door leaf eases operation and reduces hinge wear.

name: Improved acoustic insulation
rationale: Better sound transmission class (STC) rating required for noise control.

name: Enhanced fire resistance rating
rationale: Higher fire rating ensures compliance with building code compartmentation requirements.

name: Reduced air leakage
rationale: Lower infiltration improves energy efficiency and indoor comfort.

name: Greater durability
rationale: More durable materials extend service life and reduce maintenance.

name: Lower cost
rationale: Budget constraints push toward more economical door leaf solutions.

name: Improved aesthetic finish
rationale: Architectural expectations demand visually appealing door leaf appearance.

name: Improved accessibility compliance
rationale: Building codes and accessibility standards (e.g., ADA) require door thresholds to be low-profile or beveled to ensure wheelchair and walker accessibility.

name: Reduced tripping hazard
rationale: High or abrupt thresholds create tripping risks, especially in high-traffic areas; design seeks to minimize height changes.

name: Improved weather sealing
rationale: Thresholds serve as part of the building envelope to prevent air and water infiltration, requiring adequate sealing and height.

name: Greater structural durability
rationale: Thresholds must withstand foot traffic, rolling loads (carts, wheelchairs), and environmental exposure without excessive wear.

name: Reduced material cost
rationale: Budget constraints drive selection of simpler, less expensive threshold materials and profiles.

name: Enhanced thermal performance
rationale: Thermally broken threshold designs reduce heat loss/gain at the door bottom, improving energy efficiency.

name: Lower maintenance requirement
rationale: Durable materials like aluminum or stainless steel with corrosion-resistant finishes reduce ongoing maintenance needs.

name: Better acoustic insulation
rationale: Door thresholds with gaskets and tight seals help reduce sound transmission between spaces.

name: Optimised transition height between floor finishes
rationale: Threshold must accommodate differences in floor finish thicknesses (e.g., tile to carpet) while providing a smooth transition.

name: Improved weather sealing
rationale: Door sills need to provide a good seal against rain, drafts, and dust ingress; engineering best practice calls for weathertight thresholds.

name: Greater structural load capacity
rationale: Door sills must support foot traffic loads and in some cases point loads from wheelchairs, carts, or heavy doors; structural adequacy is a core requirement.

name: Reduced thermal bridging
rationale: Sills are often thermal bridges at the building envelope; minimizing conductive heat loss improves energy performance.

name: Eliminated water penetration risk
rationale: Water intrusion at the sill can cause rot, mould, and interior damage; architectural detailing aims to prevent water entry.

name: Lower air leakage
rationale: Building airtightness standards require minimal air leakage at transitions; reduced leakage improves HVAC efficiency and comfort.

name: Optimized accessibility height
rationale: Threshold height impacts wheelchair and mobility-aid accessibility; codes and universal design principles push for low or flush sills.

name: Enhanced durability against corrosion
rationale: Sills are exposed to moisture and foot traffic; selecting corrosion-resistant materials or coatings extends service life.

name: Constrained thermal movement
rationale: Temperature changes cause expansion/contraction; excessive movement can compromise seals and structural connections, so it should be limited.

name: Adequate drainage provision
rationale: Sills must allow water to drain away from the building; weep holes, sloping, or drainage channels are common architectural strategies.

name: adequate structural support for door head
rationale: The door head must bear the load above the door opening; adequate structural support ensures the lintel or header can carry the load from the wall above without deflection or failure.

name: reduced clearance height at door head
rationale: Architectural constraints sometimes require a lower door head height for aesthetic or spatial reasons, which reduces the clear opening height.

name: higher door head dimension for accessibility
rationale: Building codes and accessibility standards often require minimum clear height at the door head to allow passage of people and equipment.

name: restricted thermal bridging at door head
rationale: Thermal performance requirements push to minimise heat loss through the door head assembly by limiting thermal bridging between interior and exterior.

name: enhanced weather sealing at door head
rationale: The door head joint is vulnerable to water ingress; better sealing is needed to prevent moisture damage and air leakage.

name: increased structural support
rationale: Door jambs must support the weight of the door and resist operational forces; increased structural support ensures stability and durability.

name: improved sealing pressure
rationale: Door jambs need adequate sealing against air, water, and sound infiltration, driving a need for improved sealing.

name: reduced thermal bridging
rationale: In energy-efficient design, door jambs should minimize thermal bridging to prevent heat loss.

name: higher fire resistance
rationale: Fire-rated door assemblies require jambs with higher fire resistance to maintain compartmentation.

name: limited dimensional tolerance
rationale: Precise fit between door and jamb requires limited dimensional tolerances to ensure proper operation and sealing.

name: optimized fastener strength
rationale: Fasteners attaching the jamb to the wall structure must have optimized strength to resist forced entry and daily use.

name: minimised moisture absorption
rationale: Door jambs exposed to weather or humidity should have minimised moisture absorption to prevent rot, swelling, or corrosion.

name: adequate acoustic insulation
rationale: For sound-rated doors, the jamb assembly needs adequate acoustic insulation to meet STC ratings.

name: eliminated operational interference
rationale: Door jambs must be designed so that operational interference (binding, rubbing) is eliminated for smooth door operation.

name: Increased load-bearing capacity
rationale: Door hinges must withstand the weight of the door and repeated use, requiring sufficient strength and load capacity.

name: Improved corrosion resistance
rationale: Hinges are exposed to environmental moisture and need resistance to rust and corrosion for longevity.

name: Reduced friction
rationale: Lower friction between hinge knuckles and pin ensures smooth door operation and reduces wear over time.

name: Improved alignment precision
rationale: Precise hinge alignment is critical for proper door fit, swing, and latching without binding.

name: Reduced material fatigue
rationale: Repeated door opening/closing cycles create cyclical stress; minimising fatigue extends hinge service life.

name: Increased durability
rationale: Hinges must endure frequent use over many years without failure, demanding robust construction and materials.

name: Limited lateral play
rationale: Excessive side-to-side movement in a hinge can cause door sagging or misalignment; this should be minimised.

name: Reduced installation complexity
rationale: Simpler hinge designs and mounting methods reduce labour costs and installation errors.

name: Improved aesthetic finish
rationale: Visible hinges contribute to the door's appearance; a quality finish (e.g., brushed, painted, plated) is often desired.

name: Increased durability
rationale: Door stops need to withstand repeated impact forces from doors; higher durability ensures longer service life and prevents premature failure.

name: Reduced noise impact
rationale: Door stops should minimize noise generated when a door strikes them; quieter operation is a key design consideration.

name: Adequate holding force
rationale: Door stops must provide sufficient resistance to hold a door in the open or stopped position without slipping.

name: Minimised protrusion
rationale: Door stops should have a low profile to avoid being a tripping hazard and to maintain aesthetic cleanliness of the floor or wall.

name: Greater impact absorption
rationale: The door stop should absorb kinetic energy from door impact to protect both the door and the wall from damage.

name: Improved corrosion resistance
rationale: Especially for exterior or high-humidity environments, corrosion resistance extends the functional life of metal door stops.

name: Reduced installation complexity
rationale: Simpler installation reduces labor cost and potential for improper mounting, improving reliability.

name: Enhanced aesthetic integration
rationale: Door stops should visually complement the door and surrounding finish for cohesive interior design.

name: Lower material cost
rationale: Minimizing material cost helps keep the overall product affordable while meeting functional requirements.

name: Improved ergonomic comfort
rationale: Door knobs should be comfortable to grasp and operate, increasing user satisfaction and ease of use.

name: Reduced force to operate
rationale: Door knobs should require minimal physical effort to turn, especially for accessibility compliance (e.g., ADA standards).

name: Enhanced durability
rationale: Door knobs undergo frequent use and must resist wear, corrosion, and mechanical failure over time.

name: Restricted unauthorized access
rationale: Door knobs with locking mechanisms must limit access to authorized users, constraining the ability to open the door without a key.

name: Higher aesthetic appeal
rationale: The visual design and finish of the door knob contribute to the overall interior design statement and user experience.

name: Lower cost
rationale: Budget constraints pressure the selection of cost-effective door knob materials and manufacturing processes.

name: Improved accessibility compliance
rationale: Building codes and accessibility standards (e.g., ADA) increasingly demand lever handles or easily operable hardware, pressuring door knob design toward better accessibility.

name: Minimised maintenance requirement
rationale: Frequent maintenance of door hardware is undesirable; designs that reduce cleaning, lubrication, or part replacement needs are favoured.

name: Greater security
rationale: Door knobs with integrated locking mechanisms must provide sufficient resistance to forced entry and picking.

name: Improved ergonomic grip
rationale: Door handles must be comfortable and easy to grip for all users, driving designs toward larger, contoured handles.

name: Reduced bacterial transmission
rationale: Hygiene considerations push toward antimicrobial materials or touchless mechanisms to minimise germ spread.

name: Enhanced durability
rationale: Handles undergo frequent use and must resist wear, corrosion, and mechanical failure over time.

name: Lower manufacturing cost
rationale: Cost constraints push toward simpler geometries, cheaper materials, and standardised production methods.

name: Greater aesthetic appeal
rationale: Door handles contribute to the overall design language of a building and must be visually coherent with interior style.

name: Restricted force to operate
rationale: Accessibility standards require that handles can be operated with minimal force, including by people with limited hand strength.

name: Improved accessibility compliance
rationale: Building codes and universal design principles mandate lever-style or accessible handle designs over round knobs.

name: Reduced vandalism susceptibility
rationale: In public buildings, handles must be robust against deliberate damage or tampering.

name: Sufficient thermal insulation
rationale: In exterior doors, handles must minimise thermal bridging to prevent condensation and heat loss.

name: Increased Security Pressure
rationale: Door locks are primarily designed to provide security; there is a strong engineering pressure to increase security features such as anti-pick, anti-bump, and anti-drill capabilities.

name: Improved Durability Pressure
rationale: Door locks must withstand repeated use and environmental exposure, creating a pressure for more durable materials and mechanisms.

name: Reduced Cost Pressure
rationale: Manufacturing and procurement cost constraints create a downward pressure on the complexity and material quality of door locks.

name: Enhanced Accessibility Pressure
rationale: Building codes and universal design principles require locks to be operable by people with varying physical abilities, pressuring for easier-to-use mechanisms.

name: Minimised Maintenance Pressure
rationale: Building operators prefer lock systems that require less frequent servicing, creating a pressure to minimise maintenance needs.

name: Greater Aesthetic Appeal Pressure
rationale: Door locks are visible hardware elements; architectural design preferences pressure for finishes and styles that complement the building's aesthetic.

name: Higher Key Control Pressure
rationale: Security best practices pressure toward lock systems with restricted key duplication and master keying capabilities.

name: Reduced Installation Complexity Pressure
rationale: Ease of installation pressures toward simpler lock designs that fit standard door preparations and require less specialized labor.

name: Improved ergonomic comfort
rationale: Door levers are operated by hand; ergonomic design increases user comfort and accessibility, especially for those with limited hand strength.

name: Reduced operating force
rationale: Building codes and accessibility standards (e.g., ADA) require door hardware to be operable with minimal force, reducing the force required to actuate the lever.

name: Enhanced durability
rationale: Door levers in high-traffic areas must withstand frequent use; increased durability reduces wear and replacement frequency.

name: Greater aesthetic appeal
rationale: Architectural design often prioritises visual harmony; a more attractive door lever complements overall interior design.

name: Lower cost
rationale: Budget constraints in construction projects drive pressure to minimise hardware costs without compromising function.

name: Restricted security risk
rationale: Door levers can be vulnerable to forced entry; design pressures exist to minimise security risks, e.g., by adding locking mechanisms or anti-pry features.

name: Adequate accessibility compliance
rationale: Societal and legal expectations (e.g., ADA compliance) demand that door levers be accessible to people with disabilities, pushing for lever designs that meet code requirements.

name: Optimised installation simplicity
rationale: Simpler installation processes reduce labour time and errors, creating pressure to design levers with standardised mounting and clear installation guides.

name: Increased security force
rationale: Deadbolts are designed to increase security by providing a locking mechanism that is more resistant to forced entry than standard locks.

name: Improved durability force
rationale: Deadbolts must withstand repeated use and attempted forced entry, driving a need for durable materials and construction.

name: Reduced ease of bypass force
rationale: A key design goal for deadbolts is to minimize vulnerabilities that would allow bypassing the lock mechanism.

name: improved latch security
rationale: Door latches must provide adequate security to prevent unauthorized entry, requiring improved locking mechanisms.

name: reduced latch failure rate
rationale: Mechanical reliability demands minimization of latch failure over many open/close cycles.

name: increased durability
rationale: Door latches experience repeated mechanical stress and must withstand wear over time.

name: lower manufacturing cost
rationale: Cost constraints in building components encourage minimizing production expenses for door latches.

name: minimised corrosion risk
rationale: Exposure to moisture and environmental conditions can corrode metallic door latches over time.

name: improved fire safety compliance
rationale: Building codes require door latches to allow egress during emergencies, influencing latch design.

name: reduced installation complexity
rationale: Simpler latch installation saves labor time and reduces errors during construction.

name: enhanced aesthetic integration
rationale: Door latches should visually complement the door and surrounding architectural style.

name: Increased strike plate durability
rationale: The strike plate must withstand repeated door closing forces without deforming or loosening, requiring robust material selection and secure fastening.

name: Improved alignment precision
rationale: Proper alignment between the latch and strike plate ensures smooth door operation and prevents binding or rattling.

name: Reduced material thickness
rationale: Thinner materials may reduce cost and weight but can compromise strength; a balance must be found between economy and performance.

name: Higher corrosion resistance
rationale: Strike plates exposed to weather or high-humidity environments require corrosion-resistant finishes (e.g., stainless steel or coated metals) to maintain function and appearance over time.

name: Greater fastener strength
rationale: Screws or bolts securing the strike plate must resist pull-out forces from repeated door latch impacts and potential forced entry attempts.

name: Eliminated sharp edges
rationale: Sharp edges on the strike plate pose a safety hazard to users and can damage door frames or finishes; deburring or chamfering is standard.

name: Optimised strike plate geometry
rationale: The shape and depth of the strike plate opening must accommodate the latch properly while providing full engagement for security and smooth operation.

name: Reduced installation complexity
rationale: Simpler strike plate designs with pre-drilled holes and clear marking reduce installer error and labour time, improving overall build quality.

name: Increased security performance
rationale: The strike plate is a critical component for door security; stronger materials and deeper latch engagement resist forced entry (e.g., kick-in attacks).

name: Increased closing force
rationale: The door closer must generate sufficient torque to overcome door weight, friction, and wind pressure to reliably close and latch the door.

name: Reduced closing speed
rationale: Safety codes (e.g., ADA) and accessibility standards require slower closing speeds to prevent doors from slamming on persons, especially those with mobility impairments.

name: Improved adjustability
rationale: Field-adjustable closing speed, sweep, and latch force help fine-tune performance across varying environmental and usage conditions.

name: Reduced size
rationale: Architectural aesthetics and space constraints often demand compact door closers that fit within narrow door frames or concealed installations.

name: Higher durability
rationale: Door closers experience thousands of cycles per year; materials and seals must resist wear, corrosion, and fluid leakage over the product lifecycle.

name: Reduced cost
rationale: Budget constraints on construction projects pressure designers to select lower-cost components without compromising critical safety performance.

name: Improved fire-rated compliance
rationale: Building codes require door closers on fire doors to ensure automatic closure in case of fire; compliance with UL/EN fire standards is mandatory.

name: Better corrosion resistance
rationale: Door closers in exterior, marine, or high-humidity environments require corrosion-resistant materials (e.g., stainless steel) to maintain function.

name: Reduced noise emission
rationale: In hospitals, libraries, and hotels, quiet door operation is an architectural requirement, driving demand for hydraulic dampening and silent closer mechanisms.

name: Improved security
rationale: A peephole provides a secure way to visually identify visitors before opening the door, improving overall security.

name: Reduced visibility distortion
rationale: Optical quality of the peephole lens should minimise distortion to allow clear identification of visitors.

name: Greater field of view
rationale: A wider angle of view allows the occupant to see more of the area outside the door, improving situational awareness.

name: Lower installation cost
rationale: Budget constraints on door hardware push towards using simpler, less expensive peephole models.

name: Restricted aperture size
rationale: The peephole aperture must be small enough to prevent someone outside from seeing in or inserting tools, while still providing adequate viewing.

name: Enhanced durability
rationale: Door hardware is subject to repeated use and tampering attempts, requiring robust construction materials.

name: Eliminated reverse viewing
rationale: Peepholes should be designed so that someone outside cannot see through the lens into the interior, a key privacy requirement.

name: Adequate privacy protection
rationale: Occupants expect a sense of privacy and safety; a properly designed peephole supports this cultural/architectural norm.

name: improved sealing pressure
rationale: Door sweeps are designed to seal the gap under a door; a force to improve sealing ensures better draft prevention, energy efficiency, and sound control.

name: reduced friction pressure
rationale: Excessive friction between the door sweep and floor can impede door operation and cause wear; minimizing friction is a common design consideration.

name: higher durability pressure
rationale: Door sweeps must withstand repeated contact with flooring, weather exposure, and foot traffic; greater durability is a key performance requirement.

name: minimised air infiltration pressure
rationale: A primary function of a door sweep is to block air leakage; minimizing air infiltration supports building energy performance and comfort.

name: adequate compression pressure
rationale: The door sweep must have sufficient compression against the floor threshold to form an effective seal without binding the door.

name: Increased security against forced entry
rationale: The primary function of a door chain/security chain is to provide a physical barrier that resists forced entry, thus a design pressure to increase security is fundamental.

name: Improved ease of operation
rationale: Users need to easily engage and disengage the chain from inside; poor ergonomics could discourage use, so improving ease of use is a key design pressure.

name: Reduced vulnerability to tampering from outside
rationale: A door chain must resist manipulation tools (e.g., wires, cutters) reaching through the door gap, so minimising tamper vulnerability is critical.

name: Greater durability against wear and corrosion
rationale: As a mechanical component exposed to frequent use and sometimes outdoor conditions, the chain and its hardware must resist corrosion and fatigue over time.

name: Limited gap opening for intrusion prevention
rationale: The chain must restrict the door opening to a small gap (typically 3-6 inches) to prevent a person or arm from reaching through, so restricting the gap is a design pressure.

name: Enhanced compatibility with door frame materials
rationale: The chain must be securely mountable to various door and frame materials (wood, metal, uPVC); improved compatibility strengthens the overall assembly.

name: Lower cost of manufacturing
rationale: Affordability is a market pressure; minimising production cost while maintaining safety and security is a common design constraint.

name: Adequate visibility for indoor aesthetics
rationale: As a visible indoor fixture, the door chain should have a finish and appearance that suits the interior design, applying a pressure for adequate visual quality.

name: Eliminated risk of accidental self-locking
rationale: The design must prevent the chain from accidentally engaging when closing the door, which could trap occupants inside or damage the door.

name: increased structural strength
rationale: Door panels must resist wind loads, impact loads, and forced entry, requiring adequate structural strength.

name: improved thermal insulation
rationale: Door panels contribute to building envelope thermal performance, requiring higher insulation values for energy efficiency.

name: enhanced acoustic performance
rationale: Door panels need to provide sound insulation between spaces, requiring better acoustic ratings.

name: reduced weight
rationale: Lighter door panels reduce loading on hinges, frames, and operators, making installation and operation easier.

name: lower manufacturing cost
rationale: Cost constraints drive decisions to minimise material and production expenses for door panels.

name: restricted material thickness
rationale: Thinner door panels may be required to fit within frames or to reduce weight, but this conflicts with strength requirements.

name: improved fire resistance
rationale: Fire-rated door panels must achieve specified fire-resistance ratings for safety compliance.

name: enhanced aesthetic finish
rationale: Door panels contribute to the visual quality of interior and exterior spaces, driving demand for better surface finishes and materials.

name: reduced thermal bridging
rationale: Minimising heat transfer through the door panel assembly improves overall building energy performance.

name: Improved thermal insulation
rationale: Vision panels in doors often require improved thermal insulation properties to reduce heat loss and meet energy code requirements.

name: Higher structural strength
rationale: Glazing in doors must withstand wind loads, impact forces, and door operation stresses, requiring sufficient structural strength.

name: Enhanced safety glazing
rationale: Building codes typically require tempered or laminated safety glass in door vision panels to prevent injury from breakage.

name: Adequate fire resistance rating
rationale: Fire-rated doors with vision panels require glazing that meets the same fire resistance rating as the door assembly.

name: Reduced solar heat gain
rationale: Low solar heat gain coefficient (SHGC) glazing may be desired to minimize unwanted heat gain through vision panels.

name: Minimised thermal bridging
rationale: The frame and edge seal of vision panels can create thermal bridging, so minimising this improves overall door thermal performance.

name: Greater visible light transmittance
rationale: Vision panels are intended to provide visibility and daylight, so higher visible light transmittance supports their functional purpose.

name: Restricted size of vision panel
rationale: Larger vision panels reduce door structural integrity and thermal performance, so size may be restricted relative to door dimensions.

name: Optimised condensation resistance
rationale: Vision panels should be designed to resist condensation formation through appropriate thermal performance of glazing and edge seals.

name: higher structural load capacity
rationale: Door transoms must support the weight of the door panel and any glazing above, requiring adequate structural capacity.

name: improved weather sealing
rationale: Transoms at door openings must resist air and water infiltration to maintain building envelope integrity.

name: reduced thermal bridging
rationale: Transom frames can act as thermal bridges; minimizing heat transfer improves energy performance.

name: adequate fire resistance rating
rationale: Door transoms often require fire-rated assemblies to comply with building codes for compartmentation.

name: minimised water penetration risk
rationale: Transom joints and interfaces are vulnerable to water ingress; detailing should prevent moisture damage.

name: optimised sightline proportion
rationale: The visual proportion of the transom relative to the door affects aesthetic harmony and daylight provision.

name: increased acoustic insulation
rationale: Transoms with glazing or gaps can compromise sound transmission class ratings; enhanced acoustic performance is often required.

name: Increased structural support for Door Sidelight
rationale: Door sidelights require adequate structural framing and support to bear loads from the door assembly and transfer them to the surrounding wall structure.

name: Improved thermal insulation for Door Sidelight
rationale: Door sidelights often use glazing which is a thermal weak point; improved insulation (e.g., double glazing, low-E coatings) reduces heat loss.

name: Enhanced weather sealing for Door Sidelight
rationale: Proper weatherstripping and sealing around the sidelight prevents air and water infiltration.

name: Reduced heat gain through Door Sidelight
rationale: Solar heat gain through sidelight glazing should be minimised using solar control glass or shading to maintain indoor comfort.

name: Increased security for Door Sidelight
rationale: Sidelights adjacent to doors are potential break-in points; stronger glazing (laminated/tempered) and secure framing are needed.

name: Reduced glass breakage risk for Door Sidelight
rationale: Sidelight glazing should be designed with tempered or laminated glass to minimise the risk of breakage from impact or thermal stress.

name: Adequate daylight admission through Door Sidelight
rationale: Sidelights provide natural light to entry areas; sufficient glazing area and light transmittance are desired for architectural and wayfinding purposes.

name: Restricted visual privacy compromise at Door Sidelight
rationale: Transparent sidelights can compromise privacy at doorways; frosted or obscured glass may be needed to limit visibility from outside.

name: Improved acoustic performance for Door Sidelight
rationale: Sidelight glazing and frame assemblies should provide adequate sound insulation where doors face noisy environments.

name: Maximised opening width
rationale: Sliding doors are designed to maximise the clear opening width compared to hinged doors, as the door panels slide parallel to the wall rather than swinging outward.

name: Reduced floor space requirement
rationale: Sliding doors do not require a swing radius, thus they minimise the floor area needed for door operation, which is a key design pressure in tight spaces.

name: Improved thermal insulation
rationale: Modern sliding doors incorporate thermal breaks, double/triple glazing, and weatherstripping to enhance thermal performance and reduce heat loss.

name: Greater airtightness and weather sealing
rationale: Sliding doors must be designed with effective seals to prevent air and water infiltration, which puts pressure on achieving higher airtightness standards.

name: Reduced operational effort (smooth sliding)
rationale: The sliding mechanism should minimise friction and effort required to open/close the door, placing a design pressure on low-resistance track and roller systems.

name: Optimised structural support for glass panels
rationale: Large glass panels in sliding doors require adequate framing and structural support to withstand wind loads and impact, driving pressure for optimised structural design.

name: Improved acoustic performance
rationale: Sliding doors often form part of building envelope; design pressure exists to enhance sound insulation through thicker glass and better seals.

name: Eliminated condensation risk
rationale: Thermal bridging at sliding door frames can cause condensation; design must avoid this risk through thermal breaks and proper installation.

name: Lower maintenance requirements
rationale: Sliding doors have tracks and rollers that require cleaning and adjustment; design pressures aim to reduce maintenance through self-cleaning tracks and durable materials.

name: improved energy efficiency
rationale: Revolving doors reduce air infiltration compared to swing doors, improving building energy efficiency by minimizing heat loss/gain.

name: reduced air infiltration
rationale: The design of revolving doors inherently limits the amount of outside air entering the building, reducing HVAC load.

name: enhanced user convenience
rationale: Revolving doors can accommodate high-traffic flow and allow hands-free operation, improving convenience for users.

name: restricted accessibility
rationale: Revolving doors can be difficult for people with disabilities, those with luggage, or emergency egress, creating accessibility constraints.

name: greater security control
rationale: Revolving doors can be integrated with access control systems to manage entry/exit, providing enhanced security.

name: higher maintenance cost
rationale: Revolving doors have more mechanical parts than standard doors, leading to greater maintenance requirements and costs.

name: reduced egress capacity
rationale: Revolving doors typically cannot serve as primary emergency egress due to slower evacuation rates compared to swing doors.

name: optimized space utilization
rationale: Revolving doors can be designed to fit specific architectural layouts, optimizing entrance space usage.

name: eliminated drafts
rationale: The continuous sealing action of revolving doors prevents drafts that would otherwise occur with conventional doors.

name: Improved weather sealing
rationale: Bi-fold doors require robust weather sealing to prevent air and water infiltration, which is a common design pressure.

name: Enhanced thermal insulation
rationale: Energy efficiency requirements drive better insulation values for large glazed door assemblies.

name: Reduced operational friction
rationale: Smooth folding and sliding operation is critical; minimizing friction in tracks and hinges is a key engineering concern.

name: Greater structural rigidity
rationale: Large spans of bi-fold doors need adequate structural support to resist wind loads and maintain alignment.

name: Limited weight per panel
rationale: Heavy panels increase stress on hinges, tracks, and operating mechanisms; lighter panels are preferred for durability and ease of use.

name: Maximised glass area
rationale: Architectural preference for unobstructed views and natural light drives larger glass panels within the door system.

name: Minimised frame profile
rationale: Slim frame profiles are desired for aesthetic reasons, but must be balanced against structural and sealing requirements.

name: Adequate acoustic performance
rationale: Sound transmission through large glass doors is a concern, especially in residential or office settings near noise sources.

name: Eliminated water pooling risk
rationale: Bottom tracks and sills must be designed to prevent water accumulation, which can cause corrosion and operational issues.

name: Improved accessibility
rationale: Automatic doors improve accessibility for people with disabilities, parents with strollers, and those carrying items, making building entry more inclusive.

name: Reduced manual effort
rationale: Automatic doors eliminate the need for manual pushing or pulling, reducing physical effort for all users.

name: Increased energy loss
rationale: Automatic doors may have longer open times or imperfect seals compared to manual doors, potentially increasing heat loss or cooling loss.

name: Enhanced traffic flow
rationale: Automatic doors facilitate smoother pedestrian traffic flow in high-traffic entrances, reducing congestion.

name: Higher maintenance requirements
rationale: Automatic doors have motors, sensors, and control systems that require regular maintenance compared to simpler manual doors.

name: Improved safety compliance
rationale: Building codes and accessibility regulations often mandate automatic or power-assisted doors in commercial and public buildings.

name: Reduced manual operation failures
rationale: Automatic doors remove the risk of doors being left ajar or improperly closed by users, though they introduce electronic failure risks.

name: Increased initial cost
rationale: Automatic door systems are more expensive to purchase and install than standard manual doors due to the additional hardware and wiring.

name: Constrained installation space
rationale: Automatic doors require adequate space for sensors, sliding mechanisms or swing arcs, and safety zones, which may constrain placement.

name: Improved fire resistance rating
rationale: Fire doors must have adequate fire-resistance ratings (e.g., 30, 60, 90 minutes) to compartmentalize fire and smoke, a core engineering safety requirement.

name: Enhanced self-closing mechanism reliability
rationale: Fire doors must reliably self-close and latch to maintain compartmentation integrity; regulations require automatic closing devices.

name: Reduced air gaps and smoke leakage
rationale: Smoke seals and tight tolerances are needed around fire doors to limit smoke spread, a critical life safety objective.

name: Adequate door width for egress capacity
rationale: Fire doors on egress paths must meet minimum width requirements per building codes to allow sufficient occupant evacuation.

name: Greater hardware durability and latching strength
rationale: Fire door hardware (hinges, locks, panic bars) must withstand repeated use and remain functional during a fire event.

name: Lower thermal conductivity of door core
rationale: Fire door cores are designed with insulating materials to limit heat transfer through the door assembly during fire exposure.

name: Restricted unauthorized propping or wedging open
rationale: Architectural and life safety practice requires that fire doors not be blocked or wedged open to ensure automatic closure in a fire.

name: Improved signage and visibility of fire door markings
rationale: Fire doors should be clearly labelled with fire ratings and 'Keep Closed' signage to inform occupants and maintenance staff.

name: Minimized gaps between door and frame during installation
rationale: Installation tolerances for gaps between the door leaf and frame must be tightly controlled to preserve the fire rating.

name: Improved thermal insulation
rationale: Flush doors should provide adequate thermal insulation to meet energy performance requirements.

name: Enhanced fire resistance
rationale: Building codes require flush doors in certain locations to have fire-resistance ratings to slow fire spread.

name: Greater acoustic insulation
rationale: Flush doors may need sound transmission class (STC) ratings for privacy and noise control between spaces.

name: Higher structural stiffness
rationale: Flush doors require adequate stiffness to resist warping and maintain dimensional stability over time.

name: Reduced manufacturing cost
rationale: Cost constraints push toward simpler core materials and construction methods for flush doors.

name: Minimised weight
rationale: Lighter flush doors are easier to operate, install, and place less stress on hinges and frames.

name: Limited moisture absorption
rationale: Moisture causes swelling, delamination, and decay in flush door materials, so low moisture absorption is critical.

name: Better dimensional stability
rationale: Flush doors must resist warping, twisting, and expansion/contraction with changing environmental conditions.

name: Adequate surface durability
rationale: Flush door facings must withstand impact, abrasion, and cleaning without degrading visually or structurally.

name: Improved thermal insulation
rationale: Panelled doors typically have less insulation than solid doors; there is a design pressure to increase thermal performance.

name: Reduced weight
rationale: Panelled doors can be heavy due to solid wood panels; reducing weight may ease operation and hinge stress.

name: Enhanced aesthetic appeal
rationale: Panelled doors are often chosen for visual character; there is pressure to enhance appearance through panel detailing.

name: Improved acoustic performance
rationale: Panelled doors may transmit sound through panels; acoustic improvement is a design pressure for interior doors.

name: Reduced manufacturing cost
rationale: Cost efficiency pressures exist to reduce material use and simplify panel joinery while maintaining appearance.

name: Greater structural stiffness
rationale: Panels can flex or warp; design pressure exists to increase stiffness and long-term dimensional stability.

name: Improved fire resistance
rationale: Fire-rated panelled doors require intumescent seals and fire-resistant panel cores, increasing fire performance.

name: Reduced air leakage
rationale: Panelled doors have joints between panels and stiles; reducing air leakage improves energy efficiency.

name: Enhanced durability
rationale: Design pressure to increase durability through better finishes, weather sealing, and robust joinery for longer service life.

name: Improved ventilation airflow
rationale: Louvred doors are designed to allow airflow while providing privacy and security, so there is a design pressure to increase ventilation capacity.

name: Reduced heat gain through opening
rationale: The louvred design can allow solar radiation and heat to pass through; there is a pressure to minimise unwanted heat transfer.

name: Enhanced visual privacy
rationale: Louvred doors provide partial visual screening; design often aims to maximise privacy while maintaining ventilation.

name: Restricted insect/vermin entry
rationale: The gaps in louvred doors must be designed to limit or prevent pests from entering the building.

name: Adequate structural stability
rationale: The louvred door must have sufficient structural strength to withstand wind loads, impacts, and daily operation.

name: Improved structural integrity
rationale: A Dutch door is split horizontally, requiring reinforced framing and hardware at the split to maintain strength and alignment over time.

name: Enhanced weather sealing
rationale: The split in a Dutch door creates two meeting edges that need effective weatherstripping to prevent air and water infiltration.

name: Reduced swing interference
rationale: Each half of a Dutch door swings independently, requiring careful coordination of hinge placement and swing arcs to avoid binding or interference.

name: Adequate locking mechanism
rationale: Dutch doors need separate or interconnected locking hardware for both halves, ensuring security when both sections are closed.

name: Optimised clearance tolerances
rationale: The split line requires precise gap tolerances to allow independent operation of each half while maintaining a weather-tight seal.

name: Increased security pressure
rationale: Garage doors are a common entry point, so there is engineering pressure to increase security features such as stronger locks, reinforced materials, and smart access controls.

name: Improved insulation pressure
rationale: Energy efficiency requirements drive pressure for improved thermal insulation in garage doors to reduce heat loss and improve building energy performance.

name: Reduced cost pressure
rationale: Budget constraints create pressure to reduce the cost of garage door procurement and installation, potentially limiting material and feature choices.

name: Greater durability pressure
rationale: Garage doors face frequent use and exposure to weather, creating pressure for greater durability and longer lifespan through robust materials and mechanisms.

name: Improved noise reduction pressure
rationale: If the garage is attached or near living spaces, there is architectural pressure for improved noise reduction to minimise operational noise disturbance.

name: Reduced maintenance pressure
rationale: There is pressure to reduce maintenance requirements for garage doors, favouring materials and designs that require less frequent servicing and repairs.

name: Enhanced aesthetic appeal pressure
rationale: As a prominent building facade element, there is architectural pressure for enhanced aesthetic appeal, including colour, finish, style, and integration with the overall building design.

name: Maximised automation convenience pressure
rationale: Cultural expectations for modern convenience create pressure for maximised automation features such as remote control, smartphone integration, and automatic safety sensors.

name: Reduced space requirement pressure
rationale: Site constraints or interior layout requirements may create pressure to reduce the space needed for garage door operation (e.g., minimal headroom or side space for tracks).

name: Improved security access control
rationale: Security requirements drive the need for better authentication, authorisation, and access logging capabilities in the access control system.

name: Enhanced integration with building management
rationale: Modern access control systems must integrate with other building systems (e.g., fire alarm, HVAC, lighting) for coordinated operation.

name: Reduced unauthorised entry risk
rationale: The primary purpose of access control is to prevent unauthorised access, so minimising breach risks is a fundamental design pressure.

name: Lower operational complexity
rationale: System administrators and end-users benefit from simpler credential management, user interfaces, and maintenance procedures.

name: Improved user convenience and throughput
rationale: Entry points must allow smooth and quick passage for authorised users, balancing security with minimal delay and friction.

name: Restricted physical access points
rationale: Architectural design pressures minimise the number of controlled access points to reduce cost and management overhead while maintaining security.

name: Greater scalability for future growth
rationale: The system must accommodate future expansion in number of users, doors, and facilities without major re-architecture.

name: Higher reliability and uptime
rationale: Access control is a life-safety-adjacent system requiring high availability; failures must be minimised and fail-safe behaviour ensured.

name: Eliminated single points of failure
rationale: Redundancy in controllers, power supplies, and network paths is needed to prevent total system loss from any one component failure.

name: Improved security access control
