rationale: Video doorbells and intercoms are primarily installed to increase security by screening visitors before granting access.

name: Higher audio and video quality
rationale: Better resolution and audio clarity improve identification of visitors and system usability.

name: Reduced vulnerability to tampering
rationale: Devices mounted at entry points must resist physical tampering, vandalism, and weather exposure.

name: Minimised installation cost
rationale: Budget constraints pressure designers to select simpler, lower-cost intercom and doorbell solutions.

name: Expanded smart home integration
rationale: Modern consumer expectations demand compatibility with smartphones, smart locks, and home automation systems.

name: Adequate weather and environmental protection
rationale: Outdoor installation requires weatherproofing (IP rating) against rain, dust, and temperature extremes.

name: Enhanced ease of use for all visitors
rationale: Accessible design principles push for simple, intuitive interfaces that accommodate people of all ages and abilities.

name: Limited power consumption
rationale: Battery-operated or low-voltage systems must minimize power draw to reduce maintenance and wiring complexity.

name: Stronger aesthetic integration with building facade
rationale: Architectural design pressures favor devices that are discreet, stylish, and blend with the entryway design.

name: Increased structural load capacity
rationale: Mullions must withstand wind loads and dead loads from glazing, requiring adequate structural strength to prevent failure.

name: Reduced thermal bridging
rationale: Mullions often act as thermal bridges in curtain wall systems; minimizing heat transfer improves energy efficiency.

name: Improved weather sealing
rationale: Mullions require proper gaskets and seals to prevent air and water infiltration at glass-to-mullion interfaces.

name: Minimized deflection under load
rationale: Excessive mullion deflection can cause glass breakage or seal failure; limiting deflection is critical for performance.

name: Optimized material cross-section
rationale: Mullion profiles should be optimized to balance strength, weight, and material cost while meeting structural requirements.

name: Reduced fabrication complexity
rationale: Simpler mullion geometries reduce manufacturing and assembly costs while maintaining aesthetic objectives.

name: Enhanced fire resistance rating
rationale: Mullions may require fire-resistant materials or intumescent coatings in fire-rated glazing assemblies.

name: Better corrosion resistance
rationale: Mullions exposed to environmental moisture must resist corrosion, typically achieved through aluminum alloy selection or protective coatings.

name: Greater dimensional tolerance control
rationale: Precise mullion dimensions and alignment are necessary for proper glass fit and uniform appearance across the façade.

name: Increased structural support
rationale: The transom as a structural component needs adequate load-bearing capacity to support the window or door assembly above it.

name: Reduced deflection
rationale: Transoms must resist bending and deflection under vertical loads to maintain proper function and appearance.

name: Enhanced weather sealing
rationale: Transoms at the junction between window/door and wall require proper sealing to prevent air and water infiltration.

name: Improved thermal performance
rationale: Transom components should minimize thermal bridging to improve overall building envelope energy efficiency.

name: Adequate clearance for operation
rationale: Transom framing must provide sufficient clearance for operable windows or doors to function without binding.

name: Reduced material thickness
rationale: Minimizing transom material thickness can reduce weight and cost while maintaining structural adequacy.

name: Better load distribution
rationale: Loads from above must be properly distributed through the transom to supporting jambs or structure below.

name: Increased structural load capacity
rationale: Spandrel panels must support increased structural loads such as wind loads, dead loads, and impact loads, requiring adequate strength and stiffness.

name: Reduced thermal bridging
rationale: Spandrel panels should minimise thermal bridging through the building envelope to improve energy performance and prevent condensation.

name: Enhanced fire resistance rating
rationale: Spandrel panels require adequate fire resistance to comply with building codes and prevent fire spread between floors.

name: Reduced water infiltration
rationale: Spandrel panels must be designed to prevent water penetration through joints and seals to maintain building envelope integrity.

name: Greater aesthetic uniformity
rationale: Spandrel panels contribute to the visual appearance of the facade and should match adjacent vision glass in colour, finish, and alignment.

name: Lower maintenance requirements
rationale: Spandrel panels should be designed with durable finishes and accessible joints to reduce ongoing maintenance costs.

name: Optimised panel thickness
rationale: Panel thickness must be optimised to balance structural requirements with weight constraints and depth limitations of the curtain wall system.

name: Reduced air leakage
rationale: Spandrel panels must be sealed to minimise air leakage through the building envelope to meet energy code requirements and prevent drafts.

name: Increased structural load resistance
rationale: Vision glass panels must resist wind loads, snow loads, and impact loads to maintain safety and integrity.

name: Improved thermal insulation
rationale: Glass panels are a major source of heat loss/gain; improving insulation reduces energy consumption.

name: Enhanced solar heat gain control
rationale: Controlling solar heat gain through glass is critical for occupant comfort and HVAC load reduction.

name: Reduced glare transmission
rationale: Excessive glare through vision glass can cause visual discomfort for occupants.

name: Higher light transmittance
rationale: Vision glass should allow adequate daylight to reduce artificial lighting needs and provide views.

name: Minimized condensation risk
rationale: Condensation on glass surfaces can lead to mold, staining, and reduced visibility.

name: Increased load sensitivity
rationale: A pressure plate as a component needs sufficient sensitivity to detect applied loads, driving a need for increased responsiveness.

name: Greater surface durability
rationale: Pressure plates must withstand repeated use and environmental wear, requiring enhanced durability.

name: Reduced mechanical complexity
rationale: Simpler mechanisms improve reliability and reduce cost, pushing toward fewer moving parts or simpler sensing.

name: Minimised activation force threshold
rationale: A lower force threshold allows activation by lighter loads, expanding usability.

name: Improved manufacturing cost efficiency
rationale: Cost pressures in production push for more economical materials and processes.

name: Improved weather sealing pressure
rationale: Capping strips are used to seal joints and prevent water ingress; there is an engineering pressure to improve weather sealing performance.

name: Enhanced durability pressure
rationale: Capping strips must resist environmental exposure; there is pressure to enhance material durability over time.

name: Reduced material cost pressure
rationale: Cost efficiency drives pressure to use less expensive materials or reduce material volume in capping strips.

name: Minimised installation complexity pressure
rationale: Simple installation is preferred to reduce labour time and error risk, pressuring towards simpler capping strip designs.

name: Greater thermal performance pressure
rationale: Capping strips at roof or wall junctions can impact thermal bridging; there is pressure to improve thermal performance.

name: increased load-bearing capacity
rationale: The anchor bracket must withstand tensile and shear loads from attached components; higher load-bearing capacity improves structural safety.

name: reduced material fatigue risk
rationale: Anchor brackets are subject to cyclic loading; minimising fatigue risk extends service life and prevents failure.

name: improved corrosion resistance
rationale: Anchor brackets exposed to environmental conditions benefit from enhanced corrosion protection to maintain structural integrity.

name: limited thermal expansion mismatch
rationale: Differential thermal expansion between the bracket and connected materials must be constrained to avoid excessive stress at connections.

name: adequate bolt-hole alignment
rationale: Precision in bolt-hole positioning ensures proper fit-up and load transfer; insufficient alignment compromises assembly quality.

name: minimised installation complexity
rationale: Simpler installation procedures reduce labour time and the risk of improper assembly in the field.

name: Enhanced load-bearing capacity
rationale: Dead load brackets must bear the weight of structural elements, so increasing load-bearing capacity ensures safety and structural integrity.

name: Reduced material fatigue
rationale: Minimising material fatigue over time prolongs the bracket's service life under dead loads.

name: Sufficient corrosion resistance
rationale: Corrosion resistance must be adequate to maintain bracket performance in environmental conditions.

name: Lower stress concentration
rationale: Reducing stress concentrations at connection points prevents premature failure of the bracket.

name: Optimised attachment design
rationale: An optimised attachment design ensures proper load transfer from supported elements to the bracket.

name: Restricted deflection
rationale: Limiting deflection under dead load prevents misalignment and damage to connected components.

name: Optimized wind resistance
rationale: Wind Load Bracket must resist wind forces; increasing its wind resistance ensures structural stability under lateral loads.

name: Reduced material stress
rationale: Design pressures aim to minimize stress concentrations in the bracket to prevent fatigue or failure under wind loading.

name: Adequate load transfer
rationale: The bracket must adequately transfer wind-induced loads to the supporting structure to maintain overall building integrity.

name: Limited deflection
rationale: Deflection of the bracket under wind pressure must be limited to avoid damage to adjacent components and maintain serviceability.

name: Enhanced connection strength
rationale: Connections between the bracket and the main structure must be strong enough to withstand uplift and lateral wind forces.

name: Reduced thermal bridging
rationale: Unitised curtain wall systems often incorporate thermal breaks to reduce heat transfer, which is a common engineering requirement for energy performance.

name: Improved structural performance
rationale: The system must withstand wind loads and building movements, driving the need for enhanced structural capacity.

name: Reduced water infiltration
rationale: Unitised systems require gaskets and seals to prevent rainwater ingress; minimising leakage is a primary design driver.

name: Greater acoustic insulation
rationale: Curtain walls must often meet acoustic performance standards, especially in urban contexts.

name: Lower weight
rationale: Reducing the weight of panels eases handling, reduces structural load on the building frame, and simplifies installation.

name: Enhanced aesthetic quality
rationale: Unitised curtain walls are a prominent architectural feature, so visual appearance and finish quality drive design choices.

name: Reduced installation time
rationale: The unitised system is designed for rapid on-site assembly; minimising installation duration is a key economic driver.

name: Improved weathertightness
rationale: Achieving a robust weather seal is critical for the system's long-term performance and durability.

name: Sufficient tolerance accommodation
rationale: The system must accommodate building movement and construction tolerances; adequate allowance for movement is essential.

name: Reduced thermal bridging pressure
rationale: Stick curtain wall systems are assembled on-site with many framing connections; engineering best practice pushes for reduced thermal bridging through the aluminum frame to improve overall building envelope thermal performance.

name: Increased structural wind load resistance pressure
rationale: As a cladding system, the stick curtain wall must resist wind loads transferred from the glazing panels to the framing. Engineers seek increased structural capacity against wind-induced pressures.

name: Reduced installation complexity pressure
rationale: Stick systems require field assembly of mullions, transoms, and glazing. Construction efficiency pressures push for reduced complexity and fewer on-site labor hours.

name: Higher water infiltration resistance pressure
rationale: With many field-assembled joints, stick curtain walls are susceptible to water leakage. Design pressure pushes for higher resistance to water infiltration through gaskets, seals, and drainage pathways.

name: Lower material weight pressure
rationale: Lighter framing sections (typically aluminum) reduce dead load on the building structure and simplify handling/erection. Engineering desire for lower weight drives section size and alloy selection.

name: Improved seismic accommodation pressure
rationale: Curtain wall systems must accommodate inter-story drift during seismic events. Design pressure pushes for improved movement capability at connections and slip joints.

name: Reduced thermal expansion issues pressure
rationale: Aluminum frames expand and contract with temperature changes. Design seeks reduced issues from thermal movement through proper joint detailing and material selection.

name: Adequate acoustic performance pressure
rationale: Architectural requirements for building envelope sound isolation push for adequate acoustic performance via glazing selection and seal integrity in the stick system.

name: Optimised sightline dimensions pressure
rationale: Architects desire optimized (slim) sightlines for aesthetics while maintaining structural depth — a conflicting design pressure that drives mullion shape optimization.

name: Increased structural load capacity
rationale: The SSG system must withstand wind loads, dead loads, and thermal expansion forces requiring adequate structural capacity.

name: Higher wind load resistance
rationale: SSG systems are exposed to wind pressures acting on the glass panels, requiring sufficient silicone sealant strength to transfer loads to the framing.

name: Improved thermal movement accommodation
rationale: Temperature differentials cause expansion and contraction of glass and frame components, requiring the silicone to accommodate movements without failure.

name: Reduced sealant degradation risk
rationale: UV exposure, moisture ingress, and environmental weathering can degrade silicone sealant over time, reducing system durability.

name: Adequate adhesion strength
rationale: Proper bonding between silicone sealant and glass/aluminum frames is critical to prevent panel detachment under load.

name: Minimized glass deflection
rationale: Excessive glass deflection under wind load can cause sealant stress and visual distortion, requiring stiffness control.

name: Restricted water infiltration
rationale: The SSG system must prevent water penetration through the glazing joints to protect interior spaces and avoid sealant deterioration.

name: Optimized silicone joint geometry
rationale: Joint width and depth dimensions directly affect the stress distribution and long-term performance of the silicone sealant.

name: Eliminated galvanic corrosion risk
rationale: Dissimilar metal contact between aluminum frames and other components can cause corrosion that compromises system integrity.

name: Improved thermal insulation
rationale: Double-skin façades inherently improve thermal insulation by creating a buffer air layer between inner and outer skins, reducing heat transfer.

name: Enhanced natural ventilation
rationale: The cavity between skins allows for stack-effect ventilation, improving airflow and reducing mechanical ventilation needs.

name: Reduced solar heat gain
rationale: The cavity can incorporate shading devices and the outer skin reduces direct solar radiation penetration, lowering cooling loads.

name: Greater acoustic insulation
rationale: The dual-layer construction with an air gap provides superior sound attenuation compared to single-skin façades.

name: Higher initial construction cost
rationale: Double-skin façades require more materials, complex framing, and specialized installation, leading to higher upfront costs.

name: Optimised energy performance
rationale: The system reduces heating and cooling energy demand through passive thermal regulation.

name: Reduced glare for occupants
rationale: Integrated shading within the cavity can diffuse direct sunlight, improving visual comfort.

name: Increased daylight penetration
rationale: The transparent outer skin allows natural light while the cavity manages overheating, enabling deeper daylight reach.

name: Limited maintenance accessibility
rationale: The cavity space can be difficult to access for cleaning and maintenance of the inner and outer skins.

name: Increased Structural Load Capacity
rationale: Point-fixed glazing systems must withstand wind loads, dead loads (glass weight), and live loads (snow, maintenance). Higher structural capacity ensures safety and code compliance.

name: Improved Thermal Performance
rationale: Point-fixed glazing must meet energy efficiency standards, requiring better insulation through insulated glass units and thermal breaks in the support structure.

name: Reduced Glass Deflection
rationale: Excessive glass deflection under wind load can cause visual distortion, seal failure, or glass breakage. Limiting deflection is critical for performance.

name: Enhanced Watertightness
rationale: Point-fixed systems have numerous penetrations through the glass, making them vulnerable to water leakage. Improved sealing and gasket design is essential.

name: Minimized Point Stress Concentration
rationale: Point fixings create high localized stresses in glass around the holes. These must be minimized through proper hole placement, edge distance, and bushing design to prevent glass breakage.

name: Reduced Material Fatigue Risk
rationale: Cyclic wind loading and thermal movements can cause fatigue in stainless steel fittings, spider arms, and glass components over the building's lifespan.

name: Adequate Seismic Accommodation
rationale: In seismic zones, the glazing system must accommodate inter-story drift without glass breakage or falling hazards, requiring adequate movement capacity at fixings.

name: Greater Transparency (Visual Clarity)
rationale: Point-fixed systems are often chosen for their minimal visual obstruction. Maximizing transparency by using smaller fixings and minimal framing is a key architectural driver.

name: Better Fabrication Tolerances
rationale: Drilled holes in tempered glass and the mating fittings require precise fabrication tolerances to avoid stress concentrations and ensure proper assembly on site.

name: Improved thermal performance pressure
rationale: The rainscreen cavity acts as a ventilation and drainage layer; improving its thermal performance by increasing insulation or cavity depth reduces heat loss through the building envelope.

name: Reduced moisture ingress pressure
rationale: The rainscreen cavity is designed to drain and ventilate to prevent moisture accumulation; reducing moisture ingress is critical to avoid mold and structural degradation.

name: Optimised air flow pressure
rationale: Adequate air flow through the cavity is required to dry any incidental moisture and equalize pressure; optimising this flow enhances facade durability.

name: Reduced material cost pressure
rationale: Design decisions for cavity width, material selection, and support systems are often constrained by budget; there is pressure to minimise material costs while maintaining performance.

name: Greater fire safety pressure
rationale: Rainscreen cavities can act as concealed channels for fire spread; increased fire safety measures such as cavity barriers and non-combustible materials are often required by building codes.

name: Limited cavity width pressure
rationale: Structural and aesthetic constraints limit the allowable cavity width; a narrower cavity may be desired to maintain floor area or facade proportions.

name: Enhanced drainage capacity pressure
rationale: The cavity must effectively drain water that penetrates the outer cladding; enhancing drainage capacity through wider cavity or better flashing details prevents water damage.

name: Eliminated condensation risk pressure
rationale: Condensation within the cavity can lead to material deterioration; design pressures aim to eliminate this risk via ventilation, vapour control layers, and insulation placement.

name: Adequate maintenance access pressure
rationale: Sufficient cavity depth and access provisions are needed for future inspection and maintenance of the wall assembly, influencing design decisions.

name: Increased structural support requirement
rationale: The rainscreen cladding panel must be adequately supported by the building's structural framework to withstand wind loads and self-weight, necessitating increased structural support.

name: Reduced thermal bridging
rationale: Rainscreen cladding systems aim to minimise thermal bridging through the building envelope, improving overall thermal performance.

name: Improved moisture penetration resistance
rationale: The primary function of a rainscreen cladding panel is to act as a weather barrier, requiring high resistance to moisture ingress.

name: Reduced wind uplift pressure risk
rationale: Wind uplift forces act on cladding panels; design must minimise the risk of panel detachment under high wind conditions.

name: Greater fire resistance requirement
rationale: Building regulations increasingly demand higher fire performance for rainscreen cladding to prevent fire spread across building facades.

name: Reduced material weight
rationale: Lighter cladding panels reduce structural load requirements and simplify installation, creating a design pressure toward minimised weight.

name: Enhanced acoustic insulation performance
rationale: Rainscreen cladding assemblies contribute to the building envelope's acoustic performance, with design pressure for improved sound attenuation.

name: Optimised thermal insulation integration
rationale: The cladding system should be designed to accommodate and optimise continuous insulation layers for energy efficiency.

name: Reduced construction cost
rationale: Economic constraints create a design pressure toward minimising material and installation costs for the cladding system.

name: Improved thermal buffer performance
rationale: The inter-skin cavity acts as a thermal buffer zone between outer and inner building skins; increasing its thermal performance improves overall building energy efficiency.

name: Enhanced natural ventilation capacity
rationale: The cavity can be designed to facilitate stack-effect ventilation; increased airflow through the cavity helps regulate temperature and remove heat.

name: Reduced air leakage
rationale: Minimising uncontrolled air leakage in the inter-skin cavity preserves its intended thermal and ventilation performance.

name: Greater cavity depth for maintenance access
rationale: Sufficient cavity depth is needed to allow cleaning, inspection and maintenance of inner and outer skins as well as any integrated shading devices.

name: Limited solar heat gain
rationale: Solar radiation entering the cavity should be controlled via shading or selective glazing to prevent overheating in the cavity and adjacent occupied spaces.

name: Optimised cavity width for acoustic separation
rationale: A wider cavity improves sound attenuation between exterior noise sources and the interior, acting as an acoustic buffer.

name: Eliminated condensation risk
rationale: Condensation within the cavity can lead to mould and material degradation; ventilation and thermal design must prevent moisture accumulation.

name: Enhanced integration of shading devices
rationale: The cavity can house adjustable blinds or louvers; better integration allows dynamic solar control while maintaining aesthetic clarity.

name: Reduced cavity fire spread risk
rationale: A vertical inter-skin cavity can act as a flue for smoke and fire; design pressures aim to restrict fire propagation via compartmentation and fire-stopping.

name: Improved thermal insulation pressure
rationale: Ventilated facades improve thermal insulation by creating an air cavity that reduces heat transfer through the building envelope.

name: Enhanced moisture management pressure
rationale: The ventilated cavity allows moisture to drain and evaporate, preventing condensation and mold growth within the wall assembly.

name: Reduced solar heat gain pressure
rationale: The ventilation cavity and outer cladding help reduce solar heat gain by allowing heat to dissipate before reaching the inner building structure.

name: Greater durability pressure
rationale: Protecting the building envelope from weather exposure extends the lifespan of the facade system and reduces maintenance.

name: Higher acoustic performance pressure
rationale: The multi-layer construction of ventilated facades can provide improved sound insulation from external noise sources.

name: Optimised energy efficiency pressure
rationale: Ventilated facades contribute to overall building energy efficiency by reducing heating and cooling loads through improved envelope performance.

name: Limited construction complexity pressure
rationale: The additional layers and cavity in a ventilated facade system increase construction complexity compared to a simple wall assembly.

name: Sufficient fire safety pressure
rationale: Proper design of the ventilated cavity and use of non-combustible materials ensures adequate fire safety performance in the facade system.

name: Eliminated thermal bridging pressure
rationale: The continuous insulation layer in a well-designed ventilated facade helps minimize thermal bridging through the building envelope.

name: Improved structural integrity
rationale: Structural integrity of the curtain wall must be sufficient to withstand wind loads, seismic loads, and self-weight, driving design toward stronger framing and connections.

name: Enhanced thermal performance
rationale: Building energy codes and occupant comfort require improved insulation (U-value) and solar heat gain control in the curtain wall assembly.

name: Reduced air infiltration
rationale: Air leakage through curtain wall joints and seals must be minimized to meet building airtightness requirements and prevent energy loss.

name: Limited water penetration
rationale: Water ingress through the curtain wall must be restricted through proper gaskets, drainage, and pressure-equalized design to avoid interior damage.

name: Greater daylight transmission
rationale: Architectural intent often drives larger glazed areas to maximize natural daylight, affecting glass selection and mullion spacing.

name: Reduced solar heat gain
rationale: Low solar heat gain coefficient (SHGC) glazing is often required to control cooling loads, driving glass coating and shading decisions.

name: Lower embodied carbon
rationale: Sustainability targets push toward reduced embodied carbon in framing materials (aluminum, steel) and glazing, affecting material selection.

name: Optimized maintenance access
rationale: Provisions for cleaning and glazing replacement (e.g., access platforms, operable panels) influence curtain wall design for long-term maintainability.

name: Restricted deflection under wind load
rationale: Serviceability limits require that curtain wall deflections under wind pressure be constrained to prevent glass breakage and gasket failure.

name: Increased structural support for sheathing board
rationale: Sheathing boards require adequate structural support to resist wind loads and transfer loads to the building frame.

name: Reduced moisture penetration through sheathing board
rationale: Sheathing boards must resist moisture ingress to protect the building envelope and prevent degradation.

name: Improved fire resistance of sheathing board
rationale: Building codes require fire-rated assemblies; sheathing board contributes to fire resistance.

name: Reduced thermal bridging through sheathing board
rationale: Sheathing board can act as a thermal bridge if not properly designed, impacting energy performance.

name: Greater racking resistance from sheathing board
rationale: Sheathing boards provide shear strength and racking resistance to the structural frame against lateral loads.

name: Reduced material cost for sheathing board installation
rationale: Cost optimization is a key factor in material selection and installation decisions.

name: Improved dimensional stability of sheathing board
rationale: Dimensional stability under temperature and moisture variations is critical for sheathing board performance.

name: Reduced air infiltration through sheathing board
rationale: Sheathing boards contribute to the air barrier system, reducing unwanted air leakage.

name: Enhanced fastener holding capacity in sheathing board
rationale: Fastener withdrawal resistance is important for cladding attachment and overall assembly integrity.

name: Higher wind load resistance
rationale: Cladding brackets and fixing anchors must resist wind suction and pressure loads transferred from cladding panels to the structure.

name: Greater structural load capacity
rationale: The bracket/anchor must safely transfer dead and live loads from cladding to the main structure without failure.

name: Enhanced corrosion resistance
rationale: Exposure to moisture and environmental agents requires corrosion-resistant materials (e.g., stainless steel, galvanised finishes) for durability.

name: Reduced thermal bridging
rationale: Brackets penetrating the thermal envelope can create thermal bridges; minimising this improves energy performance.

name: Sufficient fatigue resistance
rationale: Cyclic wind loads and thermal movements require adequate fatigue endurance in the bracket/anchor connection.

name: Lower installation complexity
rationale: Simpler installation reduces labour cost and potential for on-site errors in bracket positioning and fixity.

name: Higher tolerance for building movement
rationale: The fixing system must accommodate differential movement between cladding and structure due to thermal, seismic, or settlement effects.

name: Restricted bracket protrusion
rationale: Aesthetic constraints may limit how far brackets project beyond the building face or internal surfaces.

name: Greater fire resistance rating
rationale: Fire-rated cladding assemblies require brackets and anchors to maintain structural integrity under fire conditions to prevent cladding collapse.

name: Increased structural load capacity
rationale: The cladding rail/carrier system must withstand wind loads, dead loads, and thermal movements, requiring sufficient structural capacity.

name: Improved corrosion resistance
rationale: Exposure to weather and moisture demands corrosion-resistant materials and coatings for long-term durability.

name: Reduced thermal bridging
rationale: The carrier system should minimise heat transfer through the building envelope to maintain thermal performance.

name: Adequate thermal movement accommodation
rationale: The system must allow for expansion and contraction due to temperature changes to prevent stress and failure.

name: Minimised material weight
rationale: Lighter materials reduce dead load on the building structure and may simplify installation, but must be balanced against strength requirements.

name: Enhanced drainage performance
rationale: Proper drainage of water ingress within the cladding system is critical to prevent moisture damage and corrosion.

name: Lower installation complexity
rationale: Simpler installation reduces labour costs and potential for errors during construction.

name: Greater dimensional tolerances
rationale: Allowable tolerances in alignment and fit are necessary to accommodate construction variations and thermal movement.

name: Improved thermal performance
rationale: Metal cladding panels are often designed with insulation backing or thermal breaks to improve the building envelope's thermal resistance, reducing heat transfer.

name: Enhanced weather resistance
rationale: Metal cladding panels must withstand wind, rain, and other environmental loads; improved sealing and interlocking systems increase weathertightness.

name: Reduced material thickness
rationale: To minimise weight and cost, there is pressure to use thinner gauge metal sheets while maintaining structural integrity.

name: Increased durability against corrosion
rationale: Protective coatings (e.g., galvanisation, PVDF) are applied to resist atmospheric corrosion, extending service life.

name: Adequate structural stiffness
rationale: Panels must have sufficient rigidity to resist wind loads without excessive deflection, often achieved via ribbed profiles or composite backing.

name: Lower installation complexity
rationale: Simple interlocking or cassette systems reduce labour time and skill requirements on site.

name: Reduced thermal bridging
rationale: Metal is highly conductive; thermal breaks or insulated sub-frameworks minimise heat loss through the cladding attachment points.

name: Expanded design flexibility
rationale: Architects push for a variety of colours, profiles, and finishes to achieve aesthetic goals with metal cladding.

name: Greater fire resistance
rationale: Non-combustible metal skins and fire-rated insulation cores are required to meet building code fire safety requirements.

name: Greater structural strength
rationale: ACM cladding panels must have sufficient structural strength to withstand wind loads, impact, and self-weight without failure.

name: Reduced combustibility
rationale: ACM panels with polyethylene cores have been associated with fire propagation risks; reducing flammability is critical for building safety compliance.

name: Improved thermal performance
rationale: ACM panels contribute to the building envelope's thermal insulation; better thermal performance improves energy efficiency and reduces heat loss.

name: Reduced material weight
rationale: Lighter cladding panels reduce structural loading on the building frame and substructure, simplifying installation and support requirements.

name: Enhanced weather resistance
rationale: ACM panels must resist moisture ingress, UV degradation, and temperature cycling to maintain durability and appearance over the building's lifespan.

name: Lower cost
rationale: Cost constraints often drive material selection; lower-cost ACM options may be preferred within budget limitations, balancing performance requirements.

name: Increased moisture resistance
rationale: Fibre cement cladding boards require adequate moisture resistance to prevent degradation, swelling, and fungal growth in exterior applications.

name: Reduced thermal conductivity
rationale: Lower thermal conductivity improves the insulation performance of the cladding system, reducing heat transfer through the building envelope.

name: Increased impact resistance
rationale: Higher impact resistance ensures the cladding can withstand physical impacts from debris, hail, or accidental contact without cracking or breaking.

name: Reduced weight
rationale: Lower weight reduces structural loading on the building frame and simplifies installation and handling.

name: Increased fire resistance
rationale: Fibre cement is valued for its non-combustible properties; higher fire resistance improves building safety and compliance with fire codes.

name: Reduced material cost
rationale: Lower material cost makes the cladding more economically viable for large-scale building projects.

name: Enhanced dimensional stability
rationale: Better dimensional stability minimises expansion and contraction with temperature and humidity changes, reducing risk of warping or cracking.

name: Reduced installation complexity
rationale: Simpler installation processes reduce labour costs and construction time while improving quality control.

name: Increased aesthetic finish quality
rationale: Higher quality surface finishes and colour retention improve the visual appeal and architectural value of the cladding.

name: Improved moisture resistance
rationale: Timber cladding must resist moisture ingress to prevent rot, warping, and biological decay, so there is a design pressure to increase moisture resistance performance.

name: Enhanced dimensional stability
rationale: Timber boards expand and contract with humidity changes; design aims to improve dimensional stability to minimize gaps, buckling, or distortion over time.

name: Reduced maintenance requirement
rationale: Building owners and architects prefer low-maintenance cladding solutions; there is pressure to reduce the frequency and cost of staining, sealing, or replacing timber boards.

name: Higher fire resistance
rationale: Building codes require cladding materials to meet fire performance standards; there is a design pressure to have adequate fire resistance through treatments or material selection.

name: Lower thermal conductivity
rationale: To contribute to building envelope thermal performance, there is a pressure to reduce the thermal conductivity of timber cladding or to design it as part of an insulated system.

name: Greater UV durability
rationale: Prolonged sun exposure causes timber to fade, gray, and degrade; there is a design pressure to increase UV resistance through coatings, finishes, or species selection.

name: Minimised material cost
rationale: Budget constraints in construction projects create a pressure to minimise the material cost of timber cladding while meeting performance requirements.

name: Improved fastener compatibility
rationale: The cladding must work reliably with fastening systems (screws, nails, hidden clips); there is pressure to design for proper fastener holding strength and corrosion compatibility.

name: Reduced aesthetic degradation over time
rationale: Visual appearance is critical for cladding; there is a design pressure to limit weathering effects like staining, checking, and uneven color change to maintain architectural intent.

name: Enhanced structural support for cladding
rationale: Stone cladding panels are heavy and require the primary structural frame to have adequate load-bearing capacity to support their weight.

name: Improved moisture barrier performance
rationale: Stone cladding panels act as a weather-resistant barrier; better water shedding and drainage reduce moisture ingress into the wall assembly.

name: Reduced thermal bridging through joints
rationale: Stone cladding integration with insulation minimizes thermal bridges at panel joints and anchor points.

name: Higher fire resistance contribution
rationale: Natural stone is non-combustible and can contribute to the overall fire resistance rating of the wall assembly.

name: Greater aesthetic quality of facade
rationale: Natural stone panels provide a high-quality, durable architectural finish that enhances the visual appeal of the building.

name: Limited stone panel thickness to reduce weight
rationale: Thinner stone panels reduce dead load on the structure, allowing for more economical frame design.

name: Optimized anchor connection design
rationale: Anchors must be carefully designed to transfer wind and seismic loads from stone panels to the structure while accommodating movement.

name: Prevented water infiltration at panel joints
rationale: Joints between stone panels must be properly sealed and drained to prevent rainwater from penetrating the wall assembly.

name: Adequate wind load resistance
rationale: Stone cladding panels must be designed and anchored to resist positive and negative wind pressures acting on the building facade.

name: Reduced thermal bridging pressure
rationale: Terracotta cladding panels require reduced thermal bridging to improve building envelope thermal performance and prevent heat loss through the cladding system.

name: Enhanced weather resistance pressure
rationale: Terracotta cladding must have enhanced weather resistance to protect the building from rain, wind, and moisture infiltration.

name: Increased structural attachment strength pressure
rationale: The cladding panels require increased structural attachment strength to ensure they are securely fastened to the building substructure and can withstand wind loads.

name: Reduced material weight pressure
rationale: Lighter terracotta panels reduce dead load on the building structure and simplify installation, though terracotta is inherently heavy.

name: Improved aesthetic finish pressure
rationale: Terracotta cladding is often selected for its visual appearance; achieving a consistent and high-quality aesthetic finish is a key design driver.

name: Lower embodied carbon pressure
rationale: Design decisions aim to lower the embodied carbon of terracotta cladding through material sourcing and manufacturing choices.

name: Greater fire resistance pressure
rationale: Terracotta is a fired clay product with inherent fire resistance; maintaining or improving this property is critical for façade safety compliance.

name: Reduced moisture absorption pressure
rationale: Minimising moisture absorption in terracotta panels prevents freeze-thaw damage, staining, and long-term degradation.

name: Optimised panel dimensions pressure
rationale: Panel dimensions must be optimised to balance structural requirements, manufacturing constraints, installation efficiency, and aesthetic module coordination.

name: Higher wind resistance
rationale: HPL cladding panels must resist wind loads, requiring increased structural capacity and attachment strength.

name: Reduced moisture absorption
rationale: HPL panels are exposed to rain and humidity; minimizing moisture ingress improves durability and prevents delamination.

name: Adequate fire resistance
rationale: Building codes require cladding materials to meet fire performance standards, especially for high-rise applications.

name: Better thermal insulation
rationale: HPL cladding systems may contribute to building envelope thermal performance, influencing energy efficiency.

name: Lower maintenance requirements
rationale: Architects and owners prefer cladding materials that require minimal upkeep over the building lifecycle.

name: Greater impact resistance
rationale: HPL panels must withstand mechanical impacts from hail, debris, or maintenance activities without cracking or breaking.

name: Reduced material thickness
rationale: Thinner panels reduce weight and material costs but must balance with structural and durability requirements.

name: Improved UV stability
rationale: HPL panels exposed to sunlight must resist fading, chalking, and surface degradation over time.

name: Constrained thermal expansion
rationale: Thermal movement must be limited to prevent panel buckling or joint failure in varying temperatures.

name: Increased flexural strength requirement
rationale: GRC panels must resist bending loads from wind and handling, requiring adequate flexural strength in the glass fiber reinforced matrix.

name: Reduced weight pressure
rationale: GRC panels are designed to be lightweight compared to traditional concrete, minimising dead load on the building structure.

name: Improved impact resistance demand
rationale: GRC panels must withstand impact loads from debris, hail, or accidental contact, requiring enhanced toughness from glass fiber reinforcement.

name: Limited thermal movement stress
rationale: GRC panels experience thermal expansion and contraction; joints and connections must be designed to restrict induced stresses.

name: Higher water resistance requirement
rationale: GRC panels as cladding must resist water penetration, requiring adequate density and surface treatment to prevent moisture ingress.

name: Reduced cracking tendency
rationale: Alkali-resistant glass fibers and proper mix design minimise shrinkage cracking in GRC panels during curing and service.

name: Reduced structural load requirement
rationale: Thin brick cladding is lighter than full brick, reducing structural load on the building frame.

name: Improved installation speed
rationale: Brick slips are easier and faster to install compared to traditional full brick masonry.

name: Reduced material cost
rationale: Thin brick slips use less material than full bricks, reducing material expenses.

name: Greater aesthetic flexibility
rationale: Brick slips can be manufactured in various colours, textures, and patterns to achieve desired aesthetics.

name: Reduced thermal mass
rationale: Thin brick cladding has lower thermal mass than full brick, which may reduce passive heating/cooling benefits.

name: Higher moisture sensitivity risk
rationale: Thin brick cladding systems can be more susceptible to moisture ingress if not properly detailed with drainage and waterproofing.

name: Reduced wall thickness requirement
rationale: Thin brick cladding occupies less depth than full brick, reducing overall wall thickness.

name: Improved sustainability profile
rationale: Thin brick cladding uses less raw material and can incorporate recycled content, improving environmental credentials.

name: Greater substrate preparation requirement
rationale: Thin brick cladding requires a well-prepared, flat substrate or backing surface for proper adhesion and performance.

name: Increased structural load resistance
rationale: Profiled metal sheet cladding must resist wind loads, snow loads, and other environmental pressures to maintain structural integrity.

name: Reduced thermal bridging
rationale: Metal cladding can create thermal bridges if not properly insulated, so reducing thermal transfer is a key design consideration.

name: Improved weather tightness
rationale: The cladding system must provide adequate water and air infiltration resistance to protect the building envelope.

name: Reduced material thickness
rationale: Thinner material reduces cost and weight but must be balanced against structural performance requirements.

name: Enhanced fire resistance rating
rationale: Building codes often require specific fire resistance levels for exterior cladding materials.

name: Greater corrosion resistance
rationale: Metal cladding must resist environmental corrosion, especially in coastal or industrial environments.

name: Lower installation complexity
rationale: Simpler installation reduces labour costs and potential for installation errors.

name: Optimised panel span capacity
rationale: Maximizing allowable spans between supports optimizes structural framing requirements and costs.

name: Reduced noise transmission
rationale: Metal cladding can transmit external noise (e.g., rain, wind) which may require acoustic mitigation.

name: Improved fire safety compliance
rationale: Building regulations and fire safety standards require cavity barriers to be properly installed to prevent fire spread within concealed spaces.

name: Higher cavity barrier density
rationale: More frequent or robust cavity barrier placement reduces fire spread risk through the cladding cavity.

name: Reduced installation cost
rationale: Economic pressure to minimise material and labour costs for cavity closer installation.

name: Minimised thermal bridging
rationale: Cavity closers can create thermal bridges; design aims to minimise this heat loss effect.

name: Adequate material durability
rationale: The cavity barrier must withstand environmental exposure and maintain integrity over the building's life.

name: Eliminated cavity ventilation bypass
rationale: Unwanted airflow through the cavity should be prevented to maintain fire compartmentation.

name: Increased energy generation efficiency
rationale: BIPV cladding panels must generate electricity efficiently; design decisions aim to maximise energy output through optimal orientation, cell technology, and minimising shading.

name: Improved thermal insulation performance
rationale: As a cladding element, BIPV panels contribute to the building envelope's thermal performance; design pressures push for better U-values and reduced heat transfer.

name: Reduced installation cost
rationale: Cost constraints drive decisions toward more economical BIPV panel systems, framing systems, and installation methods.

name: Enhanced durability and weather resistance
rationale: External cladding must withstand wind, rain, UV exposure, and thermal cycling; decisions favour more robust materials and sealing details.

name: Greater aesthetic integration
rationale: Architectural design pressures demand that BIPV panels match the visual appearance, colour, texture, and module size to blend with the building facade.

name: Reduced weight load on structure
rationale: Structural design constraints push for lighter BIPV panels to minimise additional loading on the building frame and foundation.

name: Optimised electrical performance and cabling
rationale: Electrical design decisions aim to optimise string sizing, inverter compatibility, cable routing, and minimise power losses in the BIPV system.

name: Minimised embodied carbon
rationale: Sustainability targets create pressure to reduce the carbon footprint of panel manufacturing and materials selection.

name: Adequate structural support and fixing robustness
rationale: Safety and building code requirements drive decisions toward sufficient structural fixings, brackets, and subframe capacity to secure BIPV panels against wind uplift and dead loads.

name: Improved weathertightness pressure
rationale: Parapet coping and cladding terminations require improved weathertightness to prevent water ingress at the roof edge, a critical interface where building envelope failures commonly occur.

name: Enhanced structural attachment pressure
rationale: The coping and cladding termination must have enhanced structural attachment to resist wind uplift forces and thermal movement at the parapet.

name: Reduced thermal bridging pressure
rationale: Thermal bridging at the parapet/cladding interface should be reduced to improve energy performance and prevent condensation issues.

name: Adequate drip edge detailing pressure
rationale: An adequate drip edge detail is needed to direct water away from the wall surface and prevent staining or moisture penetration.

name: Eliminated material incompatibility pressure
rationale: Material incompatibility between coping, cladding, and sealants should be eliminated to prevent galvanic corrosion and sealant failure.

name: Optimised joint and sealant placement pressure
rationale: Joint and sealant placement needs to be optimised to accommodate thermal movement while maintaining a continuous weather barrier.

name: Restricted water capillary action pressure
rationale: Capillary action at the cladding termination should be restricted through proper flashings and weeps to prevent water migration behind cladding.

name: Sufficient concealed flashing continuity pressure
rationale: Concealed flashing must provide sufficient continuity at the parapet coping and cladding termination to direct any penetrating water outward.

name: adequate structural support
rationale: The cladding panel must have adequate structural support to withstand wind loads and self-weight, ensuring safety and stability.

name: reduced thermal bridging
rationale: Minimising thermal bridging through the cladding panel improves energy efficiency and prevents condensation issues.

name: improved water tightness
rationale: Enhanced water tightness at reveals and returns prevents moisture ingress, protecting the building envelope and interior.

name: limited panel deflection
rationale: Restricting excessive panel deflection maintains visual alignment, prevents sealant failure, and reduces stress on connections.

name: enhanced drainage and ventilation
rationale: Improved drainage and ventilation behind the cladding panel reduces moisture accumulation and extends panel durability.

name: lower material weight
rationale: Using lighter materials reduces dead load on the supporting structure and eases installation logistics.

name: sufficient movement accommodation
rationale: Adequate joint sizing to accommodate thermal expansion, contraction, and building movement prevents buckling or cracking.

name: minimised visible fasteners
rationale: Reducing the visibility of fasteners improves the aesthetic appearance of the cladding system at reveals and returns.

name: higher fire resistance rating
rationale: Enhanced fire resistance is critical for cladding materials to meet building code requirements and ensure occupant safety.

name: Improved thermal insulation
rationale: Higher thermal insulation in exterior wall facades reduces heat transfer, improving energy efficiency and occupant comfort.

name: Increased structural stability
rationale: Exterior walls must withstand wind loads, seismic forces, and self-weight; greater structural stability ensures safety and longevity.

name: Reduced moisture infiltration
rationale: Preventing water penetration through the facade protects the building envelope from dampness, mold, and material degradation.

name: Enhanced aesthetic appearance
rationale: The facade contributes to the building's visual identity and architectural expression; better aesthetics improve marketability and urban context.

name: Lower construction cost
rationale: Minimising material and labor expenses for the facade zone keeps the project within budget without compromising essential performance.

name: Improved fire resistance
rationale: Exterior walls must resist fire spread between floors and adjacent buildings; better fire-rated assemblies enhance occupant safety.

name: Reduced thermal bridging
rationale: Minimising thermal bridges through the facade prevents heat loss, condensation, and energy inefficiency at structural connections.

name: Greater daylight penetration
rationale: Optimising window-to-wall ratios and glazing properties in the facade allows more natural light into interior spaces, reducing lighting energy.

name: Reduced maintenance requirements
rationale: Durable, low-maintenance facade materials and finishes lower long-term operational costs and building downtime.

name: Improved weather sealing
rationale: Coping stones must provide effective weather sealing to prevent water ingress at the top of parapet walls, protecting the building envelope.

name: Enhanced structural stability
rationale: Coping stones need adequate mechanical anchorage and structural integrity to resist wind uplift and remain securely in place.

name: Minimised thermal bridging
rationale: Coping stone assemblies should minimise thermal bridging at parapet edges to improve overall building thermal performance.

name: Reduced moisture penetration risk
rationale: Design must limit the risk of moisture penetration through joints and interfaces between coping stones and underlying wall construction.

name: Adequate freeze-thaw resistance
rationale: Coping stones must have sufficient freeze-thaw durability to withstand outdoor exposure and cyclic ice formation without spalling.

name: Eliminated water ponding
rationale: Proper slopes and drip edges on coping stones prevent water ponding and direct runoff away from the wall face.

name: Improved aesthetic integration
rationale: Coping stones contribute to the architectural expression of the building top and must harmonise with the overall facade design.

name: Sufficient overhang and drip detail
rationale: Adequate projecting overhang with a drip groove is required to shed water clear of the wall surface beneath the coping.

name: Greater lateral load resistance
rationale: Parapet walls must resist wind loads and lateral forces; a stronger core increases structural stability against overturning.

name: Reduced thermal bridging
rationale: Parapet cores often connect roof to wall assemblies; minimizing thermal bridging improves energy performance and prevents condensation.

name: Improved moisture penetration resistance
rationale: Parapets are vulnerable to water ingress at the roof-to-wall interface; enhanced waterproofing protects the core and interior.

name: Increased dead load capacity
rationale: The core must support its own weight plus any attached cladding or coping; adequate structural capacity is essential.

name: Minimised parapet height
rationale: Shorter parapets reduce wind uplift forces and material costs, but must still meet code minimums for safety.

name: Enhanced seismic performance
rationale: Parapets are susceptible to earthquake damage; a robust core with proper reinforcement improves ductility and collapse prevention.

name: Improved weatherproofing pressure
rationale: Parapet flashing is a critical component for preventing water ingress at the roof-wall intersection; better flashing design improves overall weatherproofing.

name: Enhanced durability pressure
rationale: Parapet flashing material and thickness must be optimised to withstand environmental exposure, thermal cycling, and corrosion over the building's lifespan.

name: Reduced thermal bridging pressure
rationale: Metal parapet flashing can act as a thermal bridge; designs should minimise this effect to improve energy efficiency and prevent condensation.

name: Minimised wind-driven rain infiltration pressure
rationale: Wind-driven rain at the parapet edge must be prevented from entering the building envelope; proper flashing design with seals and drip edges achieves this.

name: Adequate expansion joint provision pressure
rationale: Thermal expansion of metal flashing requires adequate joints and clearances to prevent buckling, tearing or detachment.

name: Greater corrosion resistance pressure
rationale: Parapet flashing is exposed to moisture and atmospheric pollutants; material selection (e.g., stainless steel, copper, or coated aluminium) needs corrosion resistance.

name: Eliminated improper lapping pressure
rationale: Incorrect lapping direction or inadequate overlap at flashing joints can cause water leakage; proper installation details must be enforced.

name: Higher wind uplift resistance pressure
rationale: Parapet flashing must be securely anchored to resist wind uplift forces, especially at roof corners and edges where suction pressures are highest.

name: Improved thermal resistance pressure
rationale: Parapet cavities often require higher thermal resistance to reduce heat loss and meet energy code requirements, driving a need for better insulation or cavity design.

name: Reduced moisture infiltration pressure
rationale: Parapet cavities are susceptible to water ingress, so there is pressure to minimise moisture penetration through proper flashing, drainage, and sealing.

name: Enhanced structural support pressure
rationale: The cavity and surrounding parapet must withstand wind loads and other lateral forces, requiring stronger structural framing or bracing.

name: Minimised air leakage pressure
rationale: Air barriers in parapet cavities are needed to reduce uncontrolled air leakage, improving building envelope performance and energy efficiency.

name: Adequate drainage provision pressure
rationale: Proper drainage paths (weeps, sloped flashings) must be provided to prevent water accumulation inside the parapet cavity.

name: Improved water resistance
rationale: Through-wall flashing is designed to direct water outward and prevent moisture ingress into wall assemblies; improved water resistance is a primary design pressure.

name: Enhanced durability against corrosion
rationale: Flashing materials must resist corrosion over time, especially at joints and intersections with other building elements.

name: Adequate overlap at joints
rationale: Proper overlap is critical to ensure continuous water shedding and prevent leaks at flashing seams.

name: Reduced thermal bridging
rationale: Metal flashings can conduct heat; minimizing thermal bridging through flashing design or thermal breaks improves overall wall thermal performance.

name: Eliminated gaps at penetrations
rationale: Gaps around penetrations through flashing create pathways for water and air leakage; eliminating them is essential for envelope integrity.

name: Minimised water capillary action
rationale: Capillary action can draw water through small cracks between flashing and masonry; design should minimize this phenomenon.

name: Sufficient drainage slope
rationale: Flashing should be sloped to direct water toward weep holes and away from the building interior for proper drainage.

name: Stronger end dams
rationale: End dams at flashing terminations must be robust to contain water and prevent lateral water migration within the wall assembly.

name: Restricted water ingress at transitions
rationale: Transitions between building envelope systems are common leak points; restricting water entry at these interfaces is critical.

name: Improved thermal continuity
rationale: A parapet cavity closer must improve thermal continuity at the parapet to reduce thermal bridging.

name: Higher fire resistance
rationale: Cavity closers at parapets need to provide adequate fire stopping to prevent fire spread through the cavity.

name: Reduced air leakage
rationale: The parapet cavity closer must minimise air leakage through the cavity to maintain building airtightness.

name: Minimised water ingress
rationale: A parapet cavity closer prevents water penetration into the cavity, which could cause moisture damage.

name: Adequate structural support
rationale: The cavity closer must provide sufficient structural stability at the parapet junction.

name: Eliminated cold bridging
rationale: The parapet cavity closer should eliminate thermal cold bridging at the parapet edge detail.

name: Increased lateral load resistance
rationale: The parapet tie bar/wall anchor system must provide adequate resistance to lateral wind loads and seismic forces acting on the parapet wall, transferring forces to the roof deck structure.

name: Improved corrosion resistance
rationale: Exposure to weather and moisture requires corrosion-resistant materials or coatings for the tie bar and anchor components to ensure long-term durability and structural integrity.

name: Reduced spacing between anchors
rationale: Closer spacing of wall anchors/tie bars provides more uniform load distribution and improved stability of the parapet wall, particularly at corners and edges.

name: Adequate embedment depth
rationale: Sufficient embedment of the anchor into the roof deck or structural slab is critical to develop the full tensile capacity of the tie bar and prevent pull-out failure.

name: Restricted thermal movement
rationale: Thermal expansion and contraction of the parapet wall must be accommodated while maintaining the tie bar connection integrity; excessive restraint could cause buckling or connection failure.

name: Enhanced weather resistance
rationale: Metal parapet capping must resist wind-driven rain, snow, and UV exposure; enhanced weather resistance ensures long-term durability and prevents water ingress into the parapet assembly.

name: Improved structural attachment
rationale: Stronger mechanical fastening and secure joint detailing are needed to resist wind uplift forces on the capping, preventing detachment during high winds.

name: Reduced thermal bridging
rationale: Metal capping can conduct heat; thermal bridging through the capping and its attachments should be minimised to improve building envelope thermal performance.

name: Adequate expansion provision
rationale: Metal expands and contracts with temperature changes; sufficient expansion joints and sliding cleats must be provided to avoid buckling or distortion of the capping.

name: Minimised corrosion risk
rationale: Exposed metal capping is subject to atmospheric corrosion; use of corrosion-resistant materials (e.g., stainless steel, galvanised steel, or coated aluminium) and proper drainage must be ensured to limit deterioration.

name: Improved water shedding
rationale: The capping profile should include drips and slopes to effectively shed water away from the parapet wall and roof edge, preventing water staining and accumulation.

name: Increased lateral load resistance
rationale: Brick parapets must resist wind loads and lateral pressures to prevent overturning or collapse; structural design requires adequate strength against lateral forces.

name: Increased weight load
rationale: Brick parapets add dead load to the building structure; this increased weight must be supported by the roof and load-bearing walls below.

name: Reduced moisture infiltration
rationale: Parapets are exposed to rain and weather; proper flashing, capping, and waterproofing are needed to minimise water penetration which could cause deterioration or leaks.

name: Improved thermal performance
rationale: Parapets can create thermal bridges; design pressures favour improved insulation detailing to reduce heat loss at the roof-to-wall junction.

name: Reduced cracking risk
rationale: Thermal expansion and contraction, plus freeze-thaw cycles, create stress in brick parapets; design seeks to minimise or control cracking through movement joints.

name: Increased seismic stability
rationale: Unreinforced masonry parapets are vulnerable during earthquakes; design pressures demand adequate anchorage and reinforcement for seismic resistance.

name: Enhanced durability against weathering
rationale: Exposed brick parapets face UV, rain, and temperature extremes; selection of durable brick, proper mortar, and protective cappings improve long-term performance.

name: Reduced construction cost
rationale: Budget constraints often push for simpler, less ornate parapet designs using standard brick sizes and minimal detailing to lower material and labour costs.

name: Improved aesthetic integration
rationale: Parapets contribute to building facade composition; design pressures favour proportions, cornice details, and brick patterns that harmonise with the overall architectural style.

name: Increased structural stability
rationale: Precast concrete parapets must have sufficient structural stability to resist wind loads, seismic loads, and impact forces as part of the building envelope.

name: Reduced thermal bridging
rationale: Concrete parapets can act as thermal bridges; design pressures aim to reduce heat loss through the parapet assembly.

name: Improved water penetration resistance
rationale: Parapets are exposed to rain and snow; joints and flashings must be designed for enhanced water tightness.

name: Reduced weight
rationale: Lighter precast panels reduce structural demands on the supporting frame and foundation.

name: Higher wind load resistance
rationale: Parapets experience significant wind uplift and lateral pressures; designs must ensure adequate wind load capacity.

name: Limited crack formation
rationale: Cracking in precast concrete parapets must be minimised to maintain durability and aesthetics.

name: Expanded seismic performance
rationale: Parapet connections must accommodate building movement during seismic events to prevent collapse.

name: Better aesthetics and finish quality
rationale: Parapets are visible architectural elements; design pressures seek improved surface finish and visual consistency.

name: Increased structural load capacity
rationale: Balustrade parapets must withstand lateral loads (wind, crowd pressure) and vertical loads; structural design often demands increased load capacity for safety.

name: Higher corrosion resistance
rationale: Parapets exposed to weather require corrosion-resistant materials (e.g., stainless steel, coated aluminum) to ensure durability.

name: Reduced deflection under load
rationale: Building codes limit deflection of handrails and parapets to prevent instability and ensure user safety.

name: Adequate guard height
rationale: Building codes mandate minimum parapet/guard heights (e.g., 42 inches in many jurisdictions) to prevent falls.

name: Lower maintenance requirements
rationale: Owners and architects prefer materials and finishes that reduce long-term upkeep costs for exposed parapets.

name: Increased water collection capacity
rationale: Parapet gutters must have sufficient capacity to collect and convey rainwater from the roof area, preventing overflow and water damage to the building envelope.

name: Optimised slope for drainage
rationale: Proper slope ensures positive drainage toward downspouts, preventing standing water, debris accumulation, and premature deterioration of the gutter system.

name: Reduced clogging risk
rationale: Minimising debris accumulation and blockages through design features such as leaf guards or larger openings ensures long-term drainage performance.

name: Higher structural load capacity
rationale: The gutter must withstand loads from ice, snow, standing water, and maintenance personnel without deformation or failure.

name: Minimised thermal expansion stress
rationale: Expansion joints and appropriate material selection reduce stresses from temperature fluctuations, preventing buckling or separation at joints.

name: Improved corrosion resistance
rationale: Parapet gutters are exposed to rainwater and debris; materials like stainless steel, copper, or coated metal resist corrosion and extend service life.

name: Adequate overflow provision
rationale: Overflow scuppers or secondary drainage prevent water backup and structural overloading during extreme rainfall events beyond the primary gutter capacity.

name: Eliminated water leakage at joints
rationale: Watertight joints and proper flashing details prevent moisture intrusion into the parapet wall and building interior, a critical performance requirement.

name: Greater debris exclusion
rationale: Design features such as strainers, screens, or larger gutter profiles help exclude leaves and debris that could obstruct flow.

name: Adequate drainage capacity
rationale: Scuppers must have sufficient capacity to handle design rainfall events without overflowing or causing water damage to the building envelope.

name: Reduced clogging risk
rationale: Scuppers are susceptible to debris accumulation; designs must minimize blockage likelihood to maintain drainage performance.

name: Increased opening size
rationale: Larger scupper openings improve flow capacity but must be balanced against structural and aesthetic constraints.

name: Lower overflow height
rationale: Minimizing the height of the scupper opening relative to the parapet top ensures water exits before ponding reaches dangerous levels.

name: Greater number of scuppers
rationale: Distributing drainage across multiple scupper outlets reduces the load on any single outlet and improves overall system redundancy.

name: Reduced spacing between scuppers
rationale: Closer spacing along the parapet helps prevent localized ponding and ensures even drainage distribution.

name: Improved corrosion resistance
rationale: Scupper materials (typically metal) must resist weathering and corrosion over the building's lifespan to maintain function.

name: Higher freeboard margin
rationale: Adequate freeboard (distance from scupper invert to roof surface) prevents water backup onto the roof during heavy flow events.

name: Restricted debris entry
rationale: Incorporating screens or grates reduces debris entry but must be designed to not restrict flow excessively or become clogged themselves.

name: Improved water penetration resistance at DPC
rationale: The DPC at parapet must resist water ingress from the top of the wall, so there is a design pressure to improve its water penetration resistance.

name: Increased durability of DPC material
rationale: The DPC at parapet is exposed to weather and UV, requiring durable materials that last the building's lifespan.

name: Reduced thermal bridging at parapet DPC
rationale: DPC materials can create thermal bridges; there is a design pressure to minimise heat loss at the parapet.

name: Adequate overlap and sealing at DPC joints
rationale: Joints in the DPC must be properly overlapped and sealed to maintain continuity of the damp-proof barrier.

name: Eliminated moisture bypass around DPC ends
rationale: Design must prevent water from bypassing the DPC at its terminations to ensure effective damp-proofing.

name: Enhanced structural continuity pressure
rationale: The roof-to-parapet junction requires enhanced structural continuity to resist uplift and lateral wind loads, preventing separation at the interface.

name: Optimized waterproofing integrity pressure
rationale: The junction is a critical point for water intrusion; optimized waterproofing design ensures long-term durability and prevents moisture damage.

name: Reduced thermal bridging pressure
rationale: Thermal bridging at the roof-to-parapet interface can cause energy loss and condensation; minimizing this improves building envelope performance.

name: Improved flashing detailing pressure
rationale: Proper flashing at the junction prevents water entry and ice damming; improved detailing ensures reliable performance over time.

name: Limited differential movement pressure
rationale: Differential movement between the roof deck and parapet wall can cause cracking and seal failure; restricting such movement protects the junction integrity.

name: Adequate drainage provision pressure
rationale: Scuppers and drainage at the parapet must be adequately sized to prevent ponding water at the roof edge, which could compromise the junction.

name: Minimized air leakage pressure
rationale: Air leakage at the roof-parapet junction reduces energy efficiency and can lead to moisture accumulation; minimizing leakage is essential for envelope performance.

name: Stronger edge restraint pressure
rationale: Edge restraint at the parapet base must be sufficiently strong to resist wind uplift and lateral forces acting on the roof membrane assembly.

name: Eliminated material incompatibility pressure
rationale: Dissimilar materials at the roof-parapet junction (e.g., metal flashing contacting membrane) can cause galvanic corrosion or chemical degradation; eliminating such incompatibility extends service life.

name: increased slip resistance
rationale: Stair treads must provide sufficient slip resistance to prevent falls, a key safety requirement.

name: adequate tread depth
rationale: Building codes mandate minimum tread depth to ensure comfortable and safe foot placement.

name: reduced noise generation
rationale: Stair treads should minimize noise from foot traffic for acoustic comfort in buildings.

name: higher structural strength
rationale: Treads must support live loads (people, objects) without excessive deflection or failure.

name: limited deflection under load
rationale: Excessive bending or deflection in treads can cause discomfort, noise, or safety hazards.

name: improved durability against wear
rationale: Stair treads experience high foot traffic and must resist abrasion and wear over time.

name: better fire resistance
rationale: Building fire codes require stair components to have adequate fire resistance for safe egress.

name: reduced tripping hazard at nosing
rationale: Nosing profile must be designed to minimize tripping risk while providing visual contrast.

name: adequate light reflectance value
rationale: Treads should have sufficient luminance contrast at nosing to aid visually impaired users.

name: Increased structural strength
rationale: Stair risers must be strong enough to support vertical loads from foot traffic and transfer loads to the stringers.

name: Reduced tread-to-riser overlap gap
rationale: Minimising gaps between tread and riser prevents tripping hazards and ensures structural continuity.

name: Sufficient vertical height consistency
rationale: Uniform riser heights are required by building codes for safe and comfortable stair usage.

name: Reduced material thickness for weight
rationale: Thinner riser material reduces overall stair weight, but must be balanced against structural requirements.

name: Greater fire resistance rating
rationale: Stairs often serve as fire egress paths, so risers must meet fire-rating requirements.

name: Reduced deflection under load
rationale: Limiting deflection ensures the stair feels solid and safe under pedestrian loads.

name: Increased structural capacity
rationale: A stringer in construction (e.g., stair stringer or structural stringer) must have adequate load-bearing capacity to safely support the structure above it. Engineering design pressures push for increased strength and capacity.

name: Reduced material usage
rationale: Cost efficiency drives minimizing material waste and using just enough material to meet structural requirements for the stringer component.

name: Optimized dimensional fit
rationale: The stringer must be precisely dimensioned to fit correctly within the stair or structural assembly, requiring optimized geometry.

name: Improved connection strength
rationale: Connections between the stringer and adjacent components (treads, risers, floor framing) must be strong to ensure safety and structural integrity.

name: Reduced deflection
rationale: Stringers must have limited deflection under load to meet serviceability requirements and prevent excessive movement.

rationale: Structural engineering requires minimised deflection under live loads to ensure safety, comfort, and code compliance for the ramp structure.

name: Greater handrail height
rationale: Building and accessibility codes mandate sufficient handrail height along switchback ramps for safety and user support.

name: Higher load-bearing capacity
rationale: The ramp structure must be designed for adequate load-bearing capacity to support live loads (people, wheelchairs) and dead loads.

name: Reduced depth pressure
rationale: Shaft pits are often designed to be as shallow as possible to minimise excavation costs and structural complexity.

name: Improved accessibility pressure
rationale: Shaft pits must be accessible for maintenance and inspection, which pressures designs toward greater clearances and access provisions.

name: Enhanced structural integrity pressure
rationale: Shaft pits must withstand soil/water pressures and support loads, pushing toward stronger structural design.

name: Minimised water ingress pressure
rationale: Water infiltration into shaft pits must be minimised through waterproofing and drainage design.

name: Restricted footprint pressure
rationale: Shaft pits are often constrained by surrounding structures or site boundaries, limiting their plan area.

name: Increased shaft headroom for equipment installation
rationale: Vertical transportation systems (elevators, escalators) and building services (HVAC ducts, pipes) require adequate headroom within the shaft for installation, maintenance, and code compliance. Insufficient headroom constrains equipment sizing and access.

name: Reduced shaft headroom to minimise floor-to-floor height
rationale: Architects often push for compact floor-to-floor heights to reduce building volume, material costs, and fit within zoning height limits, which directly limits the headroom available within shafts.

name: Adequate shaft headroom for fire safety compliance
