name: Reduced cross-sectional area of Riser Shaft (HVAC)
rationale: Building space efficiency pressures drive minimization of riser shaft footprints to maximise leasable floor area.

name: Increased fire rating for Riser Shaft (HVAC)
rationale: Fire and smoke spread regulations require HVAC riser shafts to have fire-rated enclosures and fire dampers to compartmentalise floors.

name: Optimised duct routing within Riser Shaft (HVAC)
rationale: Efficient HVAC design pressures for optimised arrangement of ducts, pipes, and cables within the shaft to minimise conflicts and pressure losses.

name: Reduced noise transmission via Riser Shaft (HVAC)
rationale: Acoustic design pressures require limited noise transmission through the riser shaft to adjacent occupied spaces.

name: Increased structural load capacity for Riser Shaft (HVAC)
rationale: Riser shafts support heavy mechanical equipment and ductwork, requiring adequate structural support.

name: Improved accessibility for maintenance of Riser Shaft (HVAC)
rationale: Building services maintenance requires sufficient access doors and working space within or at the riser shaft for inspections and repairs.

name: Minimised thermal bridging at Riser Shaft (HVAC)
rationale: Energy performance requirements drive minimised thermal bridging where the riser shaft penetrates building envelope or floor slabs.

name: Lower construction cost for Riser Shaft (HVAC)
rationale: Budget constraints create pressure to use standardised, less expensive materials and simpler configurations for the riser shaft.

name: Higher water pressure requirement
rationale: Water supply pipes must withstand adequate internal pressure to deliver water to upper floors and distant fixtures in a building.

name: Optimised pipe diameter for flow
rationale: Sufficient diameter is needed to maintain required flow rates without excessive friction loss.

name: Reduced corrosion risk
rationale: Corrosion must be minimised to prevent leaks, contamination, and pipe failure over time.

name: Minimised water hammer effect
rationale: Water hammer pressure surges should be reduced to prevent pipe damage and noise.

name: Greater pipe wall thickness for durability
rationale: Thicker walls provide higher pressure rating and longer service life for water supply pipes.

name: Reduced risk of freezing
rationale: Freezing must be prevented or eliminated to avoid pipe bursts in cold climates.

name: Enhanced material strength
rationale: Stronger pipe materials are needed to handle operational pressures and external loads.

name: Restricted water pressure loss
rationale: Pressure loss along the pipe run should be minimised to ensure adequate delivery pressure at fixtures.

name: Increased drainage capacity pressure
rationale: DWV pipes must have adequate diameter and slope to handle peak wastewater flows from fixtures, ensuring proper drainage without clogging or backup.

name: Reduced clogging pressure
rationale: Design should minimise obstructions and sharp bends to prevent blockages and maintain self-cleaning velocities.

name: Sufficient venting pressure
rationale: Proper venting is required to maintain neutral air pressure in drainage system, preventing trap siphonage and ensuring smooth flow.

name: Minimised pipe length pressure
rationale: Shorter pipe runs reduce material cost, installation complexity, and potential leak points, while improving drainage performance.

name: Improved material durability pressure
rationale: Pipes must resist corrosion, chemical degradation from wastewater, and mechanical damage over the building's lifespan.

name: Greater slope adequacy pressure
rationale: Adequate slope (typically 1/4 inch per foot) ensures self-cleaning flow velocities and prevents solids accumulation.

name: Reduced noise transmission pressure
rationale: DWV pipes can transmit wastewater flow noise; architectural design pressures may call for soundproofing or placement away from quiet zones.

name: Lower installation cost pressure
rationale: Cost constraints push toward optimised routing, standard fittings, and minimised material usage without compromising code compliance.

name: Optimised fixture arrangement pressure
rationale: Grouping plumbing fixtures vertically and horizontally reduces pipe runs and simplifies the DWV network layout.

name: Increased hot water temperature
rationale: Hot water heaters must provide sufficiently high water temperatures for domestic use, sanitation, and comfort, driving a need for adequate heating capacity.

name: Improved energy efficiency
rationale: Energy codes and operational cost considerations push for higher efficiency in water heating to reduce energy consumption.

name: Reduced standby heat loss
rationale: Minimizing heat loss from the tank and pipes improves overall system efficiency and reduces energy waste.

name: Reduced physical footprint
rationale: Space constraints in mechanical rooms or utility closets drive a need for smaller, more compact water heater units.

name: Increased storage capacity
rationale: Larger households or high-demand applications require greater hot water storage capacity to meet peak usage.

name: Reduced initial cost
rationale: Budget constraints and cost-sensitivity in construction projects pressure designers to choose lower-cost water heating solutions.

name: Improved safety compliance
rationale: Safety codes require temperature and pressure relief valves, proper venting, and temperature limits to prevent scalding and explosion hazards.

name: Reduced maintenance requirements
rationale: Design pressures exist to minimize servicing needs, such as anode rod replacement, sediment flushing, and part accessibility.

name: Lower inlet water pressure requirement
rationale: Some designs aim to operate reliably under lower incoming water pressure conditions to accommodate varying municipal supply pressures.

name: Improved water metering accuracy
rationale: Design pressure to increase measurement precision and reliability of the water meter component for accurate consumption tracking.

name: Reduced water meter cost
rationale: Design pressure to minimise manufacturing and installation costs of the water meter while maintaining functionality.

name: Enhanced durability against environmental factors
rationale: Pressure to improve the water meter's resistance to corrosion, temperature variations, and physical wear over time.

name: Minimised water meter size
rationale: Design pressure to reduce the physical footprint of the water meter for easier installation in tight spaces.

name: Better integration with smart building systems
rationale: Pressure to improve compatibility and data communication between the water meter and building management or IoT systems.

name: Increased reliability of shut-off valves
rationale: Shut-off valves are critical for isolating sections of a piping system; higher reliability ensures fail-safe operation during emergencies.

name: Reduced leakage from shut-off valves
rationale: Minimising leakage is a key design pressure for valves to prevent fluid loss, safety hazards, and environmental damage.

name: Lower maintenance requirements for shut-off valves
rationale: Designing for reduced maintenance needs lowers lifecycle costs and improves system availability.

name: Higher operating pressure rating for shut-off valves
rationale: Shut-off valves must withstand system operating pressures to function safely without failure.

name: Reduced size/weight of shut-off valves
rationale: Compact valve designs are often preferred for space-constrained installations, though this may conflict with flow capacity requirements.

name: Improved corrosion resistance of shut-off valves
rationale: Valves must resist corrosion from the fluid media and environment to ensure long service life.

name: Adequate flow capacity through shut-off valves
rationale: Shut-off valves must provide sufficient flow area (e.g., full-port design) to avoid excessive pressure drop when fully open.

name: Reduced cost of shut-off valves
rationale: Cost pressures push toward simpler, lower-cost valve designs while maintaining essential performance.

name: Enhanced sealing performance of shut-off valves
rationale: Effective sealing is essential for positive shut-off; improved sealing materials and designs reduce leakage when closed.

name: Increased downstream pressure stability
rationale: A PRV is designed to maintain stable downstream pressure regardless of upstream fluctuations; a key design pressure is to ensure consistent, stable output pressure.

name: Reduced pressure drop across valve
rationale: Minimising pressure loss through the valve improves system efficiency and reduces energy consumption, which is a common engineering design objective.

name: Higher maximum flow capacity
rationale: The PRV must be sized to handle peak flow demands without excessive pressure drop or instability, driving the need for adequate flow capacity.

name: Reduced installation space requirements
rationale: PRVs are often installed in confined mechanical rooms or plant spaces; smaller footprint valves are preferred for ease of installation and maintenance.

name: Improved response time to pressure fluctuations
rationale: Fast-acting PRVs are necessary to promptly respond to upstream pressure surges or demand changes, preventing downstream overpressure or starvation.

name: Reduced maintenance frequency
rationale: Designing for durability and reliability minimises the need for frequent servicing, reducing operational costs and downtime.

name: Lower material cost
rationale: Cost constraints often pressure designers to select less expensive materials and construction methods while still meeting performance requirements.

name: Greater safety margin against overpressure
rationale: Safety is paramount; the PRV must have adequate overpressure protection (e.g., relief capabilities or fail-safe design) to prevent catastrophic failure.

name: Optimised setpoint accuracy
rationale: The PRV must accurately maintain the target downstream setpoint pressure across varying flow conditions, which is its primary function.

name: Reduced backpressure risk
rationale: Backflow preventers are designed to reduce or eliminate the risk of backpressure and back-siphonage in plumbing systems, ensuring water flows in one direction only.

name: Increased regulatory compliance
rationale: Building codes and plumbing standards increasingly require backflow prevention devices to protect potable water supplies from contamination.

name: Sufficient pressure differential maintenance
rationale: The backflow preventer must maintain adequate pressure differential across its check valves to ensure proper sealing and prevent reverse flow.

name: Reduced contamination risk
rationale: The primary purpose of a backflow preventer is to minimize the risk of contaminants entering the potable water supply from cross-connections.

name: Lower installation cost
rationale: Design decisions often aim to minimize installation cost through appropriate sizing, material selection, and assembly location choices for the backflow preventer.

name: Better maintenance accessibility
rationale: Codes and good practice demand adequate clearance and accessibility around the backflow preventer for testing, inspection, and repair.

name: Increased sump pump capacity
rationale: Sump pumps must have adequate capacity to handle peak water inflow rates during heavy rain or flooding events.

name: Improved sump pump reliability
rationale: Sump pumps need reliable operation to prevent basement flooding; backup systems and quality components improve reliability.

name: Reduced sump pump power consumption
rationale: Energy-efficient sump pump operation is desired to minimize electricity costs and environmental impact.

name: Minimised sump pump noise
rationale: Sump pumps located near occupied spaces should operate quietly to avoid disturbing building occupants.

name: Sufficient sump pump head pressure
rationale: The sump pump must generate adequate head pressure to lift water from the sump pit to the discharge point against gravity and friction losses.

name: Eliminated sump pump clogging risk
rationale: Debris and sediment in sump water can clog the pump impeller; screening and proper pump selection helps prevent clogging.

name: Greater sump pump durability
rationale: Sump pumps experience frequent cycling and harsh wet conditions, requiring durable materials and construction for long service life.

name: Adequate sump pit sizing
rationale: The sump pit must be large enough to accommodate the pump and provide sufficient storage volume to prevent short cycling.

name: Reduced sump pump maintenance frequency
rationale: Minimizing required maintenance for sump pumps reduces operational burden and the risk of pump failure due to neglected maintenance.

name: Adequate water collection capacity
rationale: Sump pits must have sufficient volume and capacity to collect and hold incoming water from drainage systems to prevent overflow and flooding.

name: Reduced risk of flooding
rationale: Sump pits serve to collect water and reduce flood risk; design must minimize the chance of overflow.

name: Adequate pump installation space
rationale: The sump pit must provide sufficient space for submersible pumps, controls, and maintenance access.

name: Optimized pit depth
rationale: Depth must be optimized to ensure proper hydraulic gradient for water inflow while allowing pump operation.

name: Reduced contaminant ingress
rationale: Sump pits should be sealed or designed to minimize entry of soil, debris, or hazardous contaminants.

name: Improved structural integrity
rationale: The pit walls and base must be structurally sound to withstand soil and hydrostatic pressures.

name: Higher reliability of drainage system
rationale: The sump pit is a critical component of the drainage system; its design must support reliable operation.

name: Eliminated backflow risk
rationale: Sump pit design should prevent backflow of water into adjacent spaces or drainage lines.

name: Higher pressure rating requirement
rationale: Pipe fittings and couplings must withstand system operating pressures; higher pressure ratings increase material strength and wall thickness requirements.

name: Improved corrosion resistance need
rationale: Corrosion can degrade fittings and couplings over time, driving need for better materials or protective coatings.

name: Reduced leakage risk requirement
rationale: Leakage at joints is a primary failure mode; design must minimise leakage potential through tighter seals and better tolerances.

name: Lower material cost pressure
rationale: Cost constraints may push toward cheaper materials or simpler manufacturing, which can conflict with performance requirements.

name: Increased drainage capacity
rationale: Floor drains must handle expected water flow volumes from fixtures, cleaning, and emergencies; larger or additional drains may be needed.

name: Reduced clogging risk
rationale: Debris and sediment can block drains; design should minimise blockage through strainers, trap design, and appropriate sizing.

name: Improved accessibility for cleaning
rationale: Drains must be reachable and cleanable; accessibility affects placement, cover design, and ease of maintenance.

name: Lower odour emission
rationale: Proper trap seal depth and venting reduce sewer gas odours from floor drain fixtures.

name: Sufficient structural load capacity
rationale: Floor drain grates and bodies must withstand pedestrian and occasional vehicular loads without failure.

name: Prevented backflow
rationale: Backflow prevention devices or check valves may be needed to prevent sewage backup through floor drains.

name: Optimised slope for drainage
rationale: Floor slope towards drain must be optimised to ensure positive drainage and prevent ponding.

name: Minimised leak risk at connections
rationale: Pipe connections to floor drain must be watertight to prevent leakage into building structure.

name: Enhanced corrosion resistance
rationale: Floor drains exposed to chemicals and moisture require corrosion-resistant materials for longevity.

name: Improved water softening capacity
rationale: Water softeners need sufficient capacity to treat the building's water hardness levels, ensuring adequate soft water supply for plumbing systems and equipment.

name: Reduced maintenance requirements
rationale: Design pressure to minimise ongoing maintenance costs and complexity by selecting durable, self-cleaning, or low-maintenance water softening systems.

name: Minimised space footprint
rationale: Water softener systems compete for mechanical room space; there is pressure to select compact units that fit within allocated floor area.

name: Higher regeneration efficiency
rationale: Pressure to improve salt and water efficiency during regeneration cycles to reduce operating costs and environmental impact.

name: Lower upfront capital cost
rationale: Budget constraints create pressure to select a water softener system with lower initial purchase and installation costs.

name: Adequate flow rate capacity
rationale: The water softener must handle peak demand flow rates for the building without significant pressure drop or service interruption.

name: Improved filtration efficiency
rationale: There is a constant engineering pressure to improve the filtration efficiency of water filtration systems to meet higher water quality standards.

name: Reduced energy consumption
rationale: Water filtration systems are energy-intensive, so there is a design pressure to reduce their energy consumption for cost savings and sustainability.

name: Reduced maintenance requirements
rationale: Designers aim to reduce the frequency and complexity of maintenance to lower operational downtime and costs.

name: Increased filtration capacity
rationale: There is a pressure to increase the throughput or capacity of water filtration systems to handle larger volumes of water.

name: Reduced footprint
rationale: Space constraints in buildings create a pressure to minimize the physical footprint of water filtration equipment.

name: Improved water quality output
rationale: Regulatory and health standards drive the need for better quality filtered water.

name: Reduced chemical usage
rationale: There is a growing pressure to minimize the use of chemicals in water treatment processes for environmental and safety reasons.

name: Improved system durability
rationale: Longer lifespan and greater robustness against wear and corrosion are desired to reduce replacement costs.

name: Reduced operational costs
rationale: Overall cost pressures from building owners and operators push for lower ongoing operational expenses.

name: Increased water conservation demand
rationale: Growing emphasis on sustainable water management drives demand for greywater recycling systems to reduce potable water consumption.

name: Reduced freshwater consumption pressure
rationale: Greywater recycling directly reduces the demand for freshwater supply, making the system a tool for decreasing overall water usage.

name: Higher regulatory compliance requirements
rationale: Building codes and environmental regulations increasingly mandate or incentivize water reuse systems in new constructions.

name: Reduced wastewater discharge
rationale: Greywater recycling lessens the volume of wastewater sent to municipal treatment systems, reducing infrastructure burden.

name: Improved building sustainability rating
rationale: Green building certification schemes (e.g., LEED, BREEAM) award credits for greywater recycling, incentivizing its inclusion.

name: Optimised lifecycle cost savings
rationale: Long-term operational savings from reduced water bills and lower sewage charges create an economic pressure to adopt greywater recycling.

name: Increased water collection efficiency
rationale: Rainwater harvesting systems are designed to maximize the collection of rainwater from catchments like roofs; higher collection efficiency directly improves system performance.

name: Improved storage capacity
rationale: Larger or more optimized storage tanks allow greater water retention, reducing reliance on municipal supply and increasing system resilience.

name: Reduced contamination risk
rationale: First-flush diverters, filters, and proper tank design minimize pollutants entering stored rainwater, a critical design pressure for water quality.

name: Higher filtration quality
rationale: Better filtration systems ensure harvested rainwater meets potable or non-potable water quality standards, influencing system design.

name: Minimised maintenance requirements
rationale: Designs that reduce sediment buildup, clogging, and component wear are preferred to lower operational costs and ensure long-term reliability.

name: Expanded catchment area utilization
rationale: Integrating larger roof areas or additional hard surfaces as catchments increases water yield, a pressure that influences system sizing and layout.

name: Reduced system complexity
rationale: Simpler designs with fewer components (pumps, controls, multiple tanks) are cheaper and more robust, competing with performance-driven pressures.

name: Optimised cost-effectiveness
rationale: Economic viability is a key design pressure—balancing capital costs, maintenance, and water savings shapes decisions on tank size, materials, and treatment.

name: Adequate backup system integration
rationale: Rainwater systems often require connection to mains water or other backup sources for dry periods, influencing tank sizing and plumbing design.

name: adequate capacity for peak flow
rationale: Sanitary sewer connections must be sized to handle peak wastewater flows from the building to prevent backups and overflows.

name: reduced infiltration and inflow
rationale: Minimising groundwater infiltration and rainwater inflow into the sanitary sewer connection reduces hydraulic load and treatment costs.

name: minimised blockages and clogs
rationale: Design should prevent obstructions through proper pipe sizing, slope, and material selection to ensure reliable flow.

name: adequate slope for self-cleaning velocity
rationale: Sufficient gradient ensures wastewater flows at velocities that keep solids in suspension and prevent sedimentation.

name: restricted connection of unauthorised flows
rationale: Stormwater or other non-sanitary flows should be prevented from entering the sanitary sewer to avoid overloading the system.

name: improved durability against corrosion
rationale: Sewer gases and chemicals can cause corrosion; selecting durable materials extends the service life of the connection.

name: minimised construction cost
rationale: Cost pressures push toward economical design and installation methods while meeting functional requirements.

name: adequate access for maintenance
rationale: Provision of cleanouts and inspection points ensures the connection can be maintained and cleared if blockages occur.

name: minimised excavation and trench depth
rationale: Shallower trenches reduce excavation costs and safety risks, but must still provide adequate cover and slope.

name: adequate vent stack sizing
rationale: Vent stacks must be adequately sized to handle airflow and pressure equalization in plumbing systems, preventing trap seal loss and ensuring proper drainage.

name: reduced vent stack blockage risk
rationale: Blockages in vent stacks can cause pressure imbalances and drainage failures, so design aims to minimise obstruction risks.

name: higher vent stack termination height
rationale: Vent stack terminations must extend above the roofline to prevent sewer gases from re-entering the building, driven by code and health considerations.

name: minimised vent stack corrosion
rationale: Corrosion can compromise structural integrity and venting performance, so design choices favour corrosion-resistant materials.

name: sufficient vent stack diameter
rationale: Proper diameter ensures adequate airflow for pressure equalization in the drainage system.

name: Increased treatment capacity
rationale: Septic systems must handle peak wastewater loads; larger tank volume and leach field area increase treatment capacity and system reliability.

name: Reduced soil permeability risk
rationale: Soil clogging or inadequate percolation reduces system effectiveness; designing to avoid high permeability failure extends system life.

name: Improved effluent quality
rationale: Regulatory and environmental requirements push for better treatment performance to protect groundwater and surface water.

name: Minimised leach field area
rationale: Site constraints such as available land, setbacks, and topography often limit the footprint of the drainfield.

name: Higher maintenance accessibility
rationale: Access for periodic pumping, inspection, and repair is essential; better access reduces long-term operational costs.

name: Reduced groundwater contamination risk
rationale: Proper siting and design prevent untreated effluent from reaching aquifers, protecting drinking water sources.

name: Adequate hydraulic loading rate
rationale: Hydraulic loading must match soil absorption capacity to avoid surfacing or backup; adequate design ensures continuous function.

name: Restricted slope gradient
rationale: Steep slopes increase risk of effluent breakout and erosion; design pressures limit installation on steep terrain.

name: Expanded reserve area for replacement
rationale: Many codes require a reserved area for a future replacement leach field, pushing for larger site set-asides.

name: Improved water seal retention
rationale: A P-trap or S-trap must maintain a water seal to prevent sewer gases from entering the building; thus there is a design pressure to increase or improve water seal retention.

name: Reduced clogging risk
rationale: Traps are prone to debris accumulation; design seeks to minimise or reduce clogging risk to ensure unobstructed drainage flow.

name: Adequate trap depth
rationale: Building codes specify minimum trap seal depth (typically 2-4 inches) to ensure proper sealing; thus there is pressure for adequate depth.

name: Minimised self-siphonage
rationale: S-traps are especially prone to self-siphonage which breaks the water seal; design pressure is to minimise or prevent this occurrence.

name: Improved corrosion resistance
rationale: Traps are exposed to wastewater chemicals that cause corrosion; materials and coatings are selected for better corrosion resistance.

name: Restricted material cost
rationale: Cost constraints on plumbing components exert pressure to limit or restrict the material and manufacturing expense of the trap.

name: Greater accessibility for cleaning
rationale: Traps require periodic cleaning or rodding; design pressure to provide greater accessibility via cleanout plugs or easy disassembly.

name: Lower risk of freezing
rationale: In unheated building areas, traps may freeze and crack; design pressure to reduce or limit freezing risk through insulation or placement.

name: Enhanced flow capacity
rationale: Trap internal diameter and geometry must allow adequate drainage flow without excessive turbulence; design pressure for sufficient flow capacity.

name: improved accessibility
rationale: Cleanout access points need to be easily reachable for maintenance and inspection of plumbing/HVAC systems, driving a need for improved accessibility.

name: reduced obstruction
rationale: Cleanout access points should be placed to minimize interference with building usage, driving a need to reduce obstruction.

name: adequate size
rationale: The cleanout opening must be adequately sized to allow cleaning equipment and tools to pass through effectively.

name: minimised number
rationale: To reduce cost and potential leak points, the number of cleanout access points should be minimised while still meeting code requirements.

name: better placement
rationale: Placement of cleanout access points should be optimised relative to pipe routing and building geometry for effective maintenance.

name: Improved freeze protection
rationale: Outdoor spigots in cold climates must be freeze-proof (e.g., frost-free sillcocks) to prevent bursting. This pressure acts to increase freeze protection features.

name: Reduced leakage risk
rationale: The spigot assembly must minimise water leakage at the connection point, which drives design toward higher-quality valve mechanisms and seals.

name: Greater durability against outdoor exposure
rationale: Outdoor spigots are exposed to UV, rain, temperature swings, and physical impact, requiring robust materials (e.g., brass, stainless steel) and weather-resistant coatings.

name: Adequate water flow capacity
rationale: The spigot must provide sufficient flow rate for typical garden hose usage, influencing the internal diameter and valve design.

name: Lower installation complexity
rationale: Simple installation (e.g., standard thread patterns, accessible mounting) is pressured to reduce labour cost and compatibility issues with standard plumbing.

name: Prevented backflow contamination
rationale: Building codes require backflow prevention devices (e.g., vacuum breakers or check valves) on outdoor spigots to eliminate the risk of contaminating the potable water supply.

name: Enhanced corrosion resistance
rationale: Constant exposure to moisture and outdoor elements creates a design pressure for corrosion-resistant materials (brass, stainless steel, or durable coatings) to ensure long service life.

name: Increased electrical load capacity
rationale: The Main Distribution Board must handle growing electrical demands from additional circuits and equipment, driving the need for higher rated capacity.

name: Improved safety compliance
rationale: Regulatory standards and safety codes require enhanced protection features (e.g., adequate circuit breakers, proper insulation) in the Main Distribution Board.

name: Optimised space utilisation
rationale: Physical constraints on electrical room size drive the need for a more compact or efficiently laid out Main Distribution Board.

name: Reduced heat generation
rationale: Excessive heat from electrical components can degrade performance and cause hazards, so minimised thermal output is a design pressure.

name: Minimised installation cost
rationale: Budget constraints pressure the design to use fewer or less expensive components while still meeting requirements.

name: Restricted physical footprint
rationale: Limited floor space in the electrical room requires a smaller Main Distribution Board footprint.

name: Higher fault current rating
rationale: The Main Distribution Board must withstand and interrupt higher prospective fault currents to ensure system protection.

name: Improved accessibility for maintenance
rationale: Ease of access for servicing and operation drives the need for adequate clearance and ergonomic arrangement around the board.

name: Limited cable congestion
rationale: Overcrowding of cables entering/exiting the board can cause overheating and maintenance difficulties, so cable volumes should be constrained.

name: Improved power reliability
rationale: An ATS is used to automatically switch between primary and backup power sources during outages, directly improving power reliability for critical loads.

name: Reduced transfer time
rationale: Faster switching between power sources minimises downtime for critical systems; a key design pressure on ATS selection.

name: Higher switching capacity
rationale: The ATS must handle full rated current of the load; design tends toward adequate capacity for peak loads.

name: Reduced installation space
rationale: Limited space in electrical rooms or enclosures pressures towards compact ATS designs.

name: Improved electrical safety
rationale: Safety standards (e.g., UL 1008) require proper isolation, arc flash mitigation, and fail-safe operation, pressuring for better safety features.

name: Lower maintenance requirements
rationale: Design aims to minimise moving parts and contact wear to reduce maintenance frequency and lifecycle costs.

name: Enhanced monitoring capability
rationale: Modern ATS designs increasingly integrate remote monitoring, status indication, and communication for facility management systems.

name: Increased electrical load demand
rationale: As more electrical circuits and equipment are added to a building, the electrical load on sub distribution boards increases, requiring higher capacity or additional boards.

name: Improved safety compliance requirements
rationale: Electrical safety standards (e.g., BS 7671, IEC 60364) impose requirements for proper enclosures, fault protection, and accessibility, increasing design complexity and specifications for sub distribution boards.

name: Reduced physical space availability
rationale: Architectural constraints often limit the space allocated for electrical rooms or riser cupboards, restricting the size and configuration of sub distribution boards.

name: Higher thermal management requirements
rationale: Concentrated electrical equipment in sub distribution boards generates heat, necessitating ventilation, cooling, or derating of components, which pressures design decisions.

name: Reduced budget allocation
rationale: Project cost constraints may limit the selection of premium sub distribution board components or force downsizing of capacity.

name: Adequate short-circuit withstand capability
rationale: Sub distribution boards must be rated to withstand prospective fault currents from upstream transformers and cables, driving requirements for robust busbars and protective devices.

name: Better coordination with upstream distribution
rationale: Selective coordination between the main distribution board and sub distribution boards ensures fault isolation, pressuring designers to carefully size and specify protective devices.

name: Limited cable entry and exit points
rationale: Physical constraints of the sub distribution board enclosure restrict the number and size of cable connections, influencing layout and circuit allocation decisions.

name: Increased electrical capacity
rationale: Busbar trunking systems are designed to handle higher electrical loads, so there is a pressure to increase capacity to meet growing power distribution demands.

name: Reduced installation space
rationale: Busbar trunking systems are often preferred over cable systems for their space-saving characteristics, creating pressure to minimise the footprint.

name: Improved thermal performance
rationale: Heat dissipation is critical in busbar systems; improved thermal management ensures safety and reliability.

name: Reduced maintenance requirements
rationale: Busbar trunking systems are designed for low maintenance, with pressure to further minimise upkeep needs.

name: Enhanced short-circuit rating
rationale: Busbar trunking systems must withstand high fault currents; a higher short-circuit rating increases safety and compliance.

name: Increased current rating
rationale: Circuit breakers must be rated to handle the maximum expected current without tripping under normal conditions.

name: Improved breaking capacity
rationale: Higher fault currents require circuit breakers with greater interrupting capacity to safely clear faults.

name: Reduced response time
rationale: Faster tripping mechanisms improve protection by minimizing damage during fault conditions.

name: Minimised nuisance tripping
rationale: Circuit breakers should avoid unnecessary opening due to transient surges or harmless conditions.

name: Lower heat dissipation
rationale: Reducing resistive heating improves efficiency and prevents thermal degradation of components.

name: Enhanced coordination with downstream breakers
rationale: Selective coordination ensures that only the nearest breaker to a fault opens, maintaining power to other circuits.

name: Greater durability under short-circuit conditions
rationale: Breakers must withstand high mechanical and thermal stresses during short-circuit interruption without damage.

name: Reduced physical size
rationale: Space constraints in electrical panels drive demand for compact circuit breaker designs.

name: Improved arc extinguishing capability
rationale: Effective arc quenching is critical for safe interruption of high-energy faults in circuit breakers.

name: Improved safety coordination with Residual Current Device
rationale: Increasing the coordination and integration of the Residual Current Device with other protective devices improves overall electrical safety and reduces false tripping.

name: Reduced nuisance tripping of Residual Current Device
rationale: Minimising nuisance tripping is a design pressure to ensure the device does not interrupt power unnecessarily due to transient faults or leakage currents.

name: Higher sensitivity setting for Residual Current Device
rationale: Increasing the sensitivity (lower mA rating) of the RCD improves protection against electric shock, especially in wet or high-risk areas.

name: Lower tripping threshold for Residual Current Device
rationale: Decreasing the tripping threshold ensures faster disconnection in fault conditions, enhancing personnel safety.

name: Adequate fault current rating for Residual Current Device
rationale: Ensuring the Residual Current Device has an adequate short-circuit current rating to withstand fault conditions without damage.

name: Reduced physical size of Residual Current Device
rationale: Smaller physical footprint of the RCD is desirable for fitting in compact distribution boards, though this competes with thermal and clearance requirements.

name: Increased protection coordination
rationale: Surge protection devices must be properly coordinated with downstream equipment to ensure they activate at appropriate voltage thresholds, preventing equipment damage.

name: Reduced let-through voltage
rationale: A lower let-through voltage (clamping voltage) is desirable to better protect sensitive downstream equipment from voltage surges.

name: Higher surge current rating
rationale: A higher surge current rating (e.g., Imax or nominal discharge current) ensures the device can handle larger surge events without failing.

name: Reduced response time
rationale: Faster response time (lower nanosecond activation) is critical to clamping transient overvoltages before they propagate to sensitive equipment.

name: Adequate thermal protection
rationale: Thermal disconnectors or fusing within the SPD must be adequate to prevent fire risk during end-of-life or sustained overvoltage conditions.

name: Increased power transmission capacity
rationale: Power cables must transmit electrical power; increased capacity is a fundamental performance requirement driven by electrical load demands.

name: Reduced electrical resistance
rationale: Lower electrical resistance minimizes power loss and heat generation in cables, a core physical principle.

name: Improved insulation quality
rationale: Better insulation prevents short circuits and ensures safety; a key engineering design consideration for power cables.

name: Reduced cable weight
rationale: Lighter cables are easier to install and reduce structural support requirements, though may trade off with other properties.

name: Lower installation cost
rationale: Cost reduction is a common economic pressure in engineering design decisions for cable selection and routing.

name: Greater durability and lifespan

name: Lower maintenance requirements

name: Improved energy efficiency

name: Reduced manual meter reading costs

name: Improved power quality
rationale: Power factor correction units are designed to improve power quality by reducing reactive power and correcting the power factor, which enhances electrical system efficiency.

name: Reduced harmonic distortion
rationale: Power factor correction units, especially active ones, help reduce harmonic distortion in the electrical system, minimising negative impacts on equipment.

name: Increased energy efficiency
rationale: By correcting the power factor, the unit reduces reactive power flow, leading to lower energy losses and greater overall system efficiency.

name: Reduced electrical losses
rationale: Power factor correction minimises I²R losses in cables and transformers due to reduced reactive current, lowering overall electrical losses.

name: Optimised system capacity
rationale: Power factor correction frees up capacity in transformers and distribution equipment, allowing more active power to be delivered without upgrading infrastructure.

name: Enhanced voltage regulation
rationale: Power factor correction helps stabilise voltage levels by reducing voltage drops caused by reactive current flow, ensuring more consistent voltage supply.

name: Reduced utility penalties
rationale: Many utilities impose penalties for low power factor; correction avoids or reduces these financial penalties.

name: Lower maintenance requirements
rationale: Modern power factor correction units with automatic switching and quality components can have reduced maintenance needs compared to older systems.

name: Increased charging capacity demand

name: Reduced installation cost pressure
