rationale: The travelator must coordinate with escalators, elevators, flooring, and structural elements, creating pressure for better spatial and aesthetic integration.

name: Reduced footprint pressure
rationale: In space-constrained buildings, limiting the horizontal and vertical space occupied by the travelator mechanism is often required.

name: Higher speed pressure
rationale: To improve passenger travel time across long distances, there may be pressure to optimise belt speed within safety limits.

name: Increased sensitivity
rationale: Heat detectors need sufficient sensitivity to reliably detect fires or overheating events in a timely manner.

name: Higher temperature threshold
rationale: The temperature rating must be set appropriately above ambient to prevent false alarms while still detecting dangerous heat levels.

name: Reduced false alarm rate
rationale: Minimising nuisance alarms is critical for occupant trust and operational efficiency, requiring careful threshold tuning and placement.

name: Improved response time
rationale: Faster detection of heat events enables quicker emergency response, reducing potential damage and safety risks.

name: Minimised false alarms from steam/condensation
rationale: In environments like kitchens or boiler rooms, steam can trigger unwanted alarms; detector design should mitigate this.

name: Expanded coverage area
rationale: Adequate spatial coverage ensures all critical zones are monitored for heat events, aligning with fire safety standards.

name: Lower maintenance cost
rationale: Reducing ongoing maintenance requirements makes the system more economical and reliable over its lifecycle.

name: Improved detection sensitivity
rationale: Carbon monoxide detectors must be sensitive enough to detect low levels of CO to ensure occupant safety before dangerous accumulation.

name: Reduced false alarm rate
rationale: Excessive false alarms reduce trust in the system and lead to ignored warnings; detectors should minimize nuisance alarms.

name: Increased placement height optimization
rationale: CO is slightly lighter than air; optimal placement height (often at breathing level or on ceilings) improves detection effectiveness.

name: Limited proximity to combustion sources
rationale: Detectors placed too close to combustion appliances (furnaces, stoves) may cause nuisance alarms; appropriate distance is needed.

name: Adequate power supply reliability
rationale: Continuous operation requires reliable power (hardwired or long-life battery) to ensure 24/7 monitoring capability.

name: Minimized interference from other gases
rationale: Other household gases (hydrogen, alcohol vapors) can cause false readings; sensors should be selective to CO.

name: Enhanced audibility of alarm signal
rationale: Alarm must be loud enough (typically 85 dB) and have appropriate tone pattern to alert occupants even when sleeping.

name: Higher compliance with building codes
rationale: Regulatory standards (e.g., NFPA 720, local building codes) mandate specific installation locations, quantities, and performance criteria.

name: Restricted installation in dead air spaces
rationale: Dead air spaces (corners, behind doors) prevent proper air circulation and reduce detection effectiveness; placement should avoid these areas.

name: Improved accessibility of Manual Call Point
rationale: Manual call points need to be easily reachable and accessible to building occupants during emergencies, which is a standard fire safety engineering requirement.

name: Increased visibility of Manual Call Point
rationale: Manual call points must be clearly visible and identifiable to ensure rapid activation in fire emergencies, as per fire safety codes.

name: Reduced false alarm risk at Manual Call Point
rationale: Design pressures to minimise accidental or false activations of manual call points through protective covers or placement considerations.

name: Greater compliance with regulations for Manual Call Point placement
rationale: Building codes and fire safety regulations specify precise mounting heights, locations, and spacing for manual call points that must be followed.

name: Limited obstruction around Manual Call Point
rationale: Manual call points should be free from obstructions such as furniture, partitions, or decorative elements that could impede access during emergencies.

name: Improved panel visibility
rationale: Annunciator panels need to be clearly visible to operators to provide timely alerts; better visibility improves response times and safety monitoring.

name: Reduced false alarms
rationale: False alarms on annunciator panels desensitize operators and reduce trust in the system; minimizing false alarms improves system reliability.

name: Higher information density
rationale: Annunciator panels often need to display many alarm points; greater information density allows comprehensive status monitoring in a compact layout.

name: Reduced panel footprint
rationale: Space in control rooms is at a premium; a smaller panel footprint allows for better ergonomic layout and accommodation of other equipment.

name: Improved fire safety compliance
rationale: Building codes and fire safety regulations mandate that fire alarm control panels must meet stringent compliance standards, creating a pressure to increase/improve compliance features.

name: Higher reliability and uptime
rationale: Fire alarm systems must operate reliably during emergencies; there is a design pressure to ensure high reliability and uptime of the control panel.

name: Reduced false alarm rate
rationale: False alarms reduce trust and cause disruptions; design pressures push toward minimizing false alarm occurrences through better detection algorithms and panel sensitivity settings.

name: Greater integration with building systems
rationale: Modern buildings require fire alarm panels to integrate with HVAC, access control, and emergency communication systems, pressuring greater interoperability.

name: Restricted physical footprint
rationale: The control panel must fit within allocated electrical rooms or wall spaces, imposing a constraint on its physical size.

name: Lower power consumption
rationale: Energy efficiency requirements and backup battery capacity constraints drive a pressure toward reduced power draw.

name: Enhanced user interface clarity
rationale: Firefighters and building occupants need clear, intuitive interfaces for quick situation assessment and response.

name: Improved survivability in fire conditions
rationale: The panel must continue functioning during a fire event, requiring enhanced protection against heat, smoke, and water.

name: Minimised maintenance requirements
rationale: Building operators prefer systems that require minimal periodic maintenance to ensure ongoing functionality and reduce lifecycle costs.

name: Increased audibility pressure
rationale: Building codes (e.g., NFPA 72, ADA) require notification appliances to produce audible signals at sufficient levels above ambient noise to ensure occupant awareness during emergencies.

name: Enhanced visibility pressure
rationale: Visual notification appliances (strobes) must provide adequate light intensity and flash patterns to be seen by occupants, including those with hearing impairments, per accessibility standards.

name: Reduced false alarm pressure
rationale: Design seeks to minimize nuisance alarms and inadvertent activations of notification appliances to prevent alarm fatigue and maintain occupant responsiveness.

name: Minimised power consumption pressure
rationale: Notification appliances must operate within building electrical system limits and often rely on backup power; lower power draw extends battery life during emergencies.

name: Increased coverage area pressure
rationale: Regulatory requirements dictate that notification appliances cover defined floor areas to ensure all building occupants can perceive emergency signals.

name: Reduced installation cost pressure
rationale: Project budget constraints push toward fewer devices or simpler wiring topologies while still meeting code-mandated performance.

name: Improved audibility pressure
rationale: Sounders/horns must be clearly audible above ambient noise for fire alarm and emergency notification, driving design toward higher sound output.

name: Reduced false alarm pressure
rationale: Design pressures exist to minimise nuisance alarms triggered by environmental factors, which influences horn/sounder sensitivity and placement.

name: Higher environmental durability pressure
rationale: Sounders/horns are subject to environmental exposure (temperature, humidity, dust), demanding greater ingress protection and material robustness.

name: Reduced size/space pressure
rationale: Architectural integration pressures favour smaller, less obtrusive sounder/horn devices, especially in aesthetically sensitive areas.

name: Improved code compliance pressure
rationale: Building codes and standards (e.g., AS 1670, NFPA 72) mandate minimum sound pressure levels and coverage for sounder/horn devices.

name: Increased visibility demand
rationale: Building codes and fire alarm standards (e.g., NFPA 72, ADA) require visual alarm devices to provide adequate strobe light intensity and coverage to alert occupants, especially those with hearing impairments.

name: Higher mounting height requirement
rationale: Strobes must be mounted at specific heights (typically within 6-10 inches of ceiling or as per code) to ensure light dispersion reaches all areas of the room.

name: Minimised energy consumption
rationale: Energy efficiency requirements may push for LED-based strobes with lower power draw while maintaining required light output.

name: Reduced false alarm nuisance
rationale: Design should minimize unintended activation of strobes (e.g., from electrical noise or faulty sensors) to avoid occupant desensitization.

name: Greater synchronisation requirement
rationale: Codes often require strobes within a space to flash in synchronization to prevent triggering seizures in photosensitive individuals and ensure consistent signaling.

name: Lower cost pressure
rationale: Budget constraints push toward selecting cost-effective strobe models that still meet code requirements.

name: Adequate coverage area requirement
rationale: Each strobe must provide sufficient light intensity (measured in candela) to cover its designated room area per NFPA 72 spacing and coverage tables.

name: Restricted placement by aesthetics
rationale: Architectural considerations may limit where strobes can be placed to maintain visual appeal of interior spaces.

name: Improved accessibility compliance
rationale: ADA and similar accessibility standards mandate visual alarms in public and common-use areas to ensure equal access for individuals with hearing disabilities.

name: Increased audibility requirements
rationale: Building codes and standards (e.g., NFPA 72, AS 1670.4) require voice evacuation systems to achieve minimum audibility levels (typically 15 dB above ambient or 75 dBA) in all occupied spaces, driving demand for higher speaker density or power.

name: Improved speech intelligibility
rationale: Regulatory and performance requirements demand that emergency voice communications achieve acceptable speech intelligibility (e.g., STI > 0.5 per ISO 7240-19 or AS 1670.4), driving system design toward better speaker placement, acoustic treatment, and signal processing.

name: Reduced installation complexity
rationale: Project constraints (budget, schedule, coordination with other building services) push toward simpler, less disruptive installation approaches, potentially limiting speaker counts, cable runs, or zoning complexity.

name: Lower system cost
rationale: Capital and lifecycle cost pressures encourage selection of fewer speakers, less powerful amplifiers, and simpler control equipment to stay within project budget.

name: Expanded coverage area
rationale: Code requirements (e.g., NFPA 101, IBC, NCC) mandate voice evacuation coverage in all egress paths, common areas, and sleeping areas, driving expansion of speaker coverage to larger floor areas or multiple zones.

name: Greater redundancy and survivability
rationale: Fire and life safety codes require redundant amplifiers, emergency power supply (battery backup), and pathway survivability (e.g., 2-hour fire-rated cabling) to ensure continued operation during a fire event.

name: Improved integration with fire alarm system
rationale: Voice evacuation must operate as part of the overall fire alarm and emergency communication system, requiring tight integration with smoke detection, alarm initiation, and zone-based notification sequencing (e.g., NFPA 72).

name: Restricted zoning complexity
rationale: To avoid excessive cost and commissioning effort, project teams may prefer simpler zone layouts (e.g., fewer paging zones, no multi-channel evacuation messages) even if code would permit more granular zoned messaging.

name: Improved fire detection sensitivity
rationale: Beam smoke detectors need sufficient sensitivity to detect smoke early across large open areas, driving design toward higher sensitivity settings.

name: Reduced false alarm rate
rationale: Beam smoke detectors must avoid nuisance alarms from dust, steam, or environmental changes, creating pressure to minimise false triggering.

name: Greater coverage area per detector
rationale: Projected beam detectors are designed to cover large open spaces (up to 100m+), driving pressure to maximise the area monitored per unit.

name: Lower installation height constraints
rationale: Beam detectors must be mounted at specific heights relative to ceiling and protected area, limiting installation flexibility in architecturally complex spaces.

name: Improved alignment stability
rationale: Beam detectors require stable optical alignment; building movement or vibration creates pressure for more robust mounting and auto-alignment features.

name: Minimised obstruction of beam path
rationale: The infrared beam path must remain unobstructed by building elements like beams, ducts, or lighting, creating pressure to reduce or avoid obstacles.

name: Adequate environmental compensation
rationale: Beam detectors need compensation for gradual environmental changes (dust buildup, temperature shifts) to avoid false alarms while maintaining detection.

name: Restricted detector placement flexibility
rationale: Building layout, ceiling geometry, and occupancy constraints limit where beam detectors can be strategically placed for optimal coverage.

name: Increased reliability for smoke detection
rationale: Duct smoke detectors must reliably detect smoke in HVAC systems to prevent fire spread, so there is a design pressure to increase reliability.

name: Reduced false alarms
rationale: False alarms from duct smoke detectors can cause unnecessary building shutdowns, creating a pressure to minimise false alarms.

name: Improved sensitivity to smoke
rationale: The detector must be sensitive enough to detect smoke at low concentrations to ensure early warning.

name: Lower maintenance requirements
rationale: Duct smoke detectors in HVAC systems are often in hard-to-reach locations, so design should minimise maintenance frequency and effort.

name: Optimised airflow compatibility
rationale: The detector must function correctly across a range of duct air velocities and pressures without obstructing airflow.

name: Reduced installation cost
rationale: Cost constraints in building projects create pressure to minimise the installation cost of duct smoke detectors.

name: Enhanced compliance with fire codes
rationale: Building and fire codes mandate specific locations and performance criteria for duct smoke detectors, creating a strong pressure for compliance.

name: Greater durability in HVAC environment
rationale: Duct smoke detectors are exposed to temperature extremes, humidity, and dust within HVAC systems, requiring robust construction.

name: Restricted physical footprint
rationale: Space constraints within ductwork and mechanical rooms create pressure for a compact detector design.

name: Increased sensitivity to smoke/fire
rationale: Flame detectors must be sufficiently sensitive to reliably detect flame signatures (UV/IR) in order to trigger alarms quickly.

name: Reduced false alarm rate
rationale: Flame detectors need to discriminate between actual flames and nuisance sources (sunlight, welding, heaters) to avoid unnecessary disruptions.

name: Enhanced response speed
rationale: Flame detectors should have fast response times to enable early fire suppression and evacuation.

name: Lower cost per unit
rationale: Budget constraints drive pressure to reduce the acquisition and installation cost of flame detectors.

name: Improved environmental ruggedness
rationale: Flame detectors must withstand harsh conditions (dust, moisture, temperature extremes) typical in industrial settings.

name: Increased early fire detection
rationale: ASD systems provide very early warning of fire by continuously sampling air for smoke particles, enabling faster response.

name: Reduced false alarm rate
rationale: ASD systems use multiple detection thresholds and sophisticated algorithms to minimise nuisance alarms.

name: Higher sensitivity to smoke
rationale: ASD systems can detect extremely low concentrations of smoke particles, offering superior sensitivity.

name: Lower installation cost
rationale: ASD systems require pipe networks and specialised equipment, typically resulting in higher installation cost compared to conventional detectors.

name: Enhanced coverage of large open areas
rationale: ASD pipe networks can extend over large distances and cover high-ceiling or open spaces effectively.

name: Reduced maintenance effort
rationale: Centralised detector location and self-cleaning features can reduce maintenance frequency and effort.

name: Greater aesthetic integration
rationale: ASD sampling pipes can be concealed or made less obtrusive than visible point detectors, preserving architectural aesthetics.

name: Optimised sampling pipe network design
rationale: Pipe layout, hole placement, and airflow must be carefully designed to ensure representative air sampling across all zones.

name: Reduced impact of airflow on detection
rationale: Air conditioning and ventilation drafts can affect smoke dispersion; ASD pipe design must mitigate these effects.

name: Increased wiring reliability
rationale: Addressable loop wiring is expected to provide reliable communication in fire alarm and security systems, so there is a design pressure to increase reliability.

name: Reduced installation complexity
rationale: Addressable loop wiring must be installed in a loop topology, but designers often seek to minimise installation complexity for cost and time savings.

name: Lower wiring material cost
rationale: There is economic pressure to reduce the cost of wiring materials used in addressable loops.

name: Enhanced system scalability
rationale: Addressable loop wiring should support future expansion and addition of more devices without major rewiring.

name: Restricted cable distance
rationale: Addressable loops have maximum cable length limits due to signal attenuation, creating a pressure to keep distances within constraints.

name: Improved fault tolerance
rationale: The loop topology inherently provides fault tolerance (e.g., single break does not disable all devices), so there is pressure to maintain or improve this characteristic.

name: Adequate device addressing capacity
rationale: Addressable systems must support a sufficient number of unique device addresses on a loop to meet project requirements.

name: Reduced signal interference
rationale: Signal integrity on addressable loops must be maintained, so electromagnetic interference and noise should be minimised.

name: Optimised wiring topology
rationale: The loop should be arranged in an optimised path to balance cost, reliability, and maintainability.

name: Increased integration complexity
rationale: Conventional zone wiring systems face pressure to integrate with more building automation and control systems, increasing the complexity and scope of wiring decisions.

name: Higher reliability requirements
rationale: Building codes and safety standards impose higher reliability demands on conventional zone wiring for critical systems like fire alarms and HVAC controls.

name: Reduced material cost pressure
rationale: Project budgets and cost constraints push toward minimising material usage for conventional zone wiring without compromising functionality.

name: Limited physical space for routing
rationale: Cramped ceiling plenums, walls, and cable trays restrict the routing options and volume of conventional zone wiring that can be installed.

name: Increased signal reliability
rationale: The relay module must reliably transmit control signals; higher reliability reduces false trips or missed commands in automation systems.

name: Reduced power consumption
rationale: Relay modules consume standby and switching power; minimising consumption improves overall energy efficiency of the control system.

name: Improved switching speed
rationale: Faster response times are needed for time-critical automation sequences and to minimise relay contact wear.

name: Reduced physical footprint
rationale: Smaller module size allows denser panel layouts and easier integration into space-constrained enclosures.

name: Improved thermal dissipation
rationale: Effective heat management prolongs relay coil life and prevents overheating in enclosed panels.

name: Increased reliability requirement
rationale: Standby power systems must maintain high reliability to ensure critical building functions continue during outages.

name: Reduced physical footprint pressure
rationale: Building space is often constrained, pushing for more compact battery and power supply installations.

name: Improved energy density requirement
rationale: Advancements in battery technology drive demand for higher energy density to provide longer backup in smaller packages.

name: Reduced maintenance burden
rationale: Building operators prefer low-maintenance standby power solutions to reduce operational costs and downtime.

name: Higher capacity demand
rationale: Critical building loads (life safety, IT, medical equipment) require sufficient backup capacity to operate for required durations.

name: Increased safety compliance pressure
rationale: Building codes and fire safety regulations impose strict requirements on battery storage, ventilation, and thermal management.

name: Reduced cost constraint
rationale: Budget limitations in building projects pressure designers to minimise the capital cost of standby power systems.

name: Improved integration with renewable energy
rationale: As buildings incorporate solar and other on-site generation, battery systems are increasingly required to integrate with these sources.

name: Reduced environmental impact
rationale: Sustainability goals and regulations push for greener battery chemistries and end-of-life recyclability.

name: Improved fire detection and response speed
rationale: Fire suppression systems are designed to quickly detect and respond to fires, reducing damage and increasing safety. Integration improves coordination with other systems.

name: Reduced water damage from suppression activation
rationale: Modern fire suppression integration aims to minimize accidental discharge and water damage by using smarter detection and zoned activation.

name: Enhanced compliance with fire safety regulations
rationale: Building codes and fire safety regulations are established schemas (code frameworks) that mandate integrated fire suppression systems in most commercial and residential buildings.

name: Higher installation and maintenance costs
rationale: Integrating fire suppression with other building systems (alarms, HVAC, access control) increases upfront cost and ongoing maintenance complexity.

name: Minimised false alarm impact on building operations
rationale: Integration can reduce false alarms through cross-verification with other sensors, limiting unnecessary evacuations or disruptions.

name: Greater protection of life and property
rationale: The primary purpose of fire suppression systems is to protect occupants and assets; integration improves overall effectiveness.

name: Restricted system complexity due to interoperability constraints
rationale: Different fire suppression technologies and vendor systems may have limited interoperability, constraining how tightly they can be integrated.

name: Optimised zonal suppression response
rationale: Integration allows fire suppression to target specific zones rather than entire buildings, reducing damage and improving efficiency.

name: Improved energy efficiency through BMS optimization
rationale: BMS integration optimises HVAC, lighting, and other building systems to reduce energy consumption, a primary driver for BMS implementation.

name: Enhanced occupant comfort via fine-grained control
rationale: BMS allows precise monitoring and adjustment of temperature, humidity, air quality, and lighting to improve comfort.

name: Greater system reliability and predictive maintenance
rationale: BMS enables real-time monitoring and diagnostics, reducing downtime and extending equipment life.

name: Optimized operational cost savings over lifecycle
rationale: BMS reduces energy bills, maintenance costs, and staffing requirements, yielding long-term operational savings.

name: Increased fire safety compliance
rationale: Fire alarm riser rooms and panel rooms must comply with fire safety codes (e.g., NFPA 72, IBC), which drives demand for adequate space, accessibility, and proper environmental conditions.

name: Enhanced accessibility for maintenance
rationale: Fire alarm panels and riser equipment require regular inspection, testing, and maintenance, necessitating clear floor space and unobstructed access.

name: Reduced floor area allocation
rationale: Architects and project managers may push to minimize non-revenue-generating spaces, potentially constraining the size of the riser/panel room.

name: Greater clearance requirements
rationale: Electrical and fire alarm codes (NFPA 70, NFPA 72) mandate specific clearances around panels and equipment for safe operation and maintenance.

name: Optimized centralized location
rationale: Fire alarm riser rooms should be centrally located to ensure efficient cable routing, reduced voltage drop, and effective zonal coverage of the building.

name: Restricted adjacent hazardous uses
rationale: Fire alarm equipment rooms should be separated from hazardous areas (e.g., storage of combustibles, mechanical rooms with fuel-burning equipment) per code.

name: Improved accessibility
rationale: Fire command centres need to be easily and quickly accessible to firefighting personnel during emergencies, driving a design pressure for improved access routes, signage, and location within the building.

name: Enhanced fire resistance rating
rationale: Fire command centres must withstand fire conditions to remain operational, requiring higher fire-resistance ratings for walls, floors, doors, and structural elements surrounding the space.

name: Sufficient communication systems
rationale: The fire command centre must be equipped with adequate communication systems (PA, intercom, fire alarm panels, two-way radio) to coordinate emergency response, driving a pressure for sufficient equipment and system integration.

name: Restricted unauthorised access
rationale: Fire command centres should be secured against unauthorised entry to prevent tampering with fire control systems, requiring restricted access controls and limited entry points.

name: Minimised obstruction to equipment
rationale: The space must avoid obstructions that impede access to fire control panels, alarm systems, and communication equipment, driving a pressure for clear floor space and thoughtful layout.

name: Adequate lighting and visibility
rationale: Emergency and normal lighting must be sufficient for reading system displays and maps, driving a design pressure for adequate illumination levels and backup power.

name: Better environmental separation
rationale: The fire command centre should be separated from other building spaces with fire-rated construction to protect occupants and equipment from smoke, heat, and fire spread.

name: Eliminated fire hazards within space
rationale: Combustible materials, flammable storage, and unnecessary ignition sources must be avoided inside the fire command centre to maintain a safe operational environment during a fire event.

name: Higher reliability of backup power
rationale: The fire command centre requires an uninterrupted and reliable backup power supply to remain functional during a fire emergency when main power may be compromised.

name: Improved energy monitoring capability
rationale: A central BMS controller should have enhanced monitoring capabilities to track and optimize building energy consumption effectively.

name: Higher system integration complexity
rationale: The BMS controller must integrate diverse subsystems (HVAC, lighting, security), creating pressure for greater integration capacity.

name: Reduced response latency
rationale: Real-time control requires minimized delay between sensor input and actuator output for efficient building management.

name: Enhanced fault detection capability
rationale: The BMS should have improved diagnostic algorithms to detect equipment faults and inefficiencies early.

name: Lower operational costs pressure
rationale: Building owners desire reduced energy and maintenance costs, pressuring the BMS to optimize system operations.

name: Expanded data processing capacity
rationale: Growing sensor networks and data points require greater processing power and storage in the BMS controller.

name: Improved user interface usability
rationale: Operators need better dashboards and controls for efficient building management, driving UI improvements.

name: Limited communication bandwidth constraint
rationale: Network bandwidth restrictions constrain data flow between the BMS controller and field devices, requiring efficient protocols.

name: Increased operational efficiency pressure
rationale: The BMS Operator Workstation should provide efficient monitoring and control interfaces to allow operators to manage building systems effectively.

name: Improved user interface clarity pressure
rationale: A clear, intuitive user interface design reduces operator errors and improves system responsiveness.

name: Reduced system latency pressure
rationale: Low latency between operator input and system response is critical for effective building management and timely reactions to alarms or faults.

name: Enhanced data visualisation pressure
rationale: Advanced data visualisation (trends, dashboards, schematics) supports better decision-making by operators.

name: Minimised operator cognitive load pressure
rationale: Reducing unnecessary complexity and information overload helps operators focus on critical tasks and alarms.

name: Increased system reliability pressure
rationale: The workstation must be highly reliable to ensure continuous building monitoring and control capability.

name: Restricted unauthorised access pressure
rationale: Security controls should limit access to authorised personnel only, preventing tampering with BMS settings.

name: Improved alarm management pressure
rationale: Effective alarm prioritisation, acknowledgment, and tracking capabilities are essential for operator response to building faults.

name: Improved accessibility pressure
rationale: Field control panels need to be easily accessible for operators to adjust and monitor equipment in the field, driving a pressure toward improved accessibility.

name: Enhanced durability pressure
rationale: Field control panels are exposed to environmental conditions (weather, dust, moisture) so there is a strong pressure for enhanced durability and weatherproofing.

name: Higher reliability pressure
rationale: As a control component, the field control panel must operate reliably to ensure proper functioning of field equipment, creating a pressure for higher reliability.

name: Reduced size pressure
rationale: Field control panels often need to fit in tight spaces or enclosures, creating a pressure for reduced physical footprint.

name: Minimised cost pressure
rationale: Cost constraints in construction and industrial projects drive a pressure for minimised manufacturing and installation costs of field control panels.

name: Improved user interface pressure
rationale: Operators need clear displays and intuitive controls on field panels, creating a pressure for an improved user interface.

name: Limited power consumption pressure
rationale: Field control panels may run on limited power sources or need to minimise energy usage, driving a pressure for limited power consumption.

name: Enhanced environmental protection pressure
rationale: Physical exposure to temperature extremes, moisture, and contaminants creates a pressure for enhanced environmental protection (e.g., NEMA/IP ratings).

name: Reduced maintenance requirement pressure
rationale: Field locations are often difficult to access for maintenance, creating a pressure for reduced maintenance requirements and longer service intervals.

name: Improved network reliability
rationale: BMS communication networks require high reliability for building automation and control functions.

name: Higher data bandwidth
rationale: Modern BMS systems need greater data throughput for real-time monitoring and control.

name: Reduced latency
rationale: Low-latency communication is critical for responsive BMS control loops.

name: Enhanced cybersecurity
rationale: BMS networks are increasingly targeted by cyber attacks; robust security is essential.

name: Reduced installation cost
rationale: Cost constraints drive decisions toward simpler, less expensive network topologies.

name: Expanded coverage area
rationale: Large building complexes require BMS communication networks to span extensive areas.

name: Lower power consumption
rationale: Energy-efficient network components reduce overall building energy use.

name: Greater interoperability
rationale: BMS networks must support multiple protocols (BACnet, Modbus, etc.) for device integration.

name: Minimised signal interference
rationale: Electromagnetic interference can disrupt BMS communications, especially in wireless or mixed topologies.

name: Increased accuracy requirements
rationale: Building systems demand more precise measurements for energy efficiency and occupant comfort, driving the need for higher-accuracy sensors.

name: Enhanced reliability standards
rationale: Critical building operations require fail-safe and durable sensing components to prevent system downtime.

name: Reduced cost constraints
rationale: Budget limitations push toward selecting lower-cost sensor and transmitter options, potentially trade-off against performance.

name: Improved energy efficiency targets
rationale: Low-power sensors and transmitters are needed to reduce overall building energy consumption and meet sustainability goals.

name: Increased data communication bandwidth
rationale: Modern building management systems require higher data transmission rates from transmitters to handle real-time monitoring and analytics.

name: Minimised physical footprint
rationale: Space constraints in building cavities and equipment rooms drive demand for compact sensor and transmitter form factors.

name: Better environmental robustness
rationale: Sensors must withstand temperature extremes, humidity, dust, and vibration within building environments to maintain accuracy.

name: Eliminated wired infrastructure
rationale: Wireless sensor networks reduce installation cost and complexity, pushing toward eliminating wired transmitter connections.

name: Higher sampling frequency
rationale: Faster data acquisition enables better control loops and fault detection in building automation systems.

name: Higher positioning accuracy
rationale: Actuators must provide precise positioning for dampers to regulate airflow effectively in HVAC systems.

name: Reduced energy consumption
rationale: Energy-efficient actuators and damper drives are preferred to minimise operational costs and meet efficiency standards.

name: Greater reliability and durability
rationale: Components must withstand repeated cycling and long-term operation in building HVAC systems.

name: Lower maintenance requirements
rationale: Designs that minimise servicing needs reduce lifecycle costs and downtime.

name: Enhanced control responsiveness
rationale: Fast response times are needed to maintain stable indoor environmental conditions.

name: Reduced noise emission
rationale: Quiet operation is important for occupant comfort, especially in occupied spaces.

name: Adequate torque output
rationale: Sufficient force is required to overcome damper resistance and ensure proper operation.

name: Limited physical footprint
rationale: Compact designs are advantageous for installation in tight mechanical spaces.

name: Improved lifecycle cost
rationale: Balancing initial cost with long-term operational savings drives component selection.

name: Improved usability pressure
rationale: Usability is a core design pressure for HMIs, driving improvements in clarity, responsiveness, and user-friendliness.

name: Increased accessibility pressure
rationale: Accessibility standards (e.g., ADA, WCAG) push for inclusive design accommodating diverse user abilities.

name: Enhanced safety pressure
rationale: Safety-critical systems require HMIs to prevent operator error, provide clear warnings, and ensure fail-safe interactions.

name: Reduced cognitive load pressure
rationale: Designers aim to minimise complexity and information overload to improve operator performance and reduce errors.

name: Optimised response time pressure
rationale: Real-time control systems demand minimal latency in HMI feedback to maintain operational efficiency.

name: Minimised visual clutter pressure

name: Higher reliability pressure
rationale: HMIs must function consistently under all operating conditions to avoid downtime or hazardous situations.

name: Restricted input error pressure

name: Enhanced feedback clarity pressure

name: Increased data storage capacity

name: Higher data throughput
rationale: Data Historian Servers need to handle high-frequency data ingestion from numerous sources; higher throughput improves real-time data capture capability.

name: Reduced data latency
rationale: Minimizing the time between data generation and storage is critical for real-time monitoring and control applications.

name: Improved data compression efficiency
rationale: Better compression allows more historical data to be stored within available storage capacity, extending retention periods.

name: Higher query response performance
rationale: Fast retrieval of historical data for analysis and reporting is a critical requirement for data historian systems.

name: Reduced hardware footprint
rationale: Minimizing physical space, power consumption, and cooling requirements is often desirable in data center environments.

name: Enhanced data reliability
rationale: Data integrity and reliability are paramount for historian systems that store critical operational history.

name: Adequate redundancy provision

name: Reduced operational cost
rationale: Lowering total cost of ownership through efficient resource utilization and maintenance optimization is a common design pressure.

name: Increased reliability requirement for BMS operations
