name: Higher flow rate capacity
rationale: The check valve must allow sufficient hot water flow to meet system demand without excessive pressure drop.

name: Reduced backflow risk
rationale: The primary function of a check valve is to prevent reverse flow, so minimising backflow is essential for system safety and efficiency.

name: Improved sealing reliability
rationale: Reliable sealing prevents leakage when the valve is closed under backpressure, which is critical in hot water systems.

name: Lower pressure drop across valve
rationale: Minimising pressure loss through the check valve helps maintain adequate system pressure and reduces pump energy consumption.

name: Enhanced temperature resistance
rationale: Hot water service requires the valve materials and design to withstand elevated temperatures without degradation.

name: Sufficient hot water delivery pressure
rationale: Point-of-use water heaters must deliver hot water at adequate pressure to fixtures, driving design decisions for heating capacity and flow rate.

name: Reduced standby energy losses
rationale: Minimizing standby heat losses is a key design pressure to improve overall energy efficiency for point-of-use water heaters.

name: Limited physical footprint
rationale: Point-of-use water heaters are often installed in tight under-sink or closet spaces, constraining the allowable physical dimensions.

name: Improved heating element durability
rationale: Longevity and reliability of heating elements are a design pressure to reduce maintenance and replacement frequency.

name: Minimised scalding risk
rationale: Safety standards and user expectations require temperature regulation to prevent scalding, pushing designs toward lower maximum outlet temperatures or anti-scald valves.

name: Lower initial cost
rationale: Budget constraints in residential and commercial projects place downward pressure on the purchase and installation cost of point-of-use water heaters.

name: Improved measurement accuracy
rationale: Flow meters require accurate measurement of fluid flow rates; pressure to improve accuracy drives design decisions such as sensor selection and calibration.

name: Reduced pressure drop
rationale: Flow meters should minimise pressure loss across the device to maintain system efficiency; this drives design decisions about meter geometry and type.

name: Increased flow range capacity
rationale: Flow meters need to handle a wide range of flow rates (turndown ratio); pressure to expand the measurable range influences design choices.

name: Reduced maintenance frequency
rationale: Flow meters should require minimal maintenance to reduce operational downtime; this pressure affects material selection and design simplicity.

name: Enhanced durability against harsh conditions
rationale: Flow meters must withstand corrosive fluids, high temperatures, or pressures; pressure for stronger, more durable construction drives material and coating decisions.

name: Minimised installation cost
rationale: Economic pressure to lower upfront installation expenses influences the choice of meter type and integration method.

name: Improved isolation reliability
rationale: Gate and ball isolation valves are designed to provide reliable shut-off; there is engineering pressure to increase sealing effectiveness and operational reliability for isolation duty.

name: Reduced leakage risk
rationale: Isolation valves must minimise internal and external leakage; engineering standards push for reduced leakage to ensure system integrity and safety.

name: Minimised pressure drop across valve
rationale: Gate and ball valves in fully open position should offer minimal flow resistance; there is pressure to lower pressure drop to maintain system efficiency.

name: Higher operating pressure rating
rationale: Isolation valves must withstand system operating pressures; there is design pressure to achieve a higher pressure class rating for safety and compatibility.

name: Greater material durability
rationale: Valves are subject to wear, corrosion, and erosion; there is pressure for greater material durability to extend service life.

name: Reduced maintenance frequency
rationale: Isolation valves in critical systems should require less frequent maintenance to minimise downtime; design pressure exists to lower maintenance needs through robust design.

name: Prevented unintended opening/closing
rationale: Safety and operational requirements demand that isolation valves avoid accidental actuation; there is pressure to prevent unintended operation.

name: Optimised actuation torque
rationale: Valve design seeks an optimal balance where actuation torque is sufficient for reliable sealing but not excessive; there is pressure to optimise torque characteristics.

name: Eliminated internal contamination risk
rationale: Isolation valves must prevent debris or contaminants from bypassing the seal; there is pressure to eliminate contamination paths for system cleanliness.

name: Improved temperature regulation
rationale: The Hot Water Zone Controller must provide accurate temperature regulation to maintain occupant comfort, pushing toward better control logic and sensor accuracy.

name: Higher energy efficiency
rationale: Energy codes and sustainability goals demand that zone controllers minimize unnecessary heating, driving design toward optimized scheduling and setpoint management.

name: Reduced installation cost
rationale: Budget constraints push toward simpler, less expensive control solutions, potentially limiting advanced features or sensor integration.

name: Lower maintenance complexity
rationale: Building operators prefer controllers that are easy to troubleshoot and maintain, driving design toward fewer components and simplified wiring.

name: Enhanced communication reliability
rationale: Reliable BAS integration demands robust communication protocols (BACnet, Modbus) to prevent loss of control signals, pushing toward higher-quality network interfaces.

name: Restricted physical footprint
rationale: Space constraints in mechanical rooms or above-ceiling locations push toward compact controller designs with smaller enclosures.

name: Higher temperature accuracy
rationale: Thermostats require accurate temperature sensing to properly regulate HVAC systems; higher accuracy improves comfort and energy efficiency.

name: Improved user interface readability
rationale: Users need to easily read and interact with the thermostat; a clear display and intuitive controls enhance usability.

name: Reduced response time
rationale: Faster response to temperature changes improves system efficiency and occupant comfort; delay should be minimized.

name: Lower energy consumption
rationale: Thermostat controllers should consume minimal power themselves to contribute to overall building energy efficiency; standby power should be minimised.

name: Greater connectivity reliability
rationale: Smart thermostats rely on stable wireless or wired connections; reliable communication is essential for remote control and data logging.

name: Reduced physical footprint
rationale: A smaller thermostat device can be less visually intrusive and fit better on walls alongside other controls, though size is often standardised.

name: Enhanced durability against tampering
rationale: In public or commercial buildings, thermostats should resist accidental or intentional damage; a robust casing improves longevity.

name: Eliminated calibration drift
rationale: Temperature sensors must maintain accuracy over time; calibration drift should be prevented to avoid incorrect HVAC operation.

name: Improved exhaust capacity
rationale: The flue/exhaust vent must be adequately sized to expel combustion gases from the water heater to prevent backdraft and ensure safe operation.

name: Reduced backdraft risk
rationale: Negative pressure or blockage in the vent can cause backdrafting of combustion gases into the building, posing a health hazard.

name: Higher corrosion resistance
rationale: Exhaust vents are exposed to acidic condensate from combustion gases, requiring corrosion-resistant materials (e.g., stainless steel or AL29-4C).

name: Minimised condensation damage
rationale: Condensate from flue gases can corrode the vent and surrounding structure if not properly drained or if vent material is not suitable.

name: Adequate clearance from combustibles
rationale: Building codes (e.g., IRC, IMC) mandate specific clearance distances between exhaust vents and combustible materials to prevent fire hazards.

name: Reduced obstruction risk
rationale: The vent termination must be located away from windows, doors, or air intakes to prevent re-entrainment of exhaust gases into the building.

name: Sufficient gas pressure for water heater operation
rationale: The gas supply line must deliver adequate gas pressure and volume to the water heater for proper combustion and operation.

name: Reduced risk of gas leaks
rationale: Gas supply lines must be designed to minimise leak risks through proper materials, joints, and routing to ensure safety.

name: Adequate pipe diameter for flow capacity
rationale: The pipe diameter must be sufficient to deliver the required gas flow rate (BTU/hr) to the water heater without excessive pressure drop.

name: Optimised placement relative to water heater location
rationale: The supply line entry point and path should be optimally positioned relative to the water heater for efficient connection and maintenance access.

name: Reduced number of fittings and joints
rationale: Fewer fittings and joints reduce potential leak points and pressure losses in the gas supply system.

name: Improved compliance with gas code requirements
rationale: The gas supply line design must comply with local gas codes and regulations (e.g., proper materials, clearances, shut-off valves, venting requirements).

name: Eliminated corrosion risk
rationale: Corrosion of gas pipes can lead to leaks and failures; appropriate materials (e.g., black iron, corrosion-resistant coatings) should be specified.

name: Greater accessibility for maintenance and shut-off
rationale: The gas shut-off valve and accessible portions of the supply line must be positioned where maintenance personnel can easily reach them.

name: Increased electrical load capacity
rationale: Water heaters require sufficient electrical capacity to handle heating element loads; undersized supply can lead to breaker trips or inadequate heating.

name: Reduced wiring resistance
rationale: Lower resistance in wiring (achieved via proper gauge and connections) improves efficiency and safety for continuous high-current operation of water heaters.

name: Enhanced safety protection
rationale: Code requirements mandate GFCI or other protection for water heater circuits to prevent shock hazards, especially in wet locations.

name: Restricted voltage drop
rationale: Excessive voltage drop reduces heating element performance and can cause premature failure; wiring must be sized to keep drop within recommended limits.

name: Adequate conductor sizing
rationale: Water heaters are continuous loads, requiring conductors sized at 125% of the rated load per NEC guidelines.

name: Reduced risk of electrical fire
rationale: Proper overcurrent protection, secure connections, and appropriate insulation reduce fire risk from faulty water heater wiring.

name: Reduced leakage risk
rationale: Floor drains and drain pans must minimize water leakage to prevent structural damage and mold growth.

name: Adequate drainage capacity
rationale: Drain pans and floor drains need sufficient capacity to handle expected water flow from equipment (e.g., HVAC condensate) and floor cleaning.

name: Prevented clogging
rationale: Debris and sediment buildup can block drains, causing overflow and water damage, so clogging must be prevented.

name: Improved accessibility for maintenance
rationale: Drains and pans must be accessible for regular cleaning and inspection to ensure long-term functionality.

name: Reduced corrosion risk
rationale: Drain pan materials must resist corrosion from standing water and chemical exposure to maintain integrity over time.

name: Increased ventilation capacity
rationale: Plant/mechanical rooms house HVAC equipment that requires adequate ventilation for heat rejection and combustion air, pushing toward greater ventilation capacity.

name: Optimised equipment layout density
rationale: Mechanical rooms must efficiently house boilers, chillers, pumps, and air handlers within a constrained footprint, driving the need for optimised spatial layout.

name: Reduced noise transmission to adjacent spaces
rationale: Mechanical equipment generates significant noise; architectural design pressures push to contain noise within the plant room and limit disturbance to occupied spaces.

name: Adequate maintenance access clearances
rationale: Building codes and serviceability requirements mandate sufficient clearance around equipment for inspection, repair, and replacement.

name: Higher structural load capacity
rationale: Heavy mechanical equipment (chillers, boilers, transformers) imposes significant dead loads, requiring enhanced structural support.

name: Minimised floor area footprint
rationale: There is pressure to minimise the size of plant rooms to maximise leasable or usable floor area in a building.

name: Improved fire resistance rating
rationale: Building regulations require enhanced fire separation and fire-resistance ratings for mechanical rooms due to fuel and electrical fire risks.

name: Expanded ductwork and piping routes
rationale: The plant room must accommodate ductwork, piping, and conduit runs connecting to building systems, driving a need for larger or taller spaces.

name: Restricted ceiling height for equipment clearance
rationale: While tall equipment needs headroom, there can be pressure to restrict overall plant room height to fit within building floor-to-floor constraints.

name: Increased solar heat gain for thermal efficiency
rationale: Solar collectors require adequate solar exposure to maximise thermal energy capture; orienting and sizing the roof deck to maximise insolation is an engineering design pressure.

name: Reduced shading from adjacent structures
rationale: Obstructions or parapets casting shadows over the solar collector area reduce performance, so minimising shading is a key design pressure.

name: Greater structural load capacity for collector weight
rationale: Solar collectors and mounting systems add significant dead load; the roof deck must be designed with adequate structural capacity to support them.

name: Adequate roof area for collector array layout
rationale: Sufficient unobstructed roof area is needed to accommodate the required number of solar panels or collectors to meet energy targets.

name: Optimised roof slope for collector tilt angle
rationale: The roof slope should match or accommodate the optimal tilt angle of solar collectors for the geographic latitude to maximise annual energy yield.

name: Reduced roof penetrations and mounting complexity
rationale: Minimising the number of roof penetrations for mounting systems reduces water ingress risk and simplifies installation and maintenance.

name: Enhanced wind uplift resistance for roof-mounted collectors
rationale: Solar collectors mounted on flat or low-slope roofs are vulnerable to wind uplift forces; stronger wind-resistance detailing is required.

name: Adequate access for maintenance of collectors
rationale: Maintenance pathways and safe access around solar collector arrays are needed for cleaning, inspection, and repair, influencing roof layout.

name: Increased gas supply capacity
rationale: Gas meters need sufficient capacity to handle peak demand loads from connected gas appliances.

name: Reduced pressure drop
rationale: Minimising pressure loss across the meter ensures adequate gas pressure reaches downstream appliances.

name: Improved metering accuracy
rationale: Accurate measurement is critical for billing, safety, and monitoring gas consumption.

name: Reduced installation cost
rationale: Lower costs make the gas meter installation more economically viable.

name: Enhanced safety compliance
rationale: Gas meter design must comply with safety regulations to prevent leaks and hazards.

name: Reduced physical size
rationale: Smaller gas meters require less space and are easier to install in confined areas.

name: Greater durability against corrosion
rationale: Gas meters must withstand environmental exposure and corrosive gas constituents over their service life.

name: Restricted leakage risk
rationale: Minimising gas leakage is essential for safety, environmental, and operational reasons.

name: Adequate flow measurement range
rationale: The meter must handle both minimum and maximum expected flow rates for accurate measurement across all operating conditions.

name: Reduced pressure fluctuation
rationale: Gas pressure regulators are designed to reduce and stabilise fluctuating inlet pressures to a consistent outlet pressure, protecting downstream equipment.

name: Adequate flow capacity
rationale: The regulator must have sufficient capacity to handle the required gas flow rate without excessive pressure drop.

name: Minimised leakage risk
rationale: Gas regulators must prevent gas leaks to ensure safety; leakage paths must be eliminated or minimised.

name: Optimised response time
rationale: The regulator should respond quickly to changes in demand or inlet pressure to maintain stable outlet pressure.

name: Limited inlet pressure variation
rationale: Excessive inlet pressure variation can affect regulator performance; upstream conditions should be constrained to protect the regulator.

name: Improved material durability
rationale: Materials used in the regulator must withstand corrosive gases and long-term wear for reliable operation.

name: Reduced maintenance frequency
rationale: Design pressures aim to minimise the need for frequent maintenance interventions on the regulator.

name: Increased safety pressure
rationale: Safety codes require robust gas piping to prevent leaks and hazards.

name: Reduced cost pressure
rationale: Budget constraints push for minimizing material and installation costs for gas piping.

name: Higher capacity pressure
rationale: Demand for sufficient gas flow may require larger diameter or higher pressure-rated piping.

name: Reduced space pressure
rationale: Limited available space in building shafts or ceilings restricts pipe routing and size.

rationale: Need for adequate corrosion resistance and durability drives material optimization.

name: Maximised ease of manual operation
rationale: Valves should be easy for personnel to operate manually during emergencies or routine shutoffs.

rationale: Space and structural constraints may limit the allowable dimensions and mass of the valve installation.

name: Reduced leakage risk
rationale: Gas riser pipes must be designed to minimise gas leakage for safety reasons, requiring robust joints and materials.

rationale: Pipes should have enhanced corrosion resistance to ensure long service life and safety.

rationale: Minimising pressure drop along the riser ensures adequate gas pressure reaches upper floor outlets.

rationale: Gas flex connectors must meet stringent safety codes and standards to prevent gas leaks and fire hazards, creating pressure for enhanced safety features.

rationale: Gas flex connectors are subject to cyclic stresses from thermal expansion and vibration; engineering design seeks to minimize fatigue failure risk.

name: Improved corrosion resistance
rationale: Exposure to environmental moisture and potential chemical agents creates pressure for better corrosion-resistant materials or coatings.

name: Reduced installation complexity
rationale: Ease of installation is a practical design consideration, driving pressure to simplify connector design and minimize specialized labor requirements.

name: Higher flow capacity
rationale: Gas appliances may require adequate gas flow rates, creating pressure for greater internal diameter or optimized flow geometry to minimize pressure drop.

name: Restricted leakage risk
rationale: Gas leaks pose significant safety hazards; design pressures strongly constrain any potential leakage pathways through improved sealing and connection integrity.

name: Increased seismic safety compliance
rationale: Seismic safety codes and standards require automatic gas shutoff devices to be installed in earthquake-prone areas to prevent gas leaks and fires.

name: Reduced post-earthquake fire risk
rationale: The primary purpose of the device is to cut off gas supply during seismic events, thereby reducing the risk of fires following earthquakes.

name: Higher installation and maintenance cost
rationale: Seismic gas shutoff devices add additional upfront cost for procurement, installation, and periodic testing/maintenance compared to standard gas systems.

name: Reduced operational reliability concerns
rationale: There may be concerns about nuisance tripping (false shutoffs) from non-seismic vibrations or about the device failing to activate when needed, which can reduce reliability.

name: Improved building resilience rating
rationale: Installing seismic shutoff devices contributes to higher resilience scores in building rating systems and may be required for certain insurance or certification programs.

name: Increased detection sensitivity
rationale: Higher sensitivity allows earlier detection of smaller gas leaks, improving safety.

name: Reduced false alarm rate
rationale: Minimising false alarms ensures the sensor is trusted and avoids unnecessary shutdowns or evacuations.

name: Improved response time
rationale: Faster detection and alerting reduce the risk of gas accumulation and potential explosion.

name: Expanded coverage area
rationale: Wider coverage ensures that gas leaks in larger or irregular spaces are detected promptly.

name: Reduced maintenance frequency
rationale: Lower maintenance requirements improve system reliability and reduce operational costs.

name: Improved environmental robustness
rationale: Greater resistance to temperature, humidity, and vibration ensures consistent performance in harsh conditions.

name: Lower power consumption
rationale: Reduced energy usage extends battery life and supports sustainable building operations.

name: Minimised sensor drift
rationale: Less calibration drift maintains accurate gas concentration readings over time.

name: Optimised placement density
rationale: Proper spacing and positioning ensure no blind spots while avoiding redundancy.

name: higher pressure relief capacity
rationale: The valve must be sized to handle maximum expected overpressure scenarios to ensure safety.

name: reduced response time
rationale: Faster opening response minimises pressure buildup and risk of system failure.

name: greater set pressure accuracy
rationale: Accurate pressure setpoint ensures valve opens at the correct threshold to protect downstream equipment.

name: minimised leakage rate
rationale: Low or zero leakage at normal operating pressure prevents gas loss and environmental hazards.

name: enhanced material durability
rationale: Materials must resist corrosion and wear from gases over the valve's service life.

name: lower maintenance frequency
rationale: Reducing maintenance intervals improves reliability and operational cost efficiency.

name: adequate flow coefficient (Cv)
rationale: Sufficient Cv ensures the valve can relieve the required gas volume at set pressure.

name: restricted backpressure effect
rationale: Backpressure must be limited to avoid impairing valve lift and relief capacity.

name: optimised spring stiffness
rationale: Spring stiffness must be optimised to achieve proper blowdown and reseating characteristics.

rationale: LPG systems require strict adherence to safety codes (e.g. ventilation, leak detection, pressure relief) to prevent explosion or fire hazards.

name: Reduced leak risk pressure
rationale: LPG is highly flammable; design must minimise the potential for leaks through robust piping, fittings, and monitoring.

name: Optimised space allocation pressure
rationale: Storage tanks and equipment need adequate spatial footprint while balancing overall site layout constraints.

name: Limited environmental exposure pressure
rationale: LPG tanks and components should be sheltered from extreme weather, UV radiation, and physical damage to ensure integrity.

name: Lower maintenance burden pressure
rationale: Accessibility for inspection and servicing should be maximised to reduce ongoing operational effort and cost.

name: Adequate ventilation provision pressure

name: Eliminated ignition source proximity pressure
rationale: LPG system components must be located away from electrical sparks, open flames, and hot surfaces to prevent ignition.

name: Greater regulatory compliance pressure
rationale: Design must comply with local and international codes (e.g. NFPA 58, AS/NZS 1596, or equivalent) governing LPG storage and handling.

name: Increased gas supply reliability
rationale: Natural gas service connections must provide reliable gas supply to downstream building systems such as boilers, heaters, and kitchen equipment.

name: Higher gas flow capacity
rationale: The connection must be sized to handle peak gas demand from all connected appliances, requiring adequate flow capacity.

name: Reduced pressure drop
rationale: Minimising pressure loss across the service connection ensures sufficient gas pressure reaches terminal equipment.

name: Limited installation cost
rationale: Cost constraints typically pressure designers to minimise the expense of gas connection piping, metering, and trenching.

name: Reduced leak risk
rationale: Safety is paramount for gas systems; the design must minimise the risk of gas leaks through proper material selection, jointing, and routing.

name: Improved compliance with gas codes
rationale: Gas service connections must comply with local gas utility regulations and building codes, driving the need for code-compliant design.

name: Greater accessibility for maintenance
rationale: The gas service connection, including shut-off valves and meters, should be accessible for routine inspection, emergency shut-off, and maintenance.

name: Restricted footprint for gas infrastructure
rationale: Site constraints and architectural planning limit the space available for gas service equipment such as meter banks and regulator sets.

name: Eliminated interference with other utilities
rationale: Gas service routing must avoid or be separated from other underground utilities (electric, water, telecom) to prevent cross-utility conflicts and safety hazards.

name: Higher storage pressure capacity
rationale: CNG storage systems require higher pressure capacity to store more gas volume within the same physical tank size, directly affecting tank wall thickness and material selection.

name: Increased safety margin for pressure containment
rationale: Safety codes and standards require design pressures to include safety margins above normal operating pressure to prevent rupture or leakage.

name: Reduced material fatigue from pressure cycling
rationale: Frequent pressure cycles during filling and discharging cause material fatigue; design aims to limit stress ranges to extend service life.

name: Optimised pressure-to-weight ratio
rationale: For vehicular or transportable CNG systems, maximising storage pressure while minimising container weight is a key design driver.

name: Lower burst pressure risk
rationale: Design must ensure that the burst pressure of the storage vessel is significantly higher than the maximum allowable working pressure, reducing catastrophic failure risk.

name: Higher discharge pressure
rationale: Gas booster systems are designed to increase gas pressure from a lower inlet to a higher outlet pressure for distribution or downstream processes.

name: Improved energy efficiency
rationale: Efficiency is a key design objective to minimise operating costs and energy consumption in gas compression.

name: Reduced maintenance downtime
rationale: Designs aim to minimise maintenance requirements and downtime to ensure reliable gas supply.

name: Limited footprint
rationale: Space constraints often require gas booster systems to have a compact design, especially in retrofit or offshore applications.

name: Higher flow capacity
rationale: Sufficient flow capacity must be provided to meet the required gas demand of downstream processes.

name: Reduced vibration and noise
rationale: Gas boosters (reciprocating or centrifugal compressors) generate vibration and noise that must be controlled for safety and operational comfort.

name: Higher reliability
rationale: Reliability is critical as gas booster systems are often part of essential supply infrastructure.

name: Reduced capital cost
rationale: Cost constraints pressure designers to minimise upfront investment in equipment.

name: Adequate safety margins
rationale: Safety is paramount in high-pressure gas systems, requiring sufficient design margins for pressure containment and overpressure protection.

name: Increased safety compliance
rationale: Gas and electricity metering rooms must meet strict safety regulations to prevent fire/explosion hazards, driving pressure for enhanced safety features.

name: Improved accessibility for maintenance
rationale: Metering equipment requires regular inspection and maintenance, creating pressure for adequate access and clearances.

name: Reduced fire risk
rationale: Combining gas (flammable) and electricity (ignition source) in one room increases fire risk, driving pressure to minimise hazards through separation, ventilation, and fire-rated construction.

name: Maximised spatial efficiency
rationale: Meter rooms should be compact to minimise loss of usable floor area, creating pressure for efficient layout and equipment arrangement.

name: Restricted unauthorised access
rationale: Gas and electrical utilities are safety-critical and subject to tampering risks, driving pressure to limit access to authorised personnel only.

name: Adequate ventilation capacity
rationale: Gas metering areas require ventilation to prevent gas accumulation, while electrical equipment generates heat — both drive pressure for sufficient ventilation.

name: Improved gas meter accessibility
rationale: Gas meters need to be accessible for reading, maintenance, and emergency shut-off, placing pressure to improve access.

name: Increased ventilation requirements
rationale: Gas meter enclosures require adequate ventilation to prevent gas accumulation in case of leaks, creating a pressure for increased ventilation openings.

name: Reduced fire risk
rationale: Gas meter enclosures must be designed to minimise fire risk due to the presence of flammable gas.

name: Greater weather protection
rationale: The enclosure must protect the gas meter from weather elements such as rain, snow, and UV radiation to ensure proper functioning.

name: Enhanced security against tampering
rationale: Gas meters require protection from unauthorised access and tampering for safety and regulatory compliance.

name: Minimised enclosure size
rationale: Architectural and aesthetic considerations may pressure a smaller enclosure footprint to minimise visual impact.

name: Adequate clearance around meter
rationale: Building codes and safety regulations require sufficient clearance around the gas meter for safe operation and maintenance.

name: Sufficient structural integrity
rationale: The enclosure must have adequate structural strength to withstand loads and protect the gas meter.

name: Eliminated moisture ingress
rationale: Moisture must be prevented from entering the enclosure to avoid corrosion and damage to the gas meter.

name: Increased ventilation rate
rationale: LPG storage requires adequate ventilation to prevent gas accumulation, thus a force toward higher ventilation rates.

name: Reduced ignition sources
rationale: LPG is highly flammable; ignition sources must be minimised to avoid fire/explosion hazards.

name: Enhanced fire resistance rating
rationale: Fire-rated construction is needed for LPG storage enclosures to contain potential fires.

name: Restricted public access
rationale: Safety and regulatory norms require limiting unauthorised access to LPG storage areas.

name: Greater separation distance from other spaces
rationale: LPG stores must be set back from buildings, property lines, and ignition sources per safety codes.

name: Adequate explosion relief provisions
rationale: Explosion venting is necessary to relieve pressure in case of accidental gas ignition.

name: Minimised gas leakage potential
rationale: Leak-tight fittings, valves, and monitoring systems are critical to prevent uncontrolled gas release.

name: Improved emergency ventilation and gas detection
rationale: Gas detection systems and emergency ventilation ensure rapid response to leaks.

name: Sufficient signage and warning markings
rationale: Standard safety signage for LPG storage is required to inform personnel and emergency responders.

name: Higher compressed air output
rationale: Air compressor units are typically designed to deliver sufficient compressed air volume and pressure to meet downstream demand, driving an increase in output capacity.

name: Improved energy efficiency
rationale: There is a design pressure to optimise energy consumption of the air compressor unit, as compressors are often significant energy users in a facility.

name: Reduced maintenance requirements
rationale: Designers aim to minimise maintenance frequency and complexity for air compressor units to improve reliability and reduce operational costs.

name: Lower noise emissions
rationale: Air compressors can be noisy; there is often a pressure to reduce noise emissions through enclosures, silencers, or quieter compressor types.

name: Reduced footprint
rationale: Space constraints in plant rooms or mechanical areas create pressure to minimise the physical footprint of the air compressor unit.

name: Adequate reliability
rationale: Critical applications require the air compressor unit to have sufficient reliability, potentially including redundancy or robust components.

name: Increased pressure containment capacity
rationale: The receiver tank must withstand the maximum operating pressure of the compressed air system, requiring adequate wall thickness and material strength for safe pressure containment.

name: Optimised storage volume
rationale: Sufficient storage volume is needed to dampen pressure fluctuations, handle peak demand, and allow compressor control systems to cycle properly without short-cycling.

name: Reduced moisture accumulation
rationale: Moisture in compressed air can cause corrosion inside the tank and downstream issues; design should minimise internal moisture via drainage and proper tank orientation.

name: Minimised pressure drop
rationale: Inlet and outlet piping connections should be sized and configured to minimise pressure losses across the receiver tank, maintaining system efficiency.

name: Adequate corrosion resistance
rationale: Interior surfaces should be protected against corrosion from condensed water and contaminants, often via coatings or use of corrosion-resistant materials.

name: Restricted heat gain from environment
rationale: In hot environments, excessive heat gain can raise air temperature inside the tank, reducing density and effective storage capacity; insulation may be warranted.

name: Sufficient safety margin
rationale: Pressure vessels require design safety factors per codes (e.g., ASME BPVC) to account for material variability, cyclic loading, and worst-case operating conditions.

name: Eliminated leakage points
rationale: All welded joints, flanges, and fittings should be designed to prevent compressed air leakage, which wastes energy and reduces system pressure.

name: Optimised drain system
rationale: An effective automatic or manual condensate drain system is needed to remove accumulated moisture without losing excessive compressed air.

name: Increased set pressure accuracy
rationale: Pressure relief valves must accurately open at their set pressure to prevent overpressure conditions while avoiding unnecessary relief events; engineering standards mandate precise calibration.

name: Higher relieving capacity
rationale: The valve must be sized to handle the maximum possible flow from overpressure scenarios to safely discharge excess pressure.

name: Reduced leak rate
rationale: Seat leakage must be minimised to prevent loss of system fluid and maintain operational efficiency between relief events.

name: Minimised response time
rationale: The valve must open quickly when set pressure is exceeded to prevent damaging pressure spikes in the system.

name: Improved material corrosion resistance
rationale: Valve materials must resist corrosion from the process fluid and environment to ensure long-term reliable operation.

name: Lower blowdown pressure
rationale: The blowdown (pressure difference between opening and closing) should be minimised to reduce product loss and system disturbance after a relief event.

name: Improved separation efficiency
rationale: Higher separation efficiency ensures better removal of oil and particulates from water, a key performance requirement for oil-water separators.

name: Reduced pressure drop
rationale: Lower pressure drop across the coalescing filter minimizes energy consumption for pumping and improves system efficiency.

name: Greater flow capacity
rationale: Higher flow capacity ensures the separator can handle peak loads without bypass or overflow.

name: Reduced maintenance frequency
rationale: Less frequent maintenance reduces operational downtime and labor costs associated with filter replacement or cleaning.

name: Improved oil recovery rate
rationale: Maximizing the recovery of separated oil adds value and reduces waste disposal requirements.

name: Reduced footprint
rationale: A smaller physical footprint allows for more flexible installation in space-constrained mechanical rooms or skids.

name: Increased corrosion resistance
rationale: Enhanced corrosion resistance extends the service life of the separator in harsh, wet environments with hydrocarbons.

name: Higher drying capacity
rationale: The air dryer unit must provide sufficient drying capacity to meet the moisture removal requirements of the compressed air system, ensuring dew point specifications are achieved.

name: Optimised energy efficiency
rationale: Energy-efficient operation of the air dryer is important to minimise operational costs and overall system energy consumption.

name: Reduced pressure drop
rationale: Minimising pressure drop across the air dryer unit is critical to maintain system pressure and avoid additional compressor load.

name: Lower maintenance requirements
rationale: Design decisions should aim to reduce maintenance frequency and complexity to improve reliability and reduce downtime.

name: Restricted physical footprint
rationale: Space constraints within the mechanical room or facility layout may limit the allowable size and mounting configuration of the air dryer unit.

name: Adequate flow capacity
rationale: The air dryer must be sized to handle the full design flow rate of the compressed air system without exceeding its rated capacity.

name: Lower initial capital cost
rationale: Budget constraints may drive decisions toward more cost-effective dryer technologies or smaller units, though this can trade off against performance.

name: Improved reliability
rationale: Reliable operation of the air dryer is essential to avoid moisture-related damage downstream and maintain compressed air quality.

name: Higher distribution efficiency
rationale: Distribution piping networks must efficiently transport fluids (water, gas, steam) across buildings, driving demand for optimised pipe sizing, routing, and material selection.

name: Reduced pressure losses
rationale: Minimising frictional and dynamic pressure drops in piping is critical to maintaining adequate flow rates and reducing pumping energy requirements.

name: Sufficient thermal insulation
rationale: For heating/cooling distribution, adequate insulation is needed to limit thermal losses/gains and maintain energy performance.

name: Reduced installation cost
rationale: Budget constraints push toward minimised material usage, simpler routing, and standardised components in piping network design.

name: Greater pipe durability
rationale: Piping systems require strong, corrosion-resistant materials to ensure long service life and avoid leaks or failures.

name: Restricted spatial footprint
rationale: Architectural constraints limit the available space for pipe runs, requiring compact routing and smaller-diameter pipes where possible.

name: Optimised network layout
rationale: An optimised piping layout minimises total pipe length, number of fittings, and complexity, improving both cost and hydraulic performance.

name: Lower maintenance requirements
rationale: Design decisions aim to minimise future maintenance needs through accessible routing, durable materials, and simple joint configurations.

name: Expanded flow capacity
rationale: The network must be sized to handle peak demand flows, potentially requiring larger pipe diameters or redundant paths.

name: Optimized pressure regulation accuracy
rationale: A pressure regulator/reducing valve must accurately maintain downstream pressure within desired limits despite upstream fluctuations, requiring optimized design for precise control.

name: Reduced pressure drop across valve
rationale: Minimizing inherent pressure loss through the valve improves system efficiency and reduces energy consumption, a key design pressure for any flow control component.

name: Higher flow capacity
rationale: The valve must accommodate peak flow demands without excessive pressure drop or instability, driving the need for greater flow capacity (Cv).

name: Minimized leakage (internal/external)
rationale: Leakage past the valve seat (internal) or through stem seals (external) wastes energy and fluid; design must minimize or eliminate leakage to meet performance and safety standards.

name: Improved response time to pressure transients
rationale: The valve should quickly react to sudden changes in upstream pressure or downstream demand to prevent pressure surges or starvation, requiring enhanced dynamic response.

name: Greater material durability and corrosion resistance
rationale: The valve body and internal components must withstand operating pressures, temperature, and corrosive media over long service life, driving stronger materials and protective coatings.

name: Lower installation and maintenance complexity
rationale: Simpler valve design with fewer parts and accessible trim reduces installation cost and maintenance downtime, a practical pressure on design decisions.

name: Constrained physical envelope (size/weight)
rationale: Limited space in piping systems and skids imposes restrictions on valve overall dimensions and weight, pushing toward more compact designs.

name: Eliminated risk of cavitation and erosion
rationale: High pressure drop across the valve can cause cavitation, leading to noise, vibration, and material damage; design must eliminate or mitigate cavitation through trim selection and staging.

name: Higher compressed air pressure
rationale: Compressed air systems require adequate pressure at the service point to power pneumatic tools and equipment effectively.

name: Increased number of service points
rationale: More outlets may be needed to serve multiple workstations simultaneously without constant hose changes.

name: Reduced pressure loss in distribution
rationale: Minimising pressure drops between the compressor and the outlet ensures the service point delivers adequate working pressure.

name: Improved accessibility of service points
rationale: Service points should be conveniently located for ease of connection by operators.

name: Lower risk of moisture contamination
rationale: Moisture in compressed air can damage tools and affect product quality, so dry air delivery at the outlet is important.

name: Increased isolation reliability
rationale: The isolation valve must reliably stop flow in its closed position to allow maintenance or emergency shutdown; higher reliability is a typical engineering design requirement.

name: Reduced leakage
rationale: Minimising leakage through the valve when closed is a primary functional requirement to ensure effective isolation and prevent unintended flow.

name: Minimised pressure drop
rationale: In the open position, the valve should present minimal resistance to flow to avoid energy loss and maintain system efficiency.

name: Adequate pressure rating
rationale: The valve must be rated to withstand the maximum system operating pressure without failure, a critical safety and design consideration.

name: Reduced actuation force
rationale: Lower force required to open or close the valve improves operability, especially in manual or emergency situations.

name: Higher corrosion resistance
rationale: The valve material must resist corrosion from the working fluid to ensure long service life and maintain sealing integrity.

name: Minimised cost
rationale: Economic pressure to reduce procurement and installation costs of the valve, balanced against performance requirements.

name: Reduced maintenance frequency
rationale: Design should aim to minimise the need for periodic maintenance to reduce operational downtime and lifecycle costs.

name: Increased measurement accuracy
rationale: Pressure gauges and monitoring instruments require high accuracy to provide reliable readings for system control and safety.

name: Higher pressure rating capacity
rationale: The gauge must be rated to withstand the maximum system pressure without damage or failure.

name: Improved durability and reliability
rationale: Durable construction ensures long service life and consistent performance under operating conditions.

name: Reduced measurement lag time
rationale: Fast response time is critical for real-time monitoring and control applications.

name: Minimised calibration drift
rationale: Low drift ensures sustained accuracy over time and reduces maintenance frequency.

name: Lower cost of procurement
rationale: Budget constraints apply to instrumentation selection, though quality must not be compromised.

name: Restricted susceptibility to environmental interference
rationale: The instrument should be protected from vibration, temperature extremes, and moisture that could affect readings.

name: Enhanced ease of installation and maintenance
rationale: Simple installation and accessible maintenance features reduce lifecycle costs and downtime.

name: Better range resolution
rationale: Fine resolution allows detection of small pressure changes for precise monitoring.

name: Improved condensate drainage performance
rationale: The condensate drain/auto-drain valve must effectively remove condensate from compressed air systems to prevent moisture buildup and corrosion. Gravity and pressure differential drive drainage; the valve must be sized and positioned to overcome these forces.

name: Reduced risk of condensate backup
rationale: Condensate backup can cause water hammer, corrosion, and system inefficiency. The auto-drain valve must open reliably at appropriate intervals or levels to prevent accumulation, reducing the risk of backup into downstream equipment.

name: Higher reliability of automatic operation
rationale: The valve's solenoid, timer, or level-sensing mechanism must operate reliably over many cycles. Reliability pressure drives selection of robust components and appropriate maintenance schedules.

name: Minimised air loss during drainage
rationale: Compressed air is costly. The auto-drain valve should minimise the volume of compressed air vented along with condensate. Zero-loss or low-loss drain designs address this pressure.

name: Adequate flow capacity for peak condensate loads
rationale: During periods of high humidity or high compressor output, condensate generation increases. The drain valve must have sufficient orifice size and flow capacity to handle peak loads without clogging or flooding.

name: Reduced clogging from debris and particulates
rationale: Compressed air condensate often contains particulates, oil, and pipe scale that can clog small drain orifices. Design pressure pushes for strainers, larger passages, or self-cleaning mechanisms.

name: Lower maintenance frequency requirement
rationale: Auto-drain valves in accessible but potentially inconvenient locations benefit from designs requiring infrequent service. Maintenance pressure influences choice of valve type (e.g., electronic vs. mechanical).

name: Enhanced energy efficiency from reduced compressed air waste
rationale: By minimising air loss during drainage, the system's overall energy efficiency improves. This drives selection of smart drain valves that detect actual condensate presence rather than using fixed timers.

name: Reduced backflow risk
rationale: The primary function of a check valve is to prevent reverse flow (backflow) in piping systems, ensuring fluid flows in only one direction. This is a core engineering design pressure.

name: Improved sealing reliability
rationale: Check valves must close quickly and seal tightly to prevent leakage when flow reverses, requiring reliable sealing mechanisms.

name: Minimised pressure drop
rationale: Check valves introduce resistance to flow; designers aim to minimise pressure loss across the valve for system efficiency.

name: Lower maintenance frequency
rationale: Check valves have moving parts that can wear or jam; design pressures push for durable, low-maintenance construction.

name: Greater flow capacity
rationale: The valve must accommodate required flow rates without excessive sizing, balancing capacity against physical constraints.

name: Reduced water hammer effect
rationale: Rapid closure of check valves can cause water hammer; designs aim to minimise this through dampened or non-slam closure mechanisms.

name: Increased cooling capacity
rationale: Aftercoolers are used to cool compressed air or gas; higher cooling capacity improves system efficiency and reduces moisture content in downstream equipment.

name: Reduced pressure drop
rationale: Minimising pressure drop across the aftercooler is critical for maintaining overall system efficiency and reducing energy consumption of upstream compressors.

name: Improved heat exchanger effectiveness
rationale: Higher heat exchanger effectiveness ensures better thermal performance, reducing outlet temperature of the compressed gas and improving downstream process conditions.

name: Reduced footprint
rationale: Space constraints in industrial facilities often drive the need for compact aftercooler designs without sacrificing thermal performance.

name: Lower maintenance requirements
rationale: Aftercoolers are prone to fouling and corrosion; designs that reduce maintenance frequency improve overall plant reliability and operational costs.

name: Enhanced material durability
rationale: Selection of corrosion-resistant and thermally durable materials extends the service life of the aftercooler, especially in humid or aggressive gas environments.

name: Improved monitoring and control capability
rationale: Building management systems need enhanced monitoring and control interfaces to optimize compressor performance and energy efficiency.

name: Increased data integration requirements
rationale: Modern BMS requires integration of compressor data with broader building automation systems for coordinated control.

name: Reduced energy consumption pressure
rationale: Energy efficiency goals drive the need for optimized compressor sequencing and load management through the control interface.

name: Enhanced system reliability expectation
rationale: Critical facility operations demand reliable compressor control with failover and alarm management capabilities.

name: Restricted network bandwidth availability
rationale: BMS network limitations may constrain data polling frequency and protocol choices for compressor communication.

name: Reduced noise transmission to adjacent spaces
rationale: Compressor rooms and plant rooms contain loud mechanical equipment; reducing noise transmission to adjacent occupied spaces is a key design requirement.

name: Adequate ventilation and cooling
rationale: Mechanical equipment generates significant heat; adequate ventilation and cooling is essential for safe operation and equipment longevity.

name: Improved equipment accessibility for maintenance
rationale: Plant rooms require sufficient clearance around equipment for routine maintenance, repair, and replacement.

name: Reduced risk of fire and explosion hazards
rationale: Compressors often handle flammable gases or operate under high pressure, so fire safety and explosion prevention are critical design pressures.

name: Sufficient structural load capacity
rationale: Heavy mechanical equipment requires adequate structural support and floor loading capacity.

name: Minimised vibration transmission to structure
rationale: Rotating and reciprocating machinery generates vibrations that must be isolated to prevent structural damage and noise transfer.

name: Optimised spatial layout for equipment arrangement
rationale: Efficient arrangement of equipment, piping, and service routes optimises floor area utilisation and operational workflow.

name: Increased reliability requirement
rationale: Instrument air systems must provide reliable compressed air for pneumatic controls and instrumentation, requiring robust design and redundancy.

name: Higher pressure stability requirement
rationale: Instrument air requires stable, regulated pressure output to ensure accurate operation of pneumatic instruments and control valves.

name: Improved air quality requirement
rationale: Instrument air must be dry and oil-free to prevent damage to sensitive pneumatic instruments, necessitating dryers and filters.

name: Reduced moisture content requirement
rationale: Moisture in instrument air can cause corrosion and malfunction of pneumatic devices, so moisture content must be minimised.

name: Minimised contamination risk
rationale: Contaminants such as oil and particulates must be kept to a minimum to protect downstream instrumentation.

name: Constrained energy consumption
rationale: Air compressors consume significant energy, so design should minimise overall energy usage while meeting demand.

name: Adequate capacity sizing requirement
rationale: The system must be sized with sufficient capacity to handle peak demand for all pneumatic instruments and controls.

name: Reduced pressure drop requirement
rationale: Pressure losses in piping and components should be minimised to maintain adequate pressure at point of use.

name: Enhanced redundancy requirement
rationale: Critical facilities often require backup compressors or receivers to ensure uninterrupted instrument air supply.

name: Increased air quality requirement
rationale: The breathing air sub-system must provide adequate air quality for human respiratory needs, which drives higher filtration and conditioning requirements.

name: Higher flow rate demand
rationale: Occupant density and activity levels create demand for greater volumetric air flow through the breathing air system.

name: Reduced energy consumption pressure
rationale: Energy efficiency goals constrain fan power, conditioning loads, and overall system energy use.

name: Lower maintenance burden
rationale: Operational requirements push for reduced filter replacement frequency and simpler servicing of air handling components.

name: Minimised ductwork footprint
rationale: Space constraints within building ceilings and shafts drive the need for more compact duct routing.

name: Optimised contaminant removal
rationale: Health and safety standards require effective removal of CO2, particulates, and other airborne contaminants.

name: Sufficient redundancy for reliability
rationale: Critical facility requirements may demand backup fans or redundant filtration stages to ensure continuous operation.

name: Reduced noise emission
rationale: Acoustic comfort requirements constrain fan speeds and duct velocities to limit airborne and structure-borne noise.

name: Greater humidity control precision
rationale: Comfort and indoor air quality standards push for tighter control of absolute humidity levels in the breathing air stream.

name: Increased centralised control pressure
rationale: Centralised pneumatic control systems increase efficiency and coordination across building zones, creating a design pressure to adopt a unified network.

name: Reduced installation cost pressure
rationale: Cost constraints limit the extent and sophistication of pneumatic actuator deployment, pushing towards minimal viable configurations.

name: Improved response time pressure
rationale: Faster actuator response improves HVAC precision and comfort, driving demand for higher-performance pneumatic components.

name: Reduced maintenance complexity pressure
rationale: Simpler pneumatic layouts with fewer components are preferred to lower long-term maintenance burden and fault risk.

name: Greater energy efficiency pressure
rationale: Energy codes and sustainability goals favour optimised pneumatic control sequences that minimise compressed air waste.

name: Limited spatial integration pressure
rationale: Architectural constraints on ceiling plenum and wall space limit where pneumatic tubing and actuators can be placed.

name: Higher reliability pressure
rationale: Critical building services demand fault-tolerant pneumatic networks, pushing towards redundant or high-durability components.

name: Reduced noise transmission pressure
rationale: Pneumatic actuator venting and valve noise may need to be mitigated in acoustically sensitive spaces.

name: Enhanced scalability pressure
rationale: Future expandability of the system requires modular design so additional zones can be integrated without major rework.

name: Increased condensate collection efficiency
rationale: Higher efficiency in collecting condensate ensures proper drainage and prevents water damage, which is a core engineering requirement for HVAC condensate systems.

name: Reduced pipe clogging risk
rationale: Minimising blockages in condensate drain pipes is critical to maintain system performance and prevent overflow or leakage.

name: Adequate drainage slope
rationale: Sufficient slope in drainage piping is essential for gravity-driven condensate flow, preventing standing water and microbial growth.

name: Lower risk of condensate backup
rationale: Preventing condensate backup protects connected HVAC equipment from water damage and ensures continuous operation.

name: Enhanced corrosion resistance of drain components
rationale: Condensate is slightly acidic, so selecting corrosion-resistant materials increases system longevity and reliability.

name: Reduced installation cost
rationale: Cost constraints often push for simpler, more economical drainage designs, which may trade off against performance or durability.

name: Prevented condensate overflow onto building structure
rationale: Avoiding overflow protects building finishes, structure, and prevents slip hazards, a key safety requirement.

name: Better thermal insulation of drain lines
rationale: Insulating cold condensate drain pipes prevents surface condensation on pipes in warm humid spaces, reducing secondary moisture issues.

name: Improved security access control
rationale: Security requirements drive the need for better access control mechanisms, directly impacting the specification and placement of access control panels.

name: Reduced unauthorized access
rationale: Access control panels are central to preventing unauthorized entry, so pressures to minimize security breaches affect their design.

name: Higher integration with building management systems
rationale: Modern buildings require access control panels to integrate with broader BMS for centralized monitoring and control.

name: Limited physical footprint
rationale: Space constraints in electrical rooms or entry points drive the need for compact access control panel design.

name: Enhanced user authentication reliability
rationale: Reliable authentication (card readers, biometrics) is critical for access control panel functionality and user trust.

name: Reduced system downtime
rationale: Access control panels must have high availability and reliability to ensure continuous security operations.

name: Greater scalability for future expansion
rationale: Building expansions or tenant changes require access control systems to accommodate additional doors and users easily.

name: Lower power consumption
rationale: Energy efficiency goals may influence the choice of low-power components in access control panels.

name: Improved compliance with safety codes
rationale: Building and fire safety codes require access control panels to support emergency egress and comply with regulations.

name: Improved biometric accuracy
rationale: Biometric scanners require high precision in reading fingerprints, iris patterns, or facial features to ensure reliable identification and access control.

name: Reduced false rejection rate
rationale: Minimizing false rejections ensures authorized users are not incorrectly denied access, improving user experience and security effectiveness.

name: Enhanced processing speed
rationale: Faster scanning and matching speeds improve throughput and user convenience at access points.

name: Minimised vulnerability to spoofing
rationale: Reducing susceptibility to presentation attacks (e.g., fake fingerprints, photos) is critical for security integrity.

name: Higher durability under environmental conditions
rationale: Scanners exposed to outdoor or harsh environments need resistance to dust, moisture, temperature variations, and physical wear.

name: Improved user ergonomics
rationale: The placement and design of biometric scanners should accommodate comfortable user interaction, including height, reach, and accessibility for all users.

name: Reduced power consumption
rationale: Lower power draw is important for battery-operated or energy-efficient building systems.

name: Optimised integration with access control system
rationale: Seamless communication with the building's access control, alarm, and monitoring systems is essential for coordinated security operation.

name: Greater data security and privacy compliance
rationale: Biometric data is sensitive personal information; strong encryption, secure storage, and compliance with privacy regulations (e.g., GDPR) are critical.

name: Increased security access control
rationale: Security requirements demand that card readers provide reliable authentication to prevent unauthorized access.

name: Enhanced credential verification speed
rationale: Users expect fast credential verification to minimize wait times at entry points, driving faster processing technology.

name: Reduced power consumption
rationale: Energy efficiency goals and battery-operated scenarios push for lower power draw in reader electronics.

name: Improved environmental durability
rationale: Outdoor or harsh-condition installations require weatherproofing, tamper resistance, and rugged enclosures.

name: Lower installation and maintenance cost
rationale: Budget constraints drive use of standardized, easy-to-install readers with minimal ongoing maintenance needs.

name: Greater interoperability with access control systems
rationale: Readers must communicate with various backend systems and credential formats (Wiegand, OSDP, etc.), pushing for protocol flexibility.

name: Minimised physical footprint
rationale: Space constraints on door frames or wall surfaces encourage compact reader designs that are less intrusive.

name: Higher credential security (encryption/anti-cloning)
rationale: Modern threats demand encrypted communication and anti-cloning measures to protect credential data against replay and skimming attacks.

name: Restricted false acceptance rate
rationale: Security policy requires minimizing false accepts where unauthorized credentials are mistakenly granted access.

name: Increased access control reliability
rationale: Electric door strikes must reliably lock/unlock on command to ensure secure access control; higher reliability reduces failure risks.

name: Enhanced power efficiency
rationale: Lower power consumption reduces operational costs and heat buildup, and enables battery-backed operation during power loss.

name: Reduced electromagnetic interference
rationale: Electromagnetic noise from the strike coil can disrupt nearby sensitive electronics; minimising EMI improves system compatibility.

name: Improved mechanical durability
rationale: Door strikes experience repeated impact and latch engagement; stronger materials and wear resistance extend service life.

name: Minimised physical footprint
rationale: Compact strikes fit into standard door frames and allow easier retrofitting without extensive frame modification.

name: Greater fail-safe or fail-secure compliance
rationale: Building codes and safety requirements dictate whether the strike must lock (fail-secure) or unlock (fail-safe) upon power loss; ensuring correct configuration is critical.

name: Improved corrosion resistance
rationale: Door strikes are exposed to humidity and outdoor conditions; corrosion-resistant materials prevent jamming and electrical failures.

name: Lower installation complexity
rationale: Simplified wiring and alignment reduce labour cost and installation errors, making the strike more accessible to integrators.

name: Enhanced voltage tolerance
rationale: Wide input voltage range allows the strike to operate reliably on different power supplies and with voltage drops over long cable runs.

name: Increased holding force
rationale: A magnetic lock must generate sufficient holding force (typically 600-1200 lbs) to secure a door against forced entry, per ANSI/BHMA standards for electromagnetic locks.

name: Reduced power consumption
rationale: Maglocks are continuously powered; minimising standby current draw (e.g., ≤300 mA) is critical for energy efficiency, fire safety system battery backup duration, and heat dissipation.

name: Reduced residual magnetism
rationale: After power is cut, residual magnetism in the electromagnet core must be minimised (< 2 seconds release delay per UL 294) to ensure immediate door release for egress and fire safety.

name: Improved fire-rated integration
rationale: Maglocks must integrate seamlessly with fire-rated door assemblies and be listed/UL 10C rated to maintain door fire-resistance rating and comply with building/fire codes.

name: Greater ingress protection (IP rating)
rationale: For exterior or semi-exposed applications, the lock housing should have a sufficient IP rating (e.g., IP54 or higher) to resist moisture, dust, and environmental degradation per IEC 60529.

name: Reduced electromagnetic interference (EMI)
rationale: Maglocks generate magnetic fields that can interfere with nearby access control readers, sensors, or electronic equipment; EMI should be contained/shielded per FCC Part 15.

name: Enhanced fail-safe operation
rationale: Per fire and life safety codes (NFPA 101, IBC), maglocks must be fail-safe (unlock on power loss) to ensure free egress; this pressure drives design toward reliable power-off release mechanisms.

name: Adequate bonding/grounding
rationale: Proper electrical bonding and grounding of the lock assembly is needed per NEC to prevent shock hazard and ensure stable operation, especially in metal door frames.

name: Lower installation complexity
rationale: Maglocks require precise alignment of armature plate and electromagnet; design should minimise the need for custom brackets, shims, or complex wiring to reduce labour cost and installation errors.

name: Increased security
rationale: Electronic deadbolts are primarily designed to increase security by providing keyless or electronic access control, which is a core design pressure for this component.

name: Improved convenience
rationale: Electronic deadbolts offer convenience through keyless entry (keypad, smartphone, biometric), which is a major driving force for their adoption and design.

name: Reduced power consumption
rationale: As a battery-operated device, minimizing power consumption is a critical design pressure to extend battery life and reduce maintenance.

name: Minimised vulnerability to hacking
rationale: Electronic deadbolts face cybersecurity threats; design must minimize vulnerabilities to unauthorized remote access or tampering.

name: Enhanced durability
rationale: The physical components (motor, latch, casing) must withstand repeated use and environmental exposure, requiring enhanced durability.

name: Reduced cost
rationale: Manufacturing and retail cost pressures push toward lower-cost components and assembly to remain competitive.

name: Improved user interface
rationale: User expectations for intuitive, responsive interfaces (touchscreens, app connectivity) drive design improvements in the lock's interface.

name: Greater reliability
rationale: Reliability is paramount for a security device; failures to lock/unlock can compromise safety, so designs must ensure consistent operation.

name: Eliminated single point of failure
rationale: Design pressures push toward backup access methods (physical key override, emergency battery terminals) to avoid lockout scenarios.

name: Increased detection accuracy
rationale: The door position sensor must accurately detect whether a door is open or closed to trigger the correct building control responses.

name: Reduced false triggering
rationale: False alarms or incorrect readings from the sensor can cause unnecessary alerts or improper system behaviour, so minimising false triggers is a key design pressure.

name: Greater environmental robustness
rationale: The sensor must withstand environmental factors such as temperature, humidity, dust, and vibration near door openings without degradation in performance.

name: Minimised power consumption
rationale: Especially for battery-powered or wireless sensor deployments, minimising power draw extends operational life and reduces maintenance.

name: Improved integration compatibility
rationale: The sensor must interface reliably with building management systems, access control panels, and alarm systems, requiring standard communication protocols.

name: Lower installation complexity
rationale: Simpler installation procedures reduce labour costs and minimise disruption to existing building fabric and finishes.

name: Improved detection accuracy
rationale: REX sensors must reliably detect persons approaching an exit to ensure automatic door operation.

name: Reduced false triggering
rationale: False triggers from non-exit movements can cause nuisance door operations and security issues.

name: Enhanced response speed
rationale: Faster sensor response ensures timely door operation for safe egress.

name: Minimised power consumption
rationale: Lower energy draw supports battery-backed or low-voltage security systems.

name: Greater environmental robustness
rationale: Sensor must operate reliably across temperature, humidity, and lighting variations near exit doors.

name: Reduced installation complexity
rationale: Simpler wiring and mounting ease integration with door frames and access control systems.

name: Improved security through PIN encryption
rationale: PIN entry terminals must encrypt PINs to prevent interception during transmission, a standard security requirement.

name: Enhanced durability for outdoor/rugged use

name: Improved cable management
rationale: Neat organisation of patch cables reduces strain on connections, improves airflow, and simplifies troubleshooting, driving angled or modular patch panel designs.

name: Increased cooling airflow
rationale: Network racks and server cabinets generate significant heat; increased cooling airflow is necessary to maintain operating temperatures and prevent equipment failure.

name: Improved structural load capacity
rationale: Server cabinets must support heavy equipment loads; greater structural capacity ensures safe mounting of servers, UPS units, and other hardware.

name: Reduced power consumption
rationale: Energy efficiency is a key design consideration; lower power consumption reduces operational costs and cooling requirements.

name: Adequate cable management space
rationale: Sufficient space for cable routing and management prevents airflow obstruction, simplifies maintenance, and reduces signal interference.

name: Minimised physical footprint
rationale: Space constraints in data centers and network rooms drive the need for compact rack designs to maximize floor area utilization.

name: Enhanced seismic restraint
rationale: In seismically active regions, racks must be adequately braced and anchored to prevent toppling during earthquakes, protecting equipment and personnel.

name: Reduced acoustic noise emission
rationale: Server fans and cooling systems generate noise; lower noise levels are often required in office-adjacent or open-plan environments.

name: Greater serviceability and accessibility
rationale: Easy front and rear access for maintenance, cable changes, and component replacement improves operational efficiency.

name: Improved security and access control
rationale: Lockable doors, side panels, and access control mechanisms protect sensitive networking equipment from unauthorized physical access.

name: Increased network capacity
rationale: Network switches need sufficient capacity to handle data traffic without bottlenecks.

name: Increased port density
rationale: More ports allow connecting more devices, improving scalability.

name: Reduced latency
rationale: Low latency is critical for real-time applications and network performance.

name: Increased switching speed
rationale: Faster switching improves overall network throughput and responsiveness.

name: Reduced power consumption
rationale: Lower power usage reduces operational costs and heat generation.

name: Increased reliability
rationale: Reliable switches ensure network uptime and reduce failure points.

name: Reduced physical footprint
rationale: Smaller switches save rack space in data centers and wiring closets.

name: Enhanced security features
rationale: Security features like VLANs, ACLs, and port security protect the network.

name: Reduced cost
rationale: Lower cost makes the switch more affordable for deployment.

name: Increased network coverage range
rationale: Routers are designed to achieve greater signal coverage to connect more devices over larger distances.

name: Higher data throughput capacity
rationale: Routers need to handle increasing bandwidth demands for streaming, downloads, and multiple simultaneous connections.

name: Reduced latency
rationale: Minimising delay in data packet routing is critical for real-time applications like gaming and video calls.

name: Improved security features
rationale: Routers must incorporate stronger encryption, firewall capabilities, and threat prevention to protect the network.

name: Lower power consumption
rationale: Energy-efficient design reduces operational cost and heat dissipation, important for always-on networking equipment.

name: Minimised physical footprint
rationale: Smaller form factors allow routers to fit in constrained spaces like wiring closets or wall-mounted enclosures.

name: Enhanced reliability and uptime
rationale: Mission-critical networks demand robust hardware and failover mechanisms to prevent connectivity loss.

name: Greater number of simultaneous connections
rationale: Modern environments (offices, smart homes) require routers supporting many concurrent devices without degradation.

name: Reduced electromagnetic interference
rationale: Minimising EMI ensures stable wireless performance and compliance with regulatory standards.

name: Increased security against unauthorized access
rationale: A firewall appliance's primary purpose is to enforce security policies, so there is a design pressure to increase its security capabilities (access control, threat prevention).

name: Higher throughput performance
rationale: Network firewalls must handle increasing traffic volumes without becoming a bottleneck, driving the need for higher throughput and packet processing performance.

name: Reduced latency impact
rationale: Firewalls add processing delay; there is pressure to minimize added latency to maintain network responsiveness.

name: Improved reliability and uptime
rationale: As a critical security component, the firewall must have high availability and fault tolerance, driving pressure for redundant power, failover, and robust hardware.

name: Minimised power consumption
rationale: Lower power draw reduces operating cost and cooling requirements, but is secondary to security and performance requirements.

name: Adequate feature set for modern threats
rationale: Modern firewalls need features like deep packet inspection, intrusion prevention, and SSL decryption, pressuring for more comprehensive capabilities.

name: Improved signal coverage
rationale: WAP placement and selection is driven by the need to maximise wireless coverage area and signal strength throughout the building.

name: Higher data throughput
rationale: Design must support sufficient bandwidth for users, pushing toward higher-capacity WAP models and denser deployment.

name: Reduced interference
rationale: WAP placement must avoid co-channel and adjacent-channel interference from neighbouring WAPs and other wireless devices.

name: Limited power consumption
rationale: Energy efficiency targets may constrain WAP model selection, transmit power settings, and PoE budget allocation.

name: Minimised aesthetic impact
rationale: Architectural design preferences push toward discreet, low-visibility WAP mounting to preserve interior aesthetics.

name: Greater user device density
rationale: High-occupancy spaces require more WAPs or higher-capacity units to serve many simultaneous connections.

name: Restricted mounting constraints
rationale: Structural elements, ceiling types, and fire-rated barriers limit where WAPs can be physically installed.

name: Increased cable capacity requirement
rationale: As building systems expand, there is a need for more cables (power, data, control) to be routed, putting pressure to increase the size or number of conduit and cable trays.

name: Improved accessibility requirement
rationale: Maintenance and future upgrades demand easy access to cabling, pushing for better layout and more accessible conduit and tray designs.

name: Reduced space availability constraint
rationale: Overhead plenum and wall cavity space is limited by other building systems (HVAC, plumbing, structure), constraining the physical size and routing of conduit and cable trays.

name: Higher fire safety requirement
rationale: Fire codes demand fire-rated pathways, firestop systems, and use of non-combustible materials for conduit and cable trays, increasing their specification complexity.

name: Minimised cost pressure
rationale: Budget constraints push for minimising material, labour, and installation costs associated with conduit and cable tray systems, limiting their extent and specifications.

name: Higher electromagnetic interference (EMI) shielding requirement
