rationale: Budget constraints pressure designers to use economical materials and efficient construction methods for the shaft.

name: Sufficient overhead clearance
rationale: High-speed elevators require greater overhead space for overspeed governors, buffers, and safety mechanisms above the top landing.

name: Increased load-bearing capacity
rationale: Helipads must support the weight of helicopters during landing and parking, requiring sufficient structural load-bearing capacity.

name: Improved surface friction
rationale: Adequate surface friction is critical to prevent helicopter skidding during landing and takeoff, especially in wet conditions.

name: Expanded safety zone
rationale: Safety clear zones (obstacle-free areas) around the helipad are required by aviation regulations to prevent collision risks.

name: Reduced obstacle proximity
rationale: Buildings, poles, and other obstacles near the helipad must be minimised to comply with approach/departure path clearance requirements.

name: Improved drainage capacity
rationale: Effective drainage is needed to prevent water pooling on the helipad surface, which can create hazards for landing aircraft.

name: Higher fire suppression capability
rationale: Helipads require adequate firefighting equipment and suppression systems per aviation safety codes for emergency response.

name: Increased landing area dimension
rationale: Helipad dimensions must be sufficient to accommodate the design helicopter's rotor diameter and allow safe landing/takeoff.

name: Reduced lighting glare
rationale: Perimeter and approach lighting should be designed to minimise glare for pilots during night operations while maintaining visibility.

name: Maximised wind protection
rationale: Helipad siting should consider prevailing wind patterns to minimise crosswind and turbulence effects on helicopter operations.

name: Reduced structural dead load

name: Greater accessibility for maintenance

name: Reduced risk of water ponding on roof

name: Improved fire safety and separation

name: Higher thermal insulation performance

name: Reduced maintenance access costs

name: Limited track weight to reduce structural load

rationale: Canopy materials should meet fire safety standards to protect occupants and property in case of ignition sources.

rationale: Sound quality for announcements, PA systems, and crowd noise management is important for spectator experience and safety communications.

name: Restricted exposure to weather elements
rationale: Spectators should be sheltered from rain, excessive sun, wind, and other adverse weather conditions for comfort and safety.

rationale: Compliance with building codes for fire safety, emergency exits, and crowd management is critical in public assembly spaces.

rationale: Performers need quiet conditions to warm up vocally or instrumentally; acoustic isolation from noisy backstage areas is a standard design requirement.

rationale: Performers require adequate space to stretch, move, and practice; codes and best practices specify minimum clear floor areas per occupant.

rationale: Warm-up areas require good indoor air quality and thermal comfort to support physical activity and vocal performance, especially prior to stage exertion.

rationale: Sufficient task lighting is needed for performers to prepare and read materials; lower lighting could hinder warm-up routines.

name: Minimised background noise
rationale: Background noise from HVAC or adjacent spaces must be controlled to allow performers to hear themselves warm up.

name: Sufficient power and audio connectivity
rationale: Performers may need power outlets and audio connections for instruments, amplifiers, or backing tracks during warm-up.

name: Reduced reverberation time
rationale: Excessive reverberation can muddy vocal or instrumental warm-up; controlled acoustics with absorption help performers hear themselves clearly.

rationale: Proximity to stage and dressing rooms is important for efficient performer movement; close adjacency reduces travel time and supports show flow.

name: Improved acoustic performance
rationale: Acoustic treatments are designed to improve sound insulation and noise reduction, so there is a design pressure to increase acoustic performance.

name: Reduced material thickness
rationale: Thinner acoustic materials may be preferred to save space and cost, creating a pressure to reduce thickness where possible.

rationale: Building codes and safety requirements push for acoustic materials with higher fire resistance to meet regulatory standards.

name: Enhanced durability against environmental exposure
rationale: For exterior or exposed locations, there is pressure to use more durable acoustic materials that resist moisture, UV, and wear.

name: Lower maintenance requirements
rationale: Building operators prefer acoustic barriers that require less frequent maintenance and cleaning over their lifespan.

name: Optimised acoustic cavity depth

rationale: Simpler drainage layouts reduce construction and maintenance costs, but must balance with hydraulic performance requirements.

rationale: Regulatory requirements (e.g., NPDES, Water Framework Directive) demand treatment of stormwater runoff to remove pollutants before discharge.

name: Minimised travel distance to building entry

name: Improved structural stability

name: Enhanced accessibility for users

name: Higher aesthetic quality

name: Reduced slip hazard

name: Improved water quality

name: Increased natural light transmission

name: Improved thermal insulation

name: Reduced structural load

name: Enhanced UV protection

name: Reduced thermal stress

name: Lower maintenance requirements

name: Reduced risk of damage or vandalism

name: Lower humidity variation

name: Enhanced fire protection

name: Reduced dust accumulation

name: Adequate access clearance

name: Improved intrusion detection

name: Reduced false alarms

name: Minimized reliance on manual operation

name: Greater durability and weather resistance

name: Reduced noise level from interactive elements

name: Increased load-bearing capacity

name: Reduced fall risk

name: Sufficient handhold and foothold spacing

name: Enhanced durability and weather resistance
rationale: Being an outdoor or public-space component, the panel must withstand environmental factors, vandalism, and heavy usage, requiring robust materials and protective enclosures.

name: Reduced power consumption

name: Optimised user interface accessibility
rationale: The panel must be accessible to users of varying ages, heights, and abilities, requiring optimised placement, font sizes, contrast, and multimodal interaction methods.

name: Minimised screen glare and reflectivity
rationale: Outdoor or brightly lit environments cause screen glare which degrades usability; anti-glare coatings and sufficiently bright displays are needed to maintain visibility.

name: Higher processing and display performance
rationale: Smooth animations, touch response, and real-time interactivity demand adequate computing power and display refresh rates to avoid lag and user frustration.

name: Reduced maintenance frequency
rationale: Public interactive components experience high wear and tear; designing for low maintenance through sealed enclosures, robust connectors, and self-diagnostic features reduces lifecycle costs.

name: Greater security against tampering
rationale: Public-facing digital panels are vulnerable to tampering, hacking, and physical damage; reinforced enclosures, secure software, and alarm systems are necessary.

name: Improved content update flexibility
rationale: The panel's content and games need periodic updates to remain engaging and relevant; wireless content management and modular software design enable this flexibility.

name: Increased safety for children
rationale: Play boundary fencing must be strong enough to ensure children's safety by preventing them from leaving the play area and preventing external hazards.

name: Reduced climbing risk
rationale: Fencing should minimise climbability features to prevent children from climbing over and injuring themselves.

name: Increased visibility through fencing
rationale: Design pressure for greater visibility (e.g., mesh or spaced pickets) so caregivers can supervise children through the fence.

name: Reduced entrapment hazards
rationale: Fencing design must avoid gaps or protrusions that could trap children's heads, fingers, or clothing.

name: Adequate height for containment
rationale: Fencing needs sufficient (adequate) height to contain children and balls within the play area effectively.

name: Reduced maintenance requirements
rationale: Pressure to minimise ongoing maintenance effort and cost, favouring low-maintenance materials.

name: Improved aesthetic integration
