name: Stronger data privacy protection
rationale: User booking data and personal schedules must be protected from unauthorised access.

name: Optimised room utilisation
rationale: Maximising occupancy and reducing idle time for bookable rooms is a primary design driver.

name: Limited notification noise
rationale: Excessive or irrelevant notifications can cause user fatigue; they should be constrained to necessary alerts only.

name: Restricted unauthorized modifications
rationale: Only authorised administrators should be able to modify or override bookings to prevent abuse.

name: Adequate seating capacity
rationale: A conference table must accommodate the intended number of participants comfortably, making adequate seating capacity a key design pressure.

name: Sufficient table surface area
rationale: The table surface must be large enough to hold documents, laptops, and meeting materials for all participants.

name: Reduced visual obstructions
rationale: Table legs, supports, or central pedestals should be minimised to avoid blocking sightlines and legroom for participants.

name: Optimised shape for collaboration
rationale: The table shape (e.g., oval, boat, rectangular) should encourage face-to-face interaction and equal participation.

name: Limited table depth for reachability
rationale: The table should not be so deep that participants cannot comfortably reach the centre or converse across the table.

name: Adequate cable management capacity
rationale: Modern conference tables need provisions for power and data cabling to support laptops and AV equipment.

name: Higher structural stability
rationale: The table must be sturdy and stable to prevent wobbling during use, supporting the weight of equipment and leaning participants.

name: Restricted overall footprint
rationale: The table dimensions must fit within the available conference room space while allowing circulation pathways around it.

name: Better ergonomic height
rationale: The table height must be appropriate for seated work, typically around 730-760 mm, to ensure comfortable posture.

name: Increased ergonomic support
rationale: Ergonomic meeting chairs need increased support to ensure comfort during long meetings.

name: Reduced material cost
rationale: Manufacturers aim to reduce material costs while maintaining ergonomic quality.

name: Enhanced adjustability
rationale: Meeting chairs require enhanced adjustability features (height, armrests, lumbar support) to accommodate diverse users.

name: Improved lumbar support
rationale: Proper lumbar support is critical for ergonomic chairs to prevent back strain during meetings.

name: Reduced physical strain on users
rationale: The core purpose of ergonomic design is to reduce physical strain on the human body during prolonged sitting.

name: increased storage capacity
rationale: Credenza/side storage units are primarily designed for storage, so increasing storage capacity is a key design pressure.

name: improved accessibility
rationale: Easy access to stored items is important for furniture usability, driving improved door/drawer mechanisms and layout.

name: reduced footprint
rationale: Space constraints in office or home environments may push for a smaller floor footprint while maintaining function.

name: enhanced structural stability
rationale: The unit must be structurally stable to support the weight of stored items and resist tipping, requiring sufficient bracing and robust construction.

name: constrained overall height
rationale: Height may be limited by room proportions, sightlines, or ergonomic reach considerations for top surfaces.

name: adequate material durability
rationale: Materials must withstand regular use, loading, and wear over time, driving selection of robust materials and finishes.

name: lower manufacturing cost
rationale: Cost constraints in production push for economical materials, simplified joining methods, and efficient design.

name: optimised internal organisation
rationale: Well-organised internal compartments, shelves, and dividers improve the usability and functionality of the storage unit.

name: reduced weight
rationale: A lighter unit is easier to move, install, and transport, which may influence material choice and construction method.

name: Increased writing surface area
rationale: Larger writing surfaces accommodate more information and collaboration, improving usability in meeting and classroom settings.

name: Improved surface contrast and visibility
rationale: High-contrast, glare-free surfaces enhance readability from a distance and under various lighting conditions.

name: Enhanced durability and stain resistance
rationale: Durable, stain-resistant surfaces reduce ghosting and extend lifespan, maintaining a clean writing area.

name: Reduced surface glare and reflections
rationale: Glare from lighting or windows can impair readability; matte or low-glare finishes improve visibility.

name: Reduced marker ghosting and staining
rationale: Ghosting leaves residual marks that reduce clarity; easy-clean surfaces and quality materials prevent this.

name: Improved mounting stability and alignment
rationale: Secure, level mounting prevents wobbling and ensures the surface remains functional and safe during use.

name: Greater accessibility and ergonomic height
rationale: Mounting at appropriate heights ensures the board is usable by people of different heights and those using wheelchairs.

name: Lower maintenance effort for surface cleaning
rationale: Surfaces that are easy to clean reduce ongoing maintenance costs and keep the board consistently usable.

name: Enhanced integration with digital tools
rationale: Increasingly, whiteboards are paired with interactive or projection capabilities; surface design should accommodate digital overlay technologies.

name: Increased collaboration and interaction
rationale: Breakout and informal meeting areas are designed to foster spontaneous collaboration and interaction among occupants, which is a key architectural design intent.

name: Reduced noise and acoustic privacy
rationale: Informal meeting areas need adequate acoustic treatment to prevent noise from disrupting adjacent workspaces, requiring sound-absorbing materials and layout considerations.

name: Adequate seating capacity
rationale: Sufficient seating and flexible furniture arrangements are needed to accommodate varying group sizes using the breakout space.

name: Reduced spatial footprint
rationale: There may be pressure to minimize the area allocated to informal spaces in favor of more primary functions, depending on overall building efficiency goals.

name: Enhanced visual connection to surroundings
rationale: Breakout areas benefit from daylight and views to promote occupant well-being and a relaxed atmosphere for informal discussions.

name: Optimised flexibility of furniture layout
rationale: Furniture should be reconfigurable to support different activities (small chats, larger brainstorming sessions, individual respite) in the same space.

name: Reduced proximity to quiet focus areas
rationale: Breakout areas should be located away from quiet zones or enclosed spaces to avoid noise conflict between informal interaction and focused work.

name: Increased collaboration pressure
rationale: Workstation clusters are often designed to facilitate team collaboration, so there is a design pressure to increase shared workspaces and open layouts.

name: Reduced noise interference pressure
rationale: Acoustic comfort is critical in workstation clusters; design must reduce noise disruptions to maintain productivity.

name: Higher density occupancy pressure
rationale: Efficient use of floor space drives a pressure to maximize the number of workstations within a given area.

name: Minimised thermal discomfort pressure
rationale: Workstation clusters require adequate HVAC design to minimise temperature variations and ensure occupant comfort.

name: Optimised spatial layout pressure
rationale: Layout efficiency drives a pressure to optimise workspace arrangements for workflow and circulation.

name: Reduced visual obstruction pressure
rationale: Clear sightlines and reduced visual barriers are desired in workstation clusters for supervision and openness.

name: Improved ergonomic comfort pressure
rationale: Workstation design must increase ergonomic adjustability and comfort to prevent repetitive strain injuries.

name: Limited energy consumption pressure
rationale: Lighting and equipment loads in workstation clusters create a pressure to limit overall energy use.

name: Enhanced connectivity infrastructure pressure
rationale: Data and power connectivity must be sufficient and reliable, driving a pressure for enhanced IT infrastructure within the cluster.

name: Increased structural stability
rationale: Partition walls must have adequate structural stability to resist lateral loads and remain upright under normal conditions.

name: Reduced self-weight
rationale: Minimizing the weight of the partition wall reduces the load on the supporting floor structure and simplifies construction.

name: Improved fire resistance
rationale: Fire resistance requirements often dictate material choices and thickness for partition walls to maintain compartmentation.

name: Minimised material cost
rationale: Cost efficiency is a key design pressure affecting material selection and construction methods for low partition walls.

name: Greater acoustic performance
rationale: Acoustic insulation may be required depending on the partition's location, influencing its construction and detailing.

name: Sufficient height clearance
rationale: The wall's height must be low enough to not obstruct sightlines or spatial perception while still serving its functional purpose.

name: Eliminated moisture damage risk
rationale: Moisture protection, especially at the base, is essential to prevent deterioration of materials in the partition wall.

name: Optimised dimensional coordination
rationale: The partition's dimensions must coordinate with modular building systems, door openings, and adjacent finishes.

name: Enhanced durability
rationale: Durable materials and construction are needed to resist impact, abrasion, and everyday wear in occupied spaces.

name: Increased thermal performance pressure
rationale: Glazed screens must provide adequate thermal insulation to reduce heat loss/gain, placing upward pressure on thermal performance requirements.

name: Reduced solar heat gain pressure
rationale: To prevent overheating, glazed screens need to minimise solar heat gain, driving demand for lower solar heat gain coefficients.

name: Improved structural stability pressure
rationale: Glazed screens must withstand wind loads and other structural forces, requiring greater structural stability and robustness.

name: Increased daylight transmission pressure
rationale: As a glazed element, the screen should allow sufficient natural light penetration, placing upward pressure on visible light transmittance.

name: Reduced glare pressure
rationale: Excessive sunlight through the glazed screen can cause visual discomfort, driving pressure to minimise glare effects.

name: Greater acoustic insulation pressure
rationale: Glazed screens often serve as building envelope elements where sound transmission must be controlled, requiring better acoustic performance.

name: Reduced embodied carbon pressure
rationale: Sustainability targets create downward pressure on the embodied carbon footprint of glazing materials and frame systems.

name: Increased acoustic privacy
rationale: Meeting nooks require sufficient acoustic privacy to allow confidential conversations without disturbing adjacent spaces.

name: Reduced ambient noise intrusion
rationale: External noise from adjacent areas must be minimised to maintain a functional meeting environment.

name: Adequate seating capacity
rationale: The nook must accommodate expected number of occupants for small group meetings.

name: Optimised spatial efficiency
rationale: The nook should fit within available floor area without excessive footprint.

name: Reduced visual obstruction
rationale: Sightlines through and around the nook should be maintained for wayfinding and openness.

name: Improved ventilation adequacy
rationale: Enclosed or semi-enclosed nooks require sufficient air exchange for occupant comfort.

name: Sufficient lighting levels
rationale: Task and ambient lighting must be adequate for reading and collaboration activities.

name: Enhanced technology integration
rationale: Modern meeting expectations require power outlets, screen connectivity, and video conferencing support.

name: Increased structural load capacity
rationale: The storage wall unit must bear the weight of stored items; engineering principles dictate sufficient load-bearing capacity.

name: Improved accessibility and ergonomics
rationale: Architectural design considerations require that storage units be easily reachable and usable.

name: Reduced material weight
rationale: Lighter materials reduce structural demands on walls and supports, a common engineering optimization.

name: Maximised storage density
rationale: Efficient use of space drives the design toward higher storage volume per unit area.

name: Minimised manufacturing cost
rationale: Cost constraints typically push toward simpler designs and less expensive materials.

name: Adequate thermal insulation
rationale: If the unit is part of an exterior wall, physical principles of heat transfer require insulation properties.

name: Sufficient fire resistance
rationale: Building codes and safety regulations demand that wall components have fire-resistance ratings.

name: Reduced moisture absorption
rationale: Physical principles of material durability require protection against moisture-induced degradation.

name: Improved aesthetic finish
rationale: Cultural and user expectations often demand a visually appealing appearance for interior storage.

name: Reduced energy consumption
rationale: Energy codes and sustainability goals push for lower energy use from lighting systems.

name: Improved visual comfort
rationale: Task lighting must provide adequate illumination for visual tasks without glare to support occupant comfort and productivity.

name: Reduced glare
rationale: Glare from overhead task lighting can cause visual discomfort and must be minimised.

name: Higher light output
rationale: Certain tasks require higher illuminance levels, pushing for greater light output from fixtures.

name: Reduced heat generation
rationale: Lighting fixtures generate heat which can increase cooling loads; minimising heat output is desirable.

name: Improved controllability
rationale: Modern lighting designs demand dimming, zoning, and individual controls for flexibility and energy savings.

name: Reduced initial cost
rationale: Budget constraints push toward lower-cost lighting solutions, limiting premium features.

name: Adequate illumination levels
rationale: Task lighting must meet minimum illuminance standards for the performed activities according to lighting design standards.

name: Reduced maintenance burden
rationale: Designs favour longer-life lamps and accessible fixtures to minimise maintenance efforts and costs.

name: Improved energy efficiency pressure
rationale: Energy efficiency requirements drive BMS zone controllers to better manage HVAC zones, lighting, and equipment scheduling, reducing energy waste.

name: Enhanced occupant comfort pressure
rationale: Occupant comfort expectations push zone controllers to maintain precise temperature, humidity, and air quality setpoints per zone.

name: Higher system integration complexity pressure
rationale: The need to integrate with fire alarms, security, lighting, and other building systems increases the functional scope of zone controllers.

name: Reduced installation cost pressure
rationale: Budget constraints demand lower-cost controllers, favouring simpler, less feature-rich devices.

name: Minimised latency pressure
rationale: Real-time control requirements push for reduced communication and processing delays in zone control loops.

name: Constrained cybersecurity risk pressure
rationale: Cybersecurity threats drive the need for limited attack surfaces, secure firmware, and restricted network access on zone controllers.

name: Greater interoperability pressure
rationale: Standards such as BACnet, Modbus, and IoT protocols push zone controllers toward greater compatibility with diverse building equipment.

name: Adequate scalability pressure
rationale: Large building designs demand zone controllers that can scale to hundreds of zones without performance degradation.

name: Optimised maintenance accessibility pressure
rationale: Facility management teams require zone controllers to be easily accessible for diagnostics, firmware updates, and repairs.

name: Increased accessibility
rationale: Users need convenient access to power and data outlets in their workspace, driving a desire for more outlets and better placement.

name: Reduced clutter
rationale: Too many outlets clustered together can create visual clutter and functional confusion; design pressures aim to consolidate or strategically distribute outlets to minimise mess.

name: Enhanced safety compliance
rationale: Electrical codes and safety standards exert pressure to ensure outlets are properly rated, grounded, and spaced to prevent overheating and electrical hazards.

name: Optimised placement flexibility
rationale: Design decisions are pressured to position outlet clusters where they are most useful (e.g., near desks, meeting tables), balancing structural constraints with user convenience.

name: Reduced installation cost
rationale: Budget constraints pressure designers to minimise the number of outlet clusters and simplify wiring runs to lower material and labour costs.

name: Reduced weight
rationale: Demountable partition systems benefit from lighter components for easier handling, installation, and reconfiguration.

name: Increased acoustic performance
rationale: Partitions in office and commercial spaces require sound insulation to meet acoustic comfort standards.

name: Improved modularity
rationale: Demountable systems rely on modular components for flexibility in reconfiguration and reuse.

name: Reduced installation time
rationale: Faster installation reduces labor costs and disruption to building occupants during setup and changes.

name: Higher structural stability
rationale: Partitions must remain stable under normal use loads and minor impacts while remaining demountable.

name: Restricted material waste
rationale: Sustainability goals and green building certifications push for reduced construction waste from demountable systems.

name: Optimized spatial flexibility
rationale: The ability to reconfigure spaces easily is a core design pressure for demountable partition systems.

name: Lower lifecycle cost
rationale: Owners seek cost-effective solutions over the building lifecycle, factoring in initial installation and future reconfigurations.

name: Enhanced aesthetic finish
rationale: Visual appearance of partitions impacts occupant satisfaction and must align with interior design intent.

name: Improved acoustic performance pressure
rationale: Acoustic ceiling tiles are designed to absorb sound and reduce noise transmission, so there is a design pressure to improve acoustic performance for better sound control in interior spaces.

name: Enhanced fire resistance pressure
rationale: Building codes require ceiling systems to have adequate fire resistance ratings to prevent fire spread through ceiling plenums.

name: Reduced weight pressure
rationale: Lower weight reduces structural loading on the building frame and makes installation easier and safer.

name: Lower cost pressure
rationale: Budget constraints typically push for more economical ceiling material and installation choices.

name: Greater accessibility pressure
rationale: Suspended ceilings need to provide access to overhead mechanical, electrical, and plumbing systems for maintenance.

name: Minimised sagging pressure
rationale: Tiles must resist sagging over time under their own weight and humidity conditions to maintain a level appearance.

name: Better moisture resistance pressure
rationale: In humid environments, acoustic tiles must resist moisture absorption to prevent staining, warping, and mold growth.

name: Enhanced light reflectance pressure
rationale: Higher light reflectance from ceiling tiles improves overall lighting efficiency and reduces energy consumption.

name: Restricted thickness pressure
rationale: Limited plenum depth and clearance constraints may restrict the allowable thickness of ceiling tiles.

name: Improved ergonomic support
rationale: Ergonomic chairs are designed to provide better support for the user's posture, reducing strain.

name: Increased adjustability
rationale: More adjustable features (height, armrests, lumbar support) enhance user comfort and adaptability.

name: Enhanced lumbar support
rationale: Lumbar support is a key ergonomic feature that reduces lower back pain.

name: Reduced manufacturing cost
rationale: Cost pressures often push to minimize material and production expenses while maintaining ergonomic function.

name: Minimised material weight
rationale: Lighter materials can reduce shipping costs and improve portability, but may conflict with durability.

name: Greater durability
rationale: Durable materials extend product lifecycle and maintain ergonomic performance over time.

name: Improved aesthetic appeal
rationale: Visual design is important for office environments where the chair will be used.

name: Restricted environmental footprint
rationale: Sustainability concerns drive pressures to reduce resource consumption and waste in manufacturing.

name: Higher user satisfaction
rationale: Overall comfort and functionality directly impact user satisfaction and productivity.

name: Improved ergonomic comfort
rationale: Height-adjustable desks allow users to alternate between sitting and standing, improving ergonomic posture and reducing strain.

name: Increased user productivity
rationale: Studies show standing or adjustable desks can improve focus and productivity by allowing movement and comfort adjustments.

name: Reduced physical strain
rationale: Adjustability helps reduce back, neck, and shoulder strain associated with prolonged sitting.

name: Higher adjustability range
rationale: A wider height range accommodates more users of different heights and preferences, increasing inclusivity.

name: Lower manufacturing cost
rationale: Cost constraints may push toward simpler, less expensive adjustment mechanisms.

name: Minimised mechanical complexity
rationale: Simpler mechanisms are more reliable and easier to maintain, reducing failure points.

name: Enhanced stability at height
rationale: At maximum height, the desk must remain stable and not wobble, requiring robust structural design.

name: Greater weight capacity
rationale: Users expect to place monitors, computers, and other equipment on the desk, requiring sufficient load-bearing capacity.

name: Increased kitchen capacity
rationale: The shared kitchen must accommodate multiple users simultaneously, requiring sufficient counter space, storage, and appliance capacity for communal use.

name: Optimised workflow efficiency
rationale: Kitchen layout should follow the work triangle (sink-stove-fridge) and efficient circulation paths to support cooking activities.

name: Reduced cross-contamination risk
rationale: Shared food preparation spaces require separation of raw and cooked food zones, proper ventilation, and hygienic surfaces to prevent contamination.

name: Adequate ventilation provision
rationale: Cooking generates grease, smoke, and odours; sufficient mechanical exhaust and make-up air are required by building codes for occupied kitchens.

name: Limited noise transmission
rationale: Kitchen appliances and activity generate noise; acoustical separation from adjacent quiet spaces (e.g., study rooms, bedrooms) is needed.

name: Improved accessibility compliance
rationale: Universal design standards require accessible counter heights, knee spaces, and clear floor areas for wheelchair users in shared facilities.

name: Reduced energy consumption
rationale: Energy-efficient appliances and lighting should be specified to minimize operational costs and environmental impact.

name: Enhanced durability of finishes
rationale: High-traffic shared kitchen requires robust, water-resistant, easy-to-clean surfaces and flooring to withstand frequent use.

name: Greater natural daylight access
rationale: Daylight improves user well-being and reduces artificial lighting needs, though kitchen may compete with other spaces for perimeter placement.

name: Increased spaciousness
rationale: Shared living rooms benefit from generous floor area to accommodate multiple occupants and activities comfortably.

name: Improved natural lighting
rationale: Daylight access enhances occupant well-being and reduces artificial lighting needs in a shared social space.

name: Greater accessibility
rationale: A shared living room should be easily accessible to all occupants, including those with mobility constraints.

name: Enhanced acoustic comfort
rationale: Sound management is critical in shared spaces to support conversation and media use without disturbance.

name: Improved thermal comfort
rationale: Consistent temperature control is essential for a habitable shared social environment.

name: Reduced noise transmission
rationale: Minimizing sound transfer between the living room and adjacent spaces supports both privacy and acoustic quality.

name: Limited visual clutter
rationale: A clean, uncluttered visual environment contributes to a calm and functional shared space.

name: Sufficient electrical outlets
rationale: Adequate power points are needed to support lighting, electronics, and devices in a heavily used shared room.

name: Maximized flexibility of layout
rationale: A flexible floor plan allows reconfiguration of furniture to suit different social activities and group sizes.

name: Increased security pressure
rationale: Security requirements demand robust locking mechanisms to prevent unauthorised access, driving a need for stronger, more reliable locking components.

name: Reduced jamming pressure
rationale: Mechanical reliability concerns create pressure to minimise the risk of the locking mechanism jamming or failing during operation.

name: Improved accessibility pressure
rationale: Building codes and universal design principles push for locking hardware that is easy to operate for all users, including those with disabilities.

name: Reduced maintenance pressure
rationale: Lifecycle cost considerations drive a desire to limit the frequency and complexity of maintenance required for locking hardware.

name: Greater durability pressure
rationale: High-traffic environments demand locking sets that withstand repeated use and environmental exposure without degradation.

name: Restricted forced entry pressure
rationale: Physical security principles dictate that the locking system should resist forced entry attempts such as kicking, picking, or drilling.

name: Increased circulation flow
rationale: Circulation corridors must accommodate pedestrian traffic flow efficiently; wider or better-designed corridors support higher foot traffic.

name: Reduced obstruction
rationale: Obstructions (columns, doors, furniture) in corridors impede movement and egress, so limiting obstructions is a core design pressure.

name: Minimised corridor length
rationale: Long corridors can feel institutional and waste space; shorter, more efficient circulation paths are often preferred.

name: Adequate egress width
rationale: Building codes mandate minimum corridor widths for fire egress and accessibility; sufficient width is a regulatory pressure.

name: Enhanced wayfinding clarity
rationale: Corridors should support intuitive navigation; clear sightlines, signage, and spatial hierarchy improve wayfinding.

name: Reduced dead-end corridors
rationale: Dead-end corridors are restricted by fire codes due to egress safety concerns; they should be limited or eliminated.

name: Optimised space efficiency
rationale: Corridor area is non-programmable space; designers seek to optimize (minimize waste) while meeting functional requirements.

name: Lower acoustic intrusion
rationale: Corridors can transmit noise between adjacent spaces; design pressures push for reduced sound transmission.

name: Improved accessibility compliance
rationale: ADA and similar accessibility codes require corridors to have adequate clear width, turning radii, and slope limits.

name: Higher sub-meter granularity
rationale: Building energy management and sub-metering best practices call for greater granularity to isolate end-use consumption, enabling targeted efficiency improvements.

name: Redundant metering minimised
rationale: Cost constraints and installation simplicity drive a desire to avoid unnecessary duplicate meters where a single meter can serve the required monitoring function.

name: Improved accuracy for billing sub-meters
rationale: Tenant billing and energy allocation require sub-meters with sufficient accuracy to ensure fair distribution and regulatory compliance.

name: Lower installation cost per meter
rationale: Project budgets constrain the total spend on metering hardware and installation, pushing toward fewer or lower-cost sub-meters.

name: Better integration with BMS/energy management system
rationale: Sub-meters must communicate effectively with building management systems to enable real-time monitoring and data aggregation.

name: Improved energy efficiency
rationale: Energy codes and sustainability goals push for higher-efficiency heating systems, driving design toward improved performance per room.

name: Reduced installation cost
rationale: Budget constraints and cost optimisation favour lower-cost heating solutions, limiting system complexity or capacity.

name: Greater occupant comfort
rationale: Occupant well-being and thermal comfort requirements push for more responsive and adequate per-room heating capacity.

name: Reduced carbon footprint
rationale: Environmental regulations and societal expectations favour lower-emission heating, which may constrain certain high-output system choices.

name: Enhanced zoning flexibility
rationale: Modern HVAC design favours per-room zoning to optimise energy use and comfort, pushing for more sophisticated control systems.

name: Limited space for equipment
rationale: Physical space constraints in rooms restrict the size and capacity of heating units that can be installed.

name: Increased bandwidth demand
rationale: Modern building users require high-speed internet for work, streaming, IoT devices, and cloud services, driving the need for higher-capacity cabling infrastructure.

name: Greater coverage requirement
rationale: Large buildings or campuses need comprehensive network coverage across all floors, rooms, and exterior areas, requiring extensive cabling and access points.

name: Higher reliability pressure
rationale: Business-critical operations demand redundant, fault-tolerant cabling paths and backup connections to prevent downtime.

name: Reduced physical footprint
rationale: Architectural constraints and limited riser/ceiling space push for thinner, higher-density cables and minimized cable bundles.

name: Lower installation cost pressure
rationale: Budget limitations drive selection of cost-effective cabling materials and simpler routing, though this may conflict with performance goals.

name: Enhanced future-proofing demand
rationale: Designers must anticipate future technology upgrades (e.g., Cat6a/Cat8, fiber) to avoid costly re-cabling, favoring higher-spec infrastructure now.

name: Improved access control security
rationale: Security demands drive the need for stronger authentication and authorization mechanisms in access control systems.

name: Greater user convenience
rationale: Users expect fast, seamless entry without compromising security, pushing for touchless or mobile-based intercom solutions.

name: Reduced installation cost
rationale: Budget constraints push toward simpler, less expensive access control hardware and wiring.

name: Lower power consumption
rationale: Energy efficiency requirements limit the power draw of electronic locks, panels, and intercom units.

name: Enhanced integration with building management system
rationale: Modern smart buildings demand interoperability between access control and other building systems for centralized monitoring.

name: Minimised physical footprint of access points
rationale: Aesthetic and spatial constraints push toward compact, flush-mounted intercom and reader units.

name: Higher reliability and uptime
rationale: Critical security infrastructure must operate continuously with minimal failure rate, driving redundancy and robust components.

name: Increased power distribution capacity
rationale: The electrical distribution board must handle greater electrical loads to serve landlord circuits such as common area lighting, lifts, and fire safety systems.

name: Improved electrical safety compliance
rationale: Safety standards (e.g., IEC, local codes) require adequate protection, isolation, and earthing arrangements within the distribution board.

name: Optimised space utilisation
rationale: The board needs to be compact yet accessible for maintenance, balancing spatial constraints within electrical rooms.

name: Reduced voltage drop
rationale: Minimising voltage drop ensures reliable operation of connected landlord equipment and complies with design standards.

name: Restricted heat generation
rationale: Thermal management within the board limits heat buildup from busbars and circuit breakers to prevent overheating.

name: Increased water supply capacity
rationale: A multi-tenant building requires adequate water pressure and volume to serve all units simultaneously, especially during peak demand periods.

name: Optimized drainage flow
rationale: Drainage systems must be adequately sized and sloped to handle wastewater from multiple tenants without clogging or backup.

name: Reduced pipe friction losses
rationale: Minimising friction losses through proper pipe sizing, material selection, and layout ensures adequate pressure reaches all tenants.

name: Minimised cross-contamination risk
rationale: Backflow prevention and proper separation of potable and non-potable water supplies are critical in multi-tenant buildings to protect public health.

name: Sufficient hot water supply
rationale: Central or distributed hot water systems must be sized to meet the domestic hot water demand from all tenants.

name: Reduced installation cost
rationale: Economic pressures push toward minimising material and labour costs while still meeting code and performance requirements.

name: Greater maintenance accessibility
rationale: Plumbing systems in multi-tenant buildings require accessible shutoff valves, cleanouts, and access panels for ongoing maintenance and repairs.

name: Eliminated water hammer
rationale: Pressure surges from quick-closing valves in multiple units can cause noise and pipe damage; air chambers or arrestors should be provided.

name: Improved code compliance
rationale: Building codes and plumbing standards mandate specific sizing, materials, fixtures, and backflow prevention measures for multi-tenant occupancies.

name: Enhanced quality pressure
rationale: Architectural and design standards demand improved furniture quality and durability to meet user comfort and aesthetic requirements.

name: Adequate functionality pressure
rationale: The furniture package must provide sufficient functional pieces (desks, chairs, storage) to meet room occupancy needs.

name: Reduced lead time pressure
rationale: Project scheduling pressures demand shorter procurement and delivery times for furniture packages.

name: Increased fire safety requirements
rationale: HMOs typically house multiple unrelated tenants, increasing fire risk; regulations often mandate enhanced fire detection, alarms, and escape routes.

name: Improved space per occupant standards
rationale: HMO licensing imposes minimum room sizes and amenity standards to prevent overcrowding and ensure adequate living conditions.

name: Greater compliance with housing regulations
rationale: HMOs are heavily regulated by local authorities requiring licensing, safety certificates, and management standards.

name: Reduced rental income per occupant
rationale: Strict space standards and amenity requirements can limit the number of occupants, potentially reducing overall rental yield.

name: Limited conversion flexibility
rationale: Existing building layouts may be constrained by the need for fire compartments, sound insulation, and shared facilities, restricting redesign options.

name: Higher management and maintenance burden
rationale: HMOs require ongoing management, cleaning of common areas, waste disposal coordination, and compliance checks, increasing operational demands.

name: Minimised risk of antisocial behaviour
rationale: Regulations often require HMO landlords to implement behaviour management plans and maintain good neighbour relations.

name: Adequate kitchen and bathroom provision
rationale: Licensing standards mandate sufficient cooking, washing, and sanitary facilities relative to the number of occupants.

name: Restricted maximum occupancy number
rationale: Local authorities set caps on the number of unrelated occupants in HMOs to control density and ensure safety.

name: Increased spatial comfort
rationale: A bedsit/studio unit combines living, sleeping, and cooking in one room; users desire adequate spatial comfort despite the compact footprint.

name: Optimised space efficiency
rationale: Studio units require efficient use of limited floor area to accommodate all essential functions (sleeping, living, cooking, dining) within a single room.

name: Higher natural daylight
rationale: Natural daylight is important in small living spaces to make them feel larger and more habitable; regulations often require minimum daylight factors.

name: Reduced floor area
rationale: Economic pressures from developers and site constraints often push for minimising unit floor area to maximise unit count within a building.

name: Reduced construction cost
rationale: Cost efficiency is a key driver in residential projects; smaller, simpler studio units reduce material, labour, and servicing costs.

name: Adequate storage provision
rationale: Compact living spaces require built-in storage solutions (wardrobes, cabinets) to maintain functionality and livability without clutter.

name: Better acoustic privacy
rationale: Studio units often share party walls/floors with neighbours; adequate sound insulation is critical for occupant wellbeing and compliance with building codes.

name: Maximised flexibility of use
rationale: The single-room layout should accommodate various activities (sleeping, working, entertaining) through movable furniture or transformable elements.

name: Restricted services footprint
rationale: Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing services should occupy minimal space within the unit to preserve usable floor area.

name: Increased accessibility
rationale: Landlord common areas (lobbies, corridors, waiting areas) need to be easily accessible to tenants and visitors, driving design toward more accessible layouts and compliant paths of travel.

name: Enhanced comfort and ambiance
rationale: Common areas serve as the face of the building; higher comfort levels (lighting, temperature, aesthetics) are demanded to create a welcoming environment.

name: Reduced maintenance cost
rationale: Landlord is responsible for ongoing maintenance of common areas; design pressures push toward durable, low-maintenance materials and simpler systems.

name: Lower energy consumption
rationale: Energy codes and operational cost concerns drive design toward efficient lighting, HVAC zoning, and occupancy-based controls in common areas.

name: Optimised space efficiency
rationale: There is pressure to minimise wasted circulation space while still meeting egress and accessibility requirements, optimising net lettable area.

name: Greater code compliance for fire and life safety
rationale: Common areas must comply with strict fire safety, egress widths, travel distances, and smoke control requirements as per building codes.

name: Restricted noise transmission
rationale: Common areas adjacent to tenant spaces require acoustic separation to limit noise disturbance, affecting wall/floor assembly choices.

name: Increased storage capacity
rationale: Waste and recycling storage areas need adequate capacity to accommodate building occupants' waste generation, including separation of recyclables.

name: Improved accessibility for collection vehicles
rationale: Service vehicles need to easily access waste storage for collection, requiring adequate manoeuvring space and proximity to loading areas.

name: Reduced odour impact
rationale: Waste storage areas should be designed to minimise odour transfer to occupied spaces through ventilation, separation, and enclosure design.

name: Adequate ventilation provisions
rationale: Proper ventilation is essential to control odours, moisture, and potential fire hazards in waste storage areas.

name: Reduced fire risk
rationale: Waste storage areas pose fire hazards requiring fire-rated construction, sprinkler systems, and separation from other building areas.

name: Optimised space allocation for sorting
rationale: Building codes increasingly require dedicated sorting areas for different waste streams (general waste, paper, plastic, glass, organics).

name: Minimised pest attraction
rationale: Waste storage design must incorporate pest-proof features such as sealed enclosures, smooth finishes, and appropriate drainage to deter vermin.

name: Enhanced hygiene and washability
rationale: Floors, walls, and surfaces in waste storage areas should be easy to clean, with waterproof finishes and floor drains for hosing down.

name: Sufficient container storage space
rationale: The area must accommodate required number and sizes of bins or dumpsters for each waste stream based on building occupancy and usage.

name: Increased sleeping capacity
rationale: Sleeping lofts are typically designed to accommodate one or more sleepers; there is pressure to increase capacity to make the space more functional.

name: Reduced ceiling height constraint
rationale: Sleeping lofts often have limited headroom due to roof slope or building design; there is pressure to minimize ceiling height reduction to maintain usability.

name: Improved ventilation access
rationale: Sleeping lofts require adequate ventilation for comfort and air quality; there is pressure to improve ventilation pathways.

name: Greater natural light access
rationale: Sleeping lofts benefit from natural light for daytime use and well-being; pressure exists to maximize daylight penetration.

name: Restricted structural load
rationale: Loft floors have limited load-bearing capacity; there is pressure to keep structural loads low to ensure safety and compliance.

name: Optimised floor area utilization
rationale: Sleeping lofts are often compact spaces; there is pressure to optimize the layout for efficient use of floor area.

name: Lower thermal transmittance
rationale: Roof and wall insulation around a sleeping loft must minimize heat loss for comfort; pressure to reduce U-values.

name: Adequate egress provision
rationale: Building codes require sleeping spaces to have safe egress routes; there is pressure to ensure adequate means of escape from the loft.

name: Minimised noise transmission
rationale: Sleeping areas require acoustic privacy; there is pressure to minimize sound transmission from adjacent spaces.

name: Increased natural light
rationale: Study nooks benefit from abundant natural light to reduce eye strain and create a comfortable reading/studying environment.

name: Reduced noise intrusion
rationale: A study nook requires acoustic privacy and minimal noise disturbance for concentration and focused work.

name: Adequate desk space
rationale: Sufficient work surface area is needed to accommodate books, laptop, and study materials comfortably.

name: Improved ventilation
rationale: Proper air circulation prevents stuffiness and maintains a comfortable environment for extended study sessions.

name: Reduced visual distractions
rationale: Minimising visual clutter and distractions supports sustained concentration and productivity.

name: Optimised ergonomic seating
rationale: Ergonomic seating reduces physical discomfort during prolonged sitting, preventing back and neck strain.

name: Sufficient electrical outlets
rationale: Adequate power access is needed for charging laptops, tablets, and desk lamps without cable clutter.

name: Reduced thermal discomfort
rationale: Temperature stability prevents discomfort that can disrupt focus and concentration during study.

name: Better storage integration
rationale: Integrated shelving or storage keeps study materials organised and within reach, enhancing functionality.

name: Improved social interaction
rationale: Lounge/hangout areas are designed to foster social interaction and community building, so there is pressure to increase opportunities for gathering and socializing.

name: Enhanced comfort and relaxation
rationale: As a lounge space, user comfort through soft seating, appropriate lighting, and temperature control is a primary design pressure for relaxation.

name: Reduced noise transmission
rationale: To maintain a comfortable environment for conversation and relaxation, acoustic design must limit noise intrusion from adjacent spaces.

name: Adequate spatial capacity
rationale: The space must accommodate expected occupancy without overcrowding, requiring sufficient square footage and seating capacity.

name: Optimised flexibility of layout
rationale: Lounge areas often need to support varied activities (casual seating, events, study), creating pressure for adaptable furniture and layout configurations.

name: Improved accessibility
rationale: Universal design principles require the lounge to be accessible to all users, including those with mobility impairments.

name: Reduced visual clutter
rationale: Overly cluttered or disorganized spaces can detract from a relaxing hangout atmosphere, creating pressure for clean, organized design.

name: Enhanced natural lighting
rationale: Access to daylight improves mood and comfort in lounge environments, creating a design pressure for ample windows or skylights.

name: Restricted privacy intrusion
rationale: Users expect some degree of visual and acoustic privacy in lounge settings, limiting unwanted overlooking from other spaces or passersby.

name: Improved ventilation
rationale: Bathrooms require adequate ventilation to remove moisture and prevent mould growth.

name: Reduced moisture retention
rationale: Surfaces and finishes in bathrooms should minimise moisture retention to avoid deterioration and health hazards.

name: Adequate lighting
rationale: Sufficient lighting is needed for grooming tasks and safety in a bathroom space.

name: Greater privacy
rationale: Bathrooms and ensuites are private spaces; design decisions should enhance visual and acoustic privacy.

name: Optimised space utilisation
rationale: Bathrooms are often compact spaces requiring efficient layout of fixtures and fittings.

name: Reduced slip hazard
rationale: Wet floors in bathrooms create slip risks; floor materials and gradients should minimise this danger.

name: Eliminated water damage risk
rationale: Waterproofing and drainage must prevent water damage to building fabric and adjacent spaces.

name: Better thermal comfort
rationale: Users expect warmth in bathrooms; heating and insulation should provide comfortable thermal conditions.

name: Sufficient ventilation
rationale: Adequate air exchange is necessary to control humidity and odours in enclosed bathroom spaces.

name: Increased storage capacity
rationale: Storage spaces inherently benefit from greater capacity to accommodate belongings, clothing, and equipment.

name: Optimised space utilisation
rationale: Efficient use of floor area and vertical space is a core design goal for storage areas.

name: Improved accessibility
rationale: Storage spaces should be easily accessible to users for convenience and functionality.

name: Reduced floor area dedicated to storage
rationale: There is often pressure to minimise the footprint of storage to free up space for habitable rooms.

name: Restricted depth to avoid wasted space
rationale: Excessively deep wardrobes can lead to inaccessible storage and inefficient use of room volume.

name: Improved spatial flow pressure
rationale: Entry/mudrooms benefit from better spatial flow to transition smoothly between exterior and interior.

name: Adequate storage pressure
rationale: Mudrooms require sufficient storage for coats, shoes, and outdoor gear to remain functional.

name: Reduced dirt tracking pressure
rationale: Design should minimize the spread of dirt and moisture from exterior into the house.

name: Improved durability pressure
rationale: Mudroom surfaces need to withstand heavy use, moisture, and dirt; materials should be durable.

name: Adequate ventilation pressure
rationale: Good airflow helps dry wet gear and reduces humidity/mold risk in the mudroom.

name: Optimized layout efficiency pressure
rationale: An efficient layout allows multiple people to use the mudroom simultaneously without congestion.

name: Restricted visual exposure pressure
rationale: Mudrooms should offer some privacy or screening so that clutter is not immediately visible from main living areas.

name: Sufficient lighting pressure
rationale: Adequate lighting is needed for finding items, changing shoes, and safety in the entry zone.

name: Limited energy loss pressure
rationale: The entry/mudroom should be designed to minimize heat loss when the exterior door is opened frequently.

name: Increased structural load capacity
rationale: Timber frames must bear vertical and lateral loads; a pressure exists to increase load-bearing capacity.

name: Reduced material cost
rationale: Cost efficiency drives minimization of timber usage and material expense.

name: Improved fire resistance
rationale: Timber is combustible; there is a design pressure to enhance fire resistance ratings through treatments or design.

name: Reduced thermal bridging
rationale: Timber frame details such as studs can create thermal bridges; pressure exists to limit these for energy performance.

name: Adequate bracing for lateral stability
rationale: Shear walls, diagonal bracing, or moment connections must provide sufficient lateral stability against wind/seismic forces.

name: Limited moisture content
rationale: Timber must be kept dry to prevent rot, warping, and strength degradation; moisture content must be constrained.

name: Greater span capability
rationale: Architectural openness demands longer spans, pressuring timber members to achieve greater clear spans.

name: Reduced embodied carbon
rationale: Sustainability goals pressure minimizing the carbon footprint of timber sourcing and construction.

name: Enhanced durability against biological decay
rationale: Wood is susceptible to fungi and insects; design pressures exist to improve preservative treatment and detailing for long-term durability.

name: Improved thermal resistance
rationale: Insulated wall panels are designed to provide high thermal resistance (R-value), so there is a design pressure to improve thermal insulation performance.

name: Reduced weight
rationale: Lighter panels are easier to handle, transport, and install, reducing structural load on the building frame.

name: Increased structural strength
rationale: Panels must withstand wind loads, impact, and other structural forces, creating pressure for greater strength.

name: Reduced moisture permeability
rationale: Moisture ingress can degrade insulation performance and cause mold, so lower moisture permeability is desired.

name: Lower installation cost
rationale: Cost pressures drive the need for more economical panel systems, including manufacturing and installation expenses.

name: Enhanced fire resistance
rationale: Building codes require fire-rated assemblies, creating pressure for better fire resistance in insulated panels.

name: Greater dimensional stability
rationale: Panels must resist warping, shrinking, or expanding due to temperature and humidity changes to maintain integrity.

name: Reduced air leakage
rationale: Air tightness is critical for energy performance, so minimizing air leakage through panel joints is a key design pressure.

name: Improved acoustic insulation
rationale: Sound transmission through walls is a concern in many applications, driving the need for better acoustic performance.

name: Higher load-bearing capacity
rationale: The loft floor deck must have sufficient load-bearing capacity to support live loads (people, furniture) and dead loads (flooring materials, insulation) as per building codes.

name: Reduced deflection under load
rationale: Excessive deflection can cause cracking of finishes and uncomfortable bounce, so limiting deflection is a key design pressure.

name: Adequate fire resistance rating
rationale: Building codes require floor assemblies to have a minimum fire resistance rating to prevent fire spread between floors.

name: Lower overall thickness
rationale: A thinner floor deck may be desired to maximize headroom in the loft space below or above the deck.

name: Enhanced acoustic insulation
rationale: Sound transmission through the loft floor deck may need to be controlled for occupant comfort between spaces.

name: Reduced thermal bridging
rationale: The floor deck assembly should minimise thermal bridging to improve overall building energy performance.

name: Greater durability against moisture
rationale: The loft floor deck must resist moisture damage from potential leaks, condensation, or humidity to maintain structural integrity over time.

name: Increased structural load capacity
rationale: The roof truss/rafter system must bear dead loads, live loads (snow, rain), and wind loads. Higher structural capacity ensures safety and code compliance.

name: Reduced material weight
rationale: Lighter materials reduce the dead load on the truss system and supporting walls, allowing for longer spans and more efficient structural design.

name: Improved connection stiffness
rationale: Stiffer connections at truss joints (nail plates, bolts, or welds) improve overall structural integrity and load transfer between members.

name: Reduced deflection under load
rationale: Limiting deflection prevents damage to roofing materials, ceiling finishes, and ensures serviceability requirements are met per building codes.

name: Enhanced fire resistance rating
rationale: Fire-rated assemblies or treatments may be required for the roof structure to meet building code fire separation and protection requirements.

name: Reduced thermal bridging
rationale: Minimizing thermal bridging through the roof truss system improves overall building envelope thermal performance and reduces energy loss.

name: Increased daylight penetration
rationale: Skylights are primarily designed to bring natural daylight into interior spaces; thus a design pressure exists to increase daylight penetration through skylights.

name: Reduced heat gain
rationale: Skylights can be sources of unwanted solar heat gain; there is a design pressure to reduce heat gain to maintain thermal comfort and energy efficiency.

name: Reduced heat loss
rationale: Skylights are thermal weak points in building envelopes; there is a design pressure to reduce heat loss through skylights in cold climates.

name: Improved structural integrity
rationale: Skylights must withstand wind, snow, and impact loads; a design pressure exists to improve structural integrity to ensure safety and durability.

name: Reduced water leakage risk
rationale: Skylights are prone to water ingress at their junctions with the roof; there is a strong design pressure to reduce water leakage risk through proper flashing and sealing.

name: Enhanced glare control
rationale: Uncontrolled direct sunlight through skylights can cause visual discomfort; design pressure exists to enhance glare control using diffusers, shades, or orientation strategies.

name: Improved energy efficiency
rationale: Building codes and sustainability goals drive a design pressure to improve energy efficiency of skylights through better glazing, insulation, and coatings.

name: Reduced condensation risk
rationale: Condensation on skylights can cause water damage and mold; design pressure exists to reduce condensation risk through thermal breaks, insulated glazing, and ventilation.

name: Lower maintenance requirements
rationale: Skylights are often difficult and expensive to access for cleaning and repair; there is a design pressure to minimise maintenance requirements through durable materials and self-cleaning coatings.

name: Increased space efficiency pressure
rationale: Sliding doors do not require swing clearance, which increases usable floor space in tight areas.

name: Improved accessibility pressure
rationale: Sliding doors are easier to operate for individuals with mobility challenges compared to swinging doors.

name: Reduced wall space usage pressure
rationale: When open, a sliding/barn door occupies wall space parallel to the opening, reducing usable wall area for furniture or other elements.

name: Limited privacy pressure
rationale: Sliding doors, especially barn door styles, often have gaps around the edges that reduce sound insulation and visual privacy compared to traditional hinged doors.

name: Enhanced aesthetic appeal pressure
rationale: Barn doors and sliding doors are often chosen for their rustic or modern aesthetic appeal as design features.

name: Reduced structural load pressure
rationale: Sliding door hardware must support the door's weight transferred to the top track or floor, imposing structural considerations on the supporting wall or header.

name: Optimized clearance requirement pressure
rationale: Sliding doors eliminate the need for door swing clearance zones, optimizing floor plan layouts in constrained spaces.

name: Improved loft accessibility
rationale: Building codes and accessibility standards demand that loft access ladders or stairs provide safe and convenient access, especially if the loft is habitable or used for storage.

name: Reduced space consumption
rationale: Space within a building is valuable, so there is a design pressure to minimise the footprint of access elements like ladders and stairs to free up floor area for other uses.

name: Improved structural safety
rationale: Engineering safety requirements push for stronger, more stable construction to prevent collapse or accidents during use.

name: Reduced cost
rationale: Budget constraints push for lower-cost materials and simpler designs for loft access solutions.

name: Greater ease of use
rationale: Users prefer access ladders or stairs that are comfortable and easy to operate, especially for frequent loft use.

name: Lower installation complexity
rationale: Simpler installation reduces labour time and the need for structural modifications, which is a common pressure in retrofit scenarios.

name: increased structural load capacity
rationale: The deck must support expected live loads (people, furniture) and dead loads (materials); higher load capacity ensures safety and durability.

name: improved weather resistance
rationale: As an outdoor component, the deck must resist moisture, UV, temperature changes, and precipitation to prevent rot, warping, and deterioration.

name: enhanced slip resistance
rationale: Outdoor decks are exposed to rain, snow, and moisture, making slip-resistant surfaces critical for user safety.

name: adequate drainage performance
rationale: Proper drainage prevents water pooling, reducing risk of rot, mold, and structural damage on the deck surface.

name: sufficient fire resistance
rationale: Building codes often require fire-resistant materials for decks attached to structures, especially in wildfire-prone areas.

name: minimised material degradation
rationale: Reducing rot, corrosion, and UV degradation extends deck lifespan and reduces maintenance costs.

name: limited thermal expansion effects
rationale: Outdoor decks experience temperature fluctuations; controlling expansion/contraction prevents warping and fastener issues.

name: reduced structural deflection
rationale: Limiting deflection under load ensures user comfort and prevents damage to decking materials and railings.

name: eliminated trip hazards
rationale: Uneven boards, protruding fasteners, and level changes create safety risks; eliminating these hazards is critical for accessibility and liability.

name: Increased cooling capacity
rationale: In hot climates or spaces with high cooling loads, there is an engineering pressure to increase the cooling capacity of mini-split units to adequately condition the space.

name: Improved energy efficiency
rationale: Building energy codes and sustainability goals create a strong design pressure to improve the energy efficiency (SEER rating) of mini-split systems.

name: Reduced installation cost
rationale: Budget constraints typically pressure designers to select lower-cost mini-split units, reducing upfront installation expenses.

name: Reduced noise level
rationale: Occupant comfort requirements pressure designers to choose quieter indoor and outdoor units, especially in bedrooms or quiet zones.

name: Reduced refrigerant line length
rationale: Manufacturer limitations on refrigerant line length and elevation difference between indoor and outdoor units constrain placement decisions.

name: Adequate outdoor unit ventilation
rationale: The outdoor condenser unit requires sufficient clearance for airflow and heat rejection, pressuring designers to locate it in an unobstructed location.

name: Increased electrical capacity
rationale: Electrical Sub-Boards need to handle growing electrical loads from additional equipment and occupants, driving a need for higher capacity.

name: Improved safety compliance
rationale: Electrical safety standards and regulations require enhanced protection features, proper grounding, and compliance with codes.

name: Reduced installation cost
rationale: Budget constraints drive the need to minimise material, labour, and equipment costs for electrical sub-board installation.

name: Limited physical space
rationale: Electrical rooms or enclosures have constrained space which restricts the size and configuration of sub-boards.

name: Improved accessibility for maintenance
rationale: Sub-boards must be easily accessible for routine maintenance, troubleshooting, and emergency shutdowns.

name: Reduced heat generation
rationale: Heat dissipation from electrical components must be managed to prevent overheating, requiring efficient design and ventilation.

name: Enhanced coordination with other systems
rationale: Sub-boards must integrate effectively with upstream distribution boards and downstream loads, requiring careful coordination.

name: Improved indoor air quality
rationale: Mechanical ventilation and ERV systems are designed to supply fresh outdoor air and exhaust stale indoor air, directly improving indoor air quality (IAQ) by diluting pollutants, CO2, and odors.

name: Higher energy efficiency
rationale: Energy Recovery Ventilators (ERVs) recover heat and moisture from exhaust air to precondition incoming fresh air, reducing the heating and cooling load on HVAC systems.

name: Reduced humidity levels
rationale: ERVs transfer moisture between airstreams, helping to control indoor humidity; in humid climates they can reduce excessive moisture infiltration.

name: Lower energy consumption
rationale: By recovering energy from exhaust air, ERVs reduce the overall energy consumption of the HVAC system for conditioning outdoor ventilation air.

name: Adequate ventilation rates
rationale: Building codes and standards (e.g., ASHRAE 62.1) mandate minimum ventilation rates per occupant and floor area, driving the need for sufficient mechanical ventilation capacity.

name: Increased bandwidth demand
rationale: Modern building systems and user expectations require higher data throughput for streaming, conferencing, and data transfer.

name: Greater cable density
rationale: More devices (IoT sensors, AV displays, access points) require more cable runs within the building.

name: Optimised cable routing and organisation
rationale: Cable management and structured routing is critical to avoid interference and enable maintenance.

name: Reduced cable clutter
rationale: Aesthetic and spatial requirements call for minimising visible cable runs and reducing visual impact.

name: Limited cable length runs
rationale: Signal degradation over long distances (especially for AV and high-speed data) imposes constraints on cable lengths.

name: Higher cost pressure for premium cabling
rationale: Higher category cabling (Cat6a, fiber) and shielded cables increase material and installation costs.

name: Improved future-proofing capacity
rationale: Design must accommodate future technology upgrades (e.g., higher bandwidth standards) without major retrofitting.

name: Eliminated electromagnetic interference risk
rationale: Proper separation from power cables and use of shielded cabling to avoid signal interference.

name: Improved insulation requirement
rationale: Garden shed conversions typically need additional insulation to meet building regulations for habitable spaces.

name: Maximised natural light pressure
rationale: Shed conversions often lack windows; adding glazing improves daylight access and living quality.

name: Minimised structural alteration
rationale: Owners typically prefer to retain the existing shed structure to reduce cost and complexity.

name: Adequate ventilation requirement
rationale: Converting a shed to a habitable space requires proper ventilation to prevent condensation and ensure air quality.

name: Restricted footprint expansion
rationale: Planning permissions often limit the size increase of existing outbuildings to preserve garden space.

name: Sufficient electrical capacity
rationale: Existing shed electrical supply is usually inadequate for a habitable space; upgrading is needed.

name: Improved damp-proofing
rationale: Sheds are typically not damp-proofed to habitable standards; moisture protection must be added.

name: Minimised planning restriction risks
rationale: Local planning authorities may have restrictive policies on converting outbuildings to living spaces.

name: Higher ceiling height requirement
rationale: Standard shed ceiling heights may be below the minimum required for habitable rooms in building codes.

name: Improved acoustic separation
rationale: As a secondary dwelling often located close to the main house and property boundary, there is a design pressure to increase acoustic separation to ensure privacy and noise control between the granny flat, the main residence, and neighbouring properties.

name: Maximised space efficiency
rationale: Granny flats typically have limited square footage, creating a strong design pressure to maximise the efficient use of every square metre for living, sleeping, cooking, and bathroom functions within a compact footprint.

name: Adequate natural light
rationale: Being a standalone small dwelling, there is pressure to ensure adequate natural light penetrates all habitable rooms, especially given potential overshadowing from the main house, fences, or neighbouring structures.

name: Reduced construction cost
rationale: Granny flats are often budget-sensitive projects intended to provide affordable additional accommodation or rental income, creating pressure to minimise construction costs through efficient design, standardised components, and simple forms.

name: Minimised footprint on backyard
rationale: Homeowners typically wish to preserve outdoor living space, garden areas, and setback from the main house, creating pressure to minimise the building's footprint and limit its impact on the usable backyard area.

name: Expanded accessibility
rationale: Granny flats are often intended for aging parents or relatives, creating pressure to incorporate accessible design features such as step-free entry, wider doorways, and accessible bathroom fixtures.

name: Sufficient energy performance
rationale: Building codes increasingly require energy-efficient design; there is pressure to ensure sufficient insulation, thermal performance, and energy-efficient systems to meet compliance and minimize ongoing utility costs for occupants.

name: Restricted height
rationale: Local planning regulations and neighbourhood character provisions often impose height limits on secondary dwellings, creating pressure to restrict the building height to comply with zoning and avoid overshadowing neighbours.

name: Improved accessibility compliance
rationale: Building codes and accessibility standards (e.g., ADA) require accessible entrances to meet slope, width, and surface requirements, driving a need for improved ramp design.

name: Reduced slope gradient
rationale: Accessibility standards mandate a maximum slope (e.g., 1:12) to ensure safe wheelchair and mobility aid usage, pushing designers to reduce steepness.

name: Increased ramp width
rationale: To accommodate wheelchairs, walkers, and passing space, codes often require minimum ramp widths of 36-48 inches, pressuring wider designs.

name: Enhanced surface friction
rationale: Safety requirements necessitate slip-resistant surfaces on ramps to prevent accidents in wet or icy conditions, driving a demand for better traction.

name: Eliminated tripping hazards
rationale: Ramp transitions and edges must be flush and free of obstacles to avoid falls, requiring hazards to be minimized or eliminated.

name: Greater landing area provision
rationale: Building codes require level landings at the top, bottom, and at changes in direction of ramps to allow resting and maneuvering, demanding more space.

name: Sufficient handrail integration
rationale: Ramps with rises greater than 6 inches require handrails on both sides per accessibility codes, pressing for adequate handrail design.

name: Reduced overall footprint impact
rationale: Site constraints and existing building geometry may limit the space available for ramp extension, creating pressure to minimize the ramp's footprint.

name: Increased slip resistance
rationale: Grab rails and handrails must provide adequate slip resistance to ensure user safety, especially in wet or high-moisture areas like bathrooms and stairwells.

name: Greater structural strength
rationale: Handrails and grab rails must bear significant loads (e.g., body weight, pulling forces) and must be designed with sufficient structural strength to prevent failure.

name: Optimised ergonomic placement
rationale: Handrails need to be positioned at appropriate heights and angles to accommodate users of varying abilities, improving accessibility and comfort.

name: Reduced corrosion susceptibility
rationale: Grab rails and handrails, particularly in bathrooms or outdoor settings, must resist corrosion to maintain structural integrity and hygiene.

name: Minimised installation clearance gaps
rationale: Clearance gaps between handrails and walls must be kept small to prevent clothing or limbs from getting trapped, ensuring user safety.

name: Improved accessibility pressure
rationale: Building codes and universal design principles push for step-free thresholds to ensure wheelchair and mobility aid access.

name: Reduced trip hazard pressure
rationale: Step-free thresholds eliminate abrupt level changes that pose tripping risks, especially important in high-traffic areas.

name: Increased weather sealing pressure
rationale: Thresholds at grade level must resist water ingress; step-free designs require careful detailing to maintain weathertightness.

name: Reduced thermal bridging pressure
rationale: Eliminating a physical step can reduce thermal bridging at the threshold, improving energy performance.

name: Increased drainage design pressure
rationale: Step-free thresholds at exterior doors must incorporate drainage solutions to prevent water pooling and ingress.

name: Higher structural continuity pressure
rationale: Removing a step may require alternative structural load transfer paths, demanding greater structural coordination.

name: Reduced construction cost pressure
rationale: Step-free thresholds can simplify construction by eliminating step formwork, but may increase costs in retrofits; net effect perceived as cost-saving in new builds.

name: Greater regulatory compliance pressure
rationale: Accessibility regulations (e.g., ADA, Building Code Part M) mandate or strongly recommend step-free thresholds at accessible entrances.

name: Eliminated level change pressure
rationale: A step-free threshold by definition eliminates the vertical level change, removing the physical barrier.

name: Improved waterproofing
rationale: Waterproofing is critical for wet rooms and walk-in showers to prevent water damage to adjacent spaces and structure.

name: Adequate drainage slope
rationale: Proper floor slope toward drain is essential to prevent standing water and ensure effective drainage in a wet room.

name: Enhanced slip resistance
rationale: Floor surfaces in wet areas must have adequate slip resistance to ensure user safety.

name: Reduced water leakage risk
rationale: Minimizing the risk of water leakage through joints, seals, and transitions is a primary design concern.

name: Lower moisture accumulation
rationale: Reducing moisture buildup helps prevent mold, mildew, and material degradation in the shower space.

name: Better accessibility
rationale: Walk-in showers are often designed with barrier-free entry for improved accessibility and universal design.

name: Optimised ventilation
rationale: Proper ventilation is needed to manage humidity and moisture levels in the enclosed wet room space.

name: Restricted water spray outside enclosure
rationale: Containing water spray within the shower area is important to avoid wetting adjacent bathroom zones.

name: Sufficient drainage capacity
rationale: The drain must handle peak water flow rates to prevent flooding or standing water during use.

name: Improved reliability and coverage
rationale: Emergency call systems must be highly reliable and have adequate coverage to ensure calls for help are received and responded to promptly. This is a core engineering requirement for life-safety systems.

name: Reduced false alarms
rationale: False alarms can desensitize responders and waste resources, so minimising false triggers is a key design pressure for call systems.

name: Enhanced audibility and clarity
rationale: Audible alerts and voice communications must be clear and loud enough to be heard throughout the intended area, especially in noisy or emergency conditions.

name: Minimised response time
rationale: System design should aim to minimise the time between a call being placed and the response being initiated, as this is critical in emergencies.

name: Greater integration with fire and security systems
rationale: Coordinating emergency call systems with fire alarms, security systems, and building management systems improves overall emergency response effectiveness.

name: Lower maintenance requirements
rationale: Systems requiring less frequent maintenance are more dependable and cost-effective over their lifecycle.

name: Increased accessibility demand
rationale: Building codes and accessibility standards (e.g., ADA) require wider doorways to accommodate wheelchairs and mobility devices, exerting pressure to increase doorway width.

name: Improved egress flow
rationale: Fire safety and emergency egress codes often mandate wider doorways to ensure safe occupant evacuation, driving wider dimensions.

name: Reduced structural intrusion
rationale: Wider doorways may compromise structural wall integrity or load-bearing capacity, creating pressure to limit doorway width.

name: Constrained spatial layout
rationale: Room dimensions, wall lengths, and adjacent functional zones may physically restrict how wide a doorway can be built, exerting a constraining pressure.

name: Enhanced aesthetic proportion
rationale: Design preferences for grand or open-feeling spaces may favor wider doorways for visual continuity and proportion, especially in public or formal areas.

name: Improved accessibility
rationale: Level-access bedrooms are designed for accessibility, especially for wheelchair users or people with mobility impairments. There is a strong engineering/regulatory pressure to increase accessibility features.

name: Reduced step-free threshold
rationale: Level-access implies minimal or no step at the entrance threshold to allow easy access for all users.

name: Greater floor space
rationale: Adequate clear floor space is needed for wheelchair maneuverability and turning circles within the bedroom.

name: Adequate doorway width
rationale: Doorways must be wide enough to accommodate wheelchairs and mobility aids, typically minimum 900mm clear opening.

name: Eliminated level changes within room
rationale: Any internal level changes or steps within the bedroom would compromise the level-access design intent.

name: Optimised accessible bathroom proximity
rationale: Level-access bedrooms are often designed in conjunction with an accessible bathroom nearby to support users with mobility needs.

name: Lower sill heights for windows
rationale: Windows with lower sill heights allow seated users or wheelchair users to have external views, improving quality of life.

name: Adequate power outlet placement
rationale: Power outlets should be placed at accessible heights (not too low) for ease of use by all occupants.

name: Sufficient emergency egress accessibility
rationale: Emergency escape routes from a level-access bedroom must accommodate people with mobility impairments.

name: Increased accessibility requirements
rationale: An adapted kitchen for individuals with disabilities requires greater accessibility, including lower countertops, accessible storage, and maneuverable space.

name: Enhanced safety compliance
rationale: Safety codes for accessible kitchens demand non-slip flooring, proper clearances, and safe appliance placement.

name: Expanded clear floor space
rationale: ADA and similar accessibility standards require minimum clear floor space for wheelchair maneuverability in adapted kitchens.

name: Reduced counter height
rationale: Adapted kitchens typically require lower counter heights (approx. 28-34 inches) to accommodate wheelchair users.

name: Limited upper cabinet reach
rationale: Upper cabinets in adapted kitchens should be limited in height or include pull-down mechanisms for accessibility.

name: Adequate knee clearance
rationale: Sinks and work surfaces in adapted kitchens require sufficient knee clearance (minimum 27 inches high, 30 inches wide) for wheelchair access.

name: Restricted appliance depth
rationale: Appliances in adapted kitchens may need to be shallower or have front-facing controls for accessibility.

name: Optimised workflow layout
rationale: The kitchen layout should be optimised for efficient workflow while accommodating accessibility needs, such as a U-shaped or L-shaped configuration.
