name: Higher structural integrity
rationale: Fire-rated windows must maintain structural integrity under fire conditions to prevent collapse and maintain compartmentation.

name: Reduced cost
rationale: Budget constraints create a design pressure to minimise the cost of fire-rated windows while still meeting code requirements.

name: Minimised weight
rationale: Heavier fire-rated glazing assemblies put more load on supporting structures, creating pressure for lighter-weight solutions.

name: Improved visible light transmittance
rationale: Architects prefer fire-rated windows with high light transmittance for visual connectivity and daylighting, creating pressure for better clarity.

name: Restricted frame thickness
rationale: Slim sightlines are aesthetically preferred, creating pressure to minimise frame profile thickness while maintaining fire resistance.

name: Adequate fire-rating compliance
rationale: Building codes and fire safety regulations mandate minimum fire-resistance ratings for interior windows in certain locations, creating a compliance pressure.

name: Lower installation complexity
rationale: Simpler installation reduces labour cost and risk of improper fitting, creating pressure for easier-to-install designs.

name: Improved acoustic insulation
rationale: The primary function of an acoustic interior window is to provide sound insulation; there is a design pressure to improve its acoustic performance.

name: Reduced material thickness
rationale: Thinner materials may be desirable to fit within tight wall/frame assemblies, though this may conflict with acoustic performance.

name: Increased airtightness
rationale: Airtight seals around the window are critical to prevent sound leakage and improve overall acoustic performance.

name: Reduced cost
rationale: Budget constraints typically create a pressure to minimise construction and material costs for interior components.

name: Enhanced frame rigidity
rationale: A stiffer window frame reduces vibration transmission and improves acoustic isolation performance.

name: Greater glass thickness
rationale: Thicker glass panes generally provide better sound attenuation, creating a pressure to increase glass thickness.

name: Optimised laminated glass layering
rationale: Using laminated glass with optimized acoustic interlayers improves sound transmission loss across frequencies.

name: Reduced installation gaps
rationale: Minimising gaps during installation prevents acoustic flanking paths that degrade overall performance.

name: Better STC rating compliance
rationale: Acoustic interior windows must meet or exceed specified Sound Transmission Class (STC) ratings per building codes or acoustic consultant requirements.

name: Improved thermal insulation
rationale: Steel-frame windows benefit from enhanced thermal insulation to reduce heat transfer through the frame and glass, improving energy efficiency.

name: Increased structural rigidity
rationale: Steel frames require adequate stiffness to support glass panels and resist deformation under load, necessitating increased structural rigidity.

name: Reduced thermal bridging
rationale: Steel is highly conductive; minimizing thermal bridging through the frame is critical to prevent heat loss and condensation issues.

name: Lower material weight
rationale: Reducing the weight of the steel frame component can simplify installation and reduce structural load on surrounding walls.

name: Adequate acoustic insulation
rationale: Interior windows should provide sufficient sound attenuation between spaces; steel frames and glazing need to be designed for adequate acoustic performance.

name: Minimised frame thickness
rationale: Slimmer steel profiles are often desired for aesthetic reasons and to maximize glass area and natural light transmission.

name: Increased thermal insulation
rationale: Timber-frame windows provide better thermal insulation than metal-frame alternatives, reducing heat loss through the building envelope.

name: Reduced heat loss
rationale: Timber has naturally lower thermal conductivity, helping to minimise heat transfer through the window frame.

name: Enhanced aesthetic appeal
rationale: Timber frames offer a warm, natural aesthetic that complements interior design, creating visual harmony.

name: Reduced maintenance requirements
rationale: Interior timber windows are less exposed to weather, reducing the need for frequent upkeep compared to exterior timber.

name: Increased structural rigidity
rationale: Timber provides adequate structural strength for framing interior window openings, supporting glazing and loads.

name: Reduced material cost
rationale: Timber is often more cost-effective than aluminium or uPVC for interior window frames, lowering overall project costs.

name: Improved acoustic insulation
rationale: Timber frames can contribute to better sound attenuation between interior spaces due to material density.

name: Limited moisture resistance
rationale: Timber is susceptible to moisture damage and warping if not properly treated, constraining its use in humid interior environments.

name: Greater sustainability
rationale: Timber is a renewable resource with lower embodied carbon than synthetic materials, aligning with sustainable design principles.

name: Increased thermal insulation
rationale: Aluminium frames have high thermal conductivity, so design pressures aim to improve insulation through thermal breaks or double/triple glazing to reduce heat loss.

name: Reduced heat transfer
rationale: Minimising thermal bridging through the aluminium frame is a key design pressure to improve energy efficiency and occupant comfort.

name: Adequate structural strength
rationale: The aluminium frame must have sufficient strength and stiffness to support the glazing and resist operational loads, wind loads, and building movements.

name: Reduced material weight
rationale: Aluminium is lightweight compared to other frame materials like steel or timber, which is a design advantage for ease of installation and reduced structural load.

name: Minimised condensation risk
rationale: Aluminium's high thermal conductivity can lead to cold surfaces and condensation; design pressures aim to reduce this through thermal breaks and proper glazing specifications.

name: Enhanced acoustic performance
rationale: Interior windows need to provide sound insulation; design pressures push for better acoustic sealing and appropriate glazing to reduce noise transmission.

name: Improved airtightness
rationale: Proper sealing around the aluminium frame is necessary to prevent drafts and air leakage, improving energy efficiency and comfort.

name: Lower material cost
rationale: Aluminium window systems have cost implications; design pressures aim to minimise material and fabrication costs while meeting performance requirements.

name: Greater durability and corrosion resistance
rationale: Aluminium can be susceptible to corrosion in certain environments; design pressures push for protective coatings, anodising, or powder coating to ensure long-term durability.

name: Improved solar heat gain control
rationale: Window blinds and shades are primarily used to control solar heat gain through windows, improving thermal comfort and reducing cooling loads.

name: Enhanced visual comfort and glare reduction
rationale: Blinds and shades help manage daylight glare and visual discomfort for building occupants.

name: Greater occupant privacy control
rationale: Window treatments provide privacy for occupants, especially at ground level or in urban settings.

name: Reduced unwanted heat loss through windows
rationale: Some window shades (e.g., cellular shades) can provide insulation value, reducing heat loss in colder months.

name: Lower maintenance and cleaning requirements
rationale: Integration decisions consider ease of cleaning and maintenance over the lifecycle of the window treatment system.

name: Minimized obstruction of natural daylight
rationale: Blinds and shades should not excessively block daylight, as maximizing natural light is often a design goal.

name: Optimized automated control integration
rationale: Modern buildings often integrate blinds with building automation systems for optimal energy performance and occupant comfort.

name: Reduced glare on screens and work surfaces
rationale: Window treatments are selected to minimize screen glare in office and educational environments.

name: Better aesthetic integration with facade design
rationale: The visual appearance and integration of blinds/shades with the building facade is an architectural consideration.

name: Increased structural load capacity
rationale: Balusters must withstand lateral loads (e.g., people leaning or pushing against them) per building codes, so there is a design pressure to increase structural capacity.

name: Improved safety compliance
rationale: Building codes require balusters to meet minimum height, spacing, and load resistance for safety, creating pressure to improve compliance.

name: Reduced material cost
rationale: Budget constraints push designers to select less expensive materials or minimize material usage for balusters.

name: Minimised spindle spacing
rationale: Tighter spacing (smaller gaps) between spindles is often desired for aesthetic reasons or child safety codes, but also cost pressure to not over-space.

name: Greater aesthetic appeal
rationale: Architectural design intent often calls for visually appealing baluster shapes, materials, and finishes.

name: Eliminated maintenance requirements
rationale: There is pressure to use durable, low-maintenance materials (e.g., powder-coated metal vs. bare wood) to reduce long-term upkeep.

name: Optimised durability against weathering
rationale: For exterior applications, balusters face exposure to moisture, UV, and temperature cycles, driving a need for weather-resistant materials and coatings.

name: Increased structural support for stair nosing
rationale: Stair nosing must have sufficient structural support to withstand foot traffic and impact loads, requiring adequate connection to treads and stringers.

name: Improved slip resistance of stair nosing
rationale: Building codes and safety standards require stair nosings to have slip-resistant surfaces to prevent accidents.

name: Enhanced visibility/contrast of stair nosing
rationale: Codes often require contrasting nosing strips or markings on stair edges for visual cue to users, improving safety.

name: Reduced wear/abrasion on stair nosing edge
rationale: The leading edge of stairs experiences concentrated wear from foot traffic; durable materials or protective profiles are needed to limit deterioration.

name: Greater durability of stair nosing material
rationale: Stair nosings must be made of robust materials (e.g., metal, hard rubber) to withstand repeated use and impact.

name: Minimized tripping hazard at stair nosing
rationale: Nosing projection and height must be limited/standardized to prevent tripping, per building code requirements.

name: Reduced noise from stair nosing footfall
rationale: In some settings, softer or dampened nosing materials may be used to reduce impact noise from footsteps.

name: Adequate fire resistance of stair nosing
rationale: Stair nosings in fire-rated stairs must have appropriate fire-resistance ratings to maintain egress pathway integrity.

name: Optimized profile geometry of stair nosing
rationale: The nosing profile (radius, projection) must be optimized for both comfort and safety, balancing ergonomic and code requirements.

name: Increased load-bearing capacity
rationale: Stair stringers must support live and dead loads from stairs; structural engineering requires adequate load-bearing capacity to prevent failure.

name: Reduced deflection
rationale: Excessive deflection under load can cause cracking or discomfort; engineering standards limit deflection for safety and serviceability.

name: Improved corrosion resistance
rationale: If stringer is steel or exposed to moisture, corrosion resistance extends lifespan and maintains structural integrity.

name: Sufficient fire resistance
rationale: Building codes require stair components to meet fire-resistance ratings for means of egress.

name: Eliminated dimensional mismatch
rationale: Stringer dimensions must match stair tread/riser geometry; mismatches cause construction issues and code violations.

name: Optimized connection strength
rationale: Connections between stringer and floor/landing structure must be strong to transfer loads safely.

name: Increased fire safety pressurization
rationale: Stairwells/shafts often require fire-rated construction and pressurization systems to prevent smoke ingress during fires, per building codes.

name: Reduced floor area footprint
rationale: Stairwells take up valuable floor space; there is often pressure to minimize their footprint to maximize leasable or usable area.

name: Improved egress width adequacy
rationale: Building codes require minimum stair widths for occupant egress capacity; wider stairs improve safety and flow during evacuation.

name: Reduced construction cost
rationale: Budget constraints create pressure to minimize costs associated with stairwell construction, materials, and finishes.

name: Enhanced structural stability
rationale: Stairwells often serve as lateral force-resisting cores; increased structural robustness is needed for seismic and wind loads.

name: Restricted number of stairwells
rationale: While codes set minimum stair counts based on occupancy, there is pressure to not exceed the required number to save space and cost.

name: Sufficient natural light requirement
rationale: Some designs or codes encourage natural light in stairwells for wayfinding and occupant comfort, creating pressure for windows or glazing.

name: Lower accessibility slope requirement
rationale: Stairwells inherently involve steep slopes; in adjacent accessible routes there is pressure to minimize slope (via ramps/elevators) but for stairwells themselves steepness is inherent.

name: Increased fire resistance rating
rationale: Building codes (e.g., IBC) require stair enclosures to have a minimum fire-resistance rating (typically 1-2 hours) to protect the means of egress.

name: Improved structural stability
rationale: Stair enclosure walls must resist lateral loads (wind, seismic) and remain stable to ensure safe egress during emergencies.

name: Enhanced smoke-tightness
rationale: Stair enclosures must be smoke-tight to prevent smoke infiltration into the means of egress during a fire.

name: Reduced thermal bridging
rationale: Stair enclosure walls can act as thermal bridges between floors; minimizing conductive heat transfer improves energy efficiency.

name: Minimised wall thickness
rationale: Thinner walls preserve usable floor area within the stair enclosure and adjacent spaces, though must balance against fire and structural requirements.

name: Adequate acoustic isolation
rationale: Stair enclosures require sound attenuation between floors to meet acoustic privacy and comfort standards.

name: Restricted wall penetrations
rationale: Penetrations through stair enclosure walls (e.g., ducts, pipes) compromise fire integrity and must be limited and properly fire-stopped.

name: Higher impact resistance
rationale: Walls in high-traffic egress paths need resistance to impact from occupants, equipment, and during evacuation.

name: Optimised buildability/constructability
rationale: Design should facilitate ease of construction, especially coordination with stairs, landings, and MEP systems.

name: Increased pressurisation
rationale: Pressurised lobbies require increased air pressure relative to adjacent spaces to prevent smoke ingress during a fire.

name: Reduced air leakage
rationale: To maintain effective pressurisation, air leakage through doors, walls and construction joints must be minimised.

name: Adequate door closing force
rationale: Doors in pressurised lobbies require sufficient closing force to overcome the pressure differential and remain closed.

name: Lower smoke infiltration
rationale: The primary purpose of pressurisation is to limit smoke entry into the lobby during fire events.

name: Greater pressure differential
rationale: A sufficient pressure differential must be maintained between the pressurised lobby and adjacent spaces to ensure smoke containment.

name: Enhanced fire resistance rating
rationale: Fire doors must have adequate fire-resistance ratings (e.g., 60–90 minutes) to compartmentalize fire and protect egress paths, per building codes.

name: Improved self-closing mechanism reliability
rationale: Fire doors must reliably self-close and latch to prevent smoke and fire spread, as required by code.

name: Reduced air leakage around door perimeter
rationale: Smoke seals and tight tolerances reduce smoke infiltration into stairwells during a fire event.

name: Increased door width for egress capacity
rationale: Wider doors improve evacuation flow and comply with accessibility and egress code minimums.

name: Greater durability for high-traffic usage
rationale: Fire doors in stairwells endure frequent opening and closing; robust construction prolongs service life and maintains fire integrity.

name: Lower hardware projection to avoid obstruction
rationale: Minimizing protruding hardware reduces snagging hazard and maintains clear circulation paths in stair enclosures.

name: Minimised gaps under door for smoke control
rationale: Smaller undercuts limit smoke spread beneath the door while still allowing required clearances for operation.

name: Improved latch/lock engagement
rationale: Positive latching ensures the door remains closed during a fire, preventing failure of the fire barrier.

name: Restricted use of glazed vision panels
rationale: Fire-rated glazing is expensive and may reduce overall fire resistance; limiting panel size can maintain barrier performance.

name: Increased safety compliance
rationale: Building codes and safety regulations mandate minimum illumination levels for emergency escape routes to ensure safe evacuation.

name: Reduced energy consumption
rationale: Energy efficiency requirements push toward lower power consumption, fewer luminaires, and use of energy-saving LED technologies in emergency lighting systems.

name: Improved battery autonomy
rationale: Emergency lighting must maintain illumination for a minimum duration (typically 1-3 hours) during power failure, driving need for higher-capacity batteries.

name: Reduced maintenance burden
rationale: Regular testing and maintenance of emergency lighting systems create operational costs; designers seek to minimise number of units and simplify access for testing.

name: Enhanced visibility and wayfinding
rationale: Emergency escape lighting must clearly illuminate exit paths and signage to guide occupants to safety, requiring adequate light levels and strategic placement.

name: Lower installation cost
rationale: Budget constraints push toward fewer emergency lighting units and simpler wiring configurations to reduce capital expenditure.

name: Optimised lighting coverage
rationale: Regulations require that emergency escape lighting covers all exit routes, stairs, directional changes, and fire-fighting equipment without dark spots.

name: Increased fire suppression coverage
rationale: Sprinkler systems in stairwells must provide adequate coverage to protect the egress path, which is critical for life safety during a fire.

name: Reduced water flow pressure
rationale: If the water supply pressure is insufficient or if pipe sizing is too restrictive, the sprinkler system may not deliver adequate flow to suppress a fire in the stairwell.

name: Improved compliance with fire codes
rationale: Building codes (e.g., IBC, NFPA 13) require stairwell sprinklers to meet specific spacing, coverage, and reaction time standards, pushing for enhanced system design.

name: Restricted installation space
rationale: Stairwells often have limited clearances and confined geometry, constraining sprinkler head placement and pipe routing compared to open floor areas.

name: Greater reliability requirement
rationale: As a means of egress, stairwell sprinkler systems must have high reliability to ensure they operate when needed during an emergency, driving demand for robust design and maintenance.

name: Increased ventilation capacity pressure
rationale: Building codes and standards (e.g., ASHRAE, local building regulations) mandate minimum fresh air supply rates for occupant health and comfort, driving a need for higher ventilation capacity.

name: Improved pressurisation control pressure
rationale: To maintain indoor air quality and prevent infiltration of contaminants or unconditioned air, precise pressurisation control (positive or negative relative to adjacent spaces) is required.

name: Higher energy efficiency pressure
rationale: Energy performance targets and sustainability certifications (e.g., LEED, BREEAM, Part L) push for optimised fan efficiency, heat recovery, and demand-controlled ventilation to reduce operational energy use.

name: Reduced system noise pressure
rationale: Acoustic comfort requirements (e.g., noise criteria (NC) limits, local regulations) drive the need to limit fan and airflow noise from ventilation systems, especially in noise-sensitive spaces.

name: Reduced capital cost pressure
rationale: Project budget constraints often require minimising initial expenditure on large ductwork, high-efficiency fans, and complex control systems, creating a downward pressure on system scale and sophistication.

name: Maximised system reliability pressure
rationale: Critical facilities (e.g., hospitals, cleanrooms, laboratories) require high reliability of pressurisation and ventilation to maintain safety and operational continuity, pushing for redundancy and robust equipment selection.

name: Reduced duct space pressure
rationale: Architectural constraints on ceiling plenum depth and service riser space limit the size of ductwork, driving the need for compact layouts or higher-velocity air distribution to fit within available space.

name: Better indoor air quality pressure
rationale: Health and safety regulations (e.g., CO2 concentration limits, pollutant dilution requirements) push for sufficient outdoor air delivery and effective filtration, driving higher system capacity and performance.

name: Improved drainage capacity
rationale: Floor drains and stair drainage systems need to adequately handle anticipated water flow from cleaning, rain ingress, or fire sprinkler discharge to prevent ponding and slip hazards.

name: Reduced blockage risk
rationale: Drains must be designed to minimize clogging from debris, sediment, or solids to ensure reliable drainage.

name: Sufficient slope for drainage
rationale: Proper slope (pitch) is essential to direct water efficiently toward floor drains and prevent standing water.

name: Lower risk of water damage
rationale: Effective drainage reduces the risk of water intrusion into adjacent building elements, finishes, and structural components.

name: Adequate trap seal maintenance
rationale: Floor drain traps must retain sufficient water seal to prevent sewer gases from entering occupied spaces.

name: Minimised odour issues
rationale: Proper drain design and trap maintenance minimize unpleasant odors in stairwells and adjacent areas.

name: Enhanced accessibility compliance
rationale: Drain grates and covers must meet slip-resistance and accessibility standards to ensure safe passage for all users.

name: Increased load-bearing capacity
rationale: The stair structural frame/carriage must support dead loads (self-weight) and live loads (occupants, materials) without failure.

name: Improved structural stability
rationale: Lateral stability and resistance to overturning are critical for stair frames to ensure safety under dynamic loading.

name: Reduced deflection under load
rationale: Excessive deflection can cause discomfort, cracking of finishes, or misalignment of stair components, so minimizing deflection is a design pressure.

name: Minimised material weight
rationale: Lighter stair frames reduce dead load on supporting structures and can lower material and transportation costs.

name: Adequate fire resistance rating
rationale: Stairs often serve as means of egress and must meet fire-resistance requirements per building codes.

name: Sufficient connection strength to adjacent structures
rationale: Connections to landings, slabs, or beams must transfer loads reliably and resist differential movements.

name: Increased structural load capacity
rationale: Precast concrete stairs must be designed to carry adequate dead and live loads (e.g., occupant traffic, emergency loads) per building codes.

name: Improved fire resistance rating
rationale: Concrete stairs serve as fire-egress components and require sufficient fire-resistance duration as per fire safety codes.

name: Enhanced dimensional precision
rationale: Precast elements rely on tight tolerances and accurate fit with adjacent structural and architectural components during installation.

name: Reduced construction cost
rationale: Standardisation and repetition in precast elements aim to lower material, formwork, and labour costs.

name: Minimised weight for handling and transport
rationale: Precast stairs must be liftable and transportable; excessive self-weight increases crane capacity requirements and handling difficulty.

name: Sufficient slip resistance on tread surfaces
rationale: Stair treads require adequate slip resistance to ensure safe pedestrian circulation, especially in egress paths.

name: Increased structural stability requirement
rationale: Spiral stairs have complex geometry requiring robust structural design to ensure safety and load-bearing capacity.

name: Reduced footprint pressure
rationale: Spiral stairs are often chosen to minimize the floor area dedicated to vertical circulation compared to straight stairs.

name: Improved ergonomic comfort
rationale: Tread depth and riser height consistency along the spiral path must be optimized for safe and comfortable use.

name: Higher fire egress compliance
rationale: Building codes often restrict or impose additional requirements on spiral stairs as means of egress due to their tighter geometry.

name: Eliminated tripping hazard
rationale: Uniform tread geometry and proper handrail design are critical to prevent accidents on the narrowing side of spiral treads.

name: Maximised material efficiency
rationale: The compact form of a spiral stair inherently uses less material than a conventional stair, but optimization can further reduce waste.

name: Adequate headroom clearance
rationale: Spiral stair geometry must maintain minimum headroom (typically 6'6" or 2.0 m) throughout the helical path to avoid collisions.

name: Limited visual obstruction
rationale: Open-riser or lightweight designs may be preferred to reduce the visual bulk of the stair in a space.

name: Enhanced handrail continuity
rationale: Handrails on spiral stairs must follow the helical curve continuously without abrupt breaks to ensure user safety and code compliance.

name: Increased fire separation
rationale: Scissor stairs require enhanced fire separation between the two interlocking stair flights to maintain code-compliant egress pathways.

name: Reduced floor area footprint
rationale: Scissor stairs are chosen to minimise the floor area consumed by two separate stair enclosures, providing efficient egress within a compact footprint.

name: Improved occupant egress efficiency
rationale: The interlocking arrangement allows two separate egress paths within a single stair enclosure, improving overall evacuation capacity.

name: Reduced construction cost
rationale: Consolidating two stair flights into one shared enclosure reduces wall area, structural elements, and overall construction cost compared to separate stair towers.

name: Enhanced structural load capacity
rationale: The interlocking configuration creates complex load paths; increased structural capacity is needed to safely support both flights and transfer loads through shared landings.

name: increased tread depth for safety
rationale: Alternating tread stairs have narrow, alternating treads that can be hazardous; increasing tread depth improves foothold and safety.

name: reduced overall height for accessibility
rationale: Building codes often restrict alternating tread stairs to low-rise applications (e.g., mezzanines, lofts) due to steepness; limiting height ensures code compliance.

name: improved handrail integration
rationale: Alternating tread stairs require continuous handrails on both sides for user stability; enhancing handrail design improves safety and usability.

name: restricted use as primary egress
rationale: Most building codes (e.g., IBC) prohibit alternating tread stairs as required means of egress; their use is restricted to limited occupant loads or non-egress applications.

name: adequate structural support for cantilevered treads
rationale: Alternating tread stairs often use cantilevered steps; ensuring sufficient structural support prevents deflection and failure under load.

name: Increased ceiling height for comfort
rationale: Building codes and human comfort standards require adequate headroom for safe and comfortable movement through spaces.

name: Reduced headroom to minimise construction costs
rationale: Lower floor-to-floor heights reduce material costs, structural loads, and overall building height, leading to cost savings.

name: Adequate clearance for accessibility compliance
rationale: Accessibility standards (e.g., ADA, building codes) mandate minimum headroom clearances for barrier-free design.

name: Greater headroom for service infrastructure
rationale: Sufficient clearance is needed to accommodate HVAC ducts, electrical conduits, plumbing, and other building services above ceilings.

name: Restricted clearance to maximise floor area ratio
rationale: In tight floor-to-floor height allowances, reducing headroom can allow more usable floor area within a fixed building envelope.

name: Increased safety regulation compliance
rationale: Building codes and fire safety regulations require adequate egress routes for occupant safety.

name: Improved accessibility standards
rationale: ADA and similar accessibility codes demand accessible means of egress for persons with disabilities.

name: Higher occupant capacity requirements
rationale: Larger occupant loads require wider and more numerous egress paths to ensure safe evacuation times.

name: Reduced travel distance to exits
rationale: Building codes limit the maximum travel distance to an exit to ensure timely evacuation.

name: Minimised obstructions in egress path
rationale: Clear and unobstructed paths are critical for safe egress; furniture, equipment, or architectural features can block escape routes.

name: Increased number of exit points
rationale: Multiple exit points are required based on occupancy and building geometry to provide redundancy.

name: Enhanced wayfinding and signage clarity
rationale: Clear exit signage and wayfinding systems improve occupant orientation during emergency evacuation.

name: Limited egress route width constraints
rationale: Structural or spatial constraints may limit the possible width of egress corridors, acting as a restricting force.

name: Greater fire resistance of egress path materials
rationale: Egress routes must be constructed with fire-rated materials to remain tenable during a fire event.

name: Reduced swing clearance
rationale: Corner door pivot hinges reduce the required swing clearance compared to standard hinges, minimizing the door's arc radius into adjacent spaces.

name: Improved corner accessibility
rationale: Pivot hinge placement at the corner allows the door to swing outward from the corner point, improving access around the doorway.

name: Greater structural load on frame
rationale: Pivot hinges concentrate door weight and operational forces at single top and bottom pivot points rather than distributing across multiple hinges.

name: Reduced hinge visibility
rationale: Pivot hinges mounted at the top and bottom of the door are less visually obtrusive than standard side-mounted hinges.

name: Higher precision alignment requirement
rationale: Pivot hinge doors demand precise alignment of top and bottom pivot points to avoid binding or uneven operation.

name: Limited door weight capacity
rationale: Pivot hinge systems typically support less weight than continuous or multiple standard hinges, restricting door material choices.

name: Enhanced aesthetic continuity
rationale: The concealed or minimal pivot hinge mechanism offers a cleaner, more modern appearance that is preferred in contemporary architectural design.

name: Constrained hardware integration
rationale: Pivot hinge configurations limit locations for locks, handles, and closers due to the door's pivot geometry.

name: Increased structural stability
rationale: The corner door panel must withstand wind loads and transfer forces safely to the building structure, requiring adequate structural stability.

name: Reduced thermal bridging
rationale: Corner glass panels are prone to thermal bridging at the joint, requiring minimized heat loss for energy performance.

name: Improved weather sealing
rationale: As a moving corner element, the panel must resist water and air infiltration through enhanced sealing mechanisms.

name: Reduced operational friction
rationale: The folding mechanism requires minimized friction to ensure smooth opening and closing over the panel's lifespan.

name: Greater glazing area
rationale: Corner door panels are often designed to maximize transparency and views, driving demand for larger glass surfaces.

name: Higher insulated glass performance
rationale: Building energy codes demand adequate thermal insulation in glazed door panels, especially at exposed corners.

name: Lower panel weight
rationale: Heavy panels strain hinges and tracks; reduced weight improves operability and reduces hardware fatigue.

name: Enhanced corner joint rigidity
rationale: The mitered or hinged corner joint must be sufficiently rigid to prevent sagging and maintain alignment over time.

name: Adequate frame drainage
rationale: Corner door frames require proper drainage paths to prevent water accumulation and damage at the corner interface.

name: Enhanced sliding smoothness
rationale: The track must enable smooth sliding motion for the corner door; increased smoothness reduces friction and wear.

name: Higher load capacity
rationale: The track must support the weight of the door panels without deformation or failure.

name: Reduced clearance gap
rationale: Minimising gaps between track and door components prevents rattling and improves weather sealing.

name: Improved corrosion resistance
rationale: Track materials must resist corrosion over time, especially if exposed to moisture or outdoor conditions.

name: Minimised installation complexity
rationale: Simpler installation reduces labour cost and potential for errors during assembly at the corner junction.

name: Greater dimensional accuracy
rationale: Precise dimensions are required at the corner transition for proper alignment of sliding door panels.

name: Reduced material cost
rationale: Cost pressures push toward lighter, cheaper materials while maintaining structural integrity.

name: Enhanced durability under cyclic loading
rationale: Repeated sliding cycles create fatigue; the track must endure without cracking or deforming.

name: Increased structural stability for Corner Door Frame Assembly
rationale: Corner door frames at building corners must withstand higher wind loads and transfer forces; structural stability is a key engineering requirement.

name: Enhanced weather sealing for Corner Door Frame Assembly
rationale: Corner locations are vulnerable to water and air infiltration; improved sealing is critical for envelope performance.

name: Adequate corner clearance for Corner Door Frame Assembly
rationale: Adequate clearance at corners is needed for proper door swing and frame installation coordination.

name: Reduced thermal bridging at Corner Door Frame Assembly
rationale: Corner door frames can create thermal bridges; minimizing heat loss improves energy efficiency.

name: Minimised installation tolerance stack-up for Corner Door Frame Assembly
rationale: Tight tolerances are critical at corners where multiple building systems converge; excessive tolerance accumulation must be avoided.

name: Expanded corrosion resistance for Corner Door Frame Assembly
rationale: Exposure at corners increases vulnerability to moisture; enhanced corrosion protection extends service life.

name: Restricted frame deflection under load for Corner Door Frame Assembly
rationale: Deflection must be limited to maintain door operation and weather seal integrity under wind and impact loads.

name: Improved acoustic performance for Corner Door Frame Assembly
rationale: Corner door assemblies may be acoustically weaker; enhanced sound attenuation benefits interior comfort.

name: Lower maintenance access difficulty for Corner Door Frame Assembly
rationale: Corner frames can be harder to access for maintenance; design should minimize difficulty of future repairs.

name: Increased structural stability pressure
rationale: The corner door jamb must bear structural loads at the corner intersection, requiring sufficient strength and rigidity to maintain door alignment and frame integrity under operational stresses.

name: Improved weather sealing pressure
rationale: Corner door jambs are critical points for air and moisture infiltration; better sealing is needed to prevent drafts, water intrusion, and energy loss around the door perimeter.

name: Enhanced dimensional accuracy pressure
rationale: Precise dimensional tolerances at the corner jamb are required to ensure proper door fit, smooth operation, and alignment with surrounding wall and floor connections.

name: Reduced material stress concentration pressure
rationale: The corner geometry creates natural stress concentration points; minimizing these stresses through design features (radiused corners, reinforcement) prevents cracking and premature failure.

name: Restricted thermal bridging pressure
rationale: Corner jambs can act as thermal bridges, conducting heat/cold through the building envelope; limiting this heat transfer improves energy efficiency and prevents condensation issues.

name: Reduced water ingress pressure
rationale: Corner door thresholds are designed to minimise water ingress at door openings, especially in external or semi-exposed locations. The threshold detail must act as a barrier to rainwater entry.

name: Improved thermal performance pressure
rationale: Thresholds contribute to the thermal envelope of a building. An improved thermal break or insulated threshold reduces heat loss at the door assembly.

name: Reduced air infiltration pressure
rationale: Door thresholds must limit uncontrolled air leakage. A well-sealed threshold helps maintain indoor air quality and energy efficiency by reducing drafts.

name: Increased durability pressure
rationale: Thresholds in corner door locations experience high foot traffic and exposure to dirt, moisture, and mechanical wear. Greater durability extends service life and reduces maintenance.

name: Reduced trip hazard pressure
rationale: Building codes and accessibility standards require thresholds to be low-profile or ramped to minimise trip hazards, particularly at corner doors where approach angles may vary.

name: Enhanced accessibility compliance pressure
rationale: Threshold height and profile must comply with accessibility standards (e.g., ADA, building codes) to allow wheelchair and mobility aid users to cross without obstruction.

name: Increased thermal stress resistance
rationale: Corner door glass panels near building edges experience higher thermal gradients due to exposure to sun and shade, requiring increased resistance to thermal stress to prevent cracking.

name: Improved wind load resistance
rationale: Corner locations experience higher wind pressures (corner suction effects), so the glass panel must withstand greater wind loads.

name: Greater impact resistance
rationale: Door glass panels at corners are more vulnerable to impact from pedestrians, carts, or door swing, requiring higher impact resistance for safety.

name: Reduced edge deflection
rationale: Minimizing deflection at the edges of corner glass panels is critical to maintain seal integrity and prevent air/water infiltration under wind loads.

name: Limited solar heat gain
rationale: Corner glass panels may receive more direct sunlight across two exposures, so solar heat gain must be limited to maintain indoor comfort and reduce cooling loads.

name: Enhanced structural support at framing
rationale: The corner door frame and supporting structure must provide adequate stiffness and strength to carry the glass panel loads, especially at the vulnerable corner condition.

name: Improved corrosion resistance
rationale: Corner door hardware in exterior or high-moisture environments must resist corrosion to maintain functionality and appearance.

name: Greater load-bearing capacity
rationale: Hardware must support the weight of the door and withstand repeated use without deformation or failure.

name: Reduced operational friction
rationale: Lower friction in hinges, pivots, or sliding mechanisms ensures smooth door operation and reduces wear over time.

name: Minimised installation complexity
rationale: Simpler installation reduces labor cost and potential for errors during assembly on site.

name: Enhanced security against forced entry
rationale: Corner door hardware is a critical point in the door assembly where break-in attempts are common; stronger locking and reinforcement mechanisms are needed.

name: Improved aesthetic finish consistency
rationale: Architectural design standards often require matching finishes and seamless visual integration of hardware with the door and surrounding building elements.

name: Reduced long-term maintenance cost
rationale: Durable, low-maintenance hardware reduces lifecycle costs for building owners and facility managers.

name: Optimised dimensional tolerance
rationale: Precise dimensional tolerances ensure proper fit with door frames, preventing misalignment, binding, or air/water infiltration.

name: Better compatibility with smart access systems
rationale: Modern building trends increasingly integrate electronic access control, requiring hardware that accommodates sensors, actuators, or wiring.

name: Improved structural integrity
rationale: The frameless glass corner door system must withstand wind loads, seismic forces, and impact loads. Engineering demands for structural safety and building code compliance create pressure to increase the structural integrity of the glass panels, framing connections, and anchoring systems.

name: Enhanced thermal insulation
rationale: Energy efficiency requirements and building energy codes put pressure on the glass corner door system to have improved thermal performance, often requiring double or triple glazing, low-e coatings, and thermally broken frames.

name: Reduced risk of glass breakage
rationale: Safety concerns and building codes mandate tempered or laminated glass to minimise the risk of breakage and injury. This creates a design pressure to reduce failure probability.

name: Greater water and air infiltration resistance
rationale: Corner door systems are highly exposed to weather. Building envelope performance requirements push for better sealing, gaskets, and drainage to resist water and air leakage.

name: Lower manufacturing complexity
rationale: The unique mitered glass corner and minimal framing create geometric complexity. Cost and production constraints exert pressure to reduce manufacturing complexity through simpler joint detailing or standardised components.

name: Maximized visual transparency
rationale: The frameless corner door is often chosen for unobstructed views and seamless indoor-outdoor connection. Architectural design intent pressures the system to maximise glass area and minimise visible framing.

name: Minimised deflection under load
rationale: Excessive glass deflection can cause seal failure, visual distortion, and operational issues. Structural performance requirements push to limit deflection within acceptable limits.

name: Adequate hardware durability
rationale: Hinges, locks, and operating mechanisms must withstand repeated use and exposure. Durability requirements create pressure for more robust hardware, corrosion-resistant materials, and reliable operation cycles.

name: Eliminated condensation risk
rationale: Thermal bridging at glass edges and framing can cause condensation. Building science principles and occupant comfort push to prevent or eliminate condensation through improved edge seals and thermal breaks.

name: Increased closing force reliability
rationale: The door closer mechanism must reliably return the door to its closed position, requiring sufficient spring force or hydraulic damping to overcome friction and air resistance.

name: Reduced mechanical wear on hinge assembly
rationale: Minimizing wear on moving parts extends the lifespan of the closer mechanism and maintains consistent performance over time.

name: Improved corrosion resistance of exposed components
rationale: The mechanism may be exposed to environmental moisture, requiring corrosion-resistant materials or coatings to ensure long-term functionality.

name: Reduced size to fit within door frame constraints
rationale: The mechanism must fit within limited space available in the corner door frame without interfering with door swing or adjacent wall surfaces.

name: Optimised closing speed adjustability
rationale: Adjustable closing speed allows the mechanism to be tuned for different door weights, user needs, and accessibility requirements such as building codes.

name: Reduced manufacturing cost per unit
rationale: Lower production cost makes the mechanism more commercially viable and competitive in the market.

name: Improved aesthetic integration with door hardware
rationale: The closer mechanism should visually blend with the door's hardware aesthetic, especially in visible corner installations where it may be prominent.

name: Reduced noise during door closing operation
rationale: Quieter operation improves user comfort, particularly in noise-sensitive environments like offices, libraries, or healthcare facilities.

name: Greater tolerance to misalignment during installation
rationale: Flexibility in installation tolerances reduces the need for precision framing and simplifies the installation process for contractors.

name: Improved accessibility compliance
rationale: Building codes require automated doors to provide accessible entry/egress, driving design toward better compliance features.

name: Reduced obstruction footprint
rationale: Corner door operators must minimise protrusion into circulation paths to avoid collisions and maintain clear passage.

name: Enhanced durability for high-traffic
rationale: Corner locations often see heavy use, demanding robust materials and mechanisms to withstand repeated cycling.

name: Lower energy consumption
rationale: Energy codes and sustainability goals push toward efficient motor operation and standby power reduction.

name: Minimised maintenance requirements
rationale: Facility managers prefer operators that require less frequent servicing, especially in hard-to-access corner installations.

name: Improved safety sensing coverage
rationale: Corner geometries create blind spots; additional or better-positioned sensors are needed to prevent entrapment or impact.

name: Reduced installation complexity
rationale: Corner framing and power routing can be challenging, so designs that simplify mounting and wiring are preferred.

name: Greater weather sealing performance
rationale: Exterior corner doors face wind-driven rain and thermal bridging, requiring enhanced gaskets and insulation.

name: Restricted noise emission
rationale: Quiet operation is desired in adjacent occupied spaces to avoid disturbance from door cycling.

name: greater corner wall stud capacity
rationale: Corner wall studs must support greater loads due to intersecting walls, requiring increased structural capacity for lateral and vertical forces.

name: minimised corner wall stud deflection
rationale: Corner studs are prone to deflection from eccentric loading; limiting deflection ensures wall straightness and cladding integrity.

name: adequate nailing surface for sheathing
rationale: Corner framing must provide sufficient nailing surface for adjacent wall sheathing panels to meet structural diaphragm requirements.

name: reduced thermal bridging at corner
rationale: Corner stud assemblies often create thermal bridges; minimising this improves energy performance and reduces condensation risk.

name: stronger connection to intersecting walls
rationale: Corner studs must be strongly tied to intersecting wall framing to transfer shear loads and maintain structural continuity.

name: adequate structural support
rationale: The rough opening must have adequate structural support around the corner to maintain integrity and prevent distortion.

name: minimised thermal bridging
rationale: Corner locations are prone to thermal bridging; insulation and framing details should minimise heat loss.

name: sufficient framing dimensions
rationale: The rough opening must have sufficient width and height to accommodate the door frame and allow for proper shimming and adjustment.

name: restricted air leakage
rationale: Corner door rough openings are vulnerable to air infiltration; detailing should restrict uncontrolled air leakage.

name: adequate weatherproofing
rationale: Corner openings are more exposed to wind-driven rain; enhanced weatherproofing is needed at the rough opening.

name: limited water intrusion
rationale: Water penetration at corner door rough openings must be prevented through proper flashing and sealing.

name: better corner bracing
rationale: Corner openings reduce wall rigidity; improved corner bracing or shear panels may be required to maintain structural performance.

name: minimised deflection
rationale: Excessive deflection of the rough opening can cause door binding and operational issues; deflection should be minimised.

name: adequate clearance for door frame
rationale: Sufficient clearance around the rough opening is needed to accommodate the door frame, shims, and allow for square installation.

name: Improved corner visibility
rationale: A corner door alcove benefits from improved visibility and openness to reduce collision risks and improve wayfinding.

name: Increased alcove depth
rationale: Sufficient depth in the alcove allows doors to swing fully without obstructing the corridor or adjacent circulation paths.

name: Reduced door swing interference
rationale: Minimising the extent to which the door protrudes into the main circulation path is critical for safety and functionality.

name: Enhanced accessibility clearance
rationale: Building codes require adequate accessible maneuvering clearance at door alcoves for wheelchair users.

name: Minimised wall encroachment
rationale: Design pressures to keep the alcove's walls minimal to avoid visual obstruction and wasted floor area at the corner.

name: Increased structural stability
rationale: Angled wall intersections can provide greater structural rigidity compared to perpendicular intersections by distributing lateral loads more effectively.

name: Reduced construction complexity
rationale: Angled wall intersections often require more complex joinery, custom framing, and detailing, increasing construction difficulty and cost.

name: Improved spatial efficiency
rationale: Angled intersections can allow for more efficient use of floor space and unique room layouts compared to standard orthogonal wall intersections.

name: Eliminated right-angle constraints
rationale: Angled wall intersections remove the need for strict 90-degree corners, offering more design flexibility in floor plans.

name: Higher material waste
rationale: The non-standard angles may lead to more off-cuts and waste in materials like drywall, studs, and cladding.

name: Increased fire resistance rating
rationale: Building codes and fire safety regulations require adequate fire resistance ratings for door assemblies in corners to prevent fire spread.

name: Reduced gap clearances
rationale: Smaller gaps around door edges improve fire sealing and smoke containment performance.

name: Higher material fire rating
rationale: Materials with greater fire resistance are required to achieve the overall fire rating for the corner door assembly.

name: Minimised thermal bridging
rationale: Reducing thermal bridging through door frames and hardware helps maintain the integrity of the fire-rated assembly.

name: Improved smoke seal performance
rationale: Better smoke seals around the corner door assembly enhance overall fire protection and life safety performance.

name: Improved lateral load resistance
rationale: Stone rubble walls, due to their mass and thickness, provide increased resistance to lateral forces such as wind and seismic loads.

name: Greater compressive strength
rationale: Stone rubble masonry has high compressive strength, allowing the wall to bear heavy vertical loads without crushing.

name: Reduced tensile capacity
rationale: Stone rubble walls have very low tensile strength compared to reinforced masonry or concrete, making them susceptible to cracking under tension.

name: Limited mortar bond strength
rationale: The irregular shape of rubble stones results in limited mortar bond strength compared to dressed stone or brick masonry.

name: Increased thermal mass
rationale: The high density and mass of stone rubble walls provide significant thermal mass, helping to moderate indoor temperature fluctuations.

name: Higher construction material cost
rationale: Stone rubble walls typically require more material volume and skilled labour compared to modern cavity or framed wall systems.

name: Lower ductility
rationale: Stone rubble walls are brittle and lack ductility, making them prone to sudden failure under seismic overload without proper reinforcement.

name: Greater durability against weathering
rationale: Natural stone is highly resistant to weathering, moisture intrusion, and biological degradation compared to many other building materials.

name: Restricted ability for openings

name: Improved acoustic isolation pressure
rationale: The primary design requirement for an acoustic door system is to maximise sound transmission class (STC) rating, driving the need for better acoustic isolation through sealing, mass, and damping.

name: Reduced air leakage pressure
rationale: Acoustic performance is heavily dependent on airtight seals around door perimeters; minimising gaps and leakage paths is critical for maintaining acoustic integrity.

name: Enhanced structural rigidity pressure
rationale: The door frame and panel must resist deflection and vibration to prevent flanking paths and maintain consistent acoustic performance over time.

name: Constrained weight pressure
rationale: Heavier door assemblies provide better sound attenuation but must be balanced against operability, hinge loading, and structural support limits.

name: Optimised sealing compliance pressure
rationale: Perimeter gaskets and drop seals must provide adequate compression and conformity to irregular surfaces to eliminate acoustic leaks.

name: Minimised flanking transmission pressure
rationale: Sound can bypass the door through adjacent walls, floor, and ceiling junctions; corner details must be designed to prevent flanking paths.

name: Adequate door mass pressure
rationale: Mass-law dictates that heavier constructions provide higher sound insulation; sufficient mass must be incorporated into the door leaf assembly.

name: Optimised corner joint detailing pressure
rationale: Corner joints in the door frame and between the door and wall must be continuously sealed and structurally robust to maintain the acoustic envelope.

name: Improved thermal resistance
rationale: Composite wall assemblies are designed to have higher thermal resistance (R-value) to reduce heat transfer through the building envelope.

name: Reduced thermal bridging
rationale: Composite walls often incorporate continuous insulation and thermal break strategies to minimise thermal bridging through structural elements.

name: Enhanced moisture management
rationale: Composite wall assemblies need effective moisture control including vapour barriers, drainage planes, and air barriers to prevent condensation and water ingress.

name: Greater structural strength
rationale: Composite wall assemblies must resist wind loads, gravity loads, and other structural forces, requiring adequate strength and stiffness.

name: Reduced air leakage
rationale: Air sealing is critical in composite wall systems to control infiltration/exfiltration and improve energy performance.

name: Optimised material thickness
rationale: Material thickness in composite wall assemblies is optimised to balance thermal, structural, and space constraints without over-dimensioning.

name: Minimised embodied carbon
rationale: Design pressures increasingly aim to reduce the embodied carbon footprint of wall assembly materials through material selection and efficiency.

name: Improved fire resistance rating
rationale: Composite wall assemblies must meet building code fire resistance requirements, driving design toward higher fire ratings.

name: Reduced construction complexity
rationale: Simpler composite wall assemblies are preferred to reduce labour costs and construction errors, though this may compete with performance goals.

name: Increased lateral load resistance
rationale: Reinforced masonry walls are designed to resist lateral forces such as wind and seismic loads; increasing lateral load resistance improves structural performance and safety.

name: Reduced wall thickness
rationale: Design decisions may aim to reduce wall thickness to save material and space, but must balance against structural and insulation requirements.

name: Improved thermal insulation
rationale: Masonry walls contribute to building envelope thermal performance; improving insulation reduces energy consumption.

name: Higher compressive strength
rationale: Reinforced masonry walls must have adequate compressive strength to support vertical loads from floors and roof.

name: Reduced construction cost
rationale: Cost optimization is a key design pressure; minimizing material and labor costs while maintaining performance.

name: Enhanced seismic performance
rationale: Reinforced masonry walls are critical lateral force-resisting elements in seismic design; enhancing ductility and strength improves earthquake performance.

name: Lower embodied carbon

name: Greater fire resistance
rationale: Masonry provides inherent fire resistance; design decisions aim to maintain or improve fire rating.

name: Reduced moisture penetration
rationale: Controlling water ingress through masonry walls is critical for durability and preventing freeze-thaw damage.

name: increased structural load capacity
rationale: Structural concrete walls must have sufficient load-bearing capacity to support vertical gravity loads from floors, roofs, and other structural elements above.

name: increased lateral load resistance
rationale: Concrete walls serve as shear walls to resist lateral forces from wind and seismic events, requiring adequate strength and stiffness.

name: improved durability against environmental exposure
rationale: Concrete walls exposed to weather, moisture, and freeze-thaw cycles need enhanced durability to prevent degradation over time.

name: increased fire resistance rating
rationale: Concrete walls are often required to provide fire separation between building compartments, demanding sufficient fire resistance duration.

name: limited wall thickness
rationale: Architectural constraints and space planning often restrict wall thickness to preserve usable floor area and maintain design aesthetics.

name: minimised material cost
rationale: Project budget constraints drive the need to optimise concrete and reinforcement quantities without compromising structural safety.

name: reduced construction complexity
rationale: Simpler wall geometry and reinforcement detailing reduce labour costs, construction time, and risk of errors on site.

name: limited foundation settlement impact
rationale: Differential settlement under the wall must be minimised to prevent cracking, tilting, or structural distress.

name: adequate thermal insulation performance
rationale: Concrete walls have high thermal mass but low insulation value; additional insulation is needed to meet building energy code requirements.

name: Increased durability for Internal Wall Lining
rationale: Internal wall linings need to withstand day-to-day impacts, abrasion, and wear from building occupants and activities. Higher durability reduces maintenance costs and extends service life.

name: Improved moisture resistance for Internal Wall Lining
rationale: Internal wall linings in wet areas such as bathrooms, kitchens, and laundries require enhanced moisture resistance to prevent mould growth, delamination, and material degradation.

name: Reduced material thickness for Internal Wall Lining
rationale: Thinner linings can save costs and increase usable floor area, but must still satisfy structural and fire resistance requirements.

name: Greater acoustic performance for Internal Wall Lining
rationale: Internal wall linings contribute to sound insulation between rooms; higher acoustic performance is desired for privacy and comfort in residential and commercial buildings.

name: Lower material cost for Internal Wall Lining
rationale: Budget constraints drive pressure to select cost-effective lining materials without compromising essential performance criteria.

name: Optimised fire resistance for Internal Wall Lining
rationale: Building codes require internal wall linings to meet specific fire resistance levels (spread of flame, smoke production) to ensure occupant safety.

name: Reduced environmental impact for Internal Wall Lining
rationale: Growing sustainability requirements push for lower embodied carbon, recyclable materials, and reduced volatile organic compounds (VOCs) in wall linings.

name: Improved aesthetic finish for Internal Wall Lining
rationale: Visual appearance and surface quality of wall linings affect occupant satisfaction and design intent, driving demand for smooth, paint-ready, or decorative finishes.

name: Increased load transfer efficiency
rationale: The interface between wall and foundation must efficiently transfer vertical and lateral loads from the superstructure to the foundation system.

name: Improved structural continuity

name: Reduced moisture penetration

name: Minimised thermal bridging

name: Adequate bearing capacity
rationale: The foundation must provide sufficient bearing capacity beneath the wall to prevent excessive settlement or structural failure.

name: Reduced cracking risk

name: Improved shear resistance
rationale: Lateral forces (wind, seismic) generate shear stresses at the wall-foundation connection that must be adequately resisted.

name: Eliminated differential settlement
rationale: Uniform bearing conditions and proper foundation design are needed to avoid differential settlement that would distress the wall-foundation interface.

name: Enhanced damp-proofing adequacy
rationale: Building codes require damp-proof courses (DPC) at the wall-foundation interface to prevent rising damp from migrating into wall materials.

name: Reduced thermal bridging in Window / Door Reveal Recess
rationale: Reveal recesses are common locations for thermal bridges; minimizing them improves envelope performance.

name: Adequate weather sealing of Window / Door Reveal Recess
rationale: Reveal joints must be properly sealed to prevent air and water infiltration.

name: Reduced condensation risk at Window / Door Reveal Recess
rationale: Reveal geometry and insulation affect surface temperature and condensation potential.

name: Greater structural support for Window / Door Reveal Recess

name: Optimised daylight penetration around Window / Door Reveal Recess

name: Minimised material waste in Window / Door Reveal Recess construction

name: Enhanced acoustic isolation at Window / Door Reveal Recess
rationale: Reveal detailing and sealant application affect sound transmission through openings.

name: Eliminated moisture intrusion at Window / Door Reveal Recess

name: Reduced thermal bridging

name: Reduced glare contrast

name: optimised material thickness

name: prevented instability
