name: Optimised load distribution
rationale: The rigid frame action distributes vertical and lateral loads through bending in all members, providing good load-sharing characteristics.

name: Eliminated diagonal members
rationale: By definition, Vierendeel frames have no diagonal bracing members, which simplifies construction coordination and opens up the structural bay.

name: Better lateral stiffness
rationale: The rigid frame action provides inherent lateral stiffness, though less efficient than properly braced frames, making the system suitable for low-to-mid-rise buildings.

name: Reduced construction cost
rationale: While joint fabrication is more expensive, the elimination of diagonal bracing and simplified architectural detailing can lead to overall cost savings in certain building types.

name: Increased spatial efficiency
rationale: Interstitial service spaces (e.g., ceiling plenums, raised floors, service corridors) benefit from increased spatial efficiency to accommodate more building services (MEP, data, structural) within limited floor-to-floor heights.

name: Improved accessibility for maintenance
rationale: Interstitial spaces must be accessible for regular maintenance, repairs, and upgrades of building services. Improved accessibility reduces downtime and operational costs.

name: Reduced vertical height
rationale: Architectural constraints often push for reduced floor-to-floor heights to minimise building volume, lower construction costs, and meet zoning height restrictions, which limits the interstitial space height.

name: Minimised fire and smoke spread risk
rationale: Interstitial spaces can act as pathways for fire and smoke. Design pressures require minimised fire risk through firestopping, compartmentation, and sprinkler systems within these spaces.

name: Greater coordination with structural zones
rationale: Interstitial spaces must coordinate with structural elements (beams, slabs, columns). Greater coordination ensures services fit without clashes or excessive penetrations.

name: Restricted cross-sectional area for services
rationale: Architectural and programmatic constraints may restrict the cross-sectional area available for service runs within interstitial spaces, pressuring designers to optimise layouts.

name: Enhanced thermal and acoustic insulation
rationale: Interstitial spaces may require enhanced insulation to prevent thermal bridging between conditioned zones and to reduce noise transmission between floors.

name: Adequate clearance for building codes
rationale: Building codes mandate minimum clearances and headroom in accessible interstitial spaces for safety and egress, creating a pressure for adequate clearance dimensions.

name: Lower construction costs
rationale: There is a constant design pressure to lower construction costs by minimising the size, complexity, and material usage of interstitial service spaces.

name: Increased thermal insulation pressure
rationale: The inhabited frame cavity as a space benefits from greater thermal insulation to maintain comfortable interior temperatures and reduce energy loss.

name: Reduced moisture intrusion pressure
rationale: Moisture ingress into the cavity space must be minimised to prevent mould, rot, and degradation of building materials.

name: Greater structural load capacity pressure
rationale: The cavity as an inhabited space must support higher structural loads to accommodate occupants and furnishings safely.

name: Improved acoustic performance pressure
rationale: Better sound insulation is needed within the cavity space to ensure occupant comfort and privacy between adjacent spaces.

name: Reduced air leakage pressure
rationale: Air leakage through the cavity envelope should be minimised to ensure energy efficiency and indoor air quality control.

name: Optimised spatial efficiency pressure
rationale: The cavity space should be optimised to maximise usable floor area while accommodating structural and service elements.

name: Adequate natural daylight access pressure
rationale: As an inhabited space, sufficient daylight penetration is needed to ensure occupant wellbeing and reduce artificial lighting demand.

name: Lower embodied carbon pressure
rationale: The materials used in the cavity construction should have reduced embodied carbon to meet sustainability targets.

name: Enhanced fire safety pressure
rationale: Improved fire resistance and compartmentation within the cavity space is critical for occupant safety and regulatory compliance.

name: Increased load bearing capacity
rationale: Frame connection nodes must bear structural loads from beams and columns; higher capacity ensures structural integrity.

name: Improved fatigue resistance
rationale: Cyclic loading requires connections to resist fatigue failure over the building lifespan.

name: Reduced stress concentration
rationale: Stress concentrations at joints can lead to premature failure; minimising them improves durability.

name: Enhanced ductility
rationale: Ductile connections allow energy dissipation during seismic events, preventing brittle fracture.

name: Minimised fabrication complexity
rationale: Simpler connection details reduce fabrication cost and construction time while maintaining performance.

name: Greater bolt tension
rationale: Proper bolt pretension ensures friction grip and prevents slip in bolted connections.

name: Limited welding defects
rationale: Welding defects weaken the connection; quality control restricts porosity, cracks, and incomplete fusion.

name: Optimised connection stiffness
rationale: Appropriate stiffness balances moment transfer and rotation demands in the frame system.

name: Reduced corrosion risk
rationale: Corrosion at connection points compromises load transfer; protective coatings and material selection mitigate this.

name: higher load capacity

name: reduced thickness

name: sufficient stiffness

name: minimised bolt spacing

name: optimised plate geometry
rationale: Optimised gusset plate geometry improves load distribution and reduces stress concentrations at connections.

name: optimized haunch sizing
rationale: The haunch (a structural component, often a beam with varying depth) needs to be sized optimally to carry loads efficiently, balancing material use and structural performance.

name: reduced haunch depth

name: increased haunch reinforcement
rationale: To resist high shear and moment at the connection region (e.g., beam-column joint), the haunch may need additional reinforcement.

name: limited haunch taper angle
rationale: Fabrication and detailing constraints often restrict the maximum taper angle for practical steel or concrete haunch construction.

name: adequate haunch stiffness
rationale: The haunch must provide sufficient stiffness to control deflections and distribute forces at the connection.

name: Increased load-bearing capacity
rationale: A corbel is a structural component that projects from a wall to support a load, such as a beam or balcony. The design pressure to increase load-bearing capacity ensures the corbel can safely carry the imposed vertical loads.

name: Improved shear resistance
rationale: Corbels are subject to high shear forces at their connection to the wall. Improving shear resistance is critical to prevent failure at the support interface.

name: Reduced horizontal thrust
rationale: Corbels can generate horizontal thrust forces that may cause wall instability. Minimising horizontal thrust reduces the risk of overturning or cracking in the supporting wall.

name: Adequate reinforcement detailing
rationale: Proper reinforcement detailing (e.g., main tension reinforcement, stirrups) is essential for corbel structural integrity to avoid brittle failure modes.

name: Minimised eccentricity of load
rationale: Eccentric loading on a corbel induces additional bending moments. Minimising eccentricity helps maintain a more efficient and safer load path.

name: Increased structural stiffness
rationale: Precast concrete frames require adequate stiffness to resist lateral loads such as wind and seismic forces.

name: Reduced material weight
rationale: Lighter precast elements reduce the need for heavy lifting equipment and ease transportation and erection.

name: Enhanced connection ductility
rationale: Ductile connections in precast frames are critical for seismic performance and energy dissipation.

name: Reduced construction time
rationale: Precast systems are chosen to accelerate on-site construction schedules compared to cast-in-place concrete.

name: Higher prefabrication precision
rationale: Factory-controlled manufacturing of precast elements yields tighter tolerances and better quality control.

name: Lower on-site labour requirement
rationale: Precast frames reduce the volume of formwork, reinforcement placement, and pouring labour on site.

name: Improved thermal mass performance
rationale: Concrete's inherent thermal mass can be leveraged in precast frames for passive heating/cooling benefits.

name: Restricted architectural flexibility
rationale: Standardised precast modules may limit complex or irregular architectural geometries.

name: Eliminated on-site curing delays
rationale: Precast elements arrive fully cured, removing the need for on-site concrete curing time.

name: Increased structural load capacity
rationale: The in-situ concrete frame must bear vertical and lateral loads; higher load capacity requirements drive its design.

name: Improved fire resistance
rationale: Concrete's inherent fire resistance is a key design pressure; building codes often require fire-rated frames.

name: Reduced material cost
rationale: Cost constraints push toward minimizing concrete and reinforcement quantities.

name: Optimised construction time
rationale: Faster construction schedules place pressure on in-situ methods, which are typically slower than prefabricated alternatives.

name: Greater span length
rationale: Architectural requirements for open floor plans demand longer spans, affecting frame member sizing and reinforcement.

name: Minimised reinforcement congestion
rationale: Overcrowded reinforcement leads to constructability issues; design pressures aim to reduce congestion.

name: Enhanced seismic performance
rationale: In seismically active zones, the frame must provide ductility and strength, increasing design demands.

name: Adequate concrete cover
rationale: Durability requirements (corrosion protection) mandate sufficient concrete cover over reinforcement.

name: Reduced formwork complexity
rationale: Simpler formwork reduces labour and material costs; design pressure pushes for repetitive, simple geometries.

name: Greater structural load capacity
rationale: Glulam timber frames are designed to carry significant structural loads; there is a design pressure to increase load-bearing capacity to meet building requirements.

name: Reduced material cost
rationale: Cost efficiency is a common design pressure, pushing toward minimizing material expenses for the glulam frame.

name: Enhanced fire resistance
rationale: Building codes often demand improved fire performance from timber structural elements, driving design toward enhanced fire ratings.

name: Reduced environmental impact
rationale: Sustainability goals push for minimizing embodied carbon and ecological footprint of the timber frame system.

name: Improved dimensional stability

name: Higher compressive strength
rationale: Column pedestals must withstand high compressive loads from the column above; higher concrete compressive strength ensures structural integrity and prevents crushing.

name: Adequate dimensions for load distribution
rationale: Adequate plan dimensions and thickness are needed to distribute concentrated column loads to the footing without excessive bearing stress.

name: Sufficient reinforcement for moment resistance
rationale: Pedestals often experience bending moments from lateral loads; sufficient steel reinforcement is required to resist tension.

name: Reduced slenderness ratio
rationale: A lower slenderness ratio minimizes buckling risk in the pedestal under axial compression loads.

name: Minimised lateral displacement
rationale: Minimising lateral displacement at the pedestal level ensures stability of the supported column and overall structure.

name: Better corrosion protection
rationale: Pedestals are exposed to moisture at grade; improved corrosion protection extends the service life of reinforcement.

name: Enhanced confinement of core concrete
rationale: Proper transverse reinforcement (ties or spirals) enhances concrete confinement, improving ductility and load capacity.

name: Restricted crack width
rationale: Crack width must be controlled to prevent corrosion ingress and maintain durability of the pedestal.

name: Lower bearing stress on supporting footing
rationale: The pedestal base must distribute load to the footing; keeping bearing stress below allowable limits prevents foundation failure.

name: Improved structural performance
rationale: CLT frames are engineered for high strength-to-weight ratio, so there is an engineering pressure to improve structural performance through optimized panel layups and connections.

name: Reduced material waste
rationale: CLT manufacturing uses prefabricated panels cut to exact dimensions, minimizing on-site waste compared to conventional framing.

name: Higher fire resistance
rationale: Mass timber like CLT chars predictably in fires, maintaining structural integrity; design pressures push for sufficient fire resistance ratings.

name: Lower embodied carbon
rationale: CLT sequesters carbon and has lower embodied carbon than steel or concrete, creating physical/material pressure to minimize carbon footprint further.

name: Optimized connection detailing
rationale: Connection design is critical in CLT frames; there is pressure to optimize brackets, screws, and shear connections for load transfer.

name: Reduced moisture exposure risk
rationale: CLT is susceptible to moisture damage during construction and in service; design pressures aim to minimize moisture exposure through detailing and coatings.

name: Better acoustic insulation
rationale: CLT panels have good acoustic separation properties but flanking paths require attention; there is architectural pressure for improved acoustic performance.

name: Eliminated thermal bridging
rationale: CLT's continuous panel construction reduces thermal bridging compared to stud walls; design pressure to avoid thermal bridges entirely through insulation placement.

name: Greater prefabrication accuracy
rationale: CLT panels are CNC-machined off-site; there is strong engineering pressure for maximized prefabrication precision to ensure tight tolerances and faster assembly.

name: Improved structural integrity
rationale: The casing/enclosure must provide adequate structural support and protection to the column, especially in load-bearing conditions.

name: Reduced material weight
rationale: Lighter casing materials reduce dead load on the structure and can ease installation.

name: Higher fire resistance rating
rationale: Columns often require fire-rated enclosures to meet building code fire-resistance requirements.

name: Lower installation cost
rationale: Cost-effectiveness is a common constraint in selecting casing materials and methods.

name: Enhanced aesthetic finish
rationale: Visible column casings are often expected to have a clean, appealing architectural finish.

name: Restricted thermal bridging
rationale: Column enclosures should minimise thermal bridging to improve building envelope thermal performance.

name: Adequate moisture protection
rationale: Casing must resist moisture intrusion to prevent corrosion or degradation of the column.

name: Minimised material waste
rationale: Sustainable design practices encourage minimising waste from casing fabrication and installation.

name: Increased bolt preload
rationale: Higher bolt preload increases clamping force and joint stiffness in column splices, improving moment capacity and slip resistance under load.

name: Reduced eccentricity
rationale: Minimising load eccentricity at the splice reduces secondary bending moments and stress concentrations.

name: Sufficient splice plate thickness
rationale: Adequate plate thickness prevents local buckling and yielding at the connection, ensuring load transfer continuity.

name: Reduced weld defect probability
rationale: Minimising weld imperfections lowers the risk of brittle failure at the splice under cyclic or tensile loading.

name: Enhanced member alignment
rationale: Better alignment of upper and lower column segments ensures concentric load transfer and avoids P-delta effects.

name: Optimised bolt spacing
rationale: Proper bolt spacing according to code limits avoids net section failure and ensures uniform load distribution.

name: Lower stress concentration factor
rationale: Smooth transitions and non-welded details at splice reduce stress risers that can initiate fatigue cracks.

name: Adequate bolt shear capacity
rationale: Sufficient bolt shear strength ensures the splice can resist design shear forces without slip or failure.

name: Greater axial load capacity
rationale: Columns must support vertical compressive loads from the structure above; circular columns are efficient for axial load resistance.

name: Higher slenderness ratio
rationale: Slender columns risk buckling; engineering design often pushes for taller, thinner columns requiring careful buckling checks.

name: Reduced lateral stiffness
rationale: Circular columns may have lower moment resistance compared to rectangular sections unless properly reinforced, affecting lateral load behaviour.

name: Optimised reinforcement detailing
rationale: Spiral or hoop reinforcement in circular columns improves ductility and confinement; detailing must be optimised for seismic performance.

name: Sufficient diameter for buckling resistance
rationale: Column diameter directly affects moment of inertia and buckling capacity; larger diameters provide better stability.

name: Eliminated stress concentrations at connections
rationale: Circular columns require careful beam-column connection detailing to avoid local stress concentrations and achieve composite action.

name: Higher axial load capacity
rationale: Columns must support vertical loads from slabs, beams, and floors above; axial load capacity is a primary design pressure.

name: Greater buckling resistance
rationale: Slender columns require resistance to buckling under compressive loads, influencing cross-section dimensions.

name: Reduced cross-sectional dimensions
rationale: Architectural constraints often push for smaller columns to maximize usable floor space and visual appeal.

name: Sufficient reinforcement ratio
rationale: Steel reinforcement must be adequate to handle tensile stresses and comply with building codes.

name: Minimised material cost
rationale: Cost efficiency pressures designers to use less concrete and steel without compromising safety.

name: Higher slenderness ratio
rationale: In some structural systems, taller/narrower columns are desired for architectural effect, increasing slenderness.

name: Greater fire resistance
rationale: Building codes require columns to maintain structural integrity during fire, affecting cover thickness and material choice.

name: Reduced eccentric loading
rationale: Eccentric loads cause bending moments; designers aim to minimise eccentricity for simpler column design.

name: Improved constructability
rationale: Simple rectangular shapes are easier to form and pour, but size/complexity constraints may conflict with other pressures.

name: Increased axial load capacity
rationale: Steel I-section columns are designed to bear vertical (axial) compressive loads from the structure above; higher axial capacity is a core design pressure for column sizing and material selection.

name: Enhanced buckling resistance
rationale: Slender steel columns are susceptible to buckling under compressive loads; improving buckling resistance (e.g., through section shape, bracing, or stiffness) is a key design pressure.

name: Reduced material weight
rationale: Minimising the weight of the steel column reduces both material cost and the dead load on foundations, while still satisfying strength requirements.

name: Lower slenderness ratio
rationale: A lower slenderness ratio improves column stability and load-bearing capacity, dictating the cross-section dimensions and effective length.

name: Optimised cross-section dimensions
rationale: The flange width, flange thickness, web depth, and web thickness must be optimised to balance strength, stability, and economy for the given loading.

name: Sufficient fire resistance
rationale: Steel loses strength at elevated temperatures; ensuring adequate fire protection (e.g., intumescent coating, encasement) is a key design pressure.

name: Reduced lateral deflection under wind/seismic loads
rationale: Columns must limit lateral sway to meet serviceability criteria and avoid damage to cladding and partitions under horizontal loads.

name: Stronger connection detailing
rationale: Column-to-beam and column-to-baseplate connections must be designed to transfer moments, shear, and axial forces reliably.

name: Increased punching shear resistance
rationale: The slab-column interface must resist punching shear forces transferred from the slab to the column. Higher punching shear capacity is a critical design pressure to prevent brittle failure at this connection.

name: Reduced stress concentration
rationale: Stress concentrations at the slab-column junction can lead to cracking and failure. Minimising stress concentration through detailing (e.g., drop panels, column capitals, shear reinforcement) is a key design pressure.

name: Adequate moment transfer capacity
rationale: Unbalanced moments from gravity and lateral loads must be transferred between slab and column. Ensuring sufficient moment transfer capacity at the interface is a fundamental design pressure.

name: Minimised construction complexity
rationale: Complex detailing at the slab-column interface (e.g.,大量的 shear reinforcement, complicated formwork) increases construction cost and time. A design pressure exists to keep the connection simple and buildable.

name: Greater ductility under lateral loading
rationale: In seismic regions, the slab-column connection must exhibit ductile behaviour to dissipate energy and avoid sudden punching failure during earthquake loading.

name: Increased structural load capacity
rationale: Columns in a colonnade must bear vertical loads from the roof or upper floors, requiring sufficient load-bearing capacity.

name: Expanded spatial width
rationale: A colonnade corridor needs adequate width for pedestrian circulation and accessibility.

name: Greater column spacing
rationale: Wider column spacing creates a more open, inviting passage and improves sightlines.

name: Increased structural stability against lateral forces
rationale: The colonnade must resist wind and seismic lateral loads to ensure safety.

name: Reduced material usage
rationale: Optimizing column dimensions and spacing can reduce construction material costs while maintaining structural integrity.

name: Minimised column obstruction
rationale: Thinner or fewer columns reduce visual obstruction and improve the flow of space in the corridor.

name: Restricted deflection under load
rationale: Columns must be stiff enough to limit lateral and vertical deflection within acceptable serviceability limits.

name: Eliminated water ingress at column bases
rationale: Proper detailing around column bases in an outdoor colonnade prevents water damage and corrosion.

name: Adequate fire resistance rating
rationale: Building codes require columns to have sufficient fire resistance to maintain structural stability during a fire.

name: Increased structural support

name: Reduced spatial depth
rationale: Column niches are typically shallow recesses; excessive depth would compromise structural integrity or usable floor space, so depth is often limited.

name: Improved aesthetic integration
rationale: Designers often seek enhanced visual harmony between the niche and surrounding architectural elements.

name: Limited accessibility
rationale: Niche openings are often restricted or constrained to maintain the column's visual and structural continuity.

name: Eliminated water ingress risk
rationale: Moisture accumulation in recessed niches can cause deterioration; design pressures aim to prevent or eliminate water penetration.

name: Sufficient fire resistance
rationale: Building codes require adequate fire protection for structural columns, including any niches or recesses.

name: Increased load-bearing capacity
rationale: Columns must support vertical loads from floors and roof; higher load-bearing capacity ensures structural safety.

name: Improved lateral stability
rationale: Columns resist lateral forces (wind/seismic); greater lateral stability prevents collapse.

name: Reduced material usage
rationale: Optimising column dimensions and spacing minimises steel/concrete consumption for economy.

name: Minimised column footprint
rationale: Slender or fewer columns increase usable floor area and architectural flexibility.

name: Higher construction speed
rationale: Standardised column designs and prefabrication accelerate erection timelines.

name: Lower construction cost
rationale: Efficient column design reduces material and labour expenses.

name: Enhanced fire resistance
rationale: Fire protection requirements drive column size and material selection to maintain structural integrity during fire.

name: Restricted column spacing
rationale: Architectural programmes often impose maximum column spacing to create open floor plans.

name: Greater durability against corrosion
rationale: Columns exposed to moisture or aggressive environments require protective coatings or concrete cover for longevity.

name: Increased structural health monitoring coverage
rationale: There is a design pressure to expand monitoring coverage to more columns and structural elements for better safety assessment.

name: Improved sensor accuracy and precision
rationale: Engineering requirements push for higher-fidelity data from sensors (e.g., strain gauges, accelerometers) to detect subtle structural changes.

name: Reduced data latency and transmission delay
rationale: Real-time monitoring demands minimised lag between data acquisition and analysis for timely alerts.

name: Minimised power consumption
rationale: Wireless sensors and on-site systems are often battery-powered, so lowering energy use extends operational life and reduces maintenance.

name: Enhanced data transmission reliability
rationale: Communication links (wired or wireless) must be robust against interference to ensure continuous monitoring data flow.

name: Reduced installation and maintenance cost
rationale: Budget constraints and constructability considerations push for simpler, more economical sensor deployment and upkeep.

name: Increased resistance to environmental degradation
rationale: Sensors and cabling must withstand moisture, temperature variations, and corrosion in building environments to maintain long-term functionality.

name: Greater scalability for future expansion
rationale: The system design should accommodate adding new monitoring points without major re-engineering, supporting building lifecycle changes.

name: Limited false alarm rate
rationale: Excessive false positives reduce trust in the system; design pressures push for robust algorithms to minimise nuisance alerts.

name: adequate load distribution pressure
rationale: The cap plate must adequately distribute loads from above to the supporting structure below.

name: reduced deformation pressure
rationale: Cap plates should minimise bending or deformation under applied loads to maintain structural integrity.

name: sufficient thickness pressure
rationale: Cap plate thickness must be sufficient to resist punching shear and bearing stresses.

name: minimised deflection pressure
rationale: Deflection of the cap plate under service loads should be minimised to avoid damage to finishes.

name: enhanced corrosion resistance pressure
rationale: Exposed cap plates may require enhanced corrosion resistance for durability and aesthetics.

name: restricted size pressure
rationale: Cap plate dimensions may be restricted by architectural constraints or fit within column dimensions.

name: greater bolt capacity pressure
rationale: The cap plate connection design requires greater bolt capacity to transfer forces effectively.

name: eliminated stress concentration pressure
rationale: Stress concentrations at corners or holes in the cap plate should be eliminated to prevent failure.

name: Increased rotational stiffness
rationale: Rotational stiffness is critical for moment-resisting frames; higher stiffness reduces sway and improves structural performance.

name: Enhanced load-bearing capacity
rationale: Connections must safely transfer vertical and lateral loads; greater capacity ensures structural safety and code compliance.

name: Improved ductility
rationale: Ductility allows energy dissipation during seismic events, preventing brittle failure at connections.

name: Minimized fabrication complexity
rationale: Simpler connection details reduce fabrication cost, welding errors, and inspection requirements while maintaining performance.

name: Adequate bolt pretension
rationale: Proper bolt pretension ensures clamping force and slip resistance in bolted connections, essential for load transfer.

name: Restricted geometric misalignment
rationale: Misalignment between beam and column flanges/webs can induce eccentricities and secondary moments; limiting it preserves intended load paths.

name: Sufficient weld penetration
rationale: Full joint penetration welds are required for strength and ductility in moment connections; insufficient penetration leads to premature failure.

name: Eliminated brittle fracture risk
rationale: Use of notch-tough materials, proper detailing, and welding procedures prevents brittle fracture under low-temperature or dynamic loading.

name: Increased rotational stiffness
rationale: Moment connections in steel structures require high rotational stiffness to transfer moments between beams and columns, a fundamental engineering requirement for frame stability.

name: Improved ductility capacity
rationale: Moment connections need adequate ductility to allow plastic hinge formation under seismic loading without brittle failure.

name: Reduced bolt slip
rationale: Slip in bolted moment connections reduces stiffness and moment transfer capability, so slip must be minimized or prevented.

name: Enhanced weld quality
rationale: Welded moment connections depend on full-penetration welds with high quality to achieve designed moment capacity without premature fracture.

name: Minimised stress concentration
rationale: Stress concentrations at weld toes, cope holes, or abrupt section changes can initiate fatigue cracks or brittle fracture, so they should be minimised.

name: Greater connection strength
rationale: Moment connections must develop at least the plastic moment capacity of the connected member to satisfy strong-column-weak-beam design philosophy.

name: Adequate bolt tension
rationale: Pretensioned bolts in moment connections require adequate tension to develop friction and maintain clamping force under cyclic loading.

name: Eliminated brittle fracture risk
rationale: Brittle fracture in moment connections (e.g., at welded joints) must be prevented through appropriate material selection, detailing, and notch-toughness requirements.

name: Optimised connection detailing
rationale: Detailing of stiffeners, continuity plates, and reinforcement at moment connections must be optimised to achieve balanced strength, stiffness, and constructability.

name: Increased shear capacity
rationale: Shear connections must be designed to withstand expected shear loads, requiring adequate capacity.

name: Improved load transfer
rationale: Effective transfer of forces between connected members is essential for structural performance.

name: Reduced deformation
rationale: Limiting slip or deformation under load is critical for serviceability and structural integrity.

name: Minimised stress concentration
rationale: Stress concentrations at connection details can lead to premature failure; they should be minimised.

name: Greater ductility
rationale: Ductile behaviour allows redistribution of loads and provides warning before failure.

name: Adequate stiffness
rationale: Sufficient stiffness is needed to control deflections and maintain intended structural behaviour.

name: Eliminated bolt slip
rationale: Bolt slip in bolted shear connections can cause excessive deformations and should be prevented.

name: Optimised weld geometry
rationale: Weld geometry affects strength and fatigue performance; optimisation improves connection reliability.

name: Increased bolt strength requirement
rationale: Bolted connections must resist tensile and shear loads, requiring adequate bolt grade and diameter to prevent failure.

name: Improved fatigue resistance demand
rationale: Cyclic loading in structures imposes fatigue constraints on bolted connections, demanding enhanced design for long-term durability.

name: Reduced bolt spacing requirement
rationale: Closer bolt spacing improves load distribution and prevents local buckling or prying action in connected members.

name: Higher clamping force need
rationale: Pre-tensioning of bolts ensures joint stiffness and reduces slip in shear connections.

name: Minimised bolt hole clearance
rationale: Tighter tolerances reduce slip and improve alignment in bolted connections.

name: Adequate corrosion protection requirement
rationale: Bolted connections in exposed or aggressive environments require sufficient corrosion resistance to maintain structural integrity.

name: Increased weld strength requirement
rationale: Welded connections must be designed to withstand tensile, shear, and moment forces, requiring sufficient weld strength for structural integrity.

name: Reduced thermal distortion risk
rationale: Welding induces localized heating and cooling cycles; controlling thermal distortion is critical for fit-up and dimensional accuracy of connections.

name: Increased fatigue resistance demand
rationale: Cyclic loading in structures requires welded connections to resist fatigue cracking, demanding adequate weld profile and detail design.

name: Reduced stress concentration at weld toe
rationale: Stress concentrations at weld toes can initiate cracks; smooth transitions and proper weld profiling help minimize this risk.

name: Greater ductility requirement for seismic performance
rationale: In seismic-prone areas, welded connections must exhibit sufficient ductility to undergo inelastic deformation without brittle fracture.

name: Lower hydrogen-induced cracking susceptibility
rationale: Hydrogen from welding consumables or moisture can cause delayed cracking; using low-hydrogen electrodes and preheat reduces this risk.

name: minimized deflection

name: improved fire resistance rating
rationale: Soffits contributing to structural fire protection require a minimum fire resistance rating per building code.

name: reduced thermal bridging
rationale: The vault soffit may act as a thermal bridge between interior and exterior if not adequately insulated, affecting energy performance.

name: adequate acoustic insulation
rationale: The soffit should provide sufficient sound transmission loss to maintain acoustic comfort between spaces.

name: Higher connection stiffness

name: Reduced construction time
rationale: Bolted connections allow for faster on-site assembly compared to fully welded connections, so a mixed system balances prefabrication welding with bolted field installation to reduce overall erection time.

name: Improved fatigue resistance
rationale: Bolted connections generally exhibit better fatigue performance than welded connections due to reduced stress concentrations and lack of weld defects, so increasing bolted content improves fatigue life.

name: Lower on-site welding requirements
rationale: Mixed systems often aim to minimise field welding due to quality control challenges, weather dependency, and inspection costs associated with site welding.

name: Greater ductility under seismic loading
rationale: Bolted connections in mixed systems can provide enhanced ductility and energy dissipation capacity compared to fully rigid welded connections, which is desirable in seismic design.

name: Reduced fabrication cost

name: Higher load capacity

name: Minimised stress concentrations at joints

name: Increased tread depth
rationale: Building codes and ergonomics require a minimum tread depth for safety and comfortable foot placement on stairs.

name: Reduced tread slip risk

name: enhanced seismic bracing

rationale: Proper ventilation in the dormer roof space prevents heat buildup and moisture condensation, extending roof life.

name: Reduced weight load
rationale: Minimizing the weight of dormer roof materials reduces stress on the main roof structure and foundation.

name: Limited thermal bridging
rationale: Dormer roof junctions are common locations for thermal bridging; minimizing this improves energy efficiency and prevents condensation issues.

name: Restricted overhang dimensions
rationale: Overhangs on dormer roofs may need to be limited to maintain aesthetic proportion with the main roof and to reduce wind uplift risk.

name: Reduced thermal bridging pressure
rationale: Dormer soffits are prone to thermal bridging where they meet the main roof, so design decisions often aim to minimise heat loss.

name: Improved ventilation pressure
rationale: Soffits in dormers often require ventilation to prevent moisture buildup in roof cavities, pushing for better airflow design.

name: Enhanced weathertightness pressure
rationale: Dormer soffits are exposed to rain and wind, so design pressures push for better sealing and durability against water ingress.

name: Reduced material cost pressure
rationale: Cost considerations often push for minimising expensive materials or simplifying soffit construction.

name: Greater fire resistance pressure
rationale: Building codes may require increased fire resistance for soffit materials in dormer constructions.

name: Increased structural adequacy
rationale: Structural engineering requires the dormer fascia board to be adequately strong to support roof loads and resist wind uplift forces.

name: Reduced moisture infiltration
rationale: Building envelope design aims to minimise water penetration at fascia-roof intersections to prevent rot and interior damage.

name: Enhanced weather resistance
rationale: Fascia boards must withstand exposure to rain, sun, and temperature cycles, requiring durable materials and finishes.

name: Minimised material cost
rationale: Budget constraints typically push toward economical material choices for exterior trim components.

name: Improved aesthetic integration
rationale: The fascia board should visually complement the roof and wall finishes for a coherent architectural appearance.

name: Greater dimensional precision
rationale: Accurate cutting and alignment of fascia boards ensure proper fit with roof flashing and gutter systems.

name: Reduced maintenance frequency
rationale: Low-maintenance materials and designs are preferred for fascia boards to reduce long-term upkeep costs.

name: Adequate thermal expansion allowance
rationale: Fascia materials expand and contract with temperature changes; sufficient gaps and flexible fixings prevent buckling or cracking.

name: Eliminated pest entry points
rationale: Sealing gaps in fascia installation prevents birds, insects, and rodents from accessing roof cavities.

name: Increased structural load from snow
rationale: Dormer lintels must bear snow accumulation around dormer recesses; snow loads increase the downward force on the lintel.

name: Adequate vertical support for dormer roof
rationale: The lintel must provide sufficient support to transfer roof loads to the surrounding structure.

name: Reduced clear span deflection
rationale: To prevent cracking or sagging, deflection of the lintel over its span should be minimised.

name: Limited thermal bridging through lintel
rationale: Steel or concrete lintels can create thermal bridges; designers aim to restrict heat loss at this junction.

name: Greater fire resistance rating
rationale: Building codes often require lintels in dormer openings to have enhanced fire resistance to maintain compartmentation.

name: Increased structural support for dormer window frame
rationale: The dormer window frame must bear its own weight plus the dormer roof and window loads, requiring adequate structural capacity.

name: Enhanced weathertightness of dormer window frame
rationale: The dormer window frame is a critical junction where roof and wall meet, making it vulnerable to water ingress; increasing weathertightness is essential for durability.

name: Improved thermal performance of dormer window frame
rationale: The dormer window frame interfaces with the building envelope and thermal bridging can occur; improving insulation and thermal breaks reduces heat loss.

name: Reduced material weight of dormer window frame
rationale: Lighter dormer window frames reduce dead load on the roof structure and make installation easier, though structural adequacy must still be maintained.

name: Minimised air leakage at dormer window frame
rationale: The interface between the dormer window frame and surrounding roof/wall is prone to air leakage, which reduces energy efficiency; minimising leakage improves building performance.

name: Improved fire resistance of dormer window frame
rationale: Dormer window frames near roof penetrations may need to meet fire-resistance ratings to prevent fire spread between storeys or compartments.

name: Reduced condensation risk at dormer window frame
rationale: The dormer window frame is a thermal bridge location where surface condensation can occur; reducing this risk protects against moisture damage and mould growth.

name: Adequate dimensional accuracy of dormer window frame
rationale: The dormer window frame must fit precisely within the roof opening to ensure proper installation of windows, flashings, and finishes.

name: Improved durability of dormer window frame materials
rationale: Dormer window frames are exposed to weather extremes (rain, sun, snow) and must resist rot, corrosion, and UV degradation over the building's lifespan.

name: Increased structural support for Dormer Sill
rationale: The dormer sill must be adequately supported to carry the weight of the dormer structure above it, transferring loads to the wall below.

name: Enhanced weather sealing at Dormer Sill
rationale: The sill must be properly sealed to prevent water ingress where the dormer meets the roof slope.

name: Reduced thermal bridging at Dormer Sill
rationale: Minimizing thermal bridging through the sill area improves overall building energy performance and prevents condensation issues.

name: Improved material durability for Dormer Sill
rationale: The sill material must be durable enough to withstand prolonged exposure to rain, snow, and UV radiation.

name: Adequate flashing integration at Dormer Sill
rationale: Proper flashing details are essential at the sill to direct water away from the wall assembly below.

name: Increased structural capacity for trimming rafters
rationale: Trimmer rafters must be sized adequately to support the loads transferred from the dormer opening, ensuring structural integrity.

name: Enhanced connection strength at intersections
rationale: Joints between trimmer rafters and adjacent structural members require robust connections to resist shear and moment forces.

name: Reduced deflection under dormer load
rationale: Limiting deflection ensures the dormer structure remains within serviceability limits and prevents damage to finishes.

name: Minimized span length between supports
rationale: Shorter spans reduce bending moments and allow for more efficient member sizing or reduced member depth.

name: Increased structural load capacity
rationale: The dormer header beam must bear the weight of the dormer structure, roof, and any superimposed loads, requiring sufficient load-bearing capacity to ensure structural integrity.

name: Reduced deflection under load
rationale: Excessive deflection of the header beam can cause cracking in finishes and misalignment of dormer components, so deflection must be limited to acceptable serviceability limits.

name: Adequate connection strength
rationale: The header beam requires strong connections to supporting walls or columns to transfer loads effectively and maintain structural continuity.

name: Minimised thermal bridging
rationale: The dormer header beam can act as a thermal bridge if not properly insulated, reducing overall building envelope thermal performance and increasing heat loss.

name: Adequate fire resistance rating
rationale: The header beam may require a specific fire resistance rating depending on building codes and proximity to occupied spaces to ensure life safety.

name: Reduced moisture infiltration risk
rationale: Proper flashing and sealing around the dormer header beam is needed to prevent water ingress at the roof-wall intersection, avoiding rot and deterioration.

name: Increased daylight penetration
rationale: Shed dormers are added to bring more natural light into attic or upper-floor spaces, so there is a design pressure to increase daylight entry.

name: Improved headroom clearance
rationale: Shed dormers create additional interior volume and ceiling height in sloped roof spaces, increasing usable headroom.

name: Reduced roof snow load accumulation
rationale: The dormer's roof-to-main-roof valley can create snow drift zones; design seeks to limit snow accumulation and structural loading.

name: Minimised thermal bridging
rationale: The intersection of dormer walls with the main roof is a thermal weak point; design pressure to reduce heat loss through bridging.

name: Greater interior floor area
rationale: Shed dormers expand the usable floor area of an attic or upper storey, creating a pressure to maximise added square footage.

name: Eliminated water infiltration risk
rationale: Dormer roof-to-wall junctions and flashing details are vulnerable to leaks; design strongly aims to prevent water entry.

name: Optimised exterior aesthetic integration
rationale: The dormer's proportions, pitch, and cladding should harmonise with the main roof and facade for a cohesive appearance.

name: Lower construction cost
rationale: Budget constraints create a pressure to reduce material and labour expense for the dormer structure and finishes.

name: Sufficient structural support capacity
rationale: The dormer adds dead and live loads to the existing roof structure; design must ensure adequate load-bearing capacity.

name: increased roof pitch for snow shedding
rationale: Gable-fronted dormers require adequate roof pitch to prevent snow accumulation and water ponding at the valley intersection with the main roof, ensuring structural integrity and weatherproofing.

name: reduced dormer width to maintain roof structural continuity
rationale: Wider dormers create larger interruptions in the main roof structure, increasing load redistribution complexity and risk of structural failure; limiting width improves structural performance.

name: adequate headroom for habitable space
rationale: Building codes and architectural standards require sufficient ceiling height within dormers for occupancy, driving a need for adequate vertical dimensions.

name: limited window-to-wall ratio for thermal performance
rationale: Gable-fronted dormers often incorporate glazing at the front; excessive window area increases heat loss and solar gain, so fenestration should be constrained for energy efficiency.

name: increased roof ventilation pressure
rationale: Hipped dormers often require adequate ventilation to prevent moisture buildup and heat accumulation in the roof space.

name: reduced structural load pressure
rationale: The weight of the dormer structure and roof covering must be managed to avoid overloading the main roof structure.

name: improved daylight access pressure
rationale: A hipped dormer is typically added to bring more natural light into the attic or upper-floor space.

name: minimised thermal bridging pressure
rationale: The junction between the dormer and the main roof is prone to thermal bridging, which should be minimised for energy efficiency.

name: adequate waterproofing pressure
rationale: The dormer roof and flashing details must provide sufficient weather resistance to prevent leaks.

name: reduced wind uplift pressure
rationale: The dormer protrudes from the roof plane and can be subject to wind uplift forces that should be limited through proper design.

name: enhanced aesthetic integration pressure
rationale: The dormer should be visually cohesive with the main roof form and building style.

name: restricted headroom loss pressure
rationale: The internal ceiling slope of the hipped dormer should minimise loss of usable headroom inside the space.

name: Improved structural integrity
rationale: The Eyebrow Dormer must have adequate structural support to withstand wind and snow loads, requiring stronger framing and connections.

name: Enhanced weather sealing
rationale: Better flashing and waterproofing is needed to prevent leaks at the curved roof-wall intersection typical of eyebrow dormers.

name: Reduced thermal bridging
rationale: Continuous insulation should be maintained across the dormer to minimise heat loss through the curved roof structure.

name: Adequate headroom clearance
rationale: The dormer must provide sufficient interior space and headroom for functional use of the space beneath it.

name: Lower construction complexity
rationale: The curved geometry of eyebrow dormers introduces framing complexity; simpler detailing reduces cost and errors.

name: Maximised daylight penetration
rationale: Eyebrow dormers with appropriately sized windows allow more natural light into the attic or upper-floor space.

name: Restricted roof profile disruption
rationale: The dormer should minimally alter the original roof line to maintain architectural character and avoid visual bulk.

name: Prevented water ponding
rationale: Proper slope and drainage detailing on the curved dormer roof is essential to avoid standing water that could cause leakage.

name: Stronger connection to main roof
rationale: The dormer-to-roof junction must be robustly connected to resist uplift and lateral forces during high winds.

name: Improved daylight access
rationale: A blind dormer is a decorative dormer without windows, so there may be pressure to increase daylight access by adding windows to the dormer space.

name: Enhanced roof ventilation
rationale: Dormers can be used to improve attic ventilation; a blind dormer may be under pressure to enhance airflow despite lacking windows.

name: Reduced structural load
rationale: Being a non-functional decorative element, there may be design pressure to minimize the structural weight and load contribution of the blind dormer.

name: Minimised construction cost
rationale: As a purely aesthetic feature, there is pressure to keep the blind dormer cost low by using simpler materials and reduced detailing.

name: Lower thermal bridging risk
rationale: Blind dormers can create thermal bridging at the roof plane; design pressure exists to minimise heat loss through the dormer enclosure.

name: Increased daylight penetration
rationale: A lucarne dormer projects from a roof slope and introduces a vertical window, which increases daylight penetration into the attic or upper floor space.

name: Improved natural ventilation
rationale: The dormer's window can be opened to improve cross-ventilation and air circulation in the otherwise enclosed roof space.

name: Reduced roof structural integrity
rationale: Cutting an opening in the roof plane to insert a dormer disrupts the continuous roof structure, potentially reducing load-bearing capacity if not properly reinforced.

name: Increased usable floor area
rationale: A dormer adds headroom and usable floor space to an attic, making the area habitable.

name: Higher heat loss
rationale: The dormer introduces additional exterior surface area and glazing, increasing thermal bridging and heat loss compared to a plain roof.

name: Increased construction complexity
rationale: Building a dormer requires complex framing, flashing, and waterproofing details at the roof-dormer junction.

name: Greater rainwater leakage risk
rationale: The intersection between the dormer structure and the roof is a critical point vulnerable to water ingress if not properly detailed.

name: Improved aesthetic appeal
rationale: Lucarne dormers are historically associated with French Gothic and classical architecture, adding visual charm and character to a roof.

name: Increased snow and debris accumulation
rationale: Dormer roofs create valleys and ledges where snow, leaves, and debris can collect, increasing maintenance needs.

name: Increased ceiling height
rationale: Dormer loft spaces typically have sloped ceilings, and increasing the usable ceiling height improves habitability and headroom.

name: Enhanced daylight access
rationale: Dormer windows are designed to bring natural light into loft spaces; enhancing daylight penetration improves liveability.

name: Improved ventilation
rationale: Loft spaces can trap heat and moisture; improved ventilation supports comfort and prevents condensation.

name: Reduced heat loss
rationale: Dormer loft spaces are prone to thermal bridging and heat loss; reducing heat loss improves energy efficiency.

name: Maximised usable floor area
rationale: The sloping roofline limits usable floor space; maximising the usable area increases the space's functional value.

name: Reduced construction cost
rationale: Dormer loft conversions can be expensive; reducing construction costs makes the project more feasible.

name: Adequate structural support
rationale: Dormer loft spaces often require structural modifications; ensuring adequate support is critical for safety.

name: Better fire safety compliance
rationale: Building regulations for loft conversions require fire safety measures such as escape routes and fire doors.

name: Limited visual impact on roofline
rationale: Dormer extensions can alter the external appearance of a roof; limiting visual impact supports neighbourhood character and planning approval.

name: Improved weather sealing pressure
rationale: Ridge caps at roof peaks must provide enhanced sealing against rain and snow ingress, directly influencing material selection and overlap design.

name: Reduced wind uplift pressure
rationale: Ridge caps are vulnerable to wind uplift forces; design must minimise uplift through proper fastening and aerodynamic profiling.

name: Higher durability pressure
rationale: Ridge caps experience concentrated thermal expansion and UV exposure; greater material durability is required to prevent cracking.

name: Increased ventilation pressure
rationale: Ridge caps often incorporate ridge vents to allow hot air escape from attics; adequate ventilation capacity must be ensured.

name: Eliminated leakage risk pressure
rationale: The ridge is a critical leakage point; design must prevent water penetration through proper flashing and cap placement.

name: Optimised fastening strength pressure
rationale: Fasteners for ridge caps must be sufficient to resist both wind uplift and thermal movement without loosening over time.

name: Minimised thermal expansion stress pressure
rationale: Differential thermal expansion between ridge cap material and roof deck can cause buckling; design should minimise this stress.

name: Increased structural integrity for Hip Cap
rationale: Hip caps must withstand wind uplift, snow loads, and other environmental forces; a stronger, more durable cap improves long-term roof performance.

name: Enhanced weather sealing for Hip Cap
rationale: Hip caps serve as critical weatherproofing junctions; improved sealing prevents water ingress and moisture damage.

name: Reduced material weight for Hip Cap
rationale: Lighter hip cap materials reduce dead load on the roof structure and simplify installation while maintaining performance.

name: Improved aesthetic integration for Hip Cap
rationale: Hip caps are visible roof elements; better colour match, profile, and finish contribute to overall architectural harmony.

name: Minimised thermal bridging for Hip Cap
rationale: Metal or conductive hip cap materials can create thermal bridges; reducing this effect improves building energy efficiency.

name: Improved structural attachment
rationale: The eave cap must be securely attached to resist wind uplift and prevent detachment during storms.

name: Enhanced weather sealing
rationale: Eave caps serve as weather barriers; improved sealing prevents water ingress and protects the roof edge.

name: Reduced wind uplift force
rationale: Minimising wind uplift on the eave cap is critical to avoid component failure in high-wind conditions.

name: Minimised material corrosion
rationale: Corrosion of metal eave caps reduces service life; limiting exposure to moisture and chemicals helps maintain integrity.

name: Adequate thermal expansion allowance
rationale: Eave caps must accommodate thermal expansion and contraction to prevent buckling or stress fractures.

name: Improved structural load distribution
rationale: The rake cap must effectively distribute structural loads along the roof edge, requiring adequate load-bearing capacity and connection strength.

name: Enhanced weather sealing
rationale: The rake cap serves as a weather barrier at the roof edge, so improved sealing against water and air infiltration is a key design pressure.

name: Reduced material deflection
rationale: Minimising deflection under wind and snow loads is critical to maintain the cap's appearance and performance over time.

name: Greater corrosion resistance
rationale: As an exposed edge component, the rake cap requires higher resistance to corrosion from moisture and environmental exposure.

name: Adequate fastener pull-out strength
rationale: The attachment of the rake cap must be sufficient to resist uplift forces from wind, requiring adequate fastener pull-out resistance.

name: Limited thermal expansion effects
rationale: Thermal expansion and contraction must be constrained to prevent buckling or gap formation at the rake cap joints.

name: Optimised dimensional profile
rationale: The rake cap profile should be optimised to match architectural aesthetics while maintaining functional drainage and coverage.

name: Eliminated water ponding
rationale: Water ponding on or behind the rake cap must be prevented to avoid premature deterioration and leakage.

name: Stronger wind uplift resistance
rationale: As a roof edge component, the rake cap experiences significant uplift forces during high winds, requiring stronger attachment and structural capacity.

name: Improved waterproofing pressure
rationale: The flat roof edge cap must provide adequate waterproofing to prevent moisture ingress at the roof perimeter, a critical function of this component.

name: Enhanced wind uplift resistance pressure
rationale: Edge caps at roof perimeters are highly susceptible to wind uplift forces and must resist detachment during high wind events.

name: Reduced thermal bridging pressure
rationale: The edge cap detail should minimise thermal bridging where the roof meets the wall assembly to improve overall building energy performance.

name: Optimised material durability pressure
rationale: The edge cap must be made of durable materials (e.g., metal, PVC) that can withstand UV exposure, temperature cycles, and physical impacts over the building's lifespan.

name: Reduced installation complexity pressure
rationale: Simpler installation procedures reduce the risk of improper sealing and flashing integration, which are common failure points for roof edge caps.

name: Expanded drainage capacity pressure
rationale: The edge cap design should facilitate proper water runoff and drainage away from the roof edge to prevent ponding and water damage.

name: Adequate thermal expansion accommodation pressure
rationale: The edge cap must accommodate thermal expansion and contraction without buckling or losing its seal, especially in metal edge systems.

name: Increased structural stability of parapet cap
rationale: The parapet cap/coping requires sufficient structural stability to resist wind uplift, thermal movements, and live loads, especially at roof edges where wind pressures are higher.

name: Improved watertightness of coping joints
rationale: Coping joints must be watertight to prevent moisture penetration into the parapet wall below, which can lead to freeze-thaw damage and interior water intrusion.

name: Enhanced wind uplift resistance
rationale: Parapet caps at roof edges are subject to significant wind uplift forces, especially in high-rise buildings and hurricane-prone regions, requiring secure anchorage and adequate weight.

name: Reduced thermal expansion stress at joints
rationale: Thermal expansion and contraction of metal or stone coping materials can cause buckling or joint failure if not properly accommodated with expansion joints.

name: Minimised water ponding on coping surface
rationale: Proper slope and drip edge details on coping are essential to shed water away from the building facade and prevent ponding, staining, and accelerated corrosion.

name: Adequate anchorage to parapet wall
rationale: The coping must be securely anchored or fastened to the parapet wall below to resist wind uplift, seismic forces, and prevent dislodgement.

name: Eliminated galvanic corrosion risk at dissimilar metal contacts
rationale: When metal coping is used with dissimilar metal flashings or fasteners, galvanic corrosion can occur unless proper separation or compatible materials are specified.

name: Sufficient thermal insulation continuity at parapet
rationale: Parapet caps can create thermal bridges if insulation is interrupted; maintaining continuous insulation at the parapet improves overall building envelope thermal performance.

name: Improved ventilation flow pressure
rationale: A ventilated ridge cap is designed to enhance natural ventilation by allowing hot air to escape from the roof/attic, improving airflow and reducing heat buildup.

name: Enhanced weather resistance pressure
rationale: Ventilated ridge caps must resist water and debris intrusion while maintaining ventilation paths, requiring enhanced weatherproofing design.

name: Reduced moisture accumulation pressure
rationale: Proper ridge ventilation decreases moisture buildup by exhausting humid air, preventing condensation and rot in roof structures.

name: Minimised heat gain pressure
rationale: Effective ridge venting reduces attic heat gain in summer by exhausting hot air, lowering cooling loads on the building.

name: Adequate structural integrity pressure
rationale: The ridge cap must withstand wind uplift and snow loads while maintaining its ventilation function, requiring adequate structural design.

name: Increased snow load resistance
rationale: Snow guard cap strips are designed to resist snow loads and prevent snow slides from roofs. The component must have adequate structural capacity to withstand snow accumulation and transfer forces.

name: Reduced snow sliding risk
rationale: Snow guard cap strips function to reduce the risk of snow and ice sliding off roofs, protecting people and property below. This is a primary design function.

name: Enhanced attachment strength
rationale: The cap strip must have strong, secure attachments to the roof deck and underlying structure to transfer snow loads without detachment.

name: Improved weather sealing
rationale: Snow guard cap strips must be weather-sealed at attachment points to prevent water infiltration and maintain roof integrity.

name: Restricted icicle formation
rationale: Snow guard systems can help restrict the formation of ice dams and icicles at roof edges by managing snow retention and melt patterns.

name: Increased wind resistance pressure
rationale: Parapet walls must resist high wind uplift and lateral loads, requiring enhanced structural capacity and anchorage.

name: Reduced moisture infiltration pressure
rationale: Parapet walls are vulnerable to water intrusion at caps, coping joints, and flashing; design must minimise leakage paths.

name: Optimised thermal performance pressure
rationale: Parapet walls act as thermal bridges; improved insulation and continuous air barriers are needed to reduce heat loss.

name: Reduced structural overloading pressure
rationale: Parapet walls add dead load to the roof structure; design should minimise excessive weight while maintaining required heights and performance.

name: Enhanced drainage capacity pressure
rationale: Proper scupper and overflow drainage sizing is critical to prevent ponding at parapet walls and avoid structural overload during storms.

name: Improved waterproofing performance
rationale: The roofing membrane must resist water infiltration; higher waterproofing standards drive design decisions for material selection and seams.

name: Increased durability against UV exposure
rationale: UV radiation degrades membrane materials over time; greater UV resistance is a key design pressure for membrane composition and coatings.

name: Higher thermal insulation performance
rationale: The roofing system contributes to building thermal envelope; improved insulation values affect membrane thickness and integration with insulation layers.

name: Reduced material weight
rationale: Lighter membranes reduce structural loading on the building frame, influencing material selection and system design.

name: Minimised installation complexity
rationale: Simpler installation procedures reduce labor costs and error risks; design choices aim to minimize complicated details and specialized tooling.

name: Enhanced resistance to wind uplift
rationale: Wind uplift forces are a critical design load for roofing membranes; stronger attachment and higher puncture resistance are required.

name: Restricted thermal expansion/contraction
rationale: Temperature fluctuations cause dimensional changes in membranes; designs aim to limit movement to prevent stress and failure at joints.

name: Adequate fire resistance rating
rationale: Building codes require minimum fire performance for roof coverings; sufficient fire resistance drives material selection and system classification.

name: Better resistance to chemical exposure
rationale: Roofing membranes may be exposed to chemicals from industrial environments or ponding water; improved chemical resistance informs material formulation.

name: reduced trip hazard
rationale: Floor transition strips are designed to minimize tripping risks between different flooring surfaces, so there is a design pressure to reduce or eliminate height differences and edge catching.

name: improved aesthetic integration
rationale: Transition strips must blend visually with adjacent flooring materials, so there is a design pressure to improve color, texture, and material matching.

name: sufficient load capacity
rationale: Transition strips must withstand foot traffic, rolling loads (e.g., carts, wheelchairs), and other mechanical loads without deformation or failure.

name: minimised profile height
rationale: A lower profile reduces tripping hazard and improves accessibility compliance (e.g., ADA requirements), creating pressure to minimize the vertical height of the strip.

name: greater durability against wear
rationale: Transition strips endure repeated foot traffic and cleaning, so designs are pressured toward more durable materials and surface treatments.

name: reduced installation complexity
rationale: Simpler installation methods reduce labor cost and installation errors, so there is pressure to minimize the number of fasteners, cuts, or specialized tools needed.

name: improved moisture/air sealing
rationale: At junctions between different flooring systems, transition strips can serve as barriers against moisture migration and air infiltration, pressuring enhanced sealing performance.

name: lower material cost
rationale: Budget constraints in construction projects create a design pressure to minimize the cost of transition strip materials while meeting performance requirements.

name: Increased structural support for subfloor
rationale: Subfloors require adequate structural support to bear loads from flooring, occupants, and furnishings. Engineering principles dictate that increased support (joist sizing, spacing, material strength) improves subfloor performance and longevity.

name: Reduced moisture exposure for subfloor
rationale: Moisture is a primary threat to subfloor integrity, causing rot, mold, and delamination. Minimising moisture exposure through vapour barriers, ventilation, and drainage is a standard engineering requirement.

name: Improved subfloor flatness and levelness
rationale: A flat, level subfloor is essential for proper installation of finished flooring materials and to avoid squeaks, uneven surfaces, and premature wear. This drives decisions on subfloor thickness, material selection, and underlayment use.

name: Reduced thermal bridging through subfloor
rationale: Subfloors can act as thermal bridges, especially at edges and penetrations. Adding continuous insulation or thermal breaks reduces energy loss and improves building envelope performance.

name: Adequate acoustic isolation of subfloor
rationale: In multi-storey buildings, subfloors must provide sufficient sound transmission control (impact and airborne) between levels. This drives choices in subfloor construction, resilient layers, and mass.

name: Improved slip resistance
rationale: Anti-slip coatings and nosings are specifically designed to increase friction and prevent slipping, making improved slip resistance a primary design pressure.

name: Adequate durability
rationale: The coating or nosing must withstand foot traffic, weather exposure, and cleaning without wearing away, requiring adequate durability.

name: Reduced tripping hazard
rationale: Nosing profiles must be low-profile or smoothly transitioned to avoid creating a tripping edge, requiring the tripping hazard to be minimised.

name: Optimised profile height
rationale: The nosing height must be optimised to provide tactile feedback without exceeding accessibility code limits for vertical rise.

name: Restricted material degradation
rationale: UV exposure, moisture, and abrasion degrade anti-slip materials over time; degradation should be minimised to maintain performance.

name: Enhanced visual contrast
rationale: Building codes often require contrasting colour on stair nosings for visual impairment accessibility, making enhanced visual contrast a design pressure.

name: Increased waterproofing
rationale: Wet rooms and shower floors require high-performance waterproofing to prevent moisture damage and leakage.

name: Adequate drainage slope
rationale: Proper slope to drain is essential for water runoff and preventing standing water in wet areas.

name: Reduced slip hazard
rationale: Floor surfaces in wet areas must minimise slip risk for occupant safety.

name: Enhanced surface drainage
rationale: Efficient surface drainage prevents water accumulation and mould growth.

name: Higher moisture resistance
rationale: Materials and assemblies must resist moisture penetration and degradation over time.

name: Reduced water penetration
rationale: Minimising water ingress through floor joints and interfaces is critical for durability.

name: Greater non-slip texture
rationale: Texture or anti-slip treatment on the floor surface improves safety when wet.

name: Improved underfloor heating compatibility
rationale: Wet rooms often incorporate underfloor heating; the floor construction must accommodate this without compromising waterproofing.

name: Better subfloor stiffness
rationale: Adequate stiffness prevents tile/bedding cracking due to deflection, maintaining waterproof integrity.

name: Increased structural load capacity
rationale: The raised platform zone must support both static loads (equipment, furniture) and dynamic loads (people, activities) requiring adequate structural load capacity.

name: Improved accessibility compliance
rationale: Building codes require accessible routes and surfaces, so the raised platform must meet accessibility standards for ramps, slopes, and transitions.

name: Reduced tripping hazards
rationale: The raised platform's edges, level changes, and surface transitions must minimize tripping and fall risks for occupant safety.

name: Lower platform height
rationale: Height constraints from ceiling clearance, sightlines, or adjacent spaces may push toward a reduced platform height.

name: Greater surface area
rationale: Functional program requirements may demand a larger platform area to accommodate users or activities.

name: Enhanced material durability
rationale: The platform surface and structure should withstand wear from foot traffic and loading over the intended lifespan.

name: Restricted intrusion into adjacent zones
rationale: The platform's footprint and projections must not encroach on required clearances for neighboring spaces or circulation paths.

name: Increased structural load capacity
rationale: Timber stud frames must support vertical loads from floors, roofs, and other structural elements, requiring adequate load-bearing capacity.

name: Reduced thermal bridging
rationale: Timber stud frames are subject to thermal bridging through studs; minimising this improves overall building envelope thermal performance.

name: Improved racking resistance
rationale: Lateral wind and seismic forces demand adequate racking resistance in timber stud frames, often achieved through bracing or shear panels.

name: Reduced moisture content
rationale: Timber is susceptible to rot and dimensional changes from moisture; controlling moisture content is critical for durability and performance.

name: Optimised stud spacing
rationale: Stud spacing must be adequate to support cladding loads while balancing material efficiency and thermal performance requirements.

name: Greater fire resistance rating
rationale: Building codes require timber stud frames to achieve specified fire resistance ratings, often through fire-rated plasterboard or treatment.

name: Reduced material cost
rationale: Economic pressures demand minimising timber usage and labour cost while maintaining structural adequacy.

name: Enhanced dimensional stability
rationale: Timber expands and contracts with humidity changes; adequate stability prevents cracking of finishes and serviceability issues.

name: Restricted deflection under load
rationale: Excessive deflection of studs under lateral or vertical loads can cause damage to cladding and affect serviceability.

name: Increased structural support for cladding
rationale: Vertical counter battens provide structural support for external cladding, transferring wind and dead loads to the structure below.

name: Improved ventilation gap behind cladding
rationale: Counter battens create a vertical drainage and ventilation cavity behind cladding, essential for moisture management in rainscreen systems.

name: Reduced thermal bridging through direct cladding attachment
rationale: Counter battens help separate cladding from insulation layers, reducing direct thermal bridging compared to direct cladding fastening.

name: Adequate rain screen drainage capacity
rationale: The depth and spacing of counter battens must ensure sufficient cross-sectional area for drainage and ventilation in a rainscreen assembly.

name: Optimized batten spacing for cladding fixing
rationale: Batten spacing must be optimized to align with cladding panel/joint dimensions while providing adequate fixity.

name: Minimised material use and cost
rationale: There is economic pressure to use fewer or smaller battens to reduce material and labour costs.

name: Greater fire resistance performance
rationale: Counter battens must meet fire performance requirements, often requiring non-combustible materials or fire-rated designs.

name: Eliminated moisture entrapment behind cladding
rationale: Vertical battens promote drainage to prevent water accumulation, which could lead to rot or corrosion.

name: Improved ventilation effectiveness
rationale: Effective cavity ventilation is critical to prevent moisture buildup and ensure thermal performance in building envelopes.

name: Reduced pressure losses
rationale: Minimising pressure drops within the cavity ventilation system improves overall airflow and system efficiency.

name: Adequate airflow rate
rationale: Sufficient airflow must be maintained to remove moisture and heat from the cavity, preventing condensation and degradation.

name: Minimised obstruction to airflow
rationale: Obstructions such as debris, bridging, or tight geometries restrict cavity ventilation and reduce performance.

name: Enhanced moisture removal capacity
rationale: Moisture removal is a primary function of cavity ventilation; greater capacity protects building fabric from decay.

name: Increased structural support for cladding
rationale: The starter strip / J-channel must provide adequate structural support to hold the bottom edge of siding panels, creating a positive mechanical interlock that resists wind uplift and gravity loads.

name: Improved moisture drainage capacity
rationale: The J-channel design needs sufficient water drainage channels and weep holes to prevent water accumulation behind siding, reducing risk of moisture damage.

name: Reduced thermal expansion constraints
rationale: The starter strip should allow for thermal expansion and contraction of siding materials, so constraints on movement should be minimized to prevent buckling or warping.

name: Improved corrosion resistance
rationale: As an exterior metal component, the starter strip/J-channel requires enhanced corrosion resistance (e.g., galvanized or coated) to ensure long-term durability in weather-exposed conditions.

name: Sufficient fastening pull-out resistance
rationale: The fasteners securing the starter strip must have adequate pull-out resistance to withstand wind loads and maintain the integrity of the siding system.

name: Improved corner protection pressure
rationale: Corner trim/stop bead is designed to protect vulnerable external corners from impact and damage; engineering practice pressures designers to ensure adequate protection at building corners.

name: Enhanced moisture resistance pressure
rationale: Corner trim/stop bead often serves as a weather barrier at corners; there is pressure to ensure it adequately resists moisture ingress to prevent deterioration of the underlying structure.

name: Minimised material waste pressure
rationale: Construction efficiency pressures push toward standardised lengths and minimised cutting waste when installing corner trim/stop bead.

name: Reduced installation complexity pressure
rationale: There is pressure to make corner trim/stop bead easier and faster to install, reducing labour cost and the risk of installation errors.

name: Greater structural compatibility pressure
