rationale: Tie wire must possess sufficient tensile strength to securely fasten reinforcing bars (rebar) in concrete structures without breaking under tension during construction and concrete placement.

name: Reduced corrosion susceptibility
rationale: Tie wire should have minimised corrosion susceptibility, especially when used in exposed or moisture-prone concrete environments, to avoid weakening over time.

name: Improved ductility
rationale: Tie wire requires adequate ductility to allow twisting and bending around rebar without fracturing, enabling secure connections.

name: Sufficient gauge/diameter
rationale: The wire diameter must be adequate to provide the necessary strength and stiffness for holding rebar in place, typically 1.6 mm to 2.0 mm (16–18 gauge).

name: Lower cost per unit length
rationale: Tie wire is used in large quantities in reinforced concrete construction, so minimised material cost per unit length is desirable for project economy.

name: Improved aesthetic integration
rationale: Base molding visually bridges wall and floor; a well-integrated base molding improves spatial aesthetics and finish quality.

name: Greater durability against impact
rationale: Base molding at floor level is subject to kicks, bumps, and cleaning equipment; higher impact resistance extends service life.

name: Reduced material cost
rationale: Cost pressure to use less expensive materials or simpler profiles for base molding to stay within budget.

name: Limited profile height
rationale: Low-profile or minimal base molding is often desired in contemporary design to maintain clean sightlines and avoid visual clutter.

name: Eliminated moisture damage risk
rationale: Base molding near floors is vulnerable to water, cleaning chemicals, and humidity; materials and joints must resist moisture penetration and rot.

name: Improved ease of installation
rationale: Simpler profiles and pre-finished materials reduce installation labor time and skill requirements on site.

name: Adequate coverage of wall-floor gap
rationale: Base molding must sufficiently cover the expansion gap between wall and flooring to provide a clean finished appearance.

name: Improved structural support for casing trim
rationale: Casing trim as a component benefits from increased structural support to maintain its position and integrity within the building envelope.

name: Reduced thermal bridging at casing trim
rationale: Minimising thermal bridging around casing trim improves overall building energy performance and prevents condensation issues.

name: Enhanced weather sealing for casing trim
rationale: Adequate weather sealing around casing trim prevents water ingress and air leakage, protecting the building envelope.

name: Minimised material deflection at casing trim
rationale: Limiting deflection of casing trim material ensures long-term aesthetic and functional performance.

name: Optimised installation tolerances for casing trim
rationale: Precise installation tolerances for casing trim ensure visual alignment and proper fit with adjacent building components.

name: Increased durability protection
rationale: Chair rails protect walls from chair backs and furniture impacts, so there is a design pressure to increase the durability and protective function of the chair rail.

name: Reduced material cost
rationale: Budget constraints often pressure designers to reduce cost of decorative trim elements like chair rails.

name: Enhanced aesthetic proportion
rationale: Chair rails are traditionally placed at a specific height (about 1/3 up the wall) to create visual proportion; design pressure exists to enhance this aesthetic quality.

name: Lower maintenance requirement
rationale: Clients and building owners often desire chair rail materials and finishes that require less ongoing maintenance.

name: Adequate impact resistance
rationale: The chair rail must withstand impacts from furniture; a design pressure exists to ensure adequate impact resistance.

name: Restricted protrusion depth
rationale: Chair rails should not protrude excessively from the wall to avoid being obtrusive or easily damaged.

name: Increased visual prominence
rationale: Crown molding is traditionally a decorative feature, so design pressures often push for it to be more visually prominent to enhance aesthetic appeal.

name: Reduced material cost
rationale: Cost efficiency is a common engineering constraint, pushing toward simpler or less expensive crown molding profiles.

name: Greater structural support
rationale: Crown molding may need to bear loads or integrate with structural elements, creating a pressure for stronger attachment.

name: Improved structural integration
rationale: In joinery and moulding, quarter round trim needs improved structural integration with adjacent surfaces for durability and aesthetic finish.

name: Reduced material waste
rationale: Quarter round profiles are typically cut from longer stock; reducing waste during cutting and installation is a key design pressure.

name: Enhanced aesthetic continuity
rationale: Quarter round moulding is used at transitions (floor-to-wall, counter-to-wall); enhanced aesthetic continuity with adjoining surfaces is a design goal.

name: Reduced installation complexity
rationale: Simpler installation methods (e.g., flexible profiles, adhesive-backed options) reduce labor time and skill requirements.

name: Greater durability against impact
rationale: As a trim at floor level, quarter round is exposed to foot traffic and cleaning equipment, requiring greater impact resistance.

name: Improved aesthetic integration
rationale: Shoe molding (base shoe) is used at the junction between baseboard and flooring; there is a design pressure to improve its aesthetic integration with surrounding trim and flooring materials.

name: Reduced material cost
rationale: As a trim component, shoe molding is subject to cost optimization pressures to minimize material expense without sacrificing function.

name: Sufficient gap coverage
rationale: Shoe molding must adequately cover the expansion gap between flooring and baseboard, driving a pressure for sufficient dimensional coverage.

name: Lower profile height
rationale: There is often a design preference for a lower, less obtrusive profile to maintain clean sightlines and not compete with the baseboard.

name: Higher durability
rationale: Shoe molding is subject to impact from foot traffic and cleaning equipment, creating pressure for greater durability/resistance to damage.

name: Eliminated moisture damage risk
rationale: As a floor-level trim, shoe molding is exposed to moisture from cleaning and potential spills; design seeks to prevent or minimize moisture-related deterioration.

name: Enhanced aesthetic quality
rationale: Interior trim zones define the visual quality of interior spaces; there is architectural pressure to improve finish quality and material selection for better occupant experience.

name: Reduced material cost
rationale: Engineering and cost considerations push for minimizing expensive trim materials and simplifying detailing to stay within budget.

name: Improved durability and wear resistance
rationale: Trim zones in high-traffic areas experience wear; selecting more durable finishes is a common design pressure to extend lifecycle and reduce maintenance.

name: Reduced installation complexity
rationale: Simpler trim profiles and fewer transitions reduce labour costs and installation time, a typical pressure in construction scheduling.

name: Greater acoustic performance
rationale: Interior trim zones can affect sound absorption and reflection; there is a pressure to use acoustic-rated trim materials in noise-sensitive spaces like conference rooms.

name: Reduced thermal bridging pressure
rationale: Exterior trim zones are prone to thermal bridging where fasteners penetrate the building envelope. Engineering practice prioritises minimising thermal bridges to improve energy performance.

name: Improved weather resistance pressure
rationale: Exterior trim must provide enhanced resistance to moisture intrusion and wind-driven rain to protect the underlying building envelope, a core engineering requirement.

name: Expanded aesthetic integration pressure
rationale: Architectural design pressures demand that trim zones achieve better visual alignment, proportion, and material continuity with adjacent facade elements.

name: Reduced material waste pressure
rationale: Construction efficiency pressures call for minimised offcuts and waste when installing trim, achieved through standardised lengths and modular detailing.

name: Higher durability against UV degradation pressure
rationale: Exterior trim materials are directly exposed to solar radiation; physical/material science dictates that greater UV resistance is required to prevent embrittlement and discolouration over time.

name: Improved structural integrity of trim profile
rationale: The trim profile system must have sufficient structural integrity to withstand wind loads and other environmental pressures without deformation or failure.

name: Enhanced aesthetic alignment of trim profiles
rationale: Trim profiles play a key aesthetic role in building envelopes; precise alignment and finish quality are architecturally required.

name: Reduced thermal bridging through trim
rationale: Trim systems can act as thermal bridges if not properly designed; minimizing heat transfer improves energy performance.

name: Limited water ingress at trim joints
rationale: Trim profiles form part of the building envelope; water penetration at joints can cause moisture damage and must be prevented.

name: Adequate expansion clearance in trim profiles
rationale: Thermal expansion and contraction require adequate gaps in trim systems to prevent buckling or distortion.

name: Greater corrosion resistance of trim materials
rationale: Exterior trim profiles are exposed to weather; corrosion resistance is critical for long-term durability.

name: Minimised material waste in trim fabrication
rationale: Efficient use of materials in trim profiles reduces cost and environmental impact during fabrication.

name: Eliminated sharp edges on trim profiles
rationale: Safety and architectural finish quality require that trim profiles have no sharp exposed edges.

name: Optimised attachment fastening of trim system
rationale: Proper fastening design ensures trim remains securely attached under wind and thermal loads without loosening over time.

name: Improved corrosion resistance
rationale: Fasteners exposed to environmental moisture require corrosion-resistant materials or coatings to maintain structural integrity over time.

name: Higher tensile strength
rationale: Fasteners must withstand tensile loads without failure to ensure structural connections remain secure under design loads.

name: Reduced thermal expansion mismatch
rationale: Differences in thermal expansion coefficients between fastener and connected materials can cause loosening or stress concentrations.

name: Sufficient fatigue resistance
rationale: Cyclic loading from wind, vibration, or thermal cycling can cause fatigue failure in fasteners over the building lifespan.

name: Prevented galvanic corrosion
rationale: Dissimilar metal contact between fasteners and structural members creates galvanic corrosion risk that must be avoided.

name: Optimised installation torque
rationale: Proper preload from correct installation torque ensures joint integrity without over-stressing the fastener or damaging connected materials.

name: Reduced shear stress concentration
rationale: Geometric discontinuities at fastener holes create stress concentrations that can initiate failure under shear loading.

name: Adequate embedment depth
rationale: For anchors and screws in concrete/masonry, sufficient embedment depth is required to develop full pullout capacity.

name: Eliminated hydrogen embrittlement risk
rationale: High-strength steel fasteners are susceptible to hydrogen embrittlement; protective measures and material selection must prevent this failure mode.

name: Improved aesthetic quality
rationale: Architectural design values seek improved visual appeal and finish quality, pressuring the Paint and Finish System to deliver better aesthetics.

name: Reduced material cost
rationale: Engineering cost optimization pressures reducing material expenditures on paints and finishes.

name: Enhanced durability and protection
rationale: Physical/environmental protection requirements demand enhanced durability from the finish system to resist weathering, wear, and corrosion.

name: Lower environmental impact (VOC content)
rationale: Regulatory and cultural sustainability expectations push for reduced volatile organic compounds (VOCs) and lower environmental footprint.

name: Optimised application ease
rationale: Construction efficiency pressures push for optimized application properties such as spreadability, drying time, and workability.

name: Greater color and finish variety
rationale: Architectural and client demands for more options in color, texture, and finish variety.

name: Restricted maintenance frequency
rationale: Operational cost pressures push for reduced maintenance intervals, meaning the paint system must last longer between reapplications.

name: Higher adhesion strength
rationale: Physical requirement for strong adhesion to substrate material to prevent peeling and delamination.

name: Eliminated health hazards
rationale: Health and safety regulations and cultural norms demand elimination of toxic substances (e.g., lead, hazardous solvents) from finishes.

name: Increased seating capacity
rationale: The fixed seating area must accommodate a certain number of occupants, driving a need for greater seating capacity within the space.

name: Improved accessibility
rationale: Building codes and universal design principles require accessible routes and seating positions for people with disabilities.

name: Reduced footprint
rationale: Space constraints or program requirements may limit the overall footprint allocated to fixed seating to allow for other functions.

name: Optimised sightlines
rationale: Fixed seating in venues like theaters or stadiums requires optimised sightlines so all occupants have an unobstructed view of the stage or field.

name: Adequate structural support
rationale: Fixed seating imposes live and dead loads on the structure, requiring adequate structural support for safety.

name: Minimised row spacing
rationale: To maximise seating density within a constrained area, row spacing may be minimised, though this must balance with comfort and code requirements.

name: Increased seating capacity
rationale: Flexible seating zones are designed to accommodate varying numbers of people, driving the need for increased seating capacity.

name: Enhanced spatial flexibility
rationale: The core purpose of a flexible seating zone is to allow reconfiguration, so enhanced spatial flexibility is a key design pressure.

name: Optimised space utilisation
rationale: Flexible seating zones aim to maximise use of available floor area for multiple functions.

name: Reduced fixed furniture constraints
rationale: To maintain flexibility, permanent or fixed furniture that limits reconfiguration should be minimised.

name: Improved accessibility
rationale: Flexible seating zones must accommodate users with varying mobility needs, driving improved accessibility.

name: Increased visibility and sightlines
rationale: Tiered seating is designed to provide unobstructed views for audiences; improving sightlines is a primary design driver.

name: Optimised seating capacity
rationale: Maximising the number of seats within available space without compromising comfort or safety is a core design objective.

name: Reduced obstruction from structural elements
rationale: Structural columns or beams that block views degrade the user experience and must be minimised or positioned strategically.

name: Improved accessibility compliance
rationale: Building codes require accessible seating and circulation paths within tiered seating areas for persons with disabilities.

name: Reduced slope gradient for safety
rationale: Excessively steep tiers pose fall risks; the slope must be limited to meet safety standards and user comfort.

name: Greater structural load capacity
rationale: The terrace must support the dead load of the structure plus live loads from occupants; higher capacity ensures safety and durability.

name: Enhanced acoustic performance
rationale: Tiered seating areas in performance venues require good acoustics; design pressures include optimised materials and geometry for sound.

name: Adequate egress and evacuation paths
rationale: Fire safety codes demand sufficient, clearly marked exit routes from tiered seating areas to ensure safe evacuation.

name: Minimised construction cost
rationale: Budget constraints create pressure to reduce material and labour costs while maintaining structural integrity and design intent.

name: Increased structural load capacity
rationale: Bleacher assemblies must support the weight of spectators, requiring sufficient structural load capacity to ensure safety and stability.

name: Reduced lateral deflection
rationale: Lateral movement under crowd loading or wind must be minimized to prevent discomfort or panic among occupants.

name: Improved egress accessibility
rationale: Bleacher designs must provide adequate means of egress and accessible pathways per building codes for safe evacuation.

name: Higher sightline clarity
rationale: Riser heights and row spacing must be optimized to ensure unobstructed sightlines for spectators.

name: Reduced overall weight
rationale: Lighter bleacher assemblies reduce foundation demands and allow for portable or temporary configurations, though permanent units may prioritize robustness over weight.

name: increased seating capacity
rationale: Auditorium design requires adequate seating capacity to accommodate audience size.

name: optimised sightline clearance
rationale: Seats must be arranged to ensure unobstructed sightlines to the stage for all occupants.

name: reduced inter-row spacing
rationale: Limited floor area may drive tighter row spacing to fit more seats, though comfort may be compromised.

name: improved acoustic isolation
rationale: Seat materials and upholstery influence sound absorption and reflection, impacting acoustic quality.

name: lower seat weight
rationale: Lighter seats reduce structural floor loading and may simplify installation and reconfiguration.

name: enhanced ergonomic comfort
rationale: Occupant comfort during extended events drives seat design including cushioning, lumbar support, and dimensions.

name: greater durability
rationale: High-use public seating requires robust materials and construction to withstand frequent use and cleaning.

name: restricted unit width
rationale: Narrower seats may be specified to maximise row capacity within a given floor width.

name: adequate fire-resistance rating
rationale: Building codes require seating materials to meet fire safety standards for public assembly spaces.

name: Increased seating capacity
rationale: Design pressure to accommodate more people in a space, driving the bench seating unit to be larger or have more sections.

name: Improved ergonomic comfort
rationale: Pressure to design bench seating that is comfortable for users over extended periods, affecting seat depth, height, backrest angle, and material choice.

name: Reduced manufacturing cost
rationale: Pressure to minimise material usage and simplify fabrication processes to keep production costs low.

name: Enhanced durability against weather
rationale: Pressure for the bench to withstand outdoor exposure (rain, UV, temperature changes) through robust material selection and protective treatments.

name: Restricted physical footprint
rationale: Pressure to keep the bench size constrained to fit within site dimensions, pathways, or spatial planning limits.

name: Greater aesthetic appeal
rationale: Pressure to achieve a visually pleasing design that complements the surrounding architectural context.

name: Lower maintenance requirements
rationale: Pressure to select materials and finishes that require minimal cleaning, painting, or replacement over the bench's lifecycle.

name: Sufficient structural strength
rationale: Pressure to ensure the bench can safely support anticipated loads (people, dynamic forces) without failure or excessive deflection.

name: Eliminated sharp edges and hazards
rationale: Pressure to design the bench with rounded corners and smooth surfaces to prevent injury to users, especially in public or child-friendly settings.

name: Higher load capacity
rationale: Seat mounting brackets must withstand passenger loads and crash forces, requiring sufficient strength and load capacity.

name: Reduced weight
rationale: Minimising bracket weight reduces overall vehicle weight, improving fuel efficiency and performance.

name: Improved vibration damping
rationale: The bracket should damp vibrations transmitted from the vehicle chassis to the seat for passenger comfort.

name: Lower manufacturing cost
rationale: Cost constraints drive a need to minimise material and production expenses for the bracket.

name: Enhanced corrosion resistance
rationale: The bracket must resist corrosion from moisture and environmental exposure over the vehicle's lifespan.

name: Reduced installation complexity
rationale: Simpler bracket design reduces assembly time and potential for installation errors.

name: Greater fatigue life
rationale: Repeated loading cycles from vehicle motion and passenger ingress/egress require adequate fatigue endurance.

name: Adequate bolt-hole alignment
rationale: Precise alignment with seat frame and chassis mounting points is necessary for proper assembly.

name: Increased structural load capacity
rationale: The seat riser/step structure must support the weight of spectators, their dynamic movements (standing, jumping, stepping), and any superimposed loads from seats or equipment, requiring adequate structural strength.

name: Improved slip resistance
rationale: Step surfaces on risers must provide sufficient friction to prevent slipping, especially under wet or crowded conditions, to ensure spectator safety.

name: Reduced span between supports
rationale: To prevent excessive deflection or vibration in the riser structure, the unsupported span should be limited, requiring closer support spacing or stiffer construction.

name: Lower overall weight
rationale: Minimising the self-weight of the riser structure reduces the load on supporting beams, columns, and foundations, enabling more efficient overall structural design.

name: Greater fire resistance rating
rationale: Seating risers in assembly occupancies must meet fire-resistance requirements to allow safe egress and prevent fire spread, requiring fire-rated materials or coatings.

name: Restricted vertical deflection under load
rationale: Excessive vertical deflection of treads/risers under live load can cause discomfort, tripping hazards, or perceived instability, so deflection limits must be enforced.

name: Improved legibility for seat numbering
rationale: Seat numbering must be clearly legible from all viewing angles and distances to help spectators locate their seats efficiently, reducing congestion and confusion.

name: Higher contrast signage for visibility
rationale: Signage requires sufficient contrast (luminance, colour) against its background to be readable under varying lighting conditions, including emergency evacuation scenarios.

name: Reduced visual clutter from excessive signage
rationale: Too many signs or overly large signs can create visual clutter, detracting from the architectural aesthetics and potentially overwhelming users.

name: Optimised placement for wayfinding efficiency
rationale: Numbers and signs should be placed at consistent heights and intervals along aisles to support intuitive wayfinding and reduce the time spectators spend searching for their seats.

name: Minimised glare and reflection on signage
rationale: Glossy or reflective materials on signage can cause glare under direct or artificial lighting, reducing readability; matte finishes or anti-glare coatings help maintain legibility.

name: Enhanced durability against wear and vandalism
rationale: Stadium seating signage is subject to foot traffic, cleaning, and potential vandalism; durable materials (e.g., engraved or embossed numbering) ensure long-term legibility.

name: Increased structural load capacity
rationale: The seat rail system must withstand static and dynamic loads from seating and occupants, requiring adequate structural strength to prevent failure.

name: Improved corrosion resistance
rationale: Seat rails are exposed to environmental conditions (moisture, cleaning agents) and need enhanced corrosion protection to ensure longevity.

name: Reduced manufacturing cost
rationale: Cost constraints drive the need to minimise material usage and simplify fabrication processes for the rail system.

name: Minimised weight
rationale: Weight reduction is important for fuel efficiency (in vehicles/aircraft) or ease of installation, requiring lightweight yet strong rail profiles.

name: Improved dimensional precision
rationale: Tight tolerances are needed to ensure proper fit, smooth sliding adjustment, and reliable locking mechanisms for seat positioning.

name: Reduced wear over time
rationale: Frequent seat adjustment cycles cause mechanical wear; using hardened materials or low-friction coatings helps limit degradation.

name: Improved ease of installation
rationale: Simplified mounting interfaces and modular designs allow faster assembly and reduced labour costs during manufacturing or retrofit.

name: Restricted lateral movement
rationale: Lateral play must be minimised to ensure passenger safety and prevent rattling noises during transit or use.

name: Enhanced fire resistance
rationale: In transport applications (aircraft, rail), seat rails must meet flammability standards, requiring use of fire-retardant materials or coatings.

name: Improved accessibility compliance
rationale: Building codes and accessibility standards (e.g., ADA) mandate adequate wheelchair seating spaces in public venues, driving a need for well-designed, compliant spaces.

name: Increased maneuverability space
rationale: Wheelchair users require sufficient clear floor area and circulation space to approach, turn, and transfer comfortably, which dictates the dimensions of the seating space.

name: Enhanced user comfort and dignity
rationale: Societal expectations and inclusive design principles push for wheelchair seating that is not just minimal but also comfortable, well-located, and respectful of users.

name: Maximised sightline quality
rationale: Wheelchair seating positions should be designed to provide unobstructed views over standing spectators, often requiring raised platforms or sloped floors.

name: Reduced travel distance from entrance
rationale: Accessible routes from building entrances to wheelchair seating areas should be as short as possible to minimize effort and exposure for users with mobility impairments.

name: Limited number of wheelchair spaces per row
rationale: To maintain safe egress and avoid isolating wheelchair users, the number of wheelchair spaces grouped together is often restricted by code or good practice.

name: Adequate companion seating adjacency
rationale: Accessibility standards typically require that wheelchair spaces have adjacent companion seating to allow users to sit with family or friends.

name: Enhanced exclusivity and premium experience
rationale: VIP and premium seating boxes are designed to provide an elevated, exclusive experience for high-value guests, so there is a pressure to increase the sense of exclusivity and premium quality.

name: Improved sightlines and viewing comfort
rationale: Premium seating requires optimal sightlines to the event/performance area, driving a pressure for improved visual access and comfortable viewing angles.

name: Greater spatial luxury and generous dimensions
rationale: VIP boxes typically demand more spacious layouts, wider seats, and extra legroom compared to standard seating to justify premium pricing.

name: Enhanced acoustic privacy and sound isolation
rationale: Premium boxes often require better acoustic separation from adjacent boxes and public areas to allow private conversation without disturbance.

name: Increased level of service and amenities
rationale: Cultural expectations for VIP areas include dedicated service, catering, and premium amenities such as private bars or lounge access.

name: Restricted public access and controlled entry
rationale: To maintain exclusivity and security, public access to the VIP box must be limited or restricted through controlled entry points.

name: Reduced noise intrusion from adjacent areas
rationale: External noise from corridors, adjacent seating, or mechanical systems should be minimised to preserve the premium atmosphere.

name: Increased seating capacity
rationale: Retractable seating is designed to provide flexible capacity for different event sizes, so there is pressure to maximize the number of seats available when extended.

name: Improved ease of operation
rationale: Users and operators demand retractable seating systems that are easy to deploy and retract, requiring smoother mechanisms and simpler controls.

name: Reduced storage footprint
rationale: When retracted, the seating system should occupy minimal space to allow the venue to be used for other purposes.

name: Higher structural stability
rationale: Retractable seating must meet structural and safety codes, requiring strong frames and secure locking mechanisms to prevent collapse under load.

name: Minimised maintenance requirements
rationale: Moving parts and mechanisms in retractable seating require regular maintenance; there is pressure to reduce this burden through durable components and simpler designs.

name: Improved accessibility compliance
rationale: Building codes and accessibility standards require adequate space for wheelchair users and accessible routes within retractable seating layouts.

name: Reduced acoustic interference
rationale: Retractable seating systems can introduce noise from mechanisms and may affect the venue acoustics; there is pressure to minimize this interference.

name: Greater load-bearing capacity
rationale: The system must support audience weight safely; higher capacity per square meter is often demanded for compliance and safety.

name: Eliminated pinch points and safety hazards
rationale: Moving components of retractable seating create risks of injury; design pressures aim to prevent entrapment and sharp edges.

name: Increased visibility and prominence
rationale: Press and media seating areas need to have clear, unobstructed views of the main event space (e.g., stage, field, arena) to allow journalists and camera operators to perform their work effectively.

name: Optimized proximity to event action
rationale: Media seating must be positioned close enough to the action to capture high-quality footage and details, while maintaining safety and a professional working environment.

name: Reduced obstruction from columns or structures
rationale: Columns, railings, or other structural elements that block sightlines from media seating are unacceptable; they must be minimized or eliminated to ensure unobstructed views for cameras and reporters.

name: Enhanced acoustic separation from crowd noise
rationale: Broadcast and commentary positions require controlled acoustics to isolate media seating from excessive ambient crowd noise for clear audio transmission.

name: Adequate power and data connectivity
rationale: Media professionals require reliable access to electrical outlets, high-speed internet, and broadcast cabling at their seating positions to operate equipment.

name: Restricted public access to media zone
rationale: Uncontrolled public access to the press/media seating area would disrupt broadcasting and journalism activities; access should be restricted to credentialed media personnel only.

name: Sufficient workspace per media seat
rationale: Each media position requires adequate desk space or work surface for laptops, note-taking, and equipment, beyond what a typical spectator seat provides.

name: Lower sightline angle from seating to event
rationale: Steep sightline angles are undesirable for media seating as they distort perspective for cameras and make it harder for reporters to see the full field of play.

name: increased structural load-bearing capacity
rationale: The seating structural support system must bear live loads from occupants as well as dead loads from seating materials; engineering standards require sufficient load-bearing capacity to ensure safety and prevent collapse.

name: improved lateral stability
rationale: Lateral forces such as wind or seismic loads demand that the seating support system has adequate bracing and stiffness to resist overturning and sliding.

name: reduced structural weight
rationale: Minimising self-weight of the support structure reduces material costs, foundation loads, and can improve constructability while still meeting strength requirements.

name: minimised deflection under load
rationale: Excessive deflection of seating supports leads to discomfort for occupants and potential serviceability issues; deflection must be limited per structural codes.

name: adequate vibration damping
rationale: Crowd-induced vibrations from rhythmic activities (e.g., concerts, sports events) require the structure to have sufficient damping to prevent unacceptable motion.

name: enhanced fire resistance
rationale: Structural support systems for seating areas must meet fire-resistance ratings to ensure safe egress and prevent structural failure during a fire.

name: greater connection robustness
rationale: Connections between seating components and primary structure must be strong and ductile to transfer loads reliably and maintain structural integrity.

name: restricted cantilever length
rationale: Long cantilevers in seating structures can lead to excessive deflections and higher bending moments; limiting cantilever spans improves structural performance.

name: improved corrosion protection
rationale: If metal components are used in the seating support system, corrosion protection (e.g., galvanising, coatings) is needed to ensure long-term durability.

name: Increased egress capacity
rationale: Building codes require sufficient egress width and capacity to allow safe evacuation of all occupants based on occupancy load.

name: Improved circulation flow
rationale: Aisle layout must facilitate smooth, unobstructed movement toward exits, minimising congestion and bottlenecks.

name: Reduced travel distance to exits
rationale: Building codes impose maximum travel distance requirements from any point to the nearest exit to ensure timely evacuation.

name: Maximized accessibility for all users
rationale: Egress routes must comply with accessibility standards (e.g., ADA) to accommodate persons with disabilities, requiring adequate widths, slopes, and clearances.

name: Minimised obstruction from furnishings
rationale: Aisles and egress paths must remain clear of permanent or temporary obstructions to maintain effective width and safe passage.

name: Greater number of exit access points
rationale: Codes require a minimum number of separate exits based on occupancy load and building geometry to provide redundancy.

name: Improved wayfinding and signage clarity
rationale: Clear, illuminated exit signs and wayfinding aids are required to guide occupants to exits, especially under emergency conditions.

name: Reduced dead-end corridor length
rationale: Building codes limit the length of dead-end corridors to prevent occupants from being trapped in a non-exit direction.

name: Adequate separation between opposing egress flows
rationale: In high-occupancy spaces, aisle layouts should minimise cross-flow and counterflow to avoid confusion and delay during evacuation.

name: Increased seating comfort
rationale: Bench seats in architectural contexts are designed to provide comfortable seating for users in public or private spaces.

name: Reduced material cost
rationale: Engineering and cost considerations push for minimizing material usage while maintaining structural integrity.

name: Improved durability
rationale: Benches need to withstand outdoor weather, wear and tear, and heavy loads over time.

name: Reduced maintenance requirements
rationale: Design decisions aim to minimize the need for repairs, painting, or replacement of bench components.

name: Enhanced aesthetic appeal
rationale: Visual integration with surrounding landscape or architecture is a key design consideration.

name: Lower weight
rationale: Lighter benches are easier to install, relocate, and may reduce shipping costs.

name: Increased structural strength
rationale: The bench must safely support expected loads including multiple users and environmental forces.

name: Reduced environmental impact
rationale: Growing cultural emphasis on sustainable and eco-friendly material choices.

name: Greater accessibility compliance
rationale: Design must comply with accessibility standards to accommodate all users including those with disabilities.

name: Increased ergonomic support
rationale: A bench backrest must provide adequate ergonomic support for user comfort during sitting.

name: Increased structural stability
rationale: The backrest must be structurally stable to withstand loads from users leaning against it.

name: Reduced material use
rationale: Material efficiency is typically a design consideration to minimise cost and weight.

name: Improved weather resistance
rationale: Outdoor bench backrests need to resist weathering from sun, rain, and temperature changes.

name: Increased aesthetic appeal
rationale: The visual design of the backrest contributes to the overall aesthetic of the bench and its setting.

name: Reduced manufacturing complexity
rationale: Simpler designs can reduce production costs and assembly time.

name: Greater user safety
rationale: The backrest should have no sharp edges or pinch points and should be safe for users of all ages.

name: Optimised maintenance access
rationale: Design should allow for easy cleaning and replacement of backrest components if damaged.

name: Limited weight
rationale: A lighter backrest reduces overall bench weight, aiding transport and installation.

name: Increased structural stability
rationale: Bench legs must be stable enough to support the bench surface and loads placed on it without tipping or wobbling.

name: Sufficient load-bearing capacity
rationale: Bench legs must carry the weight of the bench and its occupants, requiring adequate strength and material selection.

name: Reduced material usage
rationale: There is typically a desire to minimise material cost and weight in bench leg design, while maintaining structural requirements.

name: Minimised lateral sway
rationale: Bench legs should resist lateral forces to prevent excessive sideways movement or buckling under load.

name: Increased ergonomic support pressure
rationale: Bench armrests need to provide adequate ergonomic support for users to rest their arms comfortably, which is a key functional requirement.

name: Improved durability pressure
rationale: Armrests must withstand repeated loading from users leaning or pushing on them, requiring robust construction and durable materials.

name: Reduced obstruction pressure
rationale: Armrests should not obstruct user movement or make the bench difficult to access, particularly for users with mobility aids.

name: Minimised material cost pressure
rationale: Cost constraints typically push for minimising material usage and fabrication complexity in bench armrests.

name: Improved aesthetic integration pressure
rationale: Armrests should visually complement the overall bench design and surrounding environment.

name: Enhanced safety pressure
rationale: Armrests must have rounded edges, no pinch points, and be securely attached to prevent injury.

name: Limited width pressure
rationale: Overly wide armrests reduce available seating space and may crowd adjacent seated users.

name: Greater structural strength pressure
rationale: Armrests must bear lateral and vertical forces from users without failure, requiring sufficient structural strength.

name: Reduced maintenance needs pressure
rationale: Armrests should be designed with weather-resistant, low-maintenance materials to minimise long-term upkeep.

name: Increased load-bearing capacity
rationale: Bench base frames must support static and dynamic loads from users and environmental conditions, requiring adequate strength and stability.

name: Improved corrosion resistance
rationale: Outdoor bench frames are exposed to weathering and moisture, requiring protective finishes or corrosion-resistant materials.

name: Reduced material waste
rationale: Efficient design and fabrication of the base frame should minimise excess material usage and offcuts.

name: Enhanced structural stability
rationale: The base frame must resist tipping, overturning, and lateral forces to ensure user safety and long-term performance.

name: Minimised weight
rationale: Reducing the frame weight can ease transportation and installation, though it must not compromise strength.

name: Sufficient anchoring force
rationale: If the bench is fixed to a substrate, the base frame must accommodate anchor points with adequate pull-out resistance.

name: Increased storage capacity
rationale: A shoe storage cubby should provide adequate capacity to accommodate the expected number of shoes for users.

name: Improved accessibility
rationale: Shoe cubbies need to be easily reachable and accessible for users to store and retrieve shoes efficiently.

name: Reduced physical footprint
rationale: Space constraints typically push for a smaller footprint to allow more room for other functions or circulation.

name: Improved ventilation
rationale: Shoes can trap moisture and odors, so ventilation or airflow through the cubby is desirable to prevent mold and smell.

name: Greater structural support
rationale: The cubby must be structurally capable of supporting the weight of stored shoes, especially if multi-tiered.

name: Reduced cost
rationale: Budget constraints drive the desire to minimize material and construction costs for the cubby.

name: Improved visual integration
rationale: The cubby should fit aesthetically within its surrounding interior design context.

name: Eliminated tripping hazard
rationale: Shoe cubbies near circulation paths should not create protruding elements or obstacles that pose safety risks.

name: Higher load capacity
rationale: The coat hook rail must have sufficient load capacity to support the weight of coats, bags, and other items hung on it without bending or detaching from the wall.

name: Reduced protrusion
rationale: To minimize hazards and optimize space usage, the coat hook rail should have a minimized protrusion from the wall to avoid obstructing circulation paths.

name: Adequate spacing between hooks
rationale: Sufficient spacing between individual hooks is needed to prevent overcrowding of hung items and allow easy access.

name: Greater durability for frequent use
rationale: The coat hook rail should be designed with enhanced durability to withstand frequent daily use in a commercial or educational setting.

name: Lower installation complexity
rationale: Simplified installation methods reduce construction time and labor costs while maintaining secure attachment.

name: Improved accessibility
rationale: Storage drawers need to be easily accessible for users to retrieve and store items efficiently.

name: Greater storage capacity
rationale: Users typically desire maximum usable space within the drawer for storing items.

name: Increased structural strength
rationale: The drawer must support the weight of stored items without sagging or failure.

name: Reduced cost
rationale: Manufacturing and material costs should be minimized for economic feasibility.

name: Minimised weight
rationale: Lighter drawers are easier to operate and place less load on supporting structures.

name: Eliminated friction
rationale: Smooth operation requires minimal friction between the drawer and its slides or runners.

name: Increased seating comfort
rationale: Cushion/seat pad design must prioritize increased comfort for occupants, influencing material choice, thickness, and ergonomic shape.

name: Improved durability
rationale: The cushion/seat pad must withstand repeated use and loading over time, requiring durable materials and construction.

name: Reduced material cost
rationale: Cost constraints pressure the design to minimize material expenses while maintaining required performance.

name: Reduced weight
rationale: Lighter cushion/seat pad reduces overall load on supporting structure and improves portability if applicable.

name: Improved fire resistance
rationale: Building codes require adequate fire resistance for upholstered furniture components to ensure safety.

name: Greater ergonomic support
rationale: Proper ergonomic design of the cushion/seat pad is needed to support the human body and prevent discomfort or injury.

name: Reduced maintenance requirements
rationale: Design should minimize the need for frequent cleaning, replacement, or repair of the cushion/seat pad.

name: Optimised thickness
rationale: Thickness must be optimized to balance comfort, support, material use, and fit within seating assembly constraints.

name: Lower environmental impact
rationale: Sustainability pressures encourage use of recycled or eco-friendly materials and reduced embodied energy in the cushion/seat pad.

name: Increased load-bearing capacity
rationale: The bench mounting bracket must have sufficient strength to support the weight of the bench and its occupants, requiring increased load-bearing capacity.

name: Greater corrosion resistance
rationale: Mounting brackets exposed to environmental conditions or moisture require greater corrosion resistance to ensure longevity and structural integrity.

name: Higher fatigue strength
rationale: Cyclic loading from bench usage creates fatigue stresses on the bracket, requiring higher fatigue strength to prevent failure over time.

name: Reduced material cost
rationale: Cost efficiency drives a need to minimise material usage in the bracket design without compromising structural performance.

name: Minimised deflection under load
rationale: Excessive deflection of the bracket under load can cause discomfort or instability for bench users, requiring minimised deflection.

name: Improved bolt hole alignment precision
rationale: Accurate bolt hole alignment is essential for proper installation and load transfer, driving improved precision in manufacturing.

name: Reduced weight
rationale: Lighter brackets reduce shipping costs and ease installation, creating a pressure to reduce bracket weight.

name: Enhanced manufacturing tolerances
rationale: Consistent fit and performance of the bracket requires enhanced manufacturing tolerances to ensure dimensional accuracy.

name: Eliminated sharp edges
rationale: Safety requirements demand that sharp edges and burrs on the bracket be eliminated to prevent injury during handling and use.

name: Improved mudroom organization
rationale: A mudroom serves as a transition zone between outdoors and indoors; organizing shoes, coats, bags, and outdoor gear is a primary functional requirement.

name: Adequate storage capacity
rationale: Mudrooms need sufficient storage (cubbies, hooks, benches, lockers) to accommodate household members' outdoor gear, preventing clutter in adjacent spaces.

name: Improved traffic flow efficiency
rationale: The entryway must allow smooth circulation for people entering and exiting, especially during peak times (e.g., family members coming/going simultaneously).

name: Minimised dirt and moisture transfer
rationale: The primary function of a mudroom is to contain dirt, mud, and moisture from outdoors, preventing it from spreading into the main living areas.

name: Eliminated entry congestion
rationale: Congestion at the entry point can create bottlenecks and frustration; sufficient space for multiple people to transition simultaneously is important.

name: Adequate durable flooring
rationale: Mudroom floors must withstand heavy foot traffic, moisture, dirt, and frequent cleaning; durable, easy-to-clean materials are essential.

name: Better thermal separation from interior
rationale: The mudroom acts as an airlock between outdoors and conditioned interior spaces; good insulation and air sealing reduce energy loss.

name: Sufficient lighting for task visibility
rationale: Adequate lighting is needed for finding items, putting on shoes, and cleaning; natural and artificial lighting both contribute to functionality.

name: Optimised seating provision
rationale: Seating (benches) is critical for comfortable shoe removal and donning; sufficient seating capacity for all household members is desirable.

name: greater seating durability
rationale: Built-in benches must withstand repeated use and loads, so greater durability of joinery and materials is a key design pressure.

name: improved structural stability
rationale: The bench structure must be stable under lateral and vertical loads, requiring improved joinery connections and bracing.

name: higher comfort and ergonomics
rationale: Benches used for sitting require ergonomically designed dimensions and angles, creating a pressure for higher comfort standards in joinery design.

name: reduced material costs
rationale: Budget constraints create a pressure to reduce material costs through efficient joinery design and material selection.

name: minimised maintenance requirements
rationale: Built-in benches should require minimal ongoing maintenance, creating a design pressure to select durable finishes and robust joinery.

name: optimised space utilisation
rationale: Built-in benches must fit within allocated floor plans and often serve dual storage/seating functions, pressuring optimised joinery design for space efficiency.

name: adequate fire resistance
rationale: Building codes require that built-in joinery meets fire-resistance standards, creating pressure for adequate fire-rated materials and construction.

name: restricted structural load on floor
rationale: The weight of built-in bench joinery must be limited to avoid overloading floor structures, creating a pressure for lighter construction.

name: improved aesthetic integration
rationale: Built-in benches must visually harmonise with surrounding architecture, creating pressure for improved detailing, finish, and material coordination.

name: greater load-bearing capacity
rationale: The wall base footing must support the vertical load from the wall above and distribute it to the ground, requiring sufficient load-bearing capacity to prevent settlement or failure.

name: increased width
rationale: A wider footing spreads the wall load over a larger soil area, reducing soil pressure and improving stability.

name: reduced soil settlement
rationale: Minimizing differential and total settlement under the footing is critical to avoid cracking or tilting of the wall above.

name: adequate reinforcement
rationale: Steel reinforcement is needed to resist tensile stresses induced by soil reaction and wall loads, preventing flexural or shear failure.

name: limited frost heave risk
rationale: Footings must be placed below the frost line or be insulated to minimize the risk of frost heave causing upward movement and structural damage.

name: Increased structural load capacity
rationale: The shoe rack system must support the weight of multiple pairs of shoes without sagging or collapsing, requiring adequate structural capacity.

name: Improved accessibility and ergonomics
rationale: Users need easy access to shoes, so the rack should be designed at comfortable heights and with convenient arrangement for daily use.

name: Enhanced durability and material quality
rationale: Frequent handling and exposure to outdoor contaminants (dirt, moisture) require durable, easy-to-clean materials.

name: Maximized storage density
rationale: Space efficiency is important in entryways and closets; the system should accommodate as many pairs as possible within the allotted footprint.

name: Reduced footprint and spatial intrusion
rationale: The shoe rack should not obstruct pathways or dominate the room; a compact design is preferred to maintain circulation space.

name: Minimized dirt and moisture transfer
rationale: Shoes carry dirt and moisture from outdoors; the rack should limit the spread of contaminants to floors and surrounding areas, e.g., via drip trays or open-air design.

name: Lower material and manufacturing cost
rationale: Cost constraints in furniture production favour simpler designs and affordable materials, balancing quality with economy.

name: Adequate ventilation and air circulation
rationale: Shoes need air circulation to prevent odour and moisture buildup; the rack design should allow airflow (e.g., slatted shelves, open backs).

name: Restricted visual clutter
rationale: A neat, organized appearance is culturally preferred in domestic entryways; the rack should minimise visible disorder through enclosed or orderly storage.

name: increased lateral stability
rationale: The retaining core must provide increased lateral stability against wind and seismic loads to maintain structural integrity.

name: minimised wall deflection
rationale: Wall deflection must be minimised to prevent cracking and ensure serviceability under lateral loads.

name: adequate shear capacity
rationale: The retaining core requires adequate shear capacity to resist horizontal forces transferred from floor diaphragms.

name: optimised reinforcement detailing
rationale: Reinforcement detailing should be optimised to ensure ductility and prevent brittle failure modes.

name: higher compressive strength
rationale: Higher compressive strength concrete is needed to resist axial and bending stresses in the retaining core.

name: limited crack width
rationale: Crack widths must be limited to ensure durability and prevent reinforcement corrosion.

name: improved load path continuity
rationale: Load path continuity must be improved to ensure forces are effectively transferred through the core to the foundation.

name: restricted out-of-plane movement
rationale: Out-of-plane movement must be restricted to prevent instability and excessive deformation of the core wall.

name: stronger foundation connection
rationale: A stronger connection between the retaining core and foundation is required to resist overturning moments and uplift forces.

name: Increased structural load capacity
rationale: Precast concrete planks must have sufficient load-bearing capacity to support dead and live loads as a structural floor or roof component.

name: Reduced span deflection
rationale: Deflection limits under service loads must be controlled to prevent cracking and serviceability issues in precast planks.

name: Improved fire resistance rating
rationale: Precast concrete planks typically require adequate fire resistance duration based on building code requirements for fire separation.

name: Reduced construction time
rationale: The prefabricated nature of precast planks aims to minimise on-site construction time compared to cast-in-place alternatives.

name: Greater span capability
rationale: Longer spans reduce the number of supporting beams required, optimising structural layout and cost efficiency.

name: Reduced material weight
rationale: Minimising the self-weight of precast planks eases transport, handling, and foundation demands while maintaining strength.

name: Improved thermal insulation performance
rationale: When used as part of the building envelope, precast concrete planks may need enhanced thermal properties to meet energy code requirements.

name: Enhanced connection ductility
rationale: Connections between precast planks and supporting structure require adequate ductility to ensure seismic or lateral load performance.

name: Reduced manufacturing tolerance
rationale: Tighter manufacturing tolerances ensure proper fit, alignment, and load transfer between precast elements on site.

name: Increased structural stability
rationale: Cast-in-place concrete walls provide high structural stability due to monolithic construction and continuity with foundations and slabs.

name: Reduced construction time
rationale: Cast-in-place concrete requires formwork setup, pouring, curing, and stripping, which can extend construction schedules compared to prefabricated systems.

name: Improved thermal mass
rationale: The density and thickness of cast-in-place concrete walls provide significant thermal mass, helping to regulate indoor temperatures.

name: Reduced material waste
rationale: Cast-in-place construction may generate less material waste compared to precast due to on-site forming to exact dimensions, though formwork waste is a consideration.

name: Higher sound insulation
rationale: Concrete walls offer excellent sound attenuation due to mass and density, reducing sound transmission between spaces.

name: Greater fire resistance
rationale: Concrete is inherently fire-resistant, providing high fire ratings without additional fireproofing treatments.

name: Limited design flexibility
rationale: Once cast, concrete walls are difficult to modify or reconfigure, limiting future adaptability and design changes.

name: Optimized load-bearing capacity
rationale: Cast-in-place concrete walls can be reinforced and designed to carry substantial vertical and lateral loads efficiently.

name: Reduced moisture vulnerability
rationale: Concrete is susceptible to moisture penetration and freeze-thaw damage if not properly waterproofed and detailed, requiring careful moisture management.

name: increased structural stability
rationale: Dry-stack masonry walls rely on interlocking geometry and gravity for stability; increased structural stability is a key design pressure.

name: reduced lateral displacement
rationale: Lateral displacement under wind or seismic loads is a critical concern; reducing it improves performance.

name: higher compressive strength
rationale: Compressive strength of masonry units and the wall assembly directly affects load-bearing capacity.

name: minimized construction complexity
rationale: Simpler construction techniques reduce labor costs and errors; minimizing complexity is a design objective.

name: improved water penetration resistance
rationale: Without mortar, joints may be vulnerable to water ingress; improving water resistance is important.

name: reduced material cost
rationale: Cost efficiency is often a driver for dry-stack systems; reducing material costs supports viability.

name: adequate shear resistance
rationale: Shear forces from wind or seismic loads must be resisted; ensuring adequate shear resistance is critical.

name: limited thermal bridging
rationale: Thermal performance is a concern; limiting thermal bridging through wall assembly design improves energy efficiency.

name: better interlocking precision
rationale: Precision of unit interlocking directly affects stability, alignment, and load transfer in dry-stack systems.

name: Greater structural stability
rationale: Gabion walls rely on gravity and mass for stability; increased structural stability ensures the wall can resist overturning and sliding forces.

name: Improved drainage performance
rationale: Gabion baskets are inherently permeable; improved drainage reduces hydrostatic pressure buildup behind the wall, enhancing long-term performance.

name: Reduced lateral earth pressure
rationale: Minimizing lateral earth pressure on the gabion wall reduces the risk of bulging or failure, particularly for retained soil applications.

name: Enhanced aesthetic integration
rationale: Gabion walls are often used as landscape features; enhanced visual integration with surroundings improves the design quality.

name: Limited material settlement
rationale: Controlling settlement of the gabion fill material prevents wall deformation and maintains structural integrity over time.

name: Adequate corrosion resistance
rationale: Gabion baskets are typically galvanized or PVC-coated; ensuring adequate corrosion resistance extends the service life of the wall.

name: Optimised thermal mass effect
rationale: Gabion walls with stone fill can provide thermal mass; optimising this effect can improve microclimate regulation near seating areas.

name: Restricted scour at base
rationale: Scour at the wall base can undermine stability; restricting scour through appropriate foundation design is critical.

name: Better seating comfort
rationale: As a sitting wall, the top surface and height should be designed for ergonomic comfort; better seating comfort improves user experience.

name: Improved structural stability
rationale: The Timber Sitting Wall should have adequate structural stability to safely support seated loads and resist overturning.

name: Enhanced durability against weathering
rationale: As an outdoor timber element, it needs increased resistance to moisture, UV, and biological degradation.

name: Reduced material cost
rationale: Construction budget constraints push toward minimising timber and fastener costs while meeting performance.

name: Adequate seating comfort
rationale: The wall serves as seating, so ergonomic height, depth, and surface finish must be sufficient for user comfort.

name: Limited thermal expansion
rationale: Timber expands and contracts with temperature and moisture changes; movements should be restricted to prevent joint failure.

name: Greater aesthetic appeal
rationale: Visual quality of timber grain, finish, and integration with landscape adds value and is often a design objective.

name: Reduced maintenance frequency
rationale: Using treated timber or protective coatings aims to minimise long-term upkeep requirements.

name: Optimised section dimensions
rationale: Cross-section sizing should be optimised to balance strength, material use, and visual bulk.

name: Prevented splintering hazard
rationale: Surface finish must eliminate sharp splinters for user safety, especially as a sitting surface.

name: Increased seating capacity
rationale: A landscape sitting wall is primarily designed to provide seating; thus a pressure to increase seating capacity directly influences its design.

name: Improved aesthetic integration
rationale: Sitting walls in landscapes are often designed to complement surrounding hardscape and planting, creating a pressure for improved visual integration.

name: Reduced material cost
rationale: Budget constraints typically impose a downward pressure on material selection and construction costs for site furnishings like sitting walls.

name: Enhanced durability against weathering
rationale: As an exterior exposed element, the sitting wall faces weathering from sun, rain, and frost, creating a pressure for greater material durability and longevity.

name: Restricted footprint size
rationale: Site constraints or programming requirements may limit the allowable footprint or linear extent of the sitting wall.

name: Higher structural stability
rationale: As a retaining or freestanding wall used for seating, structural safety requirements push for greater stability against overturning and sliding.

name: Sufficient thermal comfort (surface temperature)
rationale: Materials that absorb less heat provide better user comfort for seating; thus there is a pressure for adequate thermal performance of the wall surface.

name: Minimised maintenance requirements
rationale: Low-maintenance materials and finishes are typically preferred for landscape elements to reduce lifecycle costs and labor.

name: Improved accessibility (seating height)
rationale: Universal design standards and inclusive public space principles create a pressure for seating walls at appropriate heights for all users, including those with mobility limitations.

name: Increased seating capacity pressure
rationale: As a sitting wall, the entity is designed to accommodate people sitting; a pressure exists to maximize the number of users who can sit comfortably.

name: Improved ergonomic comfort pressure
rationale: Sitting walls need to be comfortable for users, driving a pressure for better ergonomic dimensions (seat height, depth, back support if any).

name: Reduced structural risk pressure
rationale: As a structural element supporting both planting and human loads, there is a strong engineering pressure to minimize risk of structural failure, cracking, or collapse.

name: Enhanced aesthetic integration pressure
rationale: The wall serves both as planter and seating, creating a pressure to optimize visual integration with the surrounding landscape and architectural context.

name: Limited maintenance cost pressure
rationale: Building owners typically seek to minimize long-term maintenance costs for combined planter/seating elements, driving material and design choices.

name: Sufficient drainage performance pressure
rationale: As an integrated planter, adequate drainage is critical to prevent waterlogging, root rot, and water damage to the wall structure itself.

name: Improved accessibility pressure
rationale: There is a societal and regulatory pressure for seating to be accessible to users of varying mobility levels, driving more inclusive design.

name: Reduced material cost pressure
rationale: Budget constraints create a pressure to minimize material expenditure while meeting structural and aesthetic requirements.

name: Increased structural stability
rationale: The stepped seating wall must withstand lateral earth pressures and live loads from spectators, requiring adequate structural stability.

name: Reduced deflection under load
rationale: Excessive deflection could compromise seating comfort and structural integrity, so deflection must be limited.

name: Adequate load-bearing capacity
rationale: The wall must support the dead load of the stepped structure plus live loads from occupants.

name: Sufficient drainage provision
rationale: Water accumulation behind or within the stepped wall could cause hydrostatic pressure and damage, so adequate drainage is needed.

name: Improved seismic resistance
rationale: In seismic zones, the stepped wall must resist lateral forces from earthquakes to prevent collapse.

name: Minimised material degradation
rationale: Weathering and environmental exposure can degrade the wall materials, which should be minimised for longevity.

name: increased structural stability
rationale: The perimeter sitting wall must withstand lateral earth pressures and vertical loads from users, requiring sufficient structural stability.

name: adequate load-bearing capacity
rationale: The wall must support the weight of people sitting on it as well as its own weight and any superimposed loads.

name: minimised material degradation
rationale: Exposure to weather and constant use can cause material degradation; durability is critical.

name: sufficient seating comfort
rationale: As a sitting wall, the height, width, and surface finish must accommodate comfortable seating for users.

name: restricted structural deflection
rationale: Excessive deflection under load could compromise the appearance and function of the wall.

name: enhanced thermal performance
rationale: If the wall is part of the building envelope, it may need insulation to reduce heat loss.

name: improved aesthetic appearance
rationale: The wall contributes to the visual character of the space and may require attractive materials and detailing.

name: eliminated water infiltration
rationale: Moisture penetration through the wall can cause damage and deterioration over time.

name: adequate drainage provision
rationale: Proper drainage behind and around the wall prevents water accumulation and hydrostatic pressure buildup.

name: Increased tension capacity
rationale: The ridge cable must have sufficient tension capacity to resist wind uplift and structural loads acting on the roof system.

name: Reduced sag displacement
rationale: Sag in the ridge cable must be limited to maintain the intended roof geometry and drainage slope.

name: Higher corrosion resistance
rationale: The ridge cable should have adequate corrosion resistance for long-term durability in the outdoor environment.

name: Minimised thermal expansion effects
rationale: Thermal expansion/contraction of the ridge cable must be limited or accommodated to avoid excessive stress changes.

name: Adequate connection strength
rationale: Connections at ridge cable ends must have sufficient strength to transfer the cable tension forces to the supporting structure.

name: Higher luminous efficacy
rationale: Higher luminous efficacy (lumens per watt) is a key design pressure for integrated lighting fixtures to improve energy efficiency and reduce operational costs.

name: Improved color rendering index
rationale: Better color rendering index (CRI) is desired for integrated lighting fixtures to ensure accurate color perception in the illuminated space.

name: Reduced energy consumption
rationale: Minimizing energy consumption is a fundamental design pressure for lighting fixtures to meet energy codes and sustainability goals.

name: Reduced physical size
rationale: Smaller fixture profiles are often preferred for aesthetic integration and to minimize visual obstruction in ceiling or wall installations.

name: Improved thermal management
rationale: Better thermal dissipation is needed to maintain LED performance and longevity in integrated fixtures.

name: Reduced glare
rationale: Minimizing glare is a key design pressure to ensure visual comfort and occupant well-being in spaces using integrated lighting.

name: Higher light output
rationale: Greater lumen output may be required to meet illuminance targets for specific applications.

name: Reduced manufacturing cost
rationale: Lower production cost is a persistent market pressure to make the fixture economically viable and competitive.

name: Improved dimming compatibility
rationale: Better dimming performance and compatibility with various dimmer systems is increasingly demanded for integrated lighting fixtures.

name: Increased cable tension
rationale: Valley cables in cable-stayed or suspension structures require adequate tension to maintain structural integrity and prevent sagging.

name: Reduced cable corrosion
rationale: Corrosion reduces the effective cross-section and lifespan of valley cables; minimizing corrosion is critical for durability.

name: Improved cable anchorage
rationale: Secure anchorages are essential for valley cables to transfer forces safely to the supporting structure.

name: Limited cable deflection
rationale: Excessive deflection in valley cables can lead to serviceability issues and potential fatigue under cyclic loading.

name: Sufficient cable fatigue resistance
rationale: Valley cables experience cyclic loading from wind, traffic, or thermal effects; adequate fatigue resistance is necessary for long-term performance.

name: Greater tensile strength for Perimeter Cable
rationale: Perimeter cables in tension structures require sufficient tensile strength to safely carry structural loads without failure.

name: Reduced cable sag for Perimeter Cable
rationale: Minimizing sag in perimeter cables improves structural performance and load distribution efficiency.

name: Higher corrosion resistance for Perimeter Cable
rationale: Perimeter cables exposed to environmental conditions require enhanced corrosion resistance for long-term durability.

name: Optimised cable diameter for Perimeter Cable
rationale: Selecting an adequate cable diameter balances strength requirements with practical installation and cost considerations.

name: Limited thermal expansion for Perimeter Cable
rationale: Restricting thermal expansion in perimeter cables prevents excessive elongation and maintains tension under temperature variations.

name: Higher pull-out resistance
rationale: Ground anchors must resist pull-out forces from the superstructure; higher pull-out resistance improves structural stability.

name: Improved corrosion protection
rationale: Anchors embedded in soil or concrete are exposed to moisture and chemicals; enhanced corrosion protection ensures long-term durability.

name: Greater load-bearing capacity
rationale: Foundations and ground anchors must safely transfer structural loads to the ground; greater load-bearing capacity is essential for structural safety.

name: Reduced displacement under service loads
rationale: Excessive anchor displacement can lead to structural serviceability issues; minimised movement under design loads is critical.

name: Limited susceptibility to soil corrosion
rationale: Soil conditions can be aggressive; reduced corrosion susceptibility extends anchor lifespan and reliability.

name: Adequate embedment depth
rationale: Sufficient embedment depth ensures the anchor develops its full geotechnical capacity and resists uplift forces.

name: Increased structural height
rationale: Taller masts can improve tension efficiency and antenna/receiver performance, creating a design pressure to increase height for better functionality.

name: Reduced material weight
rationale: Lighter materials reduce self-weight load on the mast and its foundations, which is critical for slender tension structures.

name: Increased tension capacity
rationale: Higher tension capacity ensures the mast can withstand wind loads and maintain structural stability under dynamic conditions.

name: Reduced lateral deflection
rationale: Limiting sway and deflection under wind or seismic loads is essential for serviceability and structural integrity of masts.

name: Optimised guy wire configuration
rationale: An optimised arrangement of tension cables/guy wires improves stability and load distribution for slender masts.

name: Greater foundation stability
rationale: Stronger foundations resist overturning moments from tension cables and wind loads acting on the mast.

name: Reduced wind load exposure
rationale: Streamlining or aerodynamic shaping of the mast reduces wind loading, a critical design factor for tall slender structures.

name: Improved dynamic response
rationale: Better damping and natural frequency tuning reduces vibration risks from vortex shedding and wind excitation.

name: Lower construction cost
rationale: Cost constraints create pressure to minimise material usage, foundation size, and erection complexity for masts.

name: Increased clamping force
rationale: A clamp/lacing system must provide sufficient clamping force to secure components, preventing slippage or loosening under load.

name: Reduced system weight
rationale: Minimising weight of the clamping and lacing hardware reduces dead load on the structure and material costs.

name: Improved corrosion resistance
rationale: Clamps and lacing components are exposed to environmental conditions; better corrosion resistance extends service life and maintains integrity.

name: Lower installation complexity
rationale: Simpler installation procedures reduce labour cost and potential for installation errors in the field.

name: Greater fatigue resistance
rationale: Cyclic loading on clamps and lacing requires adequate fatigue performance to prevent premature failure.

name: Reduced fastener count
rationale: Fewer fasteners can streamline assembly and reduce parts inventory, though must be balanced against structural requirements.

name: Improved water drainage capacity
rationale: Gutters and drainage channels must be sized to handle peak rainfall runoff to prevent overflow and water damage.

name: Reduced blockage risk
rationale: Debris accumulation can obstruct flow; design should minimise blockages through appropriate sizing, slope, and debris protection.

name: Sufficient slope gradient
rationale: Adequate slope ensures proper water flow towards downpipes and prevents standing water.

name: Lower material cost
rationale: Budget constraints push for economical material selection without compromising performance.

name: Enhanced durability against corrosion
rationale: Gutters are exposed to weather; corrosion-resistant materials (e.g., aluminium, zincalume, PVC) extend service life.

name: Greater structural load capacity
rationale: Drainage channels must withstand loads from traffic, snow, or maintenance access without deformation or failure.

name: Minimised profile height
rationale: Low-profile gutter designs are preferred for aesthetic integration and to avoid visual intrusion on the roofline.

name: Adequate overflow provision
rationale: Overflow outlets or scuppers prevent water backing up if the primary downpipe is blocked during heavy rain.

name: Reduced maintenance frequency
rationale: Self-cleaning designs, leaf guards, and smooth linings reduce the need for manual cleaning.

name: Increased tension load capacity
rationale: A turnbuckle must have adequate tension capacity to perform its structural function of adjusting and maintaining tension in cables, rods, or tie systems.

name: Reduced risk of loosening
rationale: Turnbuckles should resist inadvertent loosening under vibration or cyclic loading to maintain structural integrity.

name: Greater adjustability range
rationale: A turnbuckle needs sufficient thread length and adjustment range to accommodate installation tolerances and tensioning requirements.

name: Higher corrosion resistance
rationale: Turnbuckles in exposed or outdoor environments require corrosion resistance to maintain functionality and safety over time.

name: Reduced manufacturing cost
rationale: Economic pressures typically drive toward lower production costs while meeting performance requirements.

name: Sufficient thread engagement length
rationale: Proper thread engagement is critical to prevent thread stripping and ensure the turnbuckle can carry its rated load safely.

name: Better fatigue resistance
rationale: For dynamic loading conditions, the turnbuckle must resist fatigue failure over its design life.

name: Restricted size and weight
rationale: Space constraints and weight limitations in structural assemblies may restrict the turnbuckle's physical dimensions.

name: Minimised stress concentrations
rationale: Stress raisers at thread roots, transitions, or holes should be minimized to prevent crack initiation and premature failure.

name: Increased cable tension for anti-flap stability
rationale: Higher tension in restraint cables improves anti-flap performance by preventing excessive membrane movement under wind loads.

name: Reduced cable sag for precise restraint
rationale: Minimising sag in the cable net ensures tighter restraint of the membrane, reducing flutter and flap risks.

name: Higher cable density for distributed restraint
rationale: A denser cable net provides more points of restraint, better distributing wind loads and reducing localised membrane flapping.

name: Reduced cable spacing for finer control
rationale: Smaller spacing between cables increases the number of restraint points, improving overall anti-flap effectiveness.

name: Increased load-bearing capacity
rationale: The structural steel support frame must bear significant vertical and lateral loads from the building, requiring sufficient load-bearing capacity.

name: Improved corrosion resistance
