rationale: Construction cost constraints often push toward simpler, less ornate facade designs to minimize material and labor expenses.

name: Greater visual prominence pressure
rationale: Architectural intent for landmark buildings or expressive facades drives desire for more elaborate ornamentation to achieve visual impact.

name: Improved energy performance pressure
rationale: Facade ornamentation like shading devices, fins, or brise-soleil can enhance solar control and thermal performance, driving more expressive facade treatments.

name: Reduced maintenance burden pressure
rationale: Elaborate ornamentation creates more surfaces requiring cleaning, repair, and upkeep, creating pressure to minimize ornamental complexity.

name: Higher cultural or historical authenticity pressure
rationale: In heritage contexts or culturally sensitive sites, there is pressure to provide or restore rich facade ornamentation that reflects local traditions.

name: Lower material usage pressure
rationale: Sustainability goals and material conservation drive minimization of extraneous ornamentation to reduce embodied carbon and material waste.

name: Greater regulatory compliance pressure
rationale: Building codes and standards (e.g., for fire safety, seismic performance) may require specific decorative elements or restrict others, driving certain ornamental choices.

name: Improved aesthetic appeal
rationale: Architectural design seeks to enhance visual appeal and ambiance of interior spaces, driving investment in decorative finishes, materials, and detailing.

name: Enhanced functionality requirements
rationale: Spaces must accommodate specific uses (e.g., acoustics, lighting, durability) which drives the need for appropriate decorative treatments.

name: Greater user comfort expectations
rationale: Occupant well-being and comfort demands drive selection of pleasant colours, textures, lighting, and spatial arrangements.

name: Reduced maintenance requirements
rationale: Facilities management prefers durable, easy-to-clean surfaces, limiting the use of high-maintenance decorative finishes.

name: Stronger cultural or branding alignment
rationale: Organisational identity or local cultural context pressures the design towards specific styles, colours, and motifs.

name: Limited spatial dimensions
rationale: Tight floor plans or low ceiling heights restrict the scope of decorative elements such as large fixtures, heavy drapes, or bulky furnishings.

name: Expanded sustainability requirements
rationale: Green building certifications and environmental goals drive adoption of eco-friendly, recycled, or low-VOC materials and finishes.

name: higher color rendering accuracy
rationale: Color rendering (Ra/CRI) is a physical property of light sources; higher CRI values are often desired for accurate color perception.

name: reduced color distortion
rationale: Color distortion (e.g., low CRI) negatively impacts visual quality; minimizing distortion is a common design pressure.

name: improved visual comfort
rationale: Better color rendering contributes to occupant visual comfort and well-being, an engineering design consideration.

name: restricted color temperature variance
rationale: Inconsistent color temperatures can degrade perceived color rendering; limiting variance ensures specification compliance.

name: Improved visual comfort
rationale: Warm color lighting is often used to improve visual comfort and create a pleasant atmosphere in occupied spaces, increasing user satisfaction.

name: Reduced energy consumption
rationale: Modern warm-color LED systems can be more energy-efficient than traditional lighting, creating pressure to reduce energy usage through optimized warm lighting design.

name: Enhanced circadian alignment
rationale: Warm color temperatures in evening hours align with human circadian rhythms, increasing demand for tunable warm lighting to support health and well-being.

name: Minimized glare and harshness
rationale: Warm color lighting is inherently softer and produces less glare than cool white light, so there is pressure to minimize harsh lighting conditions through warm color choices.

name: Greater aesthetic appeal
rationale: Warm color lighting is commonly selected to enhance the aesthetic appeal of interior spaces, creating inviting and cozy environments.

name: Lower blue light emission
rationale: Warm color lighting naturally emits less blue light, reducing potential negative health impacts and supporting the design pressure for lower blue light exposure.

name: Optimized task visibility
rationale: There is a design pressure to optimize warm lighting such that it provides sufficient task illumination without compromising the warm color quality.

name: Restricted color temperature range
rationale: In some cultural contexts or design guidelines, warm color temperature ranges are restricted to certain limits to maintain consistency or avoid extreme warm tones.

name: Adequate illuminance levels
rationale: Warm lighting systems must provide adequate illuminance for the space function, creating a pressure to ensure light output meets standards despite warmer color temperatures.

name: Increased visual warmth
rationale: Warm colors (reds, oranges, yellows) are intentionally chosen to create a sense of warmth and coziness in a space, so there is a design pressure to increase the warm visual effect of the accent wall.

name: Reduced visual clutter
rationale: An accent wall is meant to be a focal point without overwhelming the space; therefore there is a design pressure to reduce visual clutter by limiting the area or complexity of the warm color application.

name: Enhanced contrast with adjacent walls
rationale: Accent walls typically rely on contrast with surrounding surfaces to stand out, so there is a pressure to increase the contrast between the warm color accent wall and adjacent walls.

name: Restricted color saturation for balance
rationale: Excessively high saturation of warm colors can be visually fatiguing or overwhelming, so there is often a pressure to restrict (limit) saturation levels to maintain visual balance in the overall room design.

name: Improved visual clarity
rationale: Clear color zoning helps occupants navigate spaces efficiently and improves wayfinding.

name: Enhanced aesthetic coherence
rationale: Well-planned color zoning harmonizes different functional areas and creates visual unity within the building.

name: Reduced visual confusion
rationale: Poorly defined color zones can cause disorientation; a clear zoning layout minimizes confusion.

name: Greater functional differentiation
rationale: Distinct color zones help differentiate functional areas such as public, private, service, and circulation zones.

name: Optimised user experience
rationale: Color zoning can improve comfort and psychological wellbeing by aligning with cultural and user preferences.

name: Reduced maintenance conflicts
rationale: Using durable, consistent color schemes across zones reduces repainting and maintenance complexity over time.

name: Maximized warm color palette
rationale: Warm colors like reds, oranges, and yellows create a welcoming and energetic atmosphere; the space named 'Warm Color Space' suggests a deliberate design pressure to optimize the use of warm hues.

name: Increased psychological warmth
rationale: Warm color spaces are designed to feel cozy and inviting, increasing the perception of warmth through color temperature.

name: Reduced visual clutter
rationale: To let warm colors be the dominant experience, distraction from excessive patterns or clutter should be minimized.

name: Improved occupant comfort
rationale: Warm color schemes are often used in social or relaxation spaces to improve the comfort and mood of occupants.

name: Lower cold color presence
rationale: Cool colors like blues and greens would conflict with the warm theme, so their presence should be restricted.

name: Increased thermal comfort
rationale: Sunroom design pressures include desire for comfortable indoor temperatures, especially during colder months, through passive solar heating.

name: Reduced heat loss
rationale: As a glass-enclosed space, sunrooms are prone to heat loss; design pressures aim to minimise thermal bridging and improve insulation.

name: Maximised solar gain
rationale: Sunrooms are designed to capture passive solar energy; maximizing solar gain is a core functional pressure.

name: Reduced overheating risk
rationale: Excessive solar gain can cause overheating; design must balance solar gain with ventilation and shading to avoid discomfort.

name: Adequate natural ventilation
rationale: Operable windows or vents are needed to regulate temperature and air quality in a sunroom.

name: Improved daylighting quality
rationale: Sunrooms should provide pleasant, diffused daylight without excessive glare.

name: Restricted UV damage
rationale: High solar exposure increases UV penetration; design pressures include using UV-resistant glazing to protect interior furnishings and occupants.

name: Increased ergonomic comfort
rationale: Dining chairs must provide comfortable seating for users during meals, requiring ergonomic design of seat height, backrest angle, and cushioning.

name: Improved structural stability
rationale: A dining chair must be structurally stable to safely support a seated person's weight without tipping or collapsing.

name: Reduced manufacturing cost
rationale: Cost constraints drive material and production choices, encouraging simpler designs and less expensive materials.

name: Minimised material usage
rationale: Efficient use of materials reduces weight, cost, and environmental impact while maintaining required strength.

name: Greater durability
rationale: Chairs must withstand repeated use over many years, requiring robust joinery, wear-resistant finishes, and strong materials.

name: Limited overall weight
rationale: A lighter chair is easier to move, rearrange, and transport, though weight must be balanced against stability and durability.

name: Sufficient seat height appropriateness
rationale: Standard dining table heights dictate a narrow acceptable range for seat height to ensure comfortable dining posture (typically ~45-48 cm).

name: Eliminated sharp edges
rationale: Safety concerns require that edges and corners be rounded or softened to prevent injury to users, especially in household settings.

name: Improved ergonomic support
rationale: Ergonomic design pressure drives better lumbar support, seat comfort, and adjustability for user health and productivity.

rationale: Cost constraints push toward simpler materials and fewer features to keep the product affordable and competitive.

name: Increased durability and lifespan
rationale: Durability requirements drive stronger frames, higher-quality casters, and wear-resistant upholstery.

name: Lower weight for portability
rationale: Lighter chairs are easier to move and ship, influencing material selection toward lighter components.

name: Enhanced aesthetic appeal
rationale: Workplace aesthetics and brand image drive pressures for modern, visually appealing chair designs.

name: Minimised environmental footprint
rationale: Sustainability concerns push toward recycled materials, reduced packaging, and lower embodied carbon.

name: Greater adjustability for user fit
rationale: Height, armrest, tilt, and lumbar adjustability are critical for accommodating diverse body types and work postures.

name: Restricted size for space efficiency
rationale: Office space constraints may limit chair footprint to ensure adequate circulation and desk fit.

name: Adequate load capacity for safety
rationale: Safety standards require the chair to support specified maximum user weight without failure, driving structural reinforcement.

name: Improved comfort pressure
rationale: A lounge chair must provide adequate comfort for sitting and relaxing, so comfort is a primary design pressure acting on the chair.

name: Enhanced ergonomic support pressure
rationale: Ergonomic design ensures proper posture and reduced strain, acting as a pressure to improve the chair's support features.

name: Increased durability pressure
rationale: The chair must withstand regular use over time, creating a pressure for durable materials and construction.

name: Reduced cost pressure
rationale: Manufacturing and material costs must be minimised to keep the product affordable and competitive.

name: Minimised weight pressure
rationale: Lighter weight improves portability and reduces shipping costs, creating a pressure to minimise mass.

name: Maximised aesthetic appeal pressure

rationale: Growing environmental awareness creates pressure to use sustainable materials and production methods.

rationale: The chair must have sufficient structural strength to support the user's weight and repeated rocking forces without failure.

name: Reduced tipping risk pressure

name: Optimized ergonomic comfort pressure
rationale: The seat angle, backrest angle, and armrest height must be optimized for comfortable seating during prolonged rocking.

name: Lower manufacturing cost pressure
rationale: Manufacturing costs should be minimized through efficient material selection and simplified construction.

name: Enhanced aesthetic appeal pressure
rationale: The chair's design should have visual appeal appropriate for its intended setting, whether traditional or modern.

rationale: Materials must be sufficiently durable to withstand repeated rocking stresses and long-term use without degradation.

name: Eliminated pinch points pressure
rationale: Design must avoid or eliminate pinch points between moving parts (e.g., between rockers and frame) to prevent finger injuries.

name: Improved portability
rationale: Folding chairs are designed to be lightweight and easily transportable, so there is a design pressure to increase portability through lighter materials and compact folding mechanisms.

name: Increased structural stability
rationale: As a load-bearing seating device, folding chairs must resist forces like weight and tipping, creating a pressure to increase structural stability and load capacity.

name: Reduced storage volume

rationale: Folding chairs are often mass-produced commodity items, creating a strong pressure to minimize production costs through material choices and simplified manufacturing.

name: Maximized user comfort
rationale: Despite being temporary seating, users expect reasonable ergonomic comfort, creating pressure to improve seat shape, back support, and padding.

name: Minimized weight
rationale: Light weight is essential for carrying, stacking, and handling folding chairs, driving design toward lighter materials like aluminum or plastic.

name: Enhanced durability
rationale: Folding chairs experience repeated assembly/disassembly cycles and variable loads, so long-term durability through robust hinges and joints is a design pressure.

name: Greater aesthetic appeal
rationale: For events and spaces where appearance matters, there is a moderate design pressure to improve visual design and finish quality.

name: Restricted complexity of mechanism
rationale: Simple folding mechanisms are more reliable and cheaper to produce, creating a pressure to limit mechanical complexity.

rationale: Bar stools require comfortable seating for users to sit for extended periods at a bar or counter.

name: Improved stability
rationale: Bar stools must be stable to prevent tipping when users sit or shift weight, especially on uneven floors.

name: Reduced weight
rationale: Lighter stools are easier to move and rearrange, though weight must be balanced with stability requirements.

name: Higher durability
rationale: Bar stools in commercial settings endure frequent use and must resist wear, scratches, and structural fatigue.

name: Lower manufacturing cost
rationale: Cost constraints drive material and production method choices for bar stool design.

name: Improved aesthetic appeal
rationale: Visual design and style influence user preference and suitability for different interior décors.

name: Reduced footprint
rationale: Smaller stool dimensions allow more seating capacity in limited bar or counter space.

name: Sufficient footrest height
rationale: Proper footrest positioning supports ergonomic seating and user comfort.

rationale: Stacking chairs need adequate ergonomic comfort for prolonged sitting, which exerts upward pressure on cushioning, back support, and seat contour design.

name: Reduced weight
rationale: A stacking chair must be lightweight to facilitate easy lifting, carrying, and stacking by users, pushing toward lighter materials and minimal construction.

rationale: The chair must stack neatly and compactly for storage efficiency, driving design decisions toward uniform shapes, nesting profiles, and stacking lugs.

rationale: Chairs undergo repeated stacking, unstacking, and loading; structural strength must be sufficient to prevent breakage at joints and stress points.

rationale: Stacking chairs must occupy minimal floor or cart space when stored, driving compact dimensions and efficient nesting geometry.

name: Improved ergonomic support
rationale: Users require adequate lumbar support, seat depth, and armrest design to prevent discomfort, pushing design toward better anthropometric fit.

name: Enhanced aesthetic appeal
rationale: Stacking chairs are often used in event and hospitality settings where visual appearance matters, driving toward cleaner lines, color options, and finish quality.

name: Eliminated tipping hazard
rationale: Safety requires that chairs remain stable when stacked and when used individually, pushing design toward wider leg spans and lower center of gravity.

name: Increased stability
rationale: A counter stool must be stable to safely support a seated user, requiring increased structural stability in its design.

name: Reduced weight
rationale: Lighter counter stools are easier to move and rearrange, creating pressure to minimize weight.

name: Improved comfort
rationale: Seating requires adequate ergonomic design for user comfort, driving increased ergonomic consideration.

name: Higher durability
rationale: Commercial and residential counter stools must withstand repeated use, creating pressure for greater durability.

name: Optimised seat height
rationale: Counter stools must match standard counter heights (typically 24-26 inch seat height), requiring optimised proportions.

name: Reduced material cost
rationale: Cost constraints in furniture production create pressure to use fewer or cheaper materials.

name: Improved aesthetic appeal
rationale: Counter stools serve as visible furniture in kitchens and bars, where visual design must complement interior style.

name: Higher stackability
rationale: Stackable stools are preferred in commercial settings for storage efficiency, creating pressure for enhanced stackability.

name: Restricted footprint
rationale: Counter stools must fit within limited space around counters and islands, driving need for a smaller footprint.

name: increased comfort
rationale: Accent chairs are designed for comfort in lounging or reading, so there is pressure to increase comfort through cushioning, ergonomics, and fabric choice.

name: improved aesthetic appeal
rationale: As an accent piece, the chair is expected to contribute visually to the space, driving pressure for improved visual design, color, and material selection.

name: minimised footprint
rationale: Space constraints in interior layouts pressure for a smaller physical footprint to allow flexible room arrangements.

name: optimised ergonomics
rationale: User health and satisfaction drive pressure for optimised ergonomic support including seat height, backrest angle, and armrest placement.

name: reduced material waste
rationale: Sustainability concerns and environmental regulations create pressure to minimise material waste in design and production.

name: Improved ergonomic support
rationale: Gaming chairs require enhanced lumbar support, adjustable armrests, and ergonomic shaping to reduce physical strain during long gaming sessions.

name: Increased adjustability features
rationale: Users demand height adjustment, recline mechanisms, tilt lock, and customizable settings to suit different body types and gaming setups.

name: Higher cushion density and durability
rationale: High-density foam and durable upholstery are needed to maintain shape and comfort over prolonged use.

name: Reduced manufacturing cost
rationale: Cost pressures push for lower material and production expenses to remain competitive in the gaming chair market.

name: Improved aesthetic appeal and branding
rationale: Gaming chair designs often incorporate racing-style aesthetics, bold color schemes, and brand logos to attract the gaming community.

name: Reduced weight for portability
rationale: Some users may prefer lighter chairs for easier movement, but this is often secondary to durability and stability.

name: Increased lumbar and neck pillow support
rationale: Separate adjustable lumbar and head/neck pillows are common features to enhance spinal alignment and neck comfort.

name: Enhanced base and gas lift stability
rationale: A sturdy metal base and reliable gas lift mechanism are critical for safety and smooth height adjustment under load.

name: Reduced noise from casters and mechanisms
rationale: Smooth, quiet-rolling casters and lubricated mechanisms reduce distracting noise during gameplay.

name: Increased accessibility requirements
rationale: Building codes and accessibility standards (e.g., ADA) demand wheelchair-accessible design features such as ramps, door widths, and clear floor space.

name: Reduced physical barriers
rationale: Design decisions aim to eliminate steps, narrow doorways, and other obstacles that impede wheelchair movement.

name: Improved maneuverability space
rationale: Turning radii and clear passage widths are critical for wheelchair navigation, driving design dimensions of corridors and rooms.

name: Eliminated level changes
rationale: Floor level changes without ramps or lifts are a primary barrier; designs aim to avoid or minimize vertical transitions.

name: Higher reachability standards
rationale: Controls, fixtures, and amenities must be within wheelchair reach ranges, influencing their mounting heights and locations.

name: Sufficient doorway width
rationale: Doorway clear width (typically minimum 32 inches) is a code requirement for wheelchair passage.

name: Restricted slope of pathways
rationale: Ramp and path slopes must be limited (e.g., max 1:12) to ensure safe and independent wheelchair use.

name: Adequate turn-around area
rationale: Clear floor space (e.g., 60-inch diameter circle) is needed for wheelchair turning, affecting room layouts.

name: Lower counter and table heights
rationale: Work surfaces, sinks, and counters may need to be lowered or have knee clearance for wheelchair users.

name: Improved ergonomic support pressure
rationale: Kneeling chairs are designed to improve posture by distributing weight between the buttocks and shins, reducing lower back strain.

name: Reduced seat height pressure
rationale: The kneeling chair typically has a lower seat height than standard chairs to allow the knees to rest on a pad, promoting a more open hip angle.

name: Enhanced knee pad comfort pressure
rationale: Padding on the knee rest must be sufficient to prevent discomfort during extended use.

name: Limited adjustability pressure
rationale: Many kneeling chairs have fewer adjustment mechanisms compared to ergonomic office chairs, constraining customization to individual user dimensions.

name: Better spinal alignment pressure
rationale: The design encourages a more upright pelvic tilt, naturally aligning the spine and reducing slouching.

name: Improved ergonomic comfort
rationale: Saddle chairs are designed to provide better ergonomic support and comfort by promoting a more natural sitting posture compared to traditional flat chairs.

name: Reduced spinal pressure
rationale: The saddle-shaped seat helps tilt the pelvis forward, reducing compressive forces on the lumbar spine and promoting better spinal alignment.

name: Increased sitting stability
rationale: The contoured saddle shape and often wider base provide increased stability for the user when seated, reducing the risk of sliding off.

name: Limited user mobility restriction
rationale: Saddle chairs typically lack armrests and have a narrower profile, which can restrict the user's ability to shift positions or get on/off the chair easily.

name: Higher leg circulation demand
rationale: The more open hip angle (approximately 135 degrees) in saddle sitting increases demand on leg muscles for stabilization and may affect blood circulation in the lower extremities.

name: Reduced hip angle compression
rationale: Saddle chairs open the hip angle to about 135 degrees compared to 90 degrees in conventional chairs, reducing compression in the hip joint and improving posture.

name: Increased adjustability requirements
rationale: Saddle chairs require more precise height and tilt adjustments to accommodate different user leg lengths and preferences, making adjustability a critical design pressure.

name: Enhanced ceremonial presence

name: Improved physical comfort

name: Greater structural stability

name: Restricted spatial footprint
rationale: Architectural constraints may limit the overall size and footprint of the throne/chair to fit within designated ceremonial spaces or platforms.

name: Higher material quality
rationale: Cultural expectations for a throne demand premium materials (fine wood, upholstery, ornamentation) to reflect status and durability.

name: Minimised maintenance requirements
rationale: Engineering pressure to reduce ongoing maintenance needs for a frequently used ceremonial object, though not a primary concern.

name: Improved accessibility
rationale: Architectural and code pressures to ensure the throne/chair is accessible for the occupant, including appropriate height and approach clearance.

name: Reduced material usage pressure
rationale: Engineering design of a cantilever chair seeks to minimize material while maintaining structural integrity.

name: Improved structural stability pressure
rationale: Cantilever chairs rely on the structural stability of the cantilever base to prevent tipping and ensure safety.

name: Enhanced ergonomic comfort pressure
rationale: User comfort through ergonomic shaping is a key design consideration for cantilever chairs.

name: Reduced production cost pressure
rationale: Manufacturing cost constraints push toward simpler, cheaper production methods.

name: Adequate cantilever deflection pressure
rationale: The cantilever design must limit deflection under load to ensure comfort and structural performance.

name: Minimised chair weight pressure
rationale: Lightweight design is important for portability and material efficiency in cantilever chairs.

name: Improved aesthetic appeal pressure
rationale: Cantilever chairs are iconic design objects where visual form and elegance are important.

name: Reduced risk of fatigue failure pressure
rationale: The cantilever structure experiences cyclic loading; fatigue resistance is critical for safety and durability.

name: Increased load capacity
rationale: Casters and glides must support the weight of furniture and equipment they carry; higher load ratings are needed for heavy items.

name: Reduced rolling resistance
rationale: Casters should roll smoothly with minimal effort; lowering friction improves usability and reduces wear on floors.

name: Improved floor protection
rationale: Glides and casters must avoid scratching, denting, or marking flooring materials; softer or coated materials reduce damage.

name: Minimised noise generation
rationale: Quieter movement is desirable in office, healthcare, and residential environments; lower noise from wheel contact improves occupant comfort.

name: Increased durability and wear resistance
rationale: Casters and glides experience repeated movement and loading; materials must resist abrasion, deformation, and fatigue over time.

name: Greater swivel manoeuvrability

rationale: Budget constraints often push for lower-cost caster and glide options, though this may conflict with durability and load capacity requirements.

name: Improved corrosion resistance

name: Enhanced braking/locking functionality
rationale: Locking casters prevent unintended movement; stronger, more reliable brake mechanisms improve safety and stability when furniture is stationary.

name: Increased lumbar support rigidity
rationale: The lumbar support insert must provide adequate rigidity to maintain spinal posture under load.

name: Reduced material thickness
rationale: Thinner materials reduce bulk and allow better integration into seat backrest assemblies.

name: Lower manufacturing cost

name: Enhanced durability under cyclic loading
rationale: The insert must withstand repeated compression and release over the product lifetime.

name: Greater occupant comfort

name: Minimised floor area per seat

name: Restricted layout flexibility

name: Eliminated obstructed sightlines

name: Adequate egress path width

name: Sufficient spacing for social distancing
rationale: Post-pandemic cultural norms and health guidelines may demand increased spacing between seats, affecting density and layout decisions.

rationale: Architectural design often prioritizes maximizing the number of seats within a given space to accommodate more occupants.

name: Improved sightlines
rationale: Ensuring clear views of the stage or focal point is a key design pressure in seating layout, especially in theatres, cinemas, and auditoriums.

name: Enhanced accessibility
rationale: Building codes and universal design principles demand accessible seating for individuals with disabilities, influencing layout decisions.

name: Reduced row spacing
rationale: Tighter row spacing may be used to fit more seats but competes with comfort and egress requirements.

name: Maximized floor area efficiency
rationale: Efficient use of floor area drives seating arrangement decisions to optimize the number of seats per square meter.

name: Improved acoustic performance
rationale: Seating layout influences sound absorption and reflection; optimized layouts enhance acoustic quality in performance spaces.

name: Reduced egress path length
rationale: Fire safety codes require that seating layouts provide short, unobstructed egress paths to exits for occupant safety.

name: Greater spectator comfort
rationale: Comfort factors such as seat width, legroom, and cushioning influence seating layout design decisions.

name: Lower construction cost
rationale: Cost pressures may lead to simpler, more compact seating layouts to reduce material and construction expenses.

name: Increased structural support
rationale: The Oculus, as a large architectural opening, requires robust structural reinforcement around its perimeter to maintain building integrity.

name: Reduced heat transfer
rationale: As a glazed or open architectural feature, the Oculus needs to minimise unwanted heat gain/loss for thermal performance.

name: Enhanced daylight penetration
rationale: The Oculus is designed to admit natural light into the building, so maximising daylight transmission is a key design pressure.

name: Limited water infiltration
rationale: As a roof or wall opening, the Oculus must be waterproofed to prevent rainwater ingress.

name: Reduced solar glare
rationale: Direct sunlight through the Oculus may cause visual discomfort, requiring shading or diffusing strategies.

name: Improved acoustic isolation
rationale: An opening like the Oculus can transmit external noise; better acoustic sealing may be desired.

name: Greater aesthetic prominence
rationale: The Oculus often serves as a signature architectural feature, so visual impact and design quality are prioritized.

name: Minimised structural deflection
rationale: Large openings must limit deflection to prevent glass breakage or seal failure.

name: Optimised natural ventilation
rationale: If operable, the Oculus can facilitate stack-effect ventilation, requiring optimised airflow design.

name: Increased airflow uniformity
rationale: The diffuser panel is designed to distribute airflow evenly; a design pressure exists to increase uniformity of air distribution across the panel to ensure consistent ventilation and thermal comfort.

name: Reduced pressure drop
rationale: Minimising pressure loss across the diffuser panel is a common design objective to improve energy efficiency of the HVAC system.

name: Improved acoustic performance
rationale: Diffuser panels often need to attenuate noise from the air distribution system, so there is a pressure to improve sound absorption or noise reduction characteristics.

name: Minimised visual obstruction
rationale: Architectural preferences often call for diffuser panels that are less visually intrusive, especially in exposed ceiling designs, driving a pressure to minimise their visual impact.

name: Increased daylight penetration
rationale: Tubular daylighting devices are designed to channel natural light into interior spaces; increasing daylight penetration enhances their core function and performance.

name: Reduced heat gain
rationale: Solar tubes can introduce unwanted solar heat gain; reducing heat gain improves thermal comfort and energy efficiency of the space.

name: Improved light diffusion quality
rationale: Diffusers at the ceiling end of solar tubes spread light evenly; improving diffusion quality enhances visual comfort and reduces glare.

name: Minimised roof penetration leakage risk
rationale: Roof penetrations for solar tubes pose a risk of water leaks; minimising this risk is critical for building envelope integrity.

name: Greater energy savings from daylighting
rationale: Effective use of tubular daylighting devices reduces reliance on artificial lighting, leading to greater energy savings in buildings.

name: Reduced installation complexity
rationale: Simplifying installation procedures for tubular daylighting devices lowers cost and construction coordination challenges.

name: Optimised tube length-to-diameter ratio
rationale: Optimising the geometric ratio of tube length to diameter maximises light transmission efficiency through the tube.

name: Lower maintenance requirements
rationale: Durable materials and sealed designs reduce the need for cleaning and servicing of tubular daylighting devices.

name: Enhanced visual connection to outdoors
rationale: While solar tubes primarily provide ambient light rather than views, enhancing any visual connection improves occupant satisfaction and well-being.

name: Increased natural light
rationale: A solarium is designed to maximise sunlight exposure, so there is a strong pressure to increase natural light penetration through glazing and orientation.

name: Improved thermal comfort
rationale: Glazed spaces experience temperature swings; there is pressure to improve thermal comfort via insulation, shading, or HVAC integration.

name: Reduced heat gain
rationale: Excessive solar gain can overheat the space; there is pressure to reduce unwanted heat gain through glazing treatments, overhangs, or ventilation.

name: Expanded usable area
rationale: As a transitional living space, there is design pressure to expand or optimise the floor area for seating, plants, or circulation.

name: Lower energy consumption
rationale: High glazing ratios can lead to energy loss; there is pressure to lower heating/cooling energy demand through efficient envelope design.

name: Better indoor-outdoor connection
rationale: A sun room typically serves as a transitional space; there is strong design pressure to enhance visual and physical connection to the outdoors.

name: Minimised glare
rationale: Extensive glazing can cause discomfort glare; there is pressure to minimise glare through shading devices, diffusing glass, or orientation.

name: Sufficient ventilation
rationale: To prevent overheating and ensure air quality, there is pressure to provide adequate natural or mechanical ventilation.

name: Eliminated condensation risk
rationale: High humidity and temperature differentials in glazed spaces create condensation risk; design pressure exists to eliminate moisture-related issues through thermal breaks and ventilation.

name: Improved accessibility
rationale: Architectural design typically seeks to improve access to storage rooms for ease of use.

name: Maximised storage capacity
rationale: Storage rooms are designed to offer as much usable storage space as possible within given constraints.

name: Sufficient ventilation
rationale: Personal storage rooms require adequate ventilation to prevent moisture buildup and maintain air quality.

name: Restricted floor area
rationale: Storage rooms are often allocated limited floor area to prioritize primary living or working spaces.

name: Minimised cost
rationale: Budget constraints typically push for lower construction costs for secondary spaces like storage rooms.

name: Eliminated clutter
rationale: Design pressures aim to avoid clutter by providing organized storage solutions.

name: Reduced ceiling plenum depth
rationale: Interstitial ceiling plenums are often used as return air paths; shallower depths reduce material costs and floor-to-floor height, which is a common design pressure in MEP coordination.

name: Increased plenum volume for air distribution
rationale: HVAC systems require adequate plenum volume to allow proper airflow and mixing of return air, particularly in deep interstitial spaces.

name: Sufficient access for MEP maintenance
rationale: Interstitial spaces need enough clearance for maintenance personnel to access mechanical, electrical, and plumbing systems.

name: Reduced fire hazard propagation
rationale: Plenums must limit spread of smoke and fire via fire dampers and compartmentation per building codes.

name: Optimised coordination with structural depth
rationale: Plenum depth must be balanced with structural beam depths and ceiling height constraints to achieve the desired floor-to-floor height.

name: Increased structural stability
rationale: The Memory Wall as a load-bearing or structural component requires sufficient stability to resist lateral and vertical loads, making increased stability a key design pressure.

name: Reduced material weight
rationale: Minimising the self-weight of the wall reduces foundation requirements and structural demands, a common engineering pressure in wall design.

name: Enhanced thermal insulation
rationale: Building envelope components like walls are often designed to improve thermal performance, so enhanced insulation is a relevant architectural pressure.

name: Reduced construction cost
rationale: Cost efficiency is a typical engineering and economic pressure influencing material selection and wall design decisions.

name: Greater durability
rationale: Long-term performance and resistance to weathering, wear, or degradation demand increased durability for the wall component.

name: Adequate acoustic performance
rationale: Walls often serve as sound barriers, so sufficient sound insulation is an architectural design pressure.

name: Reduced environmental impact
rationale: Sustainable design and cultural values increasingly pressure building components to minimise their carbon footprint and material waste.

name: Optimised spatial efficiency
rationale: The wall's thickness and layout should be optimised to not waste usable floor area, an architectural concern.

name: Lower maintenance requirements
rationale: Reducing the need for repairs and upkeep is a practical engineering pressure on wall material and finish choices.

name: Increased structural support for shelving load
rationale: Display shelving units require adequate structural support from walls or floor systems to safely bear the weight of displayed items without deflection or collapse.

name: Optimised visual accessibility of displays
rationale: Shelving units should be designed for optimal sightlines and visual access, often aided by integrated or adjacent lighting to highlight displayed merchandise.

name: Reduced cantilever deflection risk
rationale: Cantilevered shelves experience bending under load; limiting deflection prevents damage to displayed items and maintains aesthetic appearance.

name: Improved material durability for repeated handling
rationale: Display shelving units in retail environments undergo frequent handling and cleaning; durable materials resist wear and extend service life.

name: Restricted shelf depth to maintain aisle clearance
rationale: Excessive shelf depth can encroach on adjacent circulation paths; depth should be constrained to maintain accessibility and movement flow.

name: Greater load-bearing capacity per shelf
rationale: Each shelf must safely support the intended merchandise load; greater capacity ensures safety and prevents overloading failures.

name: Lower visual obstruction from shelf framing
rationale: Bulky framing can obstruct views of displayed items; minimising framing enhances the visual presentation of merchandise.

name: Enhanced adjustability for varied merchandise sizes
rationale: Adjustable shelving accommodates different product dimensions, improving flexibility and merchandising capability over fixed shelving.

name: Sufficient fire-resistance rating for compartmentation
rationale: Shelving units must comply with fire-resistance requirements to prevent fire spread between compartments, especially when constructed of combustible materials.

name: Increased visibility of awards
rationale: The cabinet should showcase awards prominently, driving pressure to increase visibility.

name: Improved security for contents
rationale: Trophies and awards are valuable and may require lockable or secure display to prevent theft or damage.

name: Sufficient storage capacity
rationale: The cabinet must accommodate current and future trophies/awards, driving need for adequate interior space.

name: Reduced dust accumulation
rationale: Enclosed or glass-fronted design reduces dust settling on displayed items, maintaining appearance.

name: Minimised cabinet footprint
rationale: The cabinet should not dominate the room layout, so floor area occupied should be limited.

name: Enhanced aesthetic integration
rationale: The cabinet's design should harmonise with surrounding interior finishes and style.

name: Maximised lighting quality
rationale: Integrated or directed lighting improves the display quality of trophies and awards.

name: Limited weight load on floor
rationale: Heavy cabinets with many awards may impose significant floor loading, which should be constrained.

name: Increased storage capacity
rationale: Media storage units need sufficient capacity to store all media assets, pushing for larger or more storage space.

name: Improved access speed
rationale: Quick retrieval of media content is critical, creating pressure for faster access mechanisms and optimized organization.

name: Enhanced data security
rationale: Media assets require protection from unauthorized access, data corruption, and loss, driving stronger security measures.

name: Reduced physical footprint
rationale: Space constraints in buildings push for more compact storage solutions while maintaining capacity.

name: Minimised operational cost
rationale: Budget limitations create pressure to reduce energy consumption, cooling requirements, and maintenance expenses for storage units.

name: Improved environmental control
rationale: Media storage often requires specific temperature and humidity conditions to preserve media integrity, pushing for better climate control systems.

name: Maximized reliability and redundancy
rationale: Media availability is critical, creating pressure for redundant storage, backup systems, and fault-tolerant designs to prevent data loss.

name: Limited heat generation
rationale: High-density storage generates significant heat that must be managed, pushing for lower-power components or better cooling integration.

name: Greater scalability
rationale: Future growth in media collections requires storage solutions that can be easily expanded without major redesign.

name: Increased natural lighting
rationale: Workshops benefit from ample natural light for detailed tasks, reducing eye strain and improving work quality.

name: Improved ventilation capacity
rationale: Hobby activities (woodworking, painting, soldering) often produce fumes, dust, or odors requiring robust ventilation for air quality and safety.

name: Expanded workspace area
rationale: Adequate floor area is needed to accommodate workbenches, tool storage, material stockpiles, and movement around large projects.

name: Adequate electrical outlets and power
rationale: Power tools, lighting, and equipment require sufficient and conveniently located electrical outlets with appropriate circuit capacity.

name: Reduced noise transmission to adjacent spaces
rationale: Workshop activities generate noise from tools and machinery that should be contained to avoid disturbing other building occupants.

name: Restricted dust and debris spread
rationale: Dust and debris from workshop activities should be contained within the space to protect adjacent areas and HVAC systems.

name: Enhanced storage capacity
rationale: Hobbyists accumulate tools, materials, and works-in-progress that require organized storage solutions.

name: Improved accessibility and circulation
rationale: Workbenches and equipment need clear circulation paths for safe movement and material handling.

name: Lower ambient temperature variation
rationale: Some hobby materials (paints, adhesives, electronics) require stable temperature conditions for proper curing and operation.

name: Increased preservation integrity
rationale: The Home Archive Room must preserve documents and artifacts, requiring controlled environmental conditions (humidity, temperature, light) to prevent deterioration.

name: Enhanced climate control
rationale: Archival storage demands precise HVAC systems to maintain stable temperature and humidity levels, preventing mold, warping, and material degradation.

name: Improved fire protection
rationale: Archives require enhanced fire suppression systems (e.g., gas-based rather than water-based) to protect irreplaceable documents and avoid water damage.

name: Reduced light exposure
rationale: UV and visible light cause fading and degradation of paper, photographs, and fabrics, so light levels must be minimized.

name: Restricted unauthorized access
rationale: Security measures such as locked doors, access control systems, and surveillance are needed to protect valuable or sensitive archival materials.

name: Minimized pest intrusion
rationale: Pests such as insects and rodents can destroy paper-based archives; building envelope and storage must be designed to prevent entry.

name: Adequate structural load capacity
rationale: Archives with dense shelving and heavy materials (books, boxes, files) require higher floor load ratings than standard occupancies.

name: Reduced humidity fluctuation
rationale: Fluctuating humidity levels accelerate chemical deterioration of paper and cause expansion/contraction of materials; stability is critical.

name: Optimized spatial layout for retrieval
rationale: Efficient shelving layout and clear circulation paths improve accessibility for archiving and retrieving materials, supporting long-term usability.

name: Increased storage capacity
rationale: Storage systems are typically designed to maximise the volume or quantity of items they can hold, making increased capacity a primary design pressure.

name: Reduced physical footprint
rationale: Storage units often need to fit within limited floor or shelf space, so minimising the footprint is a common constraint.

name: Improved structural durability
rationale: The storage box system should withstand repeated use and weight of contents, requiring enhanced structural robustness.

name: Lower material cost
rationale: Cost efficiency is a standard design pressure; reducing material expense while maintaining functionality is often a key goal.

name: Better accessibility
rationale: Users benefit from easier access to stored items, so improved accessibility (e.g., through drawers, lids, or labelling) is a design driver.

name: Adequate weight capacity
rationale: The system must be designed to support the expected load of keepsakes without failure, necessitating sufficient strength.

name: Increased energy efficiency demand
rationale: Building codes and sustainability goals push for higher energy efficiency, pressuring climate control systems to perform better with less energy.

name: Reduced operational cost requirement
rationale: Owners and facility managers seek to minimize energy bills and maintenance costs, constraining system complexity and runtime.

name: Improved thermal comfort standard
rationale: Occupant comfort expectations and indoor air quality standards drive demands for more precise temperature and humidity control.

name: Reduced environmental impact pressure
rationale: Societal and regulatory emphasis on lowering carbon footprint and refrigerant emissions restricts system design choices.

name: Greater system reliability requirement
rationale: Critical building operations demand uninterrupted climate control, pushing for redundant and robust system configurations.

name: Minimized space allocation constraint
rationale: Architectural design often allocates limited mechanical room space, constraining the size and layout of HVAC equipment.

name: Optimized indoor air quality standard
rationale: Health and ventilation standards (e.g., ASHRAE, LEED) require adequate fresh air intake and filtration, increasing system demands.

name: Lower noise emission requirement
rationale: Occupant comfort and acoustic design criteria limit allowable noise from HVAC equipment.

name: Enhanced smart control capability
rationale: Advancements in IoT and building automation push for smarter, more responsive climate control with sensors and adaptive algorithms.

name: Improved visual impact on exhibits
rationale: Display lighting must enhance the appearance of exhibits (artworks, products) to attract attention and convey value.

name: Higher colour rendering quality
rationale: Accurate colour rendering (high CRI) is critical for display applications to faithfully present colours of exhibited items.

name: Reduced glare and reflections
rationale: Glare and unwanted reflections on display surfaces or glass cases reduce visibility and viewer comfort, so must be minimised.

name: Limited UV/IR radiation on sensitive items
rationale: Ultraviolet and infrared radiation from lighting can damage light-sensitive objects (e.g., artwork, textiles), so emission must be constrained.

name: Adequate illuminance levels for viewing
rationale: Sufficient light levels (lux) are needed for clear viewing of display items while balancing conservation requirements.

name: Reduced energy consumption
rationale: Energy efficiency is a common design goal; display lighting should balance performance with lower power usage.

name: Greater flexibility and adjustability
rationale: Display layouts change; lighting should be adjustable in direction, intensity, and beam angle to accommodate reconfiguration.

name: Minimised heat output near displays
rationale: Heat from lighting can damage sensitive exhibits and affect environmental control; output should be as low as possible.

name: Improved security for artifacts
rationale: Display cases for valuable antiques and heirlooms require enhanced security features (locking mechanisms, tamper-resistant glass, alarm integration) to prevent theft or damage.

name: Enhanced environmental control
rationale: Antiques and heirlooms are sensitive to temperature, humidity, and UV light; a well-designed display case must provide adequate environmental protection (climate control, UV-filtering glass).

name: Greater visibility and accessibility
rationale: Display cases should maximise visual access for viewers through optimal lighting, clear glass, and ergonomic viewing heights while maintaining preservation requirements.

name: Reduced risk of physical damage
rationale: The display case must minimise risks of impact, vibration, and accidental contact that could damage fragile antique items; includes cushioned mounts and sturdy construction.

name: Restricted dust and pollutant ingress
rationale: Sealed or filtered display cases are needed to prevent dust, pollutants, and contaminants from accumulating on or degrading sensitive antique materials.

name: Optimised conservation-grade materials
rationale: Materials used in the case (glass, seals, liners, adhesives) must be conservation-grade to avoid chemical off-gassing or reactions that could harm heirloom artifacts.

name: Improved natural lighting
rationale: Reading nooks benefit from ample natural light to reduce eye strain and create a comfortable reading environment.

name: Reduced ambient noise
rationale: A quiet environment is essential for reading and concentration, so noise intrusion should be minimized.

name: Adequate shelving space
rationale: A personal library requires sufficient shelving to store books and reading materials.

name: Optimized seating comfort
rationale: Comfortable seating (e.g., armchair, window seat) supports prolonged reading sessions.

name: Reduced visual clutter
rationale: Minimalist design and organized storage help maintain a calm, focused atmosphere for reading.

name: Enhanced thermal comfort
rationale: Consistent, comfortable temperature is important for extended reading sessions.

name: Greater privacy
rationale: A reading nook should feel secluded and private to allow undisturbed reading.

name: Restricted foot traffic through space
rationale: The space should not be a thoroughfare to maintain a quiet, contemplative atmosphere.

name: Sufficient electrical outlets for reading lamps
rationale: Task lighting via lamps requires accessible power outlets in the reading area.

name: Enhanced security access control
rationale: A safe room or valuables vault requires strict access control mechanisms (locks, biometrics, keypads) to prevent unauthorized entry.

name: Increased structural hardening
rationale: The vault walls, floor, and ceiling must be reinforced (e.g., reinforced concrete, steel lining) to resist forced entry, drills, or explosives.

name: Reduced visibility from public areas
rationale: The location of the vault should be discreet and not easily observable from public or common areas to avoid drawing attention.

name: Minimized number of openings
rationale: Doors, windows, and other penetrations should be minimized as they are structural weak points; typically only one heavy security door is used.

name: Improved fire resistance rating
rationale: Valuables vaults require high fire-resistance ratings (e.g., 2-4 hour fire-rated construction) to protect contents from fire damage.

name: Sufficient environmental control systems
rationale: Climate control (temperature, humidity) is needed to preserve sensitive valuables like documents, art, or electronics from degradation.

name: Restricted proximity to building exterior
rationale: The vault should be located away from exterior walls to reduce risk of break-in from outside or vehicular ram-raid attacks.

name: Enhanced surveillance system coverage
rationale: Continuous CCTV monitoring and possibly motion sensors inside and around the vault are essential for security monitoring.

name: Higher blast resistance capacity
rationale: The vault may need to withstand blast loads from explosive attacks, requiring additional structural design considerations.

name: Increased tool accessibility
rationale: The pegboard wall is designed to provide easy access to tools, so there is a design pressure to maximise quick and convenient tool retrieval.

name: Higher storage density
rationale: Users typically want to store as many tools as possible within a limited wall area, driving a need for optimised tool arrangement and density.

name: Improved load capacity
rationale: The wall must bear the weight of tools without sagging or failing; stronger panels and robust mounting hardware are needed for heavier tools.

name: Reduced wall clutter
rationale: A clean, organised appearance is often desired, which pressures designers to avoid overcrowding or messy tool arrangements on the pegboard.

name: Minimised installation complexity
rationale: Simpler mounting and assembly processes reduce labour and errors, creating a design pressure to minimise complicated hardware or multi-step installations.

name: Greater durability
rationale: The pegboard must withstand repeated insertion and removal of tools and hooks, requiring robust materials that resist wear over time.
